* Shaykh: Yes, meaning that whoever denies one of the messengers denies all of them. Because what is the difference between Noah, Hud and Salih? They are all from the children of Adam. When you deny one whose messengership is established by evidence, it is as if you denied all the messengers. Just as whoever believes in some of the message and disbelieves in some of it has disbelieved in all of it. Someone says: "I believe that prayer is obligatory, but I do not believe that zakat is obligatory." We say: Now you have denied both this and that. Because your belief that prayer is obligatory but not zakat, is it from desire or from guidance? From desire. If it were from guidance, you would have believed in this just as you believed in that. So you are then not a believer, neither in this nor in that.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 29, verse 16:

It is an object (maf'ul) of a verb that has been omitted, whose estimated form is (...). Omitting the governing verb is for brevity and to draw attention to the object (ma'mul). So here (udhkur, "mention") has been omitted for brevity and to give attention to the object, which is Ibrahim, so that he is mentioned first. Ibrahim, peace be upon him, as everyone knows, is the second of the Messengers of firm resolve (ulu al-'azm). And who is the first of them? Muhammad ﷺ, then Ibrahim, then Musa, then Nuh and 'Isa. They have differed over which of them is most excellent, and the better position is to say that each of them has a distinction (maziyyah).

As for the three, Muhammad, then Ibrahim, then Musa, this order is agreed upon. Allah the Exalted tested him (Ibrahim) with two matters. One of them concerned the call to Allah, and the second concerned the most beloved thing to him. As for the call to Allah, Allah empowered his people over him so that they would burn him, and the outcome was that Allah saved him from the fire, and He said to the fire: ﴿O fire, be coolness and safety upon Ibrahim﴾ [al-Anbiya' 69].

The second matter concerned the thing most dear to him, which was his son when he reached the age of striving with him (al-sa'y), and he was his only son and his firstborn, and he was Isma'il according to the correct opinion. Allah tested him by commanding him to slaughter him. He was commanded to slaughter him himself, and he submitted and agreed, and he submitted to this command. The story is well known, and Allah the Glorified and Exalted saved him from it when He said to him: ﴿And We called to him, "O Ibrahim, you have fulfilled the vision." Indeed, that is how We reward the doers of good. Indeed, this is the clear trial﴾ [as-Saffat 104–106], and so on to the end. He was named the Khalil (intimate friend), whom Allah took as a khalil because of this matter, since he preferred the most beloved thing to him over the love of Allah the Exalted.

We have previously pointed out that some ignorant people in reality describe the Prophet ﷺ as the beloved of Allah (habib Allah) and Ibrahim as the intimate friend of Allah (khalil Allah), and this is an error. Muhammad ﷺ is also the khalil of Allah, as has been established from him[[Narrated by Muslim (532/23) from the hadith of Jundub ibn 'Abd Allah.]]. Whoever says that Muhammad is a habib and Ibrahim is a khalil has belittled the Prophet ﷺ, because the rank of love (mahabbah) is lower than the rank of intimate friendship (khullah).

﴿When he said to his people﴾ [al-'Ankabut 16]. ﴿Idh﴾ here is an adverbial expression of time, and it is in a position of accusative as a circumstantial clause (hal), meaning: at the time he was saying to his people.

As for His saying ﴿to his people﴾: who are the people (qawm)? The people are the group to which a person belongs by lineage or by aim. Everyone to whom a person is related by lineage is his people, or by aim, such that their claim and their path are one, and they are also called a people. The intended meaning of "his people" here is those to whom he is related by kinship. ﴿To his people: "Worship Allah and fear Him."﴾ The author said: (fear His punishment). ﴿Worship Allah﴾: the origin of worship (ibadah) is derived from humiliation (dhull), and from it their saying: a paved path (tariq mu'abbad), meaning a made-level path, because the servant humbles himself before the one he worships. Worship, then, is the humbling of oneself before Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, by carrying out His commands and avoiding His prohibitions. Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah defined it as: (a comprehensive term for everything that Allah loves and is pleased with of statements and actions, both outward and inward). This is a definition of it in terms of the field of worship, but its root is humiliation, because this is what its meaning in language requires: that a person humble himself before Allah the Glorified and Exalted by obeying Him, doing His commands and abstaining from His prohibitions. Know that worship is divided into two kinds:

First: submission to the cosmic command (al-amr al-kawni), and this is general for everyone, as in His saying the Exalted: ﴿There is none in the heavens and the earth but that he comes to the Most Merciful as a servant﴾ [Maryam 93]. Everyone in the heavens and the earth, believer and disbeliever, righteous and wicked, all come to Allah the Exalted with this attribute: ﴿but that he comes to the Most Merciful as a servant﴾. Is His saying the Exalted among this: ﴿Indeed, My servants, you have no authority over them, except those who follow you of the deviators﴾ [al-Hijr 42]?

* A student: If we say the exception is connected (muttasil), then it is included in it, and if we say it is disconnected (munqati'), then it is not included in it.

* The Shaykh: Correct. Are you following, everyone? We have mentioned that servitude is divided into two kinds: general, which is submission to the cosmic command, and no one is excluded from this. All people, all creation, are subject to Allah's cosmic command, is that not so? Can anyone remove sickness or death from himself? No. Its example is His saying the Exalted: ﴿There is none in the heavens and the earth but that he comes to the Most Merciful as a servant﴾. Is His saying the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, My servants﴾, addressing Iblis, among this: ﴿Indeed, My servants, you have no authority over them, except those who follow you of the deviators﴾?

The answer: if we make the exception connected, then the intended meaning of servitude is the general kind; and if we make it disconnected, then the intended meaning of servitude is the particular kind.

Particular servitude is the humbling before the legislative command, humbling before Allah's legislated command, and among it is His saying the Exalted: ﴿And the servants of the Most Merciful are those who walk upon the earth in humility﴾ [al-Furqan 63]. These humbled themselves by what? By the legislated command. Here, in the noble verse, Ibrahim said: ﴿Worship Allah﴾. Which of the two meanings does he intend?

* A student: The legislated one.

* The Shaykh: Devotion to Allah through legislated worship.

His saying: ﴿and fear Him﴾ is coordinated (ma'tuf) upon His saying: ﴿Worship Allah﴾. Coordination, as it has been said, requires difference (al-mughayarah), and we have mentioned that worship is humbling oneself to Allah the Glorified and Exalted through obedience.

And taqwa: taking a shield (wiqayah) from His punishment through obedience to Him. This is taqwa; its origin is from protection (wiqayah), so that a person guards himself from the punishment of Allah through obedience to Him. On these two explanations, coordinating taqwa upon worship is from the category of coordinating a thing upon itself, and it is well known that the eloquence of the Qur'an rejects that; that is, it rejects coordinating a thing upon itself, because that falls under repetition. So what is the difference by which the coordination requires difference? That is: if we say taqwa is taking a shield from the punishment of Allah through obeying Him, and worship is humbling oneself to Allah the Exalted through obeying Him, then their meanings become one, while coordination requires difference. So how can we explain worship with a meaning that differs from the meaning of taqwa? We say: this answer, on this basis, has one of two aspects. Either worship here in this verse is intended to mean performing the commands, and taqwa is intended to mean abstaining from the prohibitions, that is, that you guard against sins and perform acts of obedience. This aspect, I mean, that when the two words each include the meaning of the other when separate and differ when combined, has many examples, such as the faqir and the miskin, which are one thing when separate and differ when combined; birr and taqwa are one thing when separate and two things when combined.

Here we say: worship and taqwa are one thing when separate, and when combined, worship is explained as performing the commands and taqwa as abstaining from the prohibitions. This is one aspect. Or we say the second aspect: worship is intended to mean general commitment and humbling, and taqwa is intended to mean guarding against a specific action, because not everyone who performs general worship is performing taqwa. Many Muslims now worship Allah, but do they guard themselves before Him in everything? No, they do many things.

This fasting that we have now, we fast, but does the one who fasts guard himself before Allah the Mighty and Majestic in everything, such that he abandons lying, backbiting, insulting, what is forbidden, false speech, and acting upon it?

The answer: not every fasting person is like this. On this basis we say: the intended meaning of worship is general commitment and humbling, and of taqwa is that a person guards himself before his Lord in every individual instance or in every kind of sins and their instances.

﴿And fear Him﴾: the author says: (fear His punishment). Had the author explained the verse in a way that matches the wording, it would have been better; had he said: "guard yourselves against His punishment," it would have been better.

(﴿That is better for you﴾ than what you are upon of worshipping idols.) He said: ﴿That﴾, the referent is worship and taqwa.

His saying: ﴿And Ibrahim, when he said to his people: "Worship Allah and fear Him. That is better for you, if you only knew."﴾ [al-'Ankabut 16].

* Derived from it: the virtue of Ibrahim, in that he commanded his people with what has been mentioned.

* Also derived from it: it is fitting to mention those who call to Allah the Exalted in a way that raises their status, because we estimated (Ibrahim) as an object of an omitted verb whose estimate is: mention Ibrahim.

* Among the benefits of the verse: the obligation of worshipping Allah and fearing Him, from His saying: ﴿Worship Allah and fear Him﴾, because the basic form of the command (...).

* Among the benefits of the verse: that the best thing a servant can attain is worship of Allah and taqwa of Him, from His saying: ﴿That is better for you﴾.

* Among its benefits also: that none understands these things except people of knowledge. These are taken from... from where is it taken? That none perceives the goodness in worship and taqwa except people of knowledge?

* A student: ﴿That is better for you, if you only knew.﴾

The Shaykh: From the whole verse?!

* The student: ﴿if you only knew.﴾

* The Shaykh: From His saying: ﴿if you only knew.﴾

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 29, verse 17:

Then the Exalted and Glorified said: ﴿Indeed, you worship besides Allah only idols, and you invent a falsehood. Indeed, those whom you worship besides Allah do not possess for you any provision; so seek provision from Allah, and worship Him, and be grateful to Him. To Him you will be returned.﴾ [Al-'Ankabut 17].

* Among the benefits of this verse: that everything that is worshipped besides Allah is an idol (wathan) that neither benefits nor brings provision.

* And among its benefits: that calling these idols "gods" is a lie, because of His saying: ﴿and you invent a falsehood﴾.

* And among its benefits: that whoever states a ruling should state its reason ('illah).

* Student: (...)?

* The Shaykh: From His saying: ﴿Indeed, those whom you worship besides Allah do not possess for you any provision﴾.

* And among its benefits: that it is proper to derive the rational (ma'qul) from the sensory (mahsus). From where is this taken?

* Student: ﴿They do not possess for you any provision﴾.

* The Shaykh: ﴿Indeed, those whom you worship besides Allah do not possess for you any provision﴾ is a sensory proof. The way of deriving the rational from the sensory is that no one denies the sensory, whereas the rational may not even be conceived by a person, let alone acknowledged by him. So obliging a person with the sensory regarding the rational is one of the methods of debate, argument, establishing proof, and imposing obligation.

* And among the benefits of the verse: that the one to whom one must turn is Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. From where is this taken? ﴿So seek provision from Allah﴾.

* And among the benefits of the verse: that it mentions the cause of provision and the cause of its continuation; the cause of its coming into being and the cause of its persistence.

* Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: Or we say: ﴿Worship Allah﴾ is the cause of provision, and ﴿be grateful to Him﴾ is the cause of its continuation.

* And among the benefits of the verse: the obligation of thanking for blessings, because of His saying?

* Student: ﴿And be grateful to Him﴾.

* The Shaykh: ﴿And be grateful to Him.﴾ Here, is the verb transitive or intransitive? ﴿And be grateful to Him﴾: is the verb transitive or intransitive?

* Student: Transitive.

* The Shaykh: Transitive? Here, in the noble verse, is it intransitive or transitive?

* Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: Transitive? Where is the object?

* Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: Who knows the answer?

* Student: (...) ﴿And be grateful to Him﴾ (...).

* The Shaykh: Be grateful for His blessing, sincere to Him. This is according to the view that it is transitive. As for the view that it is intransitive, then "shakara" is used intransitively; you say: "shakartuhu" (I thanked him), and transitively you say: "shakartu lahu" (I thanked Him), and the object is the pronoun "hu" and not an elided one.

* And among the benefits of the verse: the affirmation of resurrection. From where do we take it?

* Student: ﴿To Him you will be returned.﴾

* The Shaykh: ﴿To Him you will be returned﴾; this will be on the Day of Resurrection, the affirmation of resurrection.

* And among its benefits: the affirmation of recompense for deeds. From where do we take it? From His saying: ﴿To Him you will be returned﴾; because the benefit of this information that they will be resurrected and recompensed is not merely resurrection without recompense, rather there must be recompense in it.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 29, verse 18:

Then He, the Exalted, said: ﴿And if you deny, then indeed nations before you denied, and upon the Messenger is only the clear delivery.﴾ [al-'Ankabut 18]

* From this verse is derived: a warning to those who deny the Messenger ﷺ, based on His saying: ﴿then indeed nations before you denied﴾, and they knew what befell them. Therefore, there is in this a warning to those who deny the Messenger ﷺ.

* Among its benefits also: that the messengers are obligated to deliver (the message). His saying: ﴿and upon the Messenger﴾, "upon" (ʿalā) indicates obligation, as Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿And for Allah upon the people is the pilgrimage to the House﴾ [Al 'Imran 97], meaning it is obligatory. So when it is said "ʿalā fulān kadhā wa kadhā" (upon so-and-so is such-and-such), it indicates obligation. Therefore, the verse derives the obligation of delivery upon whom? Upon the messengers.

* Among its benefits: is it obligatory upon them to guide the creation or not? Upon them is only the delivery. As for guidance, it belongs to Allah, the Exalted, and likewise the reckoning is upon Allah, the Exalted: ﴿So upon you is only the delivery, and upon Us is the reckoning﴾ [al-Ra'd 40].

* Among its benefits: the obligation of delivery upon the people of knowledge. From where is this taken?

* A student: ﴿And upon the Messenger is only the delivery﴾.

* The Shaykh: And the scholars are the heirs of the prophets, so it is obligatory upon them to deliver just as it is obligatory upon the messengers.

* Among its benefits: that the Qur'an includes all the doctrinal and practical rulings, and that it brought these in the most complete and clearest manner. His saying: ﴿only the clear delivery﴾ (covers) everything He sent with, because he is a messenger, so upon him is the clear delivery of everything he was sent with. The Prophet ﷺ was sent with sound, upright beliefs, with righteous deeds, and with straight statements.

Based on this, we say from this verse: we use this verse to establish that the entire Shari'ah is clear, complete and manifest, and we refute with it all the people of innovation. We refute all the people of innovation with this, because the saying of the people of innovation entails that the Prophet ﷺ did not deliver the clear delivery.

For example, those who deny the true reality of Allah's istiwa' (rising) over His Throne say: the meaning of istiwa' is istila' (seizing) over the Throne. This verse refutes these people: if the intended meaning of istiwa' were istila', this meaning would have come, even in one verse. And how many verses on istiwa' are there in the Qur'an? Seven verses, and not even one verse came in which Allah says: "He seized the Throne." So we say: you are liars, and this verse refutes you. Likewise the rest of the doubts by which the people of ta'til (negation) or the people of tamthil (likening) argue. Even the people of tamthil who say: Allah truly rose over His Throne, but His rising is like the rising of a created being over a created being, like the rising of a king upon the throne of kingship, and the like.

We say: these too are refuted by His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And upon the Messenger is only the clear delivery﴾, because the Messenger delivered the clear delivery, and there has come to us from its clarification His saying, the Exalted: ﴿There is nothing like unto Him﴾ [al-Shura 11].

If someone said: there occur now events that happen for which we see no mention in the Qur'an or in the Sunnah; so what is the answer to this verse? Do not events occur, which happened and happen, for which there is no mention (...) in the Sunnah?

* A student: (...).

* The Shaykh: Yes, we say: they are clarified by clarification of the category (jins); that is, it is not necessary that the Qur'an come with every individual instance or the Sunnah come with every individual instance, because the individual cases of matters have no limit. What do you think if Allah, glorified and exalted, had mentioned in the Qur'an every matter that will come until the Day of Resurrection? How many volumes would the Qur'an be? Volumes without limit.

But we say: these individual instances of these matters exist by their categories, their causes and their rules; that is, either they are known by analogy (qiyas), or they are left unmentioned, and silence in the place of clarification is clarification, as the Prophet ﷺ said: «What He has left silent is pardoned»[[Narrated by Abu Dawud (3800) from the hadith of 'Abdullah ibn 'Abbas.]].

The point is: we say, there is no matter that occurs except that its ruling exists in the Qur'an or the Sunnah, considered as an individual instance or as a category? As a category. So the category of this matter exists in the Qur'an, either by a general rule, or by sound analogy, or the like. But the defect and shortcoming come from one of several things: either a lack of knowledge, where a person has no knowledge, and where is the defect here? In the person. The person has not encompassed the Sunnah. A person can encompass the Qur'an, but the Sunnah a person cannot encompass; there are hadiths that come upon a person that were not occurring to his mind.

Or a deficiency in understanding, where a person has knowledge but his understanding is deficient, and it is not due to sleeping either, like some people who sleep in the lesson. Notice that people's difference in understanding is greater and more significant than their difference in knowledge. Some people derive several matters from a single proof, and another derives only one or two matters.

Third: among the causes of failing to reach, or failing to know the truth from the Qur'an and the Sunnah, is that a person has bad intention, such that he does not want the truth, and Allah forbid; he only wants his own opinion to prevail. Such a person, and Allah forbid, is prevented from reaching the correct view and knowing the truth, because he does not desire it. These are three causes.

The fourth cause: sins. Sins are humiliation and darkness, which necessitate that a person be prevented from reaching the truth of the Book of Allah and the Sunnah of His Messenger ﷺ. Indeed, sins cause forgetting what is present, just as they prevent the existence of what is absent. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿So for their breaking of their covenant We cursed them and made their hearts hard; they distort words from their places and have forgotten a portion of what they were reminded of﴾ [al-Ma'idah 13].

So these are four causes, all of which come between a person and reaching knowledge of the ruling of Allah that is in the Book and the Sunnah. As for the Book and the Sunnah themselves, they undoubtedly encompass all matters until the Day of Resurrection, because this Book is for until the Day of Resurrection.

As for the saying of someone among the people of knowledge, and it is one of the strangest things: that the Book and the Sunnah contain only the rulings of a few matters, to the point that some claim that the Qur'an and the Sunnah contain only about a tenth of matters, this is a grave error. For this reason Allah, the Exalted, said in the Qur'an: ﴿And We have sent down to you the Book as an exposition of all things﴾ [al-Nahl 89].

* Among the benefits of the verse: that the messengers are the most eloquent of creation. From where is this taken? From His saying: ﴿only the clear delivery﴾. Whether we say that "al-mubin" means "clear" or means "making manifest," and the correct view is that it means "making manifest." I think that is finished? To this point?

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 29, verse 19:

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Have they not seen﴾ [al-'Ankabut 19]. It is read with the yā' and with the tā': yanẓurū (ينظروا), with the yā' and the tā', meaning: ﴿yarawū﴾ (يرَوْا), and the second is ﴿tarawū﴾ (تَرَوْا). Both are Sab'iyyah readings (readings of the seven canonical Readers). The author (al-Mu'allif, i.e. al-Baghawi) explained the sight here in the sense of looking (al-nazar), so it is sight of the eye: ﴿Have they not seen﴾. It may also be a sight of the heart, i.e. knowledge ('ilmiyyah), meaning: "Have they not known?" We should consider which of the two is more appropriate given the context of the verse: ﴿how Allah originates creation, then repeats it﴾. ﴿Yubdi'u﴾ (يُبْدِئُ): the author says: (it is with a ḍammah on its first letter, and it has been read with a fatḥah on it; from (bada'a) and (abda'a) with the same meaning, i.e. He creates them at the beginning).

Here ﴿yubdi'u﴾ now has a Sab'iyyah reading and a shādhdh (irregular) reading. The Sab'iyyah reading is ﴿yubdi'u﴾. From where? The past tense of ﴿yubdi'u﴾ is abda'a, a quadriliteral verb.

The shādhdh reading, he says, is with a fatḥah on its first letter, ﴿yabda'u﴾. From where? From (bada'a). How do we know this is the shādhdh reading? Because the author's convention, may Allah have mercy on him, is that when he says "it has been read" (quri'a), it is shādhdh. The author says: (from (bada'a) and (abda'a)). Is this laff and nashr (a rhetorical arrangement of two items) ordered or scrambled? Scrambled, meaning it is not in order. Look now: "from (bada'a)" corresponds to which of the two readings? To the shādhdh one, ﴿yabda'u﴾, and "(abda'a)" corresponds to the Sab'iyyah reading, which is ﴿yubdi'u﴾. Truthfully, I wish the author had not done this, because a person may not understand that this is the scrambled type of laff and nashr, and it was unnecessary. If the author had said "from (abda'a) and (bada'a)," it would have been clearer for the student.

As for his saying (bi-ma'na) (with the same meaning): what does it mean? It means one meaning, i.e. (bada'a) and (abda'a) have the same meaning, namely: He creates them at the beginning, that is, how Allah the Exalted creates them at the beginning.

His saying ﴿how Allah originates creation﴾: ﴿al-khalq﴾ (الْخَلْق) here is a verbal noun used in the sense of the passive participle (ism al-maf'ul), i.e. the created: how He originates the created thing, then repeats it. The verbal noun often comes in the sense of the passive participle in the Arabic language. Among its examples is the Exalted's saying: ﴿and if they are pregnant﴾ [al-Talaq 6], where al-ḥaml (الحَمْل) in the womb means maḥmūl (what is carried). And the Prophet ﷺ said: "Whoever does an action that is not in accordance with our affair, it is rejected" [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (2697) and Muslim (1718/18), the wording of Muslim, from the hadith of 'A'ishah], meaning: mardud (rejected).

Here khalq means makhluq (created), and similar to it is the Exalted's saying: ﴿This is the creation of Allah﴾ [Luqman 11], i.e. His creation.

His saying: (﴿how Allah originates creation, then﴾ — it is ﴿He repeats it﴾, i.e. the creation as He began them). Notice that the author says: (i.e. the creation as He began them), indicating that khalq in the sense of makhluq encompasses all people.

His saying: (﴿then﴾ — it is ﴿He repeats it﴾) he estimated "huwa" (هو) so that the sentence is independent (isti'nafiyyah). Why? Because the repetition of creation cannot be witnessed; when will the repetition of creation occur? On the Day of Resurrection, in the future. But the beginning of creation can be observed; for example, we look at the creatures of Allah, how they reproduce, how they grow, how they mature, and so on, and we know it. But the repetition of creation is not possible to observe. Therefore the author, may Allah have mercy on him, estimated his saying: (﴿then﴾ — it is ﴿He repeats it﴾), lest someone imagine that it is coordinated with ﴿yubdi'u﴾, which would be incorrect, because if it were coordinated with it the meaning would be "how He originates creation, then how He repeats it," whereas observing the manner of repetition is impossible.

As for the saying of the Exalted: ﴿Have they not seen﴾: I mentioned to you that it may be knowledge, and the author proceeded with it being sight by the eye. Which of them is more comprehensive?

* Students: Knowledge.

* Other students: Sight of the heart.

* The Shaykh: Which is more comprehensive? The apparent view is that the sight of the heart is more comprehensive, because it includes what a person sees with his own eye and what he knows from others, is it not so? So it is more comprehensive.

Know that when a verse admits two meanings, one of which is more comprehensive, it is preferable to take it in the more comprehensive sense, because the more specific is included within it. By contrast, if it is taken in the more specific sense, its meaning is that we have excluded part of its indication. Accordingly, we say: it is preferable to take it as the sight of knowledge which is attained by sight and also by hearing, as the Exalted said: ﴿And He made for you hearing and sight and hearts﴾ [al-Nahl 78]. ﴿Hearing and sight﴾ are the means of knowledge, and ﴿hearts﴾ are the seat of awareness.

His saying: ﴿Indeed that is for Allah easy﴾. The author says: (﴿Indeed that﴾, the aforementioned, of the first and second creation, ﴿for Allah is easy﴾), i.e. simple. The originating of creation is easy for Allah. Read the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, the likeness of 'Isa with Allah is like that of Adam; He created him from dust, then said to him, "Be," and he was﴾ [Al 'Imran 59]. It is a simple matter for Allah.

The repetition of creation is also easy, because of His saying: ﴿It will be but one shout﴾ [al-Nazi'at 13], one shout only, ﴿and immediately they will be on the surface of the earth﴾ [al-Nazi'at 14]. And more general than that is His saying: ﴿And Our command is but one, like a glance of the eye﴾ [al-Qamar 50], without delay, one: Allah commands a thing and it is, like the blink of an eye, and this is evidence of the perfection of His power, may He be glorified and exalted.

His saying: ﴿Indeed that is for Allah easy﴾ in another verse: ﴿And it is He who originates creation and then repeats it, and that is easier for Him﴾ [al-Rum 27]. We say to these deniers of resurrection: Do you acknowledge that Allah created you at the beginning? What do they say? They say: Yes. The discourse is about those deniers who acknowledge the origination of creation: ﴿And if you asked them who created them, they would surely say, "Allah"﴾ [al-Zukhruf 87], acknowledging this matter. We say to them: Which is easier, the origination or the repetition? The answer: the repetition is easier. So how do you affirm the harder and then deny the easier? And I say "the harder," not on the basis that this is attributed to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, but because everything is easy for Him. Yet we say to these people: since origination is more intense and more difficult, the repetition is all the more to be affirmed by you.

But they affirm origination because they cannot deny it; they cannot say, "Allah did not create us; we created ourselves," or that the husband created the child in the mother's womb. This they cannot say. Therefore Allah argued against them from origination so that they would affirm repetition. And His saying: ﴿Indeed that is for Allah easy﴾: so how do they deny the second?

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 29, verse 20:

﴿Say: Travel through the earth and observe how He originated creation﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 20]. This verse, together with the one before it, may appear to present a difficulty. The first verse, ﴿Have they not seen﴾, is a reproach addressing them with the fact that they see how Allah originates creation and then restores it. Here He says: ﴿Say: Travel through the earth and observe how He originated creation﴾, which implies that until now they have not known how Allah originated creation. We say: the answer to this is that although they do see how Allah originated creation, they may deny it. So Allah the Exalted commanded His Prophet to tell them to travel in the earth: ﴿Say: Travel through the earth and observe how He originated creation﴾. Walk on the earth; look, for example, at the wild animals, look at the insects, look at the creatures of Allah, glorified and exalted is He, how do these things come into being, without our seeing for them any creator other than Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. This is by way of holding them to account, especially if we say that the first seeing is a seeing of knowledge, by way of holding them to account with what they witness on the earth after they travel in it.

As for His saying ﴿Say: Travel through the earth﴾, is the intended meaning travel with the body, travel with the heart, or both? Both together; for a person may travel with his body and observe the creatures of Allah, and he may travel with his heart and read what has been written about the creatures of Allah, is that not so? You may read a book about animals or other things while you are in your place in your room, and you have come to know what is in the eastern and western parts of the earth; the travel in that case is with the heart. So it encompasses both matters together.

Know also that travel with the feet is of no benefit if there is no travel with the heart and reflection.

If a person walks through all the wide paths of the earth while heedless, he gains nothing from that travel. Rather, there must be alertness and reflection.

* Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: He is not considered a traveler on the earth by his knowledge, which is in its place, namely the heart. Both of these are valid, because now, if we look at travel on the earth in reality, which is more: with the heart or with the feet? With the heart there is no difficulty. Rather, travel with the feet, if it is not intended for reflection, has no benefit. If it is intended for reflection, it returns to being travel with the heart, except that travel with the heart and with the feet have come together.

﴿Then observe how He originated creation﴾. We have here ﴿انْظُرُوا كَيْفَ﴾ (observe how), and in the first verse ﴿أَوَلَمْ يَرَوْا كَيْفَ﴾ (have they not seen how). It is known that ﴿انْظُرُوا﴾ and ﴿يَرَوْا﴾ are transitive verbs, so where is their object?

* Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: Where are the sons of Sibawayh?! ﴿How He originated creation﴾? And how does Allah originate creation? The verb may not need an object, brothers. It is suspended by the interrogative: when the interrogative comes, it suspends the verb (mu'allaq), suspended by the interrogative. For example: ﴿Have they not seen how Allah originates creation, then repeats it﴾, ﴿Say: Travel through the earth and observe how He originated creation﴾. The word ﴿كَيْفَ﴾ here is in the accusative position as a circumstantial qualifier (hal), and it suspends the verb from acting. This was covered for us in Ibn Malik's Alfiyya, in which chapter of grammar?

* Student: In the chapter on "ẓanna" and its sisters.

* The Shaykh: In the chapter on "ẓanna" and its sisters.

.......................... ∗∗∗ And the suspension before negation (mā) and (in) is required ∗∗∗ ..........................
And so on to its end.

(﴿Say: Travel through the earth and observe how He originated creation﴾ for those who were before you, and He caused them to die) (...)

﴿Then Allah will produce the final creation. Indeed, Allah is over all things competent﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 20].

The first [occurrence] came in the verbal form, while here it came in the nominal sentence, to convey the establishment and confirmation of this matter.

As for His saying ﴿Then Allah﴾, ﴿Allah﴾ here is a proper name for the Creator, may He be exalted, and its origin is al-Ilah; the hamza was dropped for lightness due to frequency of use, just as it was dropped in (al-nas).

Does al-Ilah mean the one worshipped in truth or in falsehood, or not? Al-Ilah means the one worshipped, whether in truth or not in truth. On this basis, ﴿Allah﴾ here is the one worshipped in truth, by the evidence of His saying: (there is no god but Allah), meaning: there is no true object of worship except Allah, the Exalted. So we say: ﴿Allah﴾ is a proper name for the Creator, may He be exalted, and its origin is al-Ilah, meaning al-ma'luh, that is, the one worshipped. The basic meaning of al-Ilah is the object of worship, in truth or in falsehood, but when you say "there is no god but Allah," the meaning is: there is no true god, that is, no god that is true except Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.

﴿Yunshi'u al-nash'ata al-akhirah﴾. He says (with madd and with qasr and sukun on the shin). How do I pronounce it with madd?

* Student: al-nasha'a.

* The Shaykh: No, ﴿al-nash'a'a﴾: ﴿Then Allah produces the final nash'a'a﴾, and with qasr and sukun on the shin: ﴿al-nash'ah﴾: ﴿Then Allah produces the final nash'ah﴾.

As for His saying ﴿yunshi'u al-nash'ah﴾, it may be a verbal noun, as you say: he strikes the blow (yadribu al-darbah), and it may be in the sense of the passive participle, that is: He produces the other produced creation; the meaning is one: that Allah, glorified and exalted, produces creation a second time.

If someone says: how do we call it a "nash'ah" when it is a restoration?

We say: the answer is that this restoration differs greatly from its predecessor; so in relation to it, it is a nash'ah, because the life of the Hereafter is not like the life of this world; the life of the Hereafter is everlasting life, and the life of this world is life of passing away. Therefore you find it deficient: man is created from weakness to strength to weakness. As for the restoration, he is created for eternity. Therefore it is called a nash'ah, even though it is a restoration, because the two states differ.

Look at the fetus in its mother's womb, about which Allah the Exalted said after mentioning its stages: ﴿Then We produced it as another creation﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 14]. Is it a production or a development? A development; but since the final development, in which the soul is breathed in, differs from the first, in the first it is inanimate in its mother's womb, then the soul is breathed into it, so it becomes a new nash'ah different from the first, and it is called a nash'ah even though it is a development from one state to another. (﴿Indeed, Allah is over all things competent﴾, and from it comes the beginning and the restoration.) This sentence is a justification for what preceded, namely that He originated creation and then restored it, because Allah is over all things competent.

Qudrah (power) is an attribute by which the agent is able to act without incapacity. Is it strength or something else? It is other than strength: strength is opposed by weakness, while this is opposed by incapacity.

This is made clear by an example: if I carry this book but with difficulty, what am I described as? Capable, but not strong. Another wanted to carry this book and was unable; this one is incapable. The third lifted it as if it were a feather in his hand; this one is capable and strong. Thus it becomes clear that qudrah is other than quwwah. Likewise, qudrah is attributed only to one who has awareness, and not to anything else: would you say of iron that it is capable?

No. Quwwah is attributed both to the one with awareness and to others: you say of iron, "strong," and you say of a man, "strong." Allah, glorified and exalted, is described both with qudrah and with quwwah: ﴿Indeed, Allah is the Provider, Possessor of power, the Firm﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 58].

Is ﴿over all things competent﴾ general or specified? It is general in its scope and is not specified by anything. The author of al-Jalalayn, al-Suyuti, said: (The intellect specified His essence, so He is not competent over it). (The intellect specified His essence), meaning the essence of Allah, (so He is not competent over it). He said this regarding the verse in Surat al-Ma'idah: ﴿To Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth and whatever is in them, and He is over all things competent﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 120]. He said that the intellect specifies this generality. We say: no one among intellects specifies this generality except a corrupt intellect that deems it impossible for voluntary acts to subsist in Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. As for the sound, upright intellect, it holds that Allah does what He wills: He descends, He settles upon the Throne, He ascends to the heaven, He laughs, He marvels, and other voluntary acts befitting His majesty, glorified and exalted is He.

So his saying (the intellect specified His essence, so He is not competent over it) is a grave error: if He is not capable over Himself, how is He capable over others? This is among the greatest impossibilities and greatest mistakes.

But if someone says: perhaps the author means that He is not capable of annihilating Himself, for example, or of creating something like Himself, we say: this is not what power relates to at all.

Power does not relate at all to the absolutely impossible; it is not included in the generality from the outset, so it is not excluded from it.

Here is a phrase some people say: "He is capable of whatever He wills." What is your opinion of this expression? This expression is wrong, because Allah the Exalted says: ﴿over all things competent﴾, all things. He is capable of what He wills and what He does not will; even what He does not will, He is capable of it, for if He willed it He would do it. It is not only what He wills.

Moreover, this expression ("capable of what He wills") contradicts what the Qur'an has brought: the Qur'an says ﴿He is over all things competent﴾ and ﴿And ever was Allah over all things competent﴾ [al-Ahzab: 27].

Furthermore, some of the people of knowledge say that this expression suggests the doctrine of the Mu'tazilah, who say that a person is independent in his deeds. They said: if a person is independent in his deeds, with no role for Allah's will in them, then it means Allah is incapable of the deeds of a human being, and this is dangerous, as is well known. What we ought to say is: He is over all things competent without qualification.

If someone says: does this not get refuted by His saying ﴿and He is, when He wills, competent to gather them﴾ [al-Shura: 29]? We say: the will here refers to what? To the gathering or to the power? To the gathering, not to the power. The meaning is that when He wills to gather them, He gathers them without incapacity, glorified and exalted is He, so it does not contradict what we have said.

They say: Iblis gathered his soldiers, or they gathered around him, and said to him: "You rejoice at the death of a scholar, but you do not rejoice at the death of a worshipper!" He said: "Yes, the worshipper, when he dies, does no harm, he dies only for himself; but the scholar, when he dies, dies on behalf of a whole world, and if he remains he corrupts matters for us."

So by the true scholars is meant those who act and call to Allah. He said: "Come, let us go, you and I, to a scholar we may ask, and to a worshipper." They say: they went to the worshipper and said to him: "Is Allah able to create the like of Himself?" He said: "Yes, Allah is able to create the like of Himself." "What is the evidence?" He said: "Because Allah is over all things competent." What happened to this man? He disbelieved. Anyone who holds this belief is a disbeliever. And it is also incorrect, whatever is possible, even if there were no difference, a great difference indeed; but even if the only difference were that this god, if supposed, is created, while the true God is uncreated. They went to the scholar and said: "Is Allah able to put even the heavens and the earth into a single egg?" He said: ﴿His command, when He intends a thing, is only that He says to it, "Be," and it is﴾ [Ya Sin: 82]. If He willed that, He would do it[[Related by Ibn 'Abd al-Barr in Jami' Bayan al-'Ilm wa Fadlihi (127).]]. So he was delivered, although the latter may seem more deniable to people than the former.

The conclusion is that when a person reads His saying ﴿Indeed, Allah is over all things competent﴾, it is not permissible for there to occur to his mind any exception to this generality; rather it should stand in its generality without distinction.

(...) Inference from the origin to the return: ﴿how He originated creation, then Allah produces the final creation﴾.

* Among its benefits: the one arguing should argue from the observed to the unseen, so that the opponent may be convinced.

* Among the benefits of the verse: the affirmation of resurrection, from His saying ﴿then Allah produces the final creation﴾.

* Among them: the affirmation of Allah's power, from His saying ﴿Indeed, Allah is over all things competent﴾.

* Among them: the generality of this power. From where is the generality derived?

* Student: ﴿over all things competent﴾.

* The Shaykh: ﴿over all things competent﴾.

* Among them: the affirmation of voluntary acts for Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, for they are part of the perfection of His power, like what? Like coming, descending, settling upon the Throne, laughing, marvelling, and the like.

* And also among them, and we have pointed this out, though it is not included in the content of the verse, is the error of one who says: "The intellect specified His essence, so He is not competent over it." Have we shown that this is not correct and clear? We said: this applies to those who deny that voluntary acts subsist in Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, who say: He is not capable of acting, and this undoubtedly is refuted for them by the Book, the Sunnah, and the consensus of the early generations.

* Student: The phrase?

* The Shaykh: They say: "The intellect specified His essence, so He is not competent over it."

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 29, verse 21–27 (part 1 of 7):

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿He punishes whom He wills and has mercy on whom He wills, and to Him you will be returned﴾ [Al-'Ankabut 21]; meaning: after the resurrection.

﴿Then Allah causes the final creation to come into being﴾. After this, He punishes whom He wills. It is also permissible that ﴿He punishes﴾ refers to punishment in this world as well, because punishment occurs both in this world and in the Hereafter. So the penalties prescribed for crimes are a form of punishment, based on the saying of the Prophet ﷺ concerning the two who engage in mutual cursing (al-mutalā'inān): «The punishment of this world is lighter than the punishment of the Hereafter»[[Narrated by Muslim (1493/4) from the hadith of 'Abdullah ibn 'Umar.]]. Likewise, the calamities that befall a person in his body, his family, and his property are also a form of punishment: ﴿And whatever affliction strikes you is because of what your hands have earned﴾ [Ash-Shura 30].

His saying ﴿He punishes﴾ uses the present-tense verb, indicating that this is an ongoing action of His, not something that happened and ended. Just as it occurs in the present, it also occurs in the future. What is punishment? Punishment is penalty, i.e., He penalizes.

His saying ﴿whom He wills﴾: it has passed us many times that when Allah the Exalted attributes an action to His will, it is always coupled with wisdom, because Allah the Exalted does not do anything merely by will alone; rather everything He does is by His will coupled with His wisdom. This is a clear matter, for whoever is punished must have committed what deserves punishment, and then there is wisdom in his punishment. Allah the Exalted never punishes whom He wills without sin, because His wisdom refuses that and His mercy refuses that, contrary to the one who said:

"It is permissible for the Master to punish the creatures, without any sin or crime having occurred."

Then he justified that by saying:

"Everything that comes from Him, exalted is He, is good, because He cannot be questioned about His actions."

This is not correct. Even if it is permissible by reason, it is prohibited by the Sharia, because Allah says in the sacred hadith: «O My servants, I have forbidden injustice to Myself and made it forbidden among you»[[Narrated by Muslim (2577/55) from the hadith of Abu Dharr.]], and Allah says in the Qur'an: ﴿And whoever does righteous deeds while he is a believer, will fear no injustice or deprivation﴾ [Ta-Ha 112]. The point is that His saying ﴿He punishes whom He wills﴾ — I said: it is coupled with what? With wisdom. Therefore He punishes only those who deserve punishment.

﴿And has mercy on whom He wills﴾. ﴿Has mercy﴾: mercy (ar-rahmah) is one of the attributes of Allah the Mighty and Majestic, and it requires bestowing favor and kindness, whether the kindness is by bringing about something beloved or by repelling something disliked. The mercy of Allah the Mighty and Majestic toward a person is either by bringing what benefits him or by repelling what harms him.

His saying ﴿has mercy on whom He wills﴾ is a present-tense verb derived from mercy, and mercy is an attribute of Allah the Mighty and Majestic, established in its true sense. Among its effects is what? Bestowing favor and kindness, or the will to bestow favor and kindness; it is not the favor, kindness, or will itself. This contradicts those who said so, among whom are the Ash'ariyyah, and behind them the extreme Mu'attilah, who are even more so. They say: mercy means the will to bestow favor, and some of them say: or the bestowal of favor. The correct view is contrary to that, because the will arises from mercy: one has mercy and so wills to do good or bestow favor. This is the position of the people of the Sunnah and the community, that mercy is an attribute established for Allah in its true sense. Those who argued against its being literal said: because mercy is weakness and softness in the one who is merciful; you find his self breaks until he shows mercy.

Our answer to this is simple: there are two aspects. First, we deny that it is a matter of weakness and softness, for we find tyrannical kings who are shown mercy, and there is no weakness or softness in them. Second, even if it is assumed that this meaning necessarily belongs to mercy in a human being, it is not necessary with respect to Allah, just as with other attributes that are established literally for the created and also established for the Creator. The concomitants and accidents that belong to the attribute of the created cannot belong to the attribute of the Creator, because of the great difference between them in essence and attributes. Just as Allah the Exalted has no likeness and no equal in His essence, so He has no likeness and no equal in His attributes.

﴿And to Him you will be returned﴾. The author, may Allah have mercy on him, said: (﴿He punishes whom He wills﴾ His punishment, ﴿and has mercy on whom He wills﴾ His mercy) — is that what you have? (﴿And to Him you will be returned﴾ you will be sent back). ﴿To Him﴾, not to other than Him; the fronting of the object conveys restriction. So the return or turning back is to Allah the Mighty and Majestic; we are not returned to anyone else. Is this general or specific? It is general for everyone: whatever people are, where is their return? To Allah the Exalted, however much they flee. So "return" means being sent back to Allah the Exalted, and when our return is to Allah, He becomes the judge between us; He judges between His servants concerning what they differed about, and judges between His servants regarding what is between Him and them, because Allah's judgment regarding His servants includes judgment concerning what is between Him and them, and judgment concerning what they differ about. The believers and the disbelievers differ, so Allah will judge between them on the Day of Resurrection; likewise, the transgressors and those wronged differ, so Allah will judge between them on the Day of Resurrection.

﴿And you cannot escape Allah in the earth or in the heaven, and you have no protector or helper other than Allah﴾ [Al-'Ankabut 22]. ﴿And you﴾: the address is either to the disbelievers or to people in general. That it is to people in general is preferable; meaning: and you, O people. That it is to the stubborn deniers is more emphatic, because they think they can overpower Allah.

His saying ﴿and you are not escaping﴾: I think we know that ﴿ma﴾ here is Hijazi or Najdi?

* Student: Hijazi.
* Shaykh: Hijazi, because the Qur'an is in the dialect of Hijaz, indeed in the dialect of Quraysh. Its subject is the pronoun ﴿antum﴾ and its predicate is ﴿bi-mu'jizin﴾, where the ba' is extra for emphasis. Ibn Malik said:

"After (ma) and (laysa) the predicate takes a ba' of jarr..."

How do we parse ﴿mu'jizin﴾?

* Student: The ba' is extra for emphasis, ﴿mu'jizin﴾ is the predicate of ﴿ma﴾ in the accusative, and the sign of its accusative is a hypothetical ya' prevented from appearing by the occupation of the position by the vowel of the extra preposition.
* Shaykh: By the sign of the case of the extra preposition. What is "vowel"? This is in fact a well-known over-elaboration according to the rules; that is, we must parse it according to the known rules of grammar. The ya' present now in ﴿bi-mu'jizin﴾ — what brought it? The ba'; the ba' brought it, not the predicate, although in reality it is itself the sign of the accusative.

The saying of Allah the Exalted ﴿and you are not escaping﴾ is from (a'jaza), so it is transitive. (ajaza) is intransitive, and (a'jaza) is transitive. When it is transitive and is an active participle, it requires an object. Where is the object? The author said: (not escaping your Lord from your pursuit), so the object is omitted, its estimate being "not escaping your Lord" or "not escaping Allah," for example; there is no obstacle. The one who escapes (mu'jiz) is the one who does what makes others unable to overtake him; for this reason some scholars said about the signs of the messengers that they are miracles (mu'jizat), because they render the enemies of the messengers unable to oppose them.

His saying ﴿in the earth or in the heaven﴾: this prepositional phrase is a circumstantial clause (hal) from ﴿mu'jizin﴾, meaning: whether you are in the earth or in the heaven, you do not escape Allah. Therefore the author said: (even if you were in it). So His saying ﴿nor in the heaven﴾ is by way of supposition, not literal reality, because people are on the earth and not in the heaven.

It has also been said that this is by way of supposition: "nor in the heaven" meaning "even if you were in it," i.e., even supposing you were in it, you would not escape Allah. It has been said that the meaning is hyperbole: you do not escape Allah whether you are in the depths of the earth or in the expanses of the heaven; you do not escape Allah, so the meaning is that you cannot escape Him wherever you are.

It has also been said that His saying ﴿nor in the heaven﴾ means the inhabitants of the heaven: that nothing is beyond Allah's power in the heavens or in the earth; the inhabitants of the heaven cannot escape Him, and the inhabitants of the earth cannot escape Him. So on this view, "you cannot escape Him in the earth, nor those in the heaven" — yes, in the manner of the poet Hassan ibn Thabit's words:

"Whoever among you satirizes the Messenger of Allah, and praises him and supports him, is equal."

We all know that the first is not the second, because the one who satirizes him cannot praise and support him; so it is on the supposition: "and the one who praises and supports him is equal," so this is similar. In any case, the meaning appears to me to be that you cannot escape Allah wherever you are, whether in the heaven or in the earth. At the time the Qur'an was revealed, "heaven" could not literally mean anything except what is high, even on mountain peaks; in our time a person can be in the heaven, i.e., in the height, though not the lowest heaven, which no one reaches: ﴿And We made the heaven a protected ceiling, yet they turn away from its signs﴾ [Al-Anbiya' 32]. Even the Prophet ﷺ and Gabriel could not enter this heaven except after seeking opening and permission.

﴿And you have no﴾: the author said in his summary explanation: (i.e., you cannot outrun Him), meaning you cannot outrun Allah; rather, if He wills to punish you, He overtakes you, for nothing escapes Allah the Exalted: ﴿Allah is never to be frustrated by anything in the heavens or on the earth; indeed He is ever Knowing and Competent﴾ [Fatir 44]. Know that the punishment of Allah the Mighty and Majestic and His overtaking a person sometimes occurs through sensible matters, where Allah decrees causes known to us that we witness, and sometimes through matters we do not perceive, where punishment comes from Allah without any cause known to us.

For example, the causes of the Messenger ﷺ's victory are sometimes unknown and sometimes known. Allah's victory for the Messenger ﷺ at the Battle of the Trench had known and witnessed causes: Allah sent upon them a wind and soldiers we do not see. The soldiers we do not see are among the matters unknown except through reports, through the Sharia; but the wind that disturbed them, overturned their cooking pots, and demolished their tents is perceptible and known. Yet the soldiers we did not see, were it not for Allah's informing us of them, we would not know them. So Allah the Mighty and Majestic overtakes a person either by known causes that appear openly, or by hidden causes that do not appear openly; then we may know them through revelation, or we may not know them.

(﴿And you have no protector other than Allah﴾, i.e., other than Him, ﴿who could protect you﴾ from Him, ﴿nor any helper﴾ who could help you against His punishment.) ﴿You have no protector other than Allah﴾: I do not know whether ﴿ma﴾ here is Najdi or Hijazi.

* Student: Najdi.
* Student: The attachment to the prepositional phrase does no harm.
* Shaykh: No; both dialects agree on it, because of the lack of ordering. ﴿Mina waliyyin﴾ is the subject — ﴿waliyyin﴾ is the subject, is it not? And ﴿lakum﴾ is the predicate, meaning: there is no protector for you other than Allah.

The author's saying: (﴿And you have no other than Allah﴾ i.e., other than Him) is correct; he expressed "other" by "beside" (dun) because of its lowly rank.

His saying the Exalted: ﴿a protector﴾: the author said: (who would prevent you from Him, ﴿nor a helper﴾ who would help you against His punishment). I do not know except that help means prevention and aid, but the correct view is that His saying ﴿a protector nor a helper﴾: the protector (wali) is the one who takes charge of a person in all his circumstances, helping him against his enemy and bringing him good even outside confrontation with an enemy. So the protector is the more general, the one who takes charge of him in bringing benefit and repelling harm. The helper is the one who only repels from you, and may not be one of your protectors, but repels from you in the specific situation where you need a helper. Support occurs in repelling what is disliked. So the protector here is more general: no one takes charge of you to bring you good and repel evil, and no one helps you against Allah to prevent punishment from you. This is a real matter: when the might of Allah descends upon a people, no one can repel that might from them or prevent them from it.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And those who disbelieve in the signs of Allah and His meeting﴾ [Al-'Ankabut 23], i.e., the Qur'an and the resurrection, ﴿those have despaired of My mercy﴾. ﴿Those who﴾ is a subject: where is its predicate?

* Student: The nominal sentence.
* Shaykh: The nominal sentence in His saying ﴿those have despaired﴾. This sentence is both a major and minor clause: where is the major? They say major and minor: if the sentence is a predicate, they call it a minor clause; if it consists of subject and predicate, it is called major. So here we have ﴿those who disbelieved﴾ up to the end of the sentence, which we call the major clause.

﴿Those have despaired﴾ is a minor clause, because it is part of the sentence, is it not? You agree it is part of the sentence: ﴿those have despaired of My mercy﴾ is part of the sentence. How so?

* Student: Because it is the predicate.
* Shaykh: Because it is the predicate. It is a subject and predicate, but as a predicate it is part of a clause. He used the nominal sentence to indicate establishment and permanence. ﴿Those who disbelieved in the signs of Allah﴾: "signs" is the plural of "aya," and an aya in the language is a sign. The signs of Allah the Exalted are of two kinds, cosmic and legislative. The cosmic signs are what He created in the heavens and the earth; they are signs because they point to their Creator, and every one of them indicates an attribute suitable to it, since the signs as a whole generally indicate the Creator, and each sign indicates a specific attribute of His. When the signs are magnificent, they indicate the existence of the Creator and His power; when firmness and perfection appear in them, they indicate wisdom, and so on. The point is that they are signs which, in their generality, indicate the existence of the Creator, and each has its own specific indication of these particular attributes. Such cosmic signs are like what? ﴿And among His signs are the night and the day and the sun and the moon﴾ [Fussilat 37], and look in Surat ar-Rum at several signs Allah the Mighty and Majestic mentioned.

The second kind of signs: the legislative signs, which are what the revealed laws brought. The cosmic signs are a very clear sign of Allah; the legislative signs are also a sign of Allah the Mighty and Majestic and of His wisdom. Why?

* Student: Because the Sharia (...).

**Shaykh:** Yes. Because the legislated signs (al-ayat al-shar'iyyah) are beyond the ability of humans to produce anything like them. All of them are reform and the prevention of corruption. Every divine law came to bring about reform. This is one point. However, reform differs from nation to nation according to its condition. Severity toward the Jews is appropriate, and leniency toward the Christians is appropriate. Combining the two in this Ummah is the most fitting of all. Although this religion, in itself, is ease (Islam is ease, with no hardship in it), compared to the religion of the Christians, the Christian religion contains many matters that are dispensed with, because their situation suits that. The religion of the Jews contains harshness, severity, heavy burdens (aṣār) and shackles (aghlāl), which Allah has removed from us through this Noble Prophet. So all these laws are signs that indicate the perfection of the One who legislated them and prescribed them for His servants. However, the first type of sign, belief in it, is easy, and reaching its reality is easy. The second type, however, involves some difficulty, because one does not recognize the perfection of the Sharia and its indication of the One who legislated it except by one who delves deeply into it and knows the wisdoms and secrets contained in these rulings. For this reason, we should delve deeply into knowing the wisdom of legislation. That is, knowing that this is permissible and this is forbidden may be easy, but knowing why this was prohibited or why that was permitted is extremely important, and it is through this that the Sharia is shown to be one of the signs of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.

As for His saying ﴿and His meeting﴾: meeting when? On the Day of Resurrection. It means they denied the meeting, which necessarily entails resurrection, because resurrection is a necessary consequence of meeting; there is no meeting except after resurrection. And the meeting with Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, is established by the Book, the Sunnah, and the consensus of the Muslims (ijma'). Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿O mankind, indeed you are laboring toward your Lord with labor and will meet Him﴾ [al-Inshiqaq 6]. That is, you will meet Him, and He will recompense you for this toil, either with good or with evil.

As for His saying ﴿and His meeting﴾, it means resurrection. Is it because those who deny resurrection believe in meeting Allah? No, they do not believe in meeting Allah, because they say, may Allah protect us, that when they are bones and dust, they cannot be resurrected in a new creation. So they denied this.

He, the Exalted, says: ﴿Those have despaired of My mercy﴾. This is their recompense for this denial: despair of the mercy of Allah. The author said: "(That is, My Paradise)." ﴿They have despaired of My mercy﴾ (that is, My Paradise). So he turned it into created mercy, and not into the mercy which is an attribute of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. This is because mercy when attributed to Allah may mean the abode of His mercy, and then it is created, as in the sacred hadith in which Allah said to Paradise: "You are My mercy; I show mercy through you to whomever I will."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (4850) and Muslim (2846/34) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]] And it is also applied to the mercy which is an attribute of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and in that case it is an uncreated attribute of Allah. Among its examples is His saying: ﴿And My mercy encompasses all things﴾ [al-A'raf 156], and His saying: ﴿Our Lord, You have encompassed all things in mercy and knowledge﴾ [Ghafir 7]. So what is meant by mercy in this verse? Is it the first type, the created mercy which is the place of mercy, or the mercy which is His attribute? The apparent meaning is that what is meant is the mercy which is His attribute, because when it is used absolutely, what is meant is the attribute. When mercy is used and attributed to Allah, what is meant is the attribute. We do not interpret it as meaning the place of mercy except when there is a contextual indicator (qarinah). If a contextual indicator is found, we act upon it; otherwise the default is that it is an attribute of Allah.

So, ﴿they have despaired of My mercy﴾: what does it mean? They have despaired that I would show them mercy, and if Allah does not show them mercy, they will not enter Paradise, correct? This is the correct meaning of the verse. What the author mentioned is also possible, meaning we do not vehemently object to it, because mercy, just as it is applied to the attribute, is also applied to the place of mercy.

﴿And for them is a painful punishment﴾ [al-Ankabut 23]. This too, glory be to Allah the Great, is two clauses: a major and a minor. ﴿And those﴾ is the subject, and ﴿for them is a punishment﴾ is a subject and predicate, and the whole clause is the predicate.

All of this is for the complete warning to them. They were deprived of good and fell into evil. For this reason He said: (﴿For them is a painful punishment﴾ which is painful). And ﴿punishment﴾ means what? Punishment was explained shortly before as a penalty. That is, for them is a painful penalty, meaning severe and painful, may Allah protect us, and that is in the Fire. There is no need to explain what punishment is in that Fire, because it is known.

(Allah the Exalted said about the story of Abraham: ﴿So there was no answer from his people﴾ [al-Ankabut 24]). Because the sentence, according to the author's view, is parenthetical (mu'taridah). From where? From His saying: ﴿And if you deny, then nations before you have denied﴾ to this point. It is a parenthetical clause. Do you understand? This is what the author and Ibn Jarir and most of the exegetes adopted. Some exegetes said that the whole speech is from the words of Abraham, and there is nothing parenthetical in it. Ibn Kathir chose this view and said that it is all from the words of Abraham.

**Student:** It is problematic.

**Shaykh:** What is the problem?

**Student:** ﴿Those have despaired of My mercy﴾. If it were from the words of Abraham, it would be problematic: ﴿And those who disbelieve in the signs of Allah and His meeting, those have despaired of My mercy﴾. So the mercy does not belong to Abraham; it belongs to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.

**Shaykh:** Is there any other meaning?

**Student:** (...)

**Shaykh:** Is it not permissible for the Prophet to say it? Because even the Messenger said it according to their view, since they hold that it is from the speech of Allah addressing the disbelievers of Quraysh.

Fine, let us look first at ﴿And if you deny, then nations before you have denied﴾ [al-Ankabut 18]. If someone says there is a problem in it, we say there is no problem, because there were nations before Abraham, correct?

And His saying: ﴿And upon the Messenger is only the clear conveyance﴾...

**Shaykh:** (...) Its apparent meaning is that it is from the speech of Allah. As for ﴿Have they not seen?﴾, there is no problem, because Abraham addresses them and says this statement. And His saying: ﴿Say, travel through the earth﴾ [al-Ankabut 20].

**Student:** There is a problem.

**Shaykh:** Is there a problem or not?

**Student:** Yes.

**Shaykh:** What is the problem?

**Student:** Because ﴿Say﴾ is addressed...

**Shaykh:** Because ﴿Say﴾ is from Allah, so it is addressed to the one addressed. In reality, we cannot say it is from the words of Abraham except by way of strained interpretation, by saying: since he was a messenger from Allah, the address of Allah, the Exalted, was upon his tongue. But even if it is attributed to Allah, it becomes strained. So the main point is that the apparent sense of the context of the verses indicates the view that this is from the speech of Allah, the Exalted, as a parenthetical interjection within the story.

﴿So there was no answer from his people except that they said, "Kill him or burn him"﴾ [al-Ankabut 24]. This is a severe answer, may Allah protect us. But first there is a problem from the standpoint of i'rab (grammatical analysis): why is the noun of (kāna) in the accusative? It is well known that (kāna) makes the noun nominative and the predicate accusative, but here the noun is accusative. Does anyone have an answer? (...)

**Student:** The noun of kāna is ﴿except that they said﴾.

**Shaykh:** And ﴿answer﴾?

**Student:** ﴿Answer﴾ is the predicate.

**Shaykh:** The predicate of kāna is fronted?

**Student:** Yes.

**Shaykh:** Like this? Fine, like this, correct. ﴿Answer﴾ then is the fronted predicate of kāna, and ﴿except that they said﴾ is the noun. The estimated sense is: "So the answer of his people was only their saying." And His saying: ﴿So there was no answer from his people except that they said﴾ conveys restriction (ḥaṣr), meaning: their answer was neither submission nor a fine rebuttal. It was, may Allah protect us, a threat of force. Likewise, O people, everyone who cannot refute the truth threatens with force if he has power over his opponent, and if he has no power, he begins to speak with insult and abuse. Because whoever has knowledge of the truth through sound logic answers it with sound logic. What did Pharaoh say to Moses? He said: ﴿He said, "If you take a god other than me, I will surely make you among the imprisoned"﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 29]. When Moses debated him on the matter in Surat al-Shu'ara': ﴿Pharaoh said, "And what is the Lord of the worlds?" He said, "Lord of the heavens and the earth and whatever is between them, if you were convinced"﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 23-24]. He mocked him: ﴿He said to those around him, "Do you not listen?"﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 25]. The answer was: ﴿He said, "Your Lord and the Lord of your forefathers, the first"﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 26]. Yes. Then he accused him of madness: ﴿He said, "Indeed, your messenger who has been sent to you is mad"﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 27]. The answer was: ﴿He said, "Lord of the east and the west and whatever is between them, if you would use reason"﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 28]. In reality you are the mad ones, but he presented it in a clear and logical manner, as if you were rational: the Lord of the east and the west, who brings the sun from the east and brings it from the west, is Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. Finally: ﴿He said, "If you take a god other than me, I will surely make you among the imprisoned"﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 29], because he could not answer him. This last statement, ﴿Lord of the east and the west﴾, resembles the statement of Abraham, peace be upon him, to the one who argued with him about Allah: ﴿Indeed, Allah brings the sun from the east, so bring it from the west﴾ [al-Baqarah 258]. Yes. Here, with Abraham (ﷺ), the answer...

**Student:** (...)

**Shaykh:** Yes, the answer: ﴿except that they said, "Kill him or burn him"﴾ is a threat of force, not of logic. This is like the case of the messengers and their opponents; it is a continuous chain that does not break. Muhammad, peace be upon him: ﴿And [recall] when those who disbelieved plotted against you to restrain you or kill you or expel you. They plot, and Allah plots﴾ [al-Anfal 30]. Likewise: ﴿except that they said, "Kill him or burn him"﴾. In another verse: ﴿They said, "Burn him and support your gods"﴾ [al-Anbiya' 68]. The reconciliation between them is simple: some of them said "kill him," and some said "burn him," and their decision settled on burning. Yes, and Allah knows best. We ask Allah for well-being.

**Student:** It is evident that the people of falsehood always (...) threatened the people of truth with force (...).

**Shaykh:** Yes, indeed, that is evident.

**Student:** (...)

**Shaykh:** Yes.

**Student:** (...)

**Shaykh:** But do not bring up negation (...).

* * *

Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿He punishes whom He wills﴾ [al-Ankabut 21]. This is the beginning of the benefits.

His saying ﴿He punishes﴾ and ﴿and has mercy﴾ contains: affirmation of voluntary actions (al-af'al al-ikhtiyariyyah) for Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. Yes, affirmation of voluntary actions for Allah. This is the position of Ahl al-Sunnah wa'l-Jama'ah (the People of the Sunnah and the Community) among the Salaf and the Imams: affirmation of voluntary actions for Allah, meaning that He does what He wills. The Ash'arites and others opposed this and said: Allah, glory be to Him and exalted, is not subject to any occurring act. They justified this by saying that a contingent thing does not subsist except in a contingent thing, and that if we affirm that actions occur to Allah, it would follow that Allah is contingent. There is no doubt that this is a false view. For we say to them: who said to you that a contingent thing does not subsist except in a contingent thing? From where did this principle come? Is it in the Quran? Is it in the Sunnah? Is it by reason?

Furthermore, we counter this corrupt principle with a principle that is more perfect and clearer: that the one who acts as He wills is more perfect than the one who does not act. Is that not so? The one who acts as He wills is more perfect than the one who does not act. So if you deprive Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, of His voluntary actions, you are in effect describing Him with the most deficient qualities. This is a matter known to all rational people: that the agent who acts as he wills is more perfect than the one who does not act, or the one who is compelled to act.

* From the benefits of the verse: affirmation of will for Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, from His saying ﴿whom He wills﴾ in both places.

* From its benefits: mercy is sought only from Allah, from His saying ﴿and has mercy﴾. This, in the form of division, indicates exclusivity: ﴿He punishes﴾ and ﴿has mercy﴾. So mercy is not sought except from Allah. Even those among the creation who show mercy, when you seek their mercy, you should make that dependent upon Allah, because if Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, willed that they not show you mercy, they would not show you mercy.

* From the benefits of the verse: affirmation of resurrection, from His saying ﴿and to Him you will be returned﴾.

* From its benefits: a warning against opposition, because if the return is to Allah, beware of opposing Him. This resembles a threat and warning against opposition.

Then Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿And you cannot cause failure [to Allah] on earth or in the heaven, and you have not besides Allah any protector or helper﴾ [al-Ankabut 22].

* From the benefits of this verse: the perfection of the power of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and that nothing can overpower Him: ﴿And you cannot cause failure on earth﴾.

* From its benefits: there is no escape for a person from the decree of Allah, whether he is in the heaven or on the earth, from His saying ﴿And you cannot cause failure on earth or in the heaven﴾.

* From its benefits: the weakness of humans in relation to the Creator, because the address ﴿you cannot cause failure﴾ is general. Humans, however powerful they become, are weak and incapable in relation to the Creator. For this reason Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿As for 'Ad, they were arrogant in the land without right and said, "Who is greater than us in strength?"﴾ Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿Did they not see that Allah, who created them, is greater than them in strength?﴾ [Fussilat 15]. The word ﴿created them﴾ came; He did not say "Allah is stronger than them" in a separate way. Since they are created, the Creator is undoubtedly stronger. The Creator is stronger than the created. So the relative pronoun with its clause functions like a reason and an indication of their weakness before Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.

* From the benefits of the verse: humans have no refuge for bringing benefit and repelling harm except in whom? In Allah. And whoever seeks help from other than Him will be disappointed: ﴿And you have not besides Allah any protector or helper﴾.

* And among them, which is a rhetorical benefit: among the particles of emphasis is the addition of letters. The addition of letters is among the particles of emphasis, as in His saying: ﴿And you have not besides Allah any protector﴾, because (min) here is additional, to convey generality or to explicitly state generality.

Then Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿And those who disbelieve in the signs of Allah and His meeting, those have despaired of My mercy, and for them is a painful punishment﴾ [al-Ankabut 23].

* From the benefits of this verse: the disbelievers do not enter Paradise, derived from His saying ﴿those have despaired of My mercy﴾.

* And from its benefits also: affirmation of the signs of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, both the cosmic and the legislated, from ﴿disbelieve in the signs of Allah﴾.

* And from its benefits: the mercy of Allah, the Exalted, toward the servants, in that He showed them of His signs that would make them believe in the like of them. Is that not so? This is from the blessing of Allah: that Allah, the Exalted, showed His servants of His signs that would make them believe in their like. For this reason, whenever some sign of Allah appears to a person, it is greater evidence of the blessing of Allah upon him and firmer in the establishment of his faith. Among this are the miracles (karamat) that occurred to some of the friends of Allah, for they increase their faith and confirm the truth they were upon. Shaykh al-Islam, may Allah have mercy on him, said: Miracles were numerous in the time of the Successors (tabi'un) rather than the Companions, because among the Companions was a faith that the Successors did not have. So they had no need for miracles to strengthen their faith as the Successors did. He mentioned this in the book al-Furqan. This is true, for when you reflect upon the miracles that are reported, you find them more numerous among the Successors. So the main point is that showing a person signs, whether legislated or decreed, is a blessing from Allah upon him, because it increases his faith and its firmness in the heart.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 29, verse 21–27 (part 3 of 7):

* Among the benefits of the verse: affirmation of seeing Allah. From where do we take this? From His words: ﴿and His meeting﴾. The People of the Sunnah and the Community (Ahl al-Sunnah wa'l-Jama'ah) have used this as evidence for affirming the vision, because meeting, when there is no obstacle, necessarily involves seeing, and no obstacle prevents it.
This question has much disagreement between the People of the Sunnah and the People of innovation (Ahl al-Bid'ah). The correct position, indicated by the Qur'an and the Sunnah, is affirming what? Affirming the vision of Allah, the Exalted, with the eye, and that in the Hereafter He is seen. As for Paradise, the believers see Him and others do not, because they are not in it. As for the plains of Resurrection (arasat al-qiyamah), the correct view is that the believers see Him and the hypocrites see Him as well, but the hypocrites see Him not as a vision of delight but as a true vision of remorse (ru'yat tandim). This is because Allah, glorified and exalted, manifests Himself to this Ummah, and among them are hypocrites; so He uncovers His shin for them, blessed and exalted is He, and commands them to prostrate.
