﴿And for them is a painful punishment﴾ [al-Ankabut 23]. This too, glory be to Allah the Great, is two clauses: a major and a minor. ﴿And those﴾ is the subject, and ﴿for them is a punishment﴾ is a subject and predicate, and the whole clause is the predicate.

All of this is for the complete warning to them. They were deprived of good and fell into evil. For this reason He said: (﴿For them is a painful punishment﴾ which is painful). And ﴿punishment﴾ means what? Punishment was explained shortly before as a penalty. That is, for them is a painful penalty, meaning severe and painful, may Allah protect us, and that is in the Fire. There is no need to explain what punishment is in that Fire, because it is known.

(Allah the Exalted said about the story of Abraham: ﴿So there was no answer from his people﴾ [al-Ankabut 24]). Because the sentence, according to the author's view, is parenthetical (mu'taridah). From where? From His saying: ﴿And if you deny, then nations before you have denied﴾ to this point. It is a parenthetical clause. Do you understand? This is what the author and Ibn Jarir and most of the exegetes adopted. Some exegetes said that the whole speech is from the words of Abraham, and there is nothing parenthetical in it. Ibn Kathir chose this view and said that it is all from the words of Abraham.

**Student:** It is problematic.

**Shaykh:** What is the problem?

**Student:** ﴿Those have despaired of My mercy﴾. If it were from the words of Abraham, it would be problematic: ﴿And those who disbelieve in the signs of Allah and His meeting, those have despaired of My mercy﴾. So the mercy does not belong to Abraham; it belongs to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.

**Shaykh:** Is there any other meaning?

**Student:** (...)

**Shaykh:** Is it not permissible for the Prophet to say it? Because even the Messenger said it according to their view, since they hold that it is from the speech of Allah addressing the disbelievers of Quraysh.

Fine, let us look first at ﴿And if you deny, then nations before you have denied﴾ [al-Ankabut 18]. If someone says there is a problem in it, we say there is no problem, because there were nations before Abraham, correct?

And His saying: ﴿And upon the Messenger is only the clear conveyance﴾...

**Shaykh:** (...) Its apparent meaning is that it is from the speech of Allah. As for ﴿Have they not seen?﴾, there is no problem, because Abraham addresses them and says this statement. And His saying: ﴿Say, travel through the earth﴾ [al-Ankabut 20].

**Student:** There is a problem.

**Shaykh:** Is there a problem or not?

**Student:** Yes.

**Shaykh:** What is the problem?

**Student:** Because ﴿Say﴾ is addressed...

**Shaykh:** Because ﴿Say﴾ is from Allah, so it is addressed to the one addressed. In reality, we cannot say it is from the words of Abraham except by way of strained interpretation, by saying: since he was a messenger from Allah, the address of Allah, the Exalted, was upon his tongue. But even if it is attributed to Allah, it becomes strained. So the main point is that the apparent sense of the context of the verses indicates the view that this is from the speech of Allah, the Exalted, as a parenthetical interjection within the story.

﴿So there was no answer from his people except that they said, "Kill him or burn him"﴾ [al-Ankabut 24]. This is a severe answer, may Allah protect us. But first there is a problem from the standpoint of i'rab (grammatical analysis): why is the noun of (kāna) in the accusative? It is well known that (kāna) makes the noun nominative and the predicate accusative, but here the noun is accusative. Does anyone have an answer? (...)

**Student:** The noun of kāna is ﴿except that they said﴾.

**Shaykh:** And ﴿answer﴾?

**Student:** ﴿Answer﴾ is the predicate.

**Shaykh:** The predicate of kāna is fronted?

**Student:** Yes.

**Shaykh:** Like this? Fine, like this, correct. ﴿Answer﴾ then is the fronted predicate of kāna, and ﴿except that they said﴾ is the noun. The estimated sense is: "So the answer of his people was only their saying." And His saying: ﴿So there was no answer from his people except that they said﴾ conveys restriction (ḥaṣr), meaning: their answer was neither submission nor a fine rebuttal. It was, may Allah protect us, a threat of force. Likewise, O people, everyone who cannot refute the truth threatens with force if he has power over his opponent, and if he has no power, he begins to speak with insult and abuse. Because whoever has knowledge of the truth through sound logic answers it with sound logic. What did Pharaoh say to Moses? He said: ﴿He said, "If you take a god other than me, I will surely make you among the imprisoned"﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 29]. When Moses debated him on the matter in Surat al-Shu'ara': ﴿Pharaoh said, "And what is the Lord of the worlds?" He said, "Lord of the heavens and the earth and whatever is between them, if you were convinced"﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 23-24]. He mocked him: ﴿He said to those around him, "Do you not listen?"﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 25]. The answer was: ﴿He said, "Your Lord and the Lord of your forefathers, the first"﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 26]. Yes. Then he accused him of madness: ﴿He said, "Indeed, your messenger who has been sent to you is mad"﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 27]. The answer was: ﴿He said, "Lord of the east and the west and whatever is between them, if you would use reason"﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 28]. In reality you are the mad ones, but he presented it in a clear and logical manner, as if you were rational: the Lord of the east and the west, who brings the sun from the east and brings it from the west, is Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. Finally: ﴿He said, "If you take a god other than me, I will surely make you among the imprisoned"﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 29], because he could not answer him. This last statement, ﴿Lord of the east and the west﴾, resembles the statement of Abraham, peace be upon him, to the one who argued with him about Allah: ﴿Indeed, Allah brings the sun from the east, so bring it from the west﴾ [al-Baqarah 258]. Yes. Here, with Abraham (ﷺ), the answer...

**Student:** (...)

**Shaykh:** Yes, the answer: ﴿except that they said, "Kill him or burn him"﴾ is a threat of force, not of logic. This is like the case of the messengers and their opponents; it is a continuous chain that does not break. Muhammad, peace be upon him: ﴿And [recall] when those who disbelieved plotted against you to restrain you or kill you or expel you. They plot, and Allah plots﴾ [al-Anfal 30]. Likewise: ﴿except that they said, "Kill him or burn him"﴾. In another verse: ﴿They said, "Burn him and support your gods"﴾ [al-Anbiya' 68]. The reconciliation between them is simple: some of them said "kill him," and some said "burn him," and their decision settled on burning. Yes, and Allah knows best. We ask Allah for well-being.

**Student:** It is evident that the people of falsehood always (...) threatened the people of truth with force (...).

**Shaykh:** Yes, indeed, that is evident.

**Student:** (...)

**Shaykh:** Yes.

**Student:** (...)

**Shaykh:** But do not bring up negation (...).

* * *

Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿He punishes whom He wills﴾ [al-Ankabut 21]. This is the beginning of the benefits.

His saying ﴿He punishes﴾ and ﴿and has mercy﴾ contains: affirmation of voluntary actions (al-af'al al-ikhtiyariyyah) for Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. Yes, affirmation of voluntary actions for Allah. This is the position of Ahl al-Sunnah wa'l-Jama'ah (the People of the Sunnah and the Community) among the Salaf and the Imams: affirmation of voluntary actions for Allah, meaning that He does what He wills. The Ash'arites and others opposed this and said: Allah, glory be to Him and exalted, is not subject to any occurring act. They justified this by saying that a contingent thing does not subsist except in a contingent thing, and that if we affirm that actions occur to Allah, it would follow that Allah is contingent. There is no doubt that this is a false view. For we say to them: who said to you that a contingent thing does not subsist except in a contingent thing? From where did this principle come? Is it in the Quran? Is it in the Sunnah? Is it by reason?

Furthermore, we counter this corrupt principle with a principle that is more perfect and clearer: that the one who acts as He wills is more perfect than the one who does not act. Is that not so? The one who acts as He wills is more perfect than the one who does not act. So if you deprive Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, of His voluntary actions, you are in effect describing Him with the most deficient qualities. This is a matter known to all rational people: that the agent who acts as he wills is more perfect than the one who does not act, or the one who is compelled to act.

* From the benefits of the verse: affirmation of will for Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, from His saying ﴿whom He wills﴾ in both places.

* From its benefits: mercy is sought only from Allah, from His saying ﴿and has mercy﴾. This, in the form of division, indicates exclusivity: ﴿He punishes﴾ and ﴿has mercy﴾. So mercy is not sought except from Allah. Even those among the creation who show mercy, when you seek their mercy, you should make that dependent upon Allah, because if Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, willed that they not show you mercy, they would not show you mercy.

* From the benefits of the verse: affirmation of resurrection, from His saying ﴿and to Him you will be returned﴾.

* From its benefits: a warning against opposition, because if the return is to Allah, beware of opposing Him. This resembles a threat and warning against opposition.

Then Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿And you cannot cause failure [to Allah] on earth or in the heaven, and you have not besides Allah any protector or helper﴾ [al-Ankabut 22].

* From the benefits of this verse: the perfection of the power of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and that nothing can overpower Him: ﴿And you cannot cause failure on earth﴾.

* From its benefits: there is no escape for a person from the decree of Allah, whether he is in the heaven or on the earth, from His saying ﴿And you cannot cause failure on earth or in the heaven﴾.

* From its benefits: the weakness of humans in relation to the Creator, because the address ﴿you cannot cause failure﴾ is general. Humans, however powerful they become, are weak and incapable in relation to the Creator. For this reason Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿As for 'Ad, they were arrogant in the land without right and said, "Who is greater than us in strength?"﴾ Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿Did they not see that Allah, who created them, is greater than them in strength?﴾ [Fussilat 15]. The word ﴿created them﴾ came; He did not say "Allah is stronger than them" in a separate way. Since they are created, the Creator is undoubtedly stronger. The Creator is stronger than the created. So the relative pronoun with its clause functions like a reason and an indication of their weakness before Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.

* From the benefits of the verse: humans have no refuge for bringing benefit and repelling harm except in whom? In Allah. And whoever seeks help from other than Him will be disappointed: ﴿And you have not besides Allah any protector or helper﴾.

* And among them, which is a rhetorical benefit: among the particles of emphasis is the addition of letters. The addition of letters is among the particles of emphasis, as in His saying: ﴿And you have not besides Allah any protector﴾, because (min) here is additional, to convey generality or to explicitly state generality.

Then Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿And those who disbelieve in the signs of Allah and His meeting, those have despaired of My mercy, and for them is a painful punishment﴾ [al-Ankabut 23].

* From the benefits of this verse: the disbelievers do not enter Paradise, derived from His saying ﴿those have despaired of My mercy﴾.

* And from its benefits also: affirmation of the signs of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, both the cosmic and the legislated, from ﴿disbelieve in the signs of Allah﴾.

* And from its benefits: the mercy of Allah, the Exalted, toward the servants, in that He showed them of His signs that would make them believe in the like of them. Is that not so? This is from the blessing of Allah: that Allah, the Exalted, showed His servants of His signs that would make them believe in their like. For this reason, whenever some sign of Allah appears to a person, it is greater evidence of the blessing of Allah upon him and firmer in the establishment of his faith. Among this are the miracles (karamat) that occurred to some of the friends of Allah, for they increase their faith and confirm the truth they were upon. Shaykh al-Islam, may Allah have mercy on him, said: Miracles were numerous in the time of the Successors (tabi'un) rather than the Companions, because among the Companions was a faith that the Successors did not have. So they had no need for miracles to strengthen their faith as the Successors did. He mentioned this in the book al-Furqan. This is true, for when you reflect upon the miracles that are reported, you find them more numerous among the Successors. So the main point is that showing a person signs, whether legislated or decreed, is a blessing from Allah upon him, because it increases his faith and its firmness in the heart.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 29, verse 21–27 (part 3 of 7):

* Among the benefits of the verse: affirmation of seeing Allah. From where do we take this? From His words: ﴿and His meeting﴾. The People of the Sunnah and the Community (Ahl al-Sunnah wa'l-Jama'ah) have used this as evidence for affirming the vision, because meeting, when there is no obstacle, necessarily involves seeing, and no obstacle prevents it.
This question has much disagreement between the People of the Sunnah and the People of innovation (Ahl al-Bid'ah). The correct position, indicated by the Qur'an and the Sunnah, is affirming what? Affirming the vision of Allah, the Exalted, with the eye, and that in the Hereafter He is seen. As for Paradise, the believers see Him and others do not, because they are not in it. As for the plains of Resurrection (arasat al-qiyamah), the correct view is that the believers see Him and the hypocrites see Him as well, but the hypocrites see Him not as a vision of delight but as a true vision of remorse (ru'yat tandim). This is because Allah, glorified and exalted, manifests Himself to this Ummah, and among them are hypocrites; so He uncovers His shin for them, blessed and exalted is He, and commands them to prostrate. Whoever used to prostrate to Allah prostrates, and whoever used to prostrate only for show and reputation is unable to, and does not prostrate. But the believers see Him as a vision of honour, and these see it as a vision of remorse, because when He is veiled from them afterward, or when they are veiled from Him afterward, it becomes more painful in their souls. Likewise the hypocrites are given light on the Day of Resurrection and then it is taken from them, and this is worse than those who were never given light at all. If someone says: how do you accept this vision and believe in it, when Allah, the Majestic and Exalted, says to Moses: ﴿You will not see Me﴾ [al-A'raf 143], and says: ﴿Vision does not perceive Him, but He perceives vision﴾ [al-An'am 103]?
The answer: as for His words to Moses, ﴿You will not see Me﴾, it is a reply to Moses' words: ﴿Show me, that I may look upon You﴾ [al-A'raf 143], and he meant now. This is why He said: ﴿Look at the mountain; if it remains in its place, then you will see Me﴾ [al-A'raf 143]. This shows that the negation of seeing is at what time? At that time. This is true: Allah, the Majestic and Exalted, is not seen in this world, yes, because of man's inability to bear it. Allah set for His messenger Moses, upon him be peace, an example with the mountain: when his Lord manifested Himself to the mountain, He made it crumble and Moses fell down unconscious.
As for His words: ﴿Vision does not perceive Him﴾, it is closer to indicating the affirmation of seeing than to indicating its negation, because Allah, may His mention be exalted, did not say "He is not seen", but said: ﴿does not perceive Him﴾. Negating the more specific (al-akhass) — because perceiving (idrak) is more specific than seeing in general (mutlaq al-ru'yah) — negating the more specific does not entail negating the more general. This is a well-known principle among the scholars: negating the more specific does not necessarily negate the more general. So here we say: this indicates that He is seen, because if He were not seen He would have said: "Vision does not see Him." Since He said: ﴿does not perceive Him﴾, it is known that He is seen but not perceived. We say: ﴿Vision does not perceive Him﴾ even in the Hereafter; it is impossible to encompass Allah, Mighty and Majestic, but He is seen. Giving an example is not objectionable, but with a difference: do we not see the sun without perceiving it? We see it and do not perceive it. Indeed we see the smallest thing, the smallest animal (...) you see it with the eye, yet you do not perceive it. Do you perceive what is in its belly or in its skin that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, created? You do not perceive it.
The summary is that negating perception does not entail negating vision; rather it is evidence for the affirmation of vision. This is why the People of the Sunnah and the Community used this verse, ﴿Vision does not perceive Him﴾, as evidence for the affirmation of vision.
* A student: Shaykh, do the disbelievers see Allah on the Day of Resurrection?
* The Shaykh: No, the disbelievers do not see Him, because He says: ﴿Nay, indeed they, that Day, will be veiled from their Lord﴾ [al-Mutaffifin 15].
* The student: And His words: ﴿O man, indeed you are toiling toward your Lord with toil, and you will meet Him﴾ [al-Inshiqaq 6] (...)..
* The Shaykh: This meeting, as regards the disbeliever, the evidence shows that he does not see Him, as regards the disbeliever.
* Among the benefits of the verse: the obligation of believing in the meeting with Allah, because Allah, exalted is He, punished those who do not believe in it by despair of His mercy.
* Among its benefits: the affirmation of mercy, from His words: ﴿those have despaired of My mercy﴾. Now, the idafah here: if we say the mercy means Paradise, it is of the type of attributing a creation to its Creator, for honour and dignity; and if we say it is an attribute of Allah, it is of the type of attributing an attribute to the one it describes.
* Among the benefits of the verse: the affirmation of punishment for the disbelievers, and that it is severe punishment, from His words: ﴿and for them is a painful punishment﴾. The verses on this are very numerous, so there is no need for much discussion of them, because they are clear, praise be to Allah.
* A student: (...) a refutation of the Qadariyyah: ﴿and you cannot cause failure on earth or in heaven﴾ [al-'Ankabut 22], where its meaning is that..
* The Shaykh: Yes, there is in it a refutation of the Qadariyyah. His words: ﴿and you cannot cause failure on earth﴾ contain a refutation of the Qadariyyah who say that man is independent in his deeds, and that the will of Allah has no part in them, because if we say that, it follows that they cause Allah to be unable. And we may say that this address is weak in this respect, because they themselves acknowledge that Allah is able over them, to destroy them if they oppose, and to uproot them with punishment.
We mentioned previously that what is attributed to Allah, the Exalted, is of two kinds. Do you remember? What is attributed to Allah is of two kinds; does anyone among you recall?
* A student: We said: what is attributed to Allah (...).
* The Shaykh: Good, the entities (a'yan).
* The student: Entities: the attribution of the Creator to the created, like the House of Allah and the she-camel of Allah.
* The Shaykh: Yes.
* The student: (...).
* The Shaykh: We mentioned that what is attributed to Allah, glorified and exalted, is of two kinds: either entities or attributes. Entities are either attributed to Allah in a general sense or in a specific sense. The first, what is attributed to Allah in a general sense, is meant to indicate that Allah, glorified and exalted, is the Creator of that thing, as in His words, Exalted: ﴿And He has subjected to you whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth, all of it from Him﴾ [al-Jathiyah 13], for this includes everything in the heavens and the earth. And there is what is specific, meant for honour and dignity, like the she-camel of Allah, the House of Allah, yes, the mosques of Allah, and what is similar to that. As for what is attributed to Allah as an attribute that does not subsist in anything other than Him, it is one of the attributes of Allah, like the speech of Allah, the power of Allah, the might of Allah, and what is similar to that. And by this the People of the Sunnah have argued that the Qur'an is created or uncreated?
* Students: Uncreated.
* The Shaykh: Uncreated, because the Qur'an is an attribute that subsists in the speaker; it is speech that subsists in the one who speaks, so it is the attribution of an attribute to the one it is an attribute of. Now, it remains for us that Allah, glorified and exalted, attributed the spirit of Adam and the spirit of Jesus to Himself. Under which of the categories does it fall?
* A student: The honouring of the created by the Creator.
* The Shaykh: The created to the Creator. Now, we said: entities.
* A student: (...) there are entities, the spirit (...) when it leaves the body, sight follows it.
* The Shaykh: The spirit is an entity, not an attribute, because it is taken and wrapped in the shroud, as came in the hadith[[Narrated by Ahmad in al-Musnad (18534) from the hadith of al-Bara' ibn 'Azib.]], and it is raised up to Allah. So it is an entity, but an unknown entity, having no counterpart; it is not like the physical entities we observe. It is an entity with no counterpart in what we observe. This is why Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿They ask you about the spirit. Say: The spirit is of the command of my Lord, and you have not been given of knowledge except a little﴾ [al-Isra' 85].
* A student: Does "servant of Allah" and "maidservant of Allah" come, for example, in the specific and general sense?
* The Shaykh: It comes in both the specific and general sense. So if we say, for example, "servant of Allah" in the general servitude, it is for the general sense, and if we say "servants of the Most Merciful", for example, it is for the specific sense.
* A student: (...)?
* The Shaykh: That is, of the spirits that He created, because spirits are created by Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and it does not mean that I placed a part of myself in it. No one says this except the Incarnationists (hululiyyah) among the Christians and their like.
Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿So the answer of his people was only that they said: Kill him or burn him﴾. We have read this: ﴿only that they said: Kill him or burn him﴾. (Or): is it for choice, or for doubt, or for enumeration? For enumeration. It is for enumeration, not for choice, because Allah said in Surat al-Anbiya': ﴿They said: Burn him﴾ [al-Anbiya' 68]. This is why, perhaps you recall, we said in its grammatical analysis (i'rab) that ﴿jawab﴾ is the predicate preceding ﴿kana﴾, and ﴿an qalu﴾ is the subject of ﴿kana﴾. (...) Now we said: "or" here is for doubt; that is not possible, because the speech of Allah, glorified and exalted, is not subject to doubt, owing to the perfection of His knowledge, glorified and exalted. For choice also, contrary to the apparent meaning of the Qur'an in Surat al-Anbiya'. For enumeration, it is correct: that is, some of them said "Burn him" and some said "Kill him", and the opinion settled on burning: ﴿only that they said: Kill him or burn him﴾.
If someone says: does burning not also result in killing?
We say: yes, but it is intended to be more torturous. They, may Allah protect us, because of their rage and the intensity of what was in their breasts against Abraham, wanted him tormented by fire, upon him be peace: ﴿only that they said: Kill him or burn him﴾. Allah is Wise, Majestic and Exalted; see how affairs proceed according to His will and wisdom. Perhaps had they killed him, this great sign would not have occurred, namely that the fire becomes coolness and peace for him; but Allah, Mighty and Majestic, is Wise. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿So Allah saved him from the fire﴾. The verse contains an ellipsis; the estimate is: they burned him, and Allah saved him from the fire. ﴿from the fire﴾ (into which they threw him, by making it for him coolness and peace).
* A student: (...)?
* The Shaykh: Indeed, yes, but ﴿So Allah saved him﴾ prevents this. The reality is that they gathered firewood and threw him into the fire, on the basis that they burned him. Now we say: "So Allah saved him from the fire into which they threw him, by making it coolness and peace for him by His command", because Allah said: ﴿O fire, be coolness and peace﴾ [al-Anbiya' 69], and it was coolness and peace. The scholars said: if Allah, Majestic and Exalted, had said only "coolness", it would have been ice upon him; but He said "and peace", so that he would be safe.
And in it: cold kills just as heat kills, and had cold not been able to kill, there would have been no need for His words "and peace."
Now (﴿Indeed in that﴾, i.e. his being saved from it, ﴿are signs﴾). ﴿Indeed in that are signs﴾. It is known that (inna) puts the subject in the accusative and the predicate in the nominative; where is its subject?
* A student: ﴿signs﴾.
* The Shaykh: ﴿signs﴾, and the lam is for emphasis. And "signs (ayat)": how do we say (inna) governs the accusative when it is kasra now? But it...
* A student: (...).
* The Shaykh:
........................... ∗∗∗ it takes kasra in the genitive and the accusative alike
He said: ﴿Indeed in that are signs﴾. "Signs" is the plural of "ayah", which means a sign. Is the context here cosmic signs or legislative ones?
Cosmic. As for its plural, the author explained it, saying: it is their not affecting him despite its greatness, its extinguishing, and the creation of a garden in its place within a short time. Thus the author explained the signs as:
First: that it did not affect him despite its greatness, because they gathered a great quantity of firewood and kindled a great fire, to the extent that it is mentioned they could not approach it, and they threw him with a catapult, a throw from afar, yes, and Allah knows best; in any case, it was certainly a great fire.
(Its extinguishing): that is, that it cooled and calmed from its flame in an instant; this is one of the signs of Allah, Mighty and Majestic.
Third: he said it was a garden, but it is enough that it was coolness and peace, that it was coolness and peace upon Abraham.
And in my view the signs are more than what the author mentioned:
Among the signs is the frustration of their scheme.
Among them: Abraham's patience and endurance, because the reality of the matter is that no one can bear this except the likes of Abraham among the steadfast messengers (ulu al-'azm).
Among them also: the reversal of this heat into coldness.
Among them: the reversal of what was a cause of destruction into peace upon him.
* A student: (...) it did not extinguish; rather it was coolness and peace for him. It was a flame and yet coolness, until it was extinguished afterward, while they saw that he had perished?
* The Shaykh: Yes indeed. Allah knows; we do not know whether it went out or remained, and the apparent meaning also is that it remained, because He said: ﴿O fire, be coolness and peace﴾. Allah, exalted is He, did not command it to go out, but said: ﴿be coolness and peace﴾. On this basis, there is room for scrutiny in the author's statement, and the correct view is that it remained as it was, yet it was coolness and peace upon Abraham.
* A student: So this is more evident in the miracle?
* The Shaykh: We said: its remaining is more evident in the miracle.
* A student: The view that from its goodness to him it had a flame (...)?
* The Shaykh: It had a flame?
* The student: From its goodness, I mean.
* The Shaykh: Yes, whoever saw it saw it blazing, or (...).
* The student: (...).
* The Shaykh: The verse remains as it is.
* The student: Because there is a benefit in it?
* The Shaykh: There is no (...) Israelite narrations in it, but the obligation is to take the apparent meaning of the Qur'an.
﴿Indeed in that are signs for a people who believe﴾ [al-'Ankabut 24] (who affirm the oneness and power of Allah, because they are the ones who benefit from them). These signs Allah restricted by saying ﴿for a people who believe﴾, excluding the people who do not believe; even if the signs are before them, they do not benefit from them, so for them there are no signs. This is why Allah said: ﴿And signs and warnings avail not a people who do not believe﴾ [Yunus 101]. Do you know of anything in speech more magnificent as a sign than the speech of Allah? No, we do not know of any; and that is the reality. Yet whoever is not a believer, when the Qur'an is recited to him, says: "tales of the ancients", as Allah said: ﴿When Our signs are recited to him, he says: tales of the ancients﴾ [al-Qalam 15]. Therefore, if you see in yourself that you are not affected by the Qur'an, then accuse yourself; accuse it, because Allah did not say of anyone: "he does not benefit from the Qur'an" except of the deniers who see nothing in the Qur'an; that is, it does not seize their hearts and their awe. This matter is one we ask Allah to save us and you from, because many people read this Qur'an yet it does not stir their feelings, and this is very dangerous for a person. A person must accuse himself of this matter until he corrects what has deviated in him and straightens what is crooked.
On this basis we say: the cosmic and legislative signs benefit only the believer. The non-believer does not benefit, may Allah protect us, because they pass over him as though, if they are cosmic signs, they were a routine matter, or by the necessity of nature. As for the earthquakes that strike people, what do they say? They say: these are ordinary volcanoes. Indeed, they are nothing. And the violent winds that destroy crops and trees, and likewise the overwhelming floods, all of these they say are natural phenomena, as if they were not a punishment from Allah, Mighty and Majestic. So have they benefited from them or not? No. Even now people have begun with eclipses, saying: these are apparent causes, and we ask Allah for safety. They publish them before they occur so that they reach people when they are reassured by them and they settle in their souls, so they neither terrify nor frighten them. The Prophet, upon him be peace, said: "Allah frightens His servants with them" [Abu Dawud (1185), and al-Bayhaqi in al-Sunan al-Kubra (6338), from the hadith of Qabisah al-Hilali, and the wording is his]. And these people have made them like the new moon of a festival, to the point that some of them addressed us with this, saying: we inform people so that they prepare and await it, so that when the eclipse comes they are ready, as if it were the crescent of Eid coming out so that they go to the prayer-ground. This is an error. I recall, and perhaps some of you who are advanced in years recall, how people, when an eclipse came, would experience fear, alarm and dread, as the Prophet, upon him be peace, commanded: they would go to the mosques and weep. Now, may Allah grant us well-being, as you see, perhaps some people when an eclipse occurs watch it with an instrument of amusement that sings and the like. The point is that these signs benefit only the believer.
* * *

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 29, verse 21–27 (part 4 of 7):

(﴿And Abraham said﴾: ﴿You have only taken, other than Allah, idols﴾ [al-'Ankabut 25], which you worship, and (mā) is a verbal-noun particle (mā maṣdariyyah), ﴿affection among you﴾ is the predicate of inna, and on the reading with the accusative it is an object of purpose (maf'ul lahu), and (mā) is a restrictive particle (mā kāffah), the meaning being: you have befriended one another through its worship.) The author, may Allah have mercy on him, has now made clear to us that His saying ﴿mawaddata﴾ has two canonical readings, or not? Two canonical readings: the reading with the nominative. We are now parsing the verse before we speak about its meaning. The reading with the nominative: ﴿Indeed, you have only taken, other than Allah, idols, affection among you﴾. On the reading with the nominative, the author parsed (mā) as a verbal-noun particle (mā maṣdariyyah), neither restrictive nor relative. The estimate according to his view: indeed your taking, other than Allah, of idols is affection among you. So the verbal noun formed from (mā) is the subject of (inna), and (mawaddatu) is the predicate of (inna), and (you have taken idols) ... we will complete the parsing of (inna) and what relates to it. On the reading with the accusative, he says it is an object of purpose. What is an object of purpose?

* Student: Maf'ul li-ajlihi (object of purpose).

* The Shaykh: They call it maf'ul li-ajlihi, meaning: you have only taken idols, other than Allah, for the sake of affection among you. Yes. But on this reading (mā) is restrictive (kāffah), so it enters upon (inna), and restrictive (mā) when it enters upon (inna) conveys exclusivity, meaning: you took the idols only for the sake of affection among you. Have you now grasped the meaning?

* Student: Yes.

* The Shaykh: On the first opinion we say: (mā), according to the author's view of course, is a verbal-noun particle, and (you have taken) is a verb converted into a verbal noun, and the estimate is: indeed your taking, other than Allah, of idols is affection among you, the predicate of (inna). On the reading with the accusative we say: (innamā) is an exclusive particle, and (mawaddatan) is an object of purpose, meaning you took it for the sake of affection. Yes, this is what the author said.

It is also said: (mā) on the reading with the nominative is a relative pronoun (ism mawṣūl), (inna) is followed by a relative pronoun, and the returning pronoun (al-'a'id) is omitted, and the estimate is: indeed that which you have taken other than Allah as idols is affection among you. On this estimate, the object of (ittakhadha) is omitted as its first object, and its second object is (awthanan). On this view we say: (inna) is a particle of emphasis that puts the subject in the accusative and the predicate in the nominative, (mā) is its subject meaning "that which," (ittakhadhtum) is the relative clause, the returning pronoun is omitted, and the estimate is: you have taken it. (Awthanan) is the second object of (ittakhadha), because ittakhadha takes two objects, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And Allah took Abraham as a intimate friend﴾ [al-Nisa' 125].

* Student: Clear (...).

* The Shaykh: Yes, clear. That is, that which you have taken as idols is the affection among you. Yes, and this estimate, that it is a relative pronoun, is also valid on the reading with the accusative: indeed that which you have taken as idols, for the sake of affection among you, does not benefit you. And the predicate on the reading with the accusative is omitted, the estimate being: does not benefit you.

Now let us return to (ittakhadha) taking two objects on the estimate that (mā) is relative. Where is its first object? It is omitted: you have taken it, which refers back to (mā), and (awthanan) is the second object. And on the view that (mā) is verbal-noun or restrictive, we say that the second object is also omitted, and the estimate is: gods, as in His saying: ﴿offerings, gods﴾ [al-Ahqaf 28]. The meaning: they took these idols as gods, with affection among them.

* Student: (...)?

* The Shaykh: (...) as a second object. No, it apparently is a circumstantial clause (hal) from awthan, because it came before it.

* Student: Affection (...)?

* The Shaykh: No, it is not suitable, because it is clearly for causation, meaning they took it for the sake of affection. For they gathered on this so that they would not scatter, and they said: we shall support the gods by seeking affection among us, so that these gods unite us in affection.

* * *

His saying: ﴿But their answer was only that they said: Kill him or burn him﴾ and so on to the end.

* Among its benefits: a demonstration of the tyranny of his people, since he guides them to the truth, and this is their response.

* Among its benefits: they disagreed about what to do with him, then they resolved that they would burn him, based on combining this verse with the verse of the Prophets: ﴿Burn him and support your gods﴾ [al-Anbiya' 68].

* Among its benefits: the complete power of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, since this burning fire became coolness and peace upon him, and this is one of the signs of Allah indicating His power.

* Among them: that whoever stands for Allah, Allah, Exalted, will save him by His refuge, meaning He saves him in the place of his destruction. Allah, Exalted, said: ﴿And Allah will deliver those who feared Him by their salvation﴾ [al-Zumar 61].

* Among its benefits also: that Allah, Glorified and Exalted, decrees for the deliverance of His friends matters beyond what occurs to the mind, for whoever imagines that this great fire would become coolness and peace, but Allah, Glorified and Exalted, decrees for His friends means of salvation that do not occur to them.

* Among the benefits of this verse: the knowledge of inanimate things of Allah, since inanimate things know their Lord and obey His command, for Allah said to this fire: ﴿O fire, be coolness and peace﴾ [al-Anbiya' 69]. (...) It benefits only the believers. From where is this derived? From His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed in that are signs for a people who believe﴾ [al-'Ankabut 24]. Is it clear? This does not contradict what came in several verses: ﴿Indeed in that are signs for a people who reason﴾ [al-Ra'd 4] and ﴿signs for a people who reflect﴾ [al-Ra'd 3], and the like, because reason, reflection and the like are requirements of faith, and whenever a person is stronger in faith he is more rational and reflective, and reflection also calls to faith, so they are mutually implicated.

* Student: Has this been established regarding deliverance from the Fire for any of the Companions (...)?

* The Shaykh: Yes, they mentioned that it has been established. Ibn Kathir, may Allah have mercy on him, mentioned this in al-Bidaya wa al-Nihaya, and said: there is no sign given to a previous prophet except that it was a sign for the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, or greater. But some of them occurred to the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, himself, and some occurred to his community, and what occurred to his community is also among his signs, since it attests to the soundness of the path they follow, so that is among the signs of the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him.

* Student: It is a refutation of the Jabriyyah, from His saying: ﴿Kill him or burn him﴾ [al-'Ankabut 24], where the action is attributed to them.

* The Shaykh: What do you say? Can we take from this a refutation of the Jabriyyah?

* Student: (...) blown by the wind, having no will and no act at all?

* The Shaykh: Yes, but they say that he kills, that a person kills, acts and does, but he is compelled to it. Unless it is said, for example, that his being a chooser (mukhayyar) in some respects, does this indicate this?

Also, after the second benefit (...), which is that causes do not produce their effect except by the will of Allah, and this is important. Causes, however strong they are, do not produce the effect except by the permission of Allah, meaning that Allah, Exalted, may prevent their influence. Fire is undoubtedly a cause of burning, yet here this causation was removed and it had no effect.

Now, ﴿He said: You have only taken, other than Allah, idols﴾ [al-'Ankabut 25], meaning that what you have taken as idols is something only affection unites you upon, and therefore the author said: (the meaning: you befriended one another through its worship), because, may Allah protect us, the people of evil befriend one another in doing evil, just as the people of good also support one another in doing good, so likewise the people of evil.

His saying: ﴿affection among you﴾ here: the word (bayn) may be read with what precedes it as an annexed construction, and it may be cut off from the annexation, so it is permissible outside the Qur'an to say (mawaddatan baynakum) and (mawaddata baynikum), and here it is in this latter form.

His saying: ﴿in the life of this world﴾ is connected to what precedes it, meaning that it is affection in the life of this world only. These polytheists befriend one another in shirk in this world only; you find them supporting and helping one another. But ﴿then on the Day of Resurrection some of you will disavow others and some of you will curse others﴾.

﴿Some of you will disavow others﴾ means deny it, as in His saying: ﴿When those who were followed disown those who followed﴾ [al-Baqarah 166], and this is undoubtedly denial and disbelief of some toward others.

﴿and some of you will curse others﴾ like His saying: ﴿And they will say: Our Lord, indeed we obeyed our masters and our elders, and they misled us from the way. Our Lord, give them double the punishment and curse them with a great curse﴾ [al-Ahzab 67–68], and the disputing of followers with leaders occurs in several verses of the Qur'an, not only in the verse of al-Baqarah. There is: ﴿Those who were arrogant said﴾ [al-A'raf 76], ﴿And those who were oppressed said﴾ [Saba' 33], and the like.

* Student: ﴿Whenever a nation enters, it curses its sister﴾ [al-A'raf 38].

* The Shaykh: And ﴿Whenever a nation enters, it curses its sister﴾. The sum is that this affection among the polytheists is only in this world. As for the Day of Resurrection, each of them disowns the other, denies him, and curses him too, and this is undoubtedly among the severest punishments. But the God-fearing, their friendship remains until the Day of Resurrection: ﴿The intimate friends that day will be enemies to one another, except the righteous﴾ [al-Zukhruf 67]. As for these, the affection between them ends with death.

He said: (﴿some of you will disavow others﴾ by the leaders disowning the followers, ﴿and some of you will curse others﴾ by the followers cursing the leaders), and the verse is general: the leaders disown the followers, and the followers disown the leaders, and likewise some of them curse others.

He said: ﴿And your refuge is the Fire﴾: ﴿your refuge﴾ (your final destination, all of you), so "refuge" means "destination," since it derives from awā yāwī, meaning he proceeded toward a thing and turned toward it.

﴿And your refuge is the Fire, and you will have no helpers﴾. This Fire Allah, Glorified and Exalted, has prepared for the disbelievers, and it now exists. The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, saw it on the night he was taken on the Night Journey. It is a fire whose torment a person cannot grasp in this world, for it has been given a superiority over the fire of this world by sixty-nine parts. I say: this Fire has been given a superiority over the fire of this world by sixty-nine parts; add to it the part that completes seventy. The Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "Upon your fire this" [agreed upon; al-Bukhari (3265), Muslim (2843/30), from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, in similar wording], or "upon the fire of this world." The fire of this world, as you know, includes a fire of extreme heat, a fire of moderate heat, and a fire that is cold compared to others, yet even so, it is measured against the highest fire of this world, and thus is given a superiority of sixty-nine parts over it.

(﴿And you will have no helpers﴾, preventing you from it.) ﴿You will have no helpers﴾: here the particle (min) is extra, for emphasis, since ﴿helpers﴾ originally is a subject whose predicate is His saying ﴿for you﴾. Meaning, no one will help you so as to prevent you from entering the Fire. Whose speech is this?

* Student: The speech of Allah.

* The Shaykh: No, this is the speech of Abraham, because he said: ﴿Then on the Day of Resurrection some of you will disavow others and some of you will curse others, and your refuge is the Fire, and you will have no helpers﴾ [al-'Ankabut 25]. This is from the speech of Abraham, peace be upon him.

* * *

Allah, Exalted, said: (﴿So Lot believed him﴾, that is, he affirmed Abraham, ﴿Lot﴾, and he was the son of his brother Haran, ﴿And [Abraham] said﴾, Abraham) to the end.

﴿So Lot believed him﴾. Faith (al-iman) linguistically means affirmation, but it is not mere affirmation; rather it is affirmation with tranquility, since the root of āmana is the root of security (amn), meaning it contains the hamza, the mim and the nun. On this basis faith is not mere affirmation, but a particular affirmation accompanied by, or including, tranquility in the matter. It takes the preposition lam as in this verse, and as in His saying: ﴿Have you believed him?﴾ [Ta-Ha 71], and likewise ﴿But you would not believe us﴾ [Yusuf 17] and several verses of this kind. It also takes the preposition ba', which is common: ﴿The Messenger believes in what was sent down to him﴾ [al-Baqarah 285], ﴿We have believed in Allah﴾ [al-'Ankabut 10], and the like. So is this a matter of synonymy, that lam means ba' and ba' means lam? Or is there a difference between them?

One may say that it is synonymy, and each of them, lam and ba', comes in the place of the other due to the frequent use of each. One may also say that they differ: lam indicates submission, while ba' indicates tranquility of the heart. So lam is for submission: ﴿So Lot believed him﴾ [al-'Ankabut 26], which implies the meaning of "yielded to," whereas ba' indicates tranquility of the heart; "āmana bihi" means he was at peace with it. Allah, Glorified and Exalted, distinguished between them in the Noble Qur'an, as in His saying: ﴿He believes in Allah and believes for the believers﴾ [al-Tawbah 61], in a single verse: ﴿believes in Allah and believes for the believers.﴾ The apparent meaning, and Allah knows best, from their occurrences in the Qur'an is that they are not synonymous and that there is a difference between them: whatever requires tranquility, or contains the meaning of tranquility, takes ba'; whatever implies the meaning of submission, even outwardly, takes lam. Pharaoh said to the sorcerers once: ﴿Have you believed him?﴾ [Ta-Ha 71], and said another time: ﴿Have you believed in him?﴾ [al-A'raf 123]. Do the two statements have the same meaning? No, based on what we have said: ﴿you believed in him﴾ means you affirmed him with tranquility and your hearts were at peace with his truthfulness, and ﴿you believed him﴾ [Ta-Ha 71] means you followed him and submitted to him. This is why he said to them: ﴿Indeed he is your chief who taught you magic﴾ [Ta-Ha 71]. So each verse is interpreted according to its meaning. Here He said: ﴿So Lot believed him﴾ [al-'Ankabut 26]. We know that Lot, peace be upon him, believed in Abraham and in him: he believed him and in him, so he believed in him with his heart and was at peace with his truthfulness, and likewise submitted to him, so faith here includes the meaning of submission and the meaning of tranquility.

* Student: Here it is said: when the two are combined they differ in meaning, and when one is used alone it conveys what the other conveys?

* The Shaykh: This does not appear; this does not appear, because in reality whenever you trace the lam, you find it in matters that do not require tranquility as a perfection; you never find "āmantu li-llah" (I believed for Allah).

* Student: Pharaoh said: ﴿You believed him before I gave you permission. Indeed he is your chief who taught you magic﴾ [Ta-Ha 71], the same wording as the other verse, he said to them...

* The Shaykh: Yes, so its meaning is that he affirmed that they were at peace with him and submitted to him. If we take the two verses together, the meaning is that he affirmed they acknowledged him and his truthfulness, and also submitted to him through his magic. This is why "āmantu li-llah" (I believed for Allah) does not occur, but "aslamtu li-llah" (I submitted to Allah) does occur in the Mighty Qur'an.

He said: ﴿So Lot believed him﴾ [al-'Ankabut 26]. The author's saying: (affirmed Abraham) shows that he holds that lam means ba'.

So when we say: the author, may Allah have mercy on him, holds that ﴿believed him﴾ means "believed in him," look at what he said: (affirmed) is the explanation of (believed), (Abraham) is the explanation of (him), (﴿Lot﴾, and he was the son of his brother Haran). That is, Abraham had a brother named Haran, son of Azar, and Haran had a son named Lot.

(﴿And [Abraham] said﴾: ﴿Indeed I am emigrating﴾ from my people ﴿to my Lord﴾, that is, to where my Lord commanded me, and he emigrated from his people, and he emigrated from the land of Iraq to al-Sham.)

His saying: ﴿And [he] said﴾: the author says the pronoun refers to Abraham, and accordingly, in recitation, you pause at ﴿So Lot believed him﴾ and do not continue with ﴿and said: Indeed I am emigrating﴾, because if you connected it you would give the impression that the speech is from Lot. Some scholars said the pronoun refers to Lot, based on the apparent context, and that Lot, peace be upon him, believed and emigrated, combining faith and emigration.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 29, verse 21–27 (part 5 of 7):

His saying: ﴿Indeed I am a emigrant (muhājir) to my Lord﴾. Here, muhājir is on the pattern of mufā'il (mufā'ala) in the Arabic language, which may denote an action shared by two or more parties, as when one says "muqātil" (fighter), and may denote an action with only one party, as when one says "musāfir" (traveller). Do you understand? The word muhājir: which of these is it? Is it something shared between two parties, or something specific to one party?
* Student: Specific.
* The Shaykh: That is, hājara in the sense of hajara (to abandon), or does hājara mean that he abandoned them and they abandoned him? Or is there the possibility that the meaning is "muhājir" in that I abandoned them and they abandoned me by my separation from them? And it may be that it belongs to the category of what has only one party, like musāfir.
* Student: (...) from the context, it is clarified by Ibrahim's words ﴿And We gave him Isaac and Jacob﴾ [al-'Ankabut 27]...
* The Shaykh: We will attach this later, God willing...
* The student: (...) here he attributed it to his Lord (...)?
* The Shaykh: That it is one-sided? Perhaps the apparent meaning supports it.
And his saying: (from my people ﴿to my Lord﴾). The author said: (to where He commanded me). That is, to the direction in which God, glorified and exalted, commanded me to travel. This is what he explained it by. Strangely, some commentators said: the author said "to where He commanded me" in order to flee from affirming a direction for God, fleeing from affirming a direction; because if we took the apparent meaning of the verse ﴿to my Lord﴾ it would be directed toward God Himself. Yes, and they hold that God, exalted is He, is not in a direction. Whose view is this?
* Student: The Ash'aris.
* The Shaykh: Yes, the view of the Ash'aris, and likewise the Jahmiyya who negate (ta'til). The Jahmiyya divided on the question of direction into two groups: one group is the incarnationist (hulūliyya), who hold that God, glorified and exalted, is in His essence in every place, and these were the earlier ones among them; and another group is those of pure negation (ta'til), who hold that God, glorified and exalted, is not in a place and not in a direction, so they say: neither inside the world nor outside it, neither connected to the world nor separate from it, neither distinct nor... We ask God for well-being. This direction is used by those who deny the exaltedness of God, the Mighty and Majestic, in His essence. They say: because if you say that God is exalted in His essence upon His Throne, it necessarily follows that He is in a direction, and if He is in a direction, it necessarily follows that He is confined, and what is confined is limited. Glory be to God! I do not know where they got these premises and conclusions. We say to them: we do not deny the matter of direction in meaning, but we deny a direction that confines God, the Mighty and Majestic, or encompasses Him; because God, exalted is He, encompasses all things. But we affirm that He has a direction, which is height (al-'uluw). So the directions are three: the direction of below, the direction of height that encompasses God, and the direction of height that does not encompass Him. Which of these is affirmed? The direction of height that does not encompass Him. As for the direction of below, it is impossible; and as for the direction of height that encompasses Him, it is also impossible, because there is nothing above God, glorified and exalted.
So how do we interpret ﴿to my Lord﴾ according to the correct view? The preferred view is that ﴿to my Lord﴾ means to my religion, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Certainly God will support whoever supports Him﴾ [al-Hajj 40], that is, whoever supports His religion. And the person who emigrates to the religion of God seeks the place in which he can establish his religion. For this reason the scholars say about hijra that it is the movement from where?
* Students: From a land of polytheism to faith.
* The Shaykh: From a land of polytheism to a land of Islam, where the religion of God, the Mighty and Majestic, is established.
And his saying: ﴿emigrant to my Lord﴾: (to) denotes the endpoint, and in it is an indication of the goodness of his intention and purpose. The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "Whoever's emigration was to God and His Messenger, his emigration is to God and His Messenger, and whoever's emigration was for worldly gain he would obtain or a woman he would marry, his emigration is to that for which he emigrated."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (54), and Muslim (1907 / 155) from the hadith of 'Umar ibn al-Khattab.]] The author said: (and he abandoned his people and emigrated from Sawad al-'Iraq to al-Sham). What is Sawad al-'Iraq? Iraq itself, the land of Iraq; it was called sawad (blackness) for the abundance of its palm trees and plants. And his saying: (to al-Sham) is well known.
* Student: (...)?
* The Shaykh: Yes, this is not entirely identical, because Sawad al-'Iraq..
* The student: It is Iraq.
* The Shaykh: But it has the blackness, Sawad al-'Iraq.
He said: (﴿Indeed He is the Mighty﴾ in His kingdom ﴿the Wise﴾ in His creation). The author, may God have mercy on him, proceeds in this manner in explaining these two names, saying: (﴿the Mighty﴾ in His kingdom, ﴿the Wise﴾ in His creation), and this contains some deficiency. He, glorified and exalted, is Mighty in His essence and in His attributes, and His might is of three types: the might of rank (izzat al-qadr), the might of subjugation (izzat al-qahr), and the might of inaccessibility (izzat al-imtina').
As for the might of inaccessibility, its meaning is that it is impossible for any deficiency to reach Him, glorified and exalted, in all His attributes and acts. As for the might of rank, it is station, majesty and greatness. As for the might of subjugation, it is strength and authority.
So no one overcomes Him, is that right or not? He is the Overcoming, and for this reason many scholars explained it as "the Overcoming." Likewise, no one can harm Him, and likewise no deficiency reaches His attributes. So the might is of three types, and these are?
* Student: Subjugation, rank, and inaccessibility.
* The Shaykh: What?
* Student: Might of subjugation and might of power..
* The Shaykh: Rank.
* The student: Rank, might, and inaccessibility.
* The Shaykh: Inaccessibility, good. The root of this word indicates strength; the root ʿ-z-z indicates strength, and from it the saying for hard ground: ard ʿazzāz, ʿazzāz meaning strong and hard.
And his saying: (﴿the Wise﴾ in His creation) contains deficiency, because the wisdom of God, the Mighty and Majestic, is not restricted to His creation alone, but is in His creation and His legislation. He is Wise in what He created, Wise in what He legislated. And "al-Hakim" is not only from ḥikma (wisdom) alone, because al-Hakim is from ḥikma, meaning the one who perfects, but it is also from ḥukm (judgment) and from ḥukm also. The pattern faʿīl, as you know in the active participle, comes in the sense of the agent for emphasis, or not? Is it not so?
Among the patterns of emphasis: faʿʿāl, or mifʿāl, or faʿūl. Then he said after them: faʿīl and faʿil are five. So it is faʿīl from ḥakama, so he is ḥākim, but it became in the sense of ḥakīm for emphasis, or because it is an attributive adjective (ṣifa mushabbaha). So it is from ḥukm, and the judgment of God, the Mighty and Majestic, divides into two parts, which are the cosmic (kawnī) and the legislative (sharʿī). So God's judgment is of two kinds: cosmic and legislative. An example of the cosmic is the saying of the brother of Yusuf: ﴿I will not leave this land until my father permits me or God judges for me﴾ [Yusuf 80]. What is this? This is cosmic, and for this reason he did not say "judge against me"; he said "judge for me," meaning decree for me. And the legislative judgment is like His saying in Surat al-Mumtahana: ﴿That is the judgment of God; He judges between you﴾ [al-Mumtahana 10]. As for ﴿He does what He wills﴾ [al-Ma'ida 1], it encompasses both matters. Where did you find ﴿He does what He wills﴾ [al-Ma'ida 1], in which surah?
* Student: At the beginning of Surat al-Ma'ida.
* The Shaykh: At the beginning of Surat al-Ma'ida, yes. So we say, my brothers: al-Hakim is derived from ḥukm and ḥikma, and ḥukm is judgment, and it is of two kinds: cosmic and legislative. The example of the cosmic is ﴿I will not leave this land until my father permits me or God judges for me﴾; the example of the legislative is ﴿That is the judgment of God; He judges between you﴾ [al-Mumtahana 10]; and the example of what combines both is ﴿Indeed God does what He wills﴾ [al-Ma'ida 1]. Good. Wisdom exists in the legislation and exists in the decree, and it is derived from where? From iḥkām, meaning perfection. It exists in the legislation, meaning that everything God legislated is in accordance with wisdom; and it exists in the decree, meaning that everything God decreed is for a wisdom. ﴿Corruption has appeared on land and sea by what the hands of people have earned﴾ [al-Rum 41]. Is corruption, in itself as corruption, a wisdom or not? No, in itself as corruption it is not a wisdom, because God does not love corruption. So it is not wisdom, but for the end for which it becomes wisdom: ﴿Corruption has appeared on land and sea by what the hands of people have earned, that He may let them taste part of what they have done, so that they may return﴾. That is the wisdom.
So is it very clear to everyone that the existence of good things is a wisdom, or not? That is, the existence of what contains good for the servants has an evident wisdom; the existence of what contains evil for the servants cannot occur from God, the Mighty and Majestic, except for a wisdom. For this reason the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "And evil is not attributed to You." [[Narrated by Muslim (771 / 201) from the hadith of 'Ali ibn Abi Talib.]] He did not say "it is not from You"; so it is not attributed to God, but everything that occurs, good and evil, is what He decreed. However, God, the Mighty and Majestic, decrees evil only for a greater benefit, and when it is for a greater benefit it becomes wisdom, does it not? It becomes wisdom. You find a person who is the most merciful of creatures toward his son bringing him to the doctor to cut his skin, so his blood flows; this is an evil, because it hurts the boy, but it is for his benefit, so the outcome is praiseworthy. And he brings him to the doctor and says: heat this iron on the fire and cauterize him with it. Cauterization is an evil in itself, but its end is praiseworthy. Likewise in circumcision, he brings him to the circumciser and says: take, cut the skin of my son's penis, yes, a sensitive place, and it is cut from his skin, but the outcome is praiseworthy.
The point is: evil may be good in view of what it leads to, even if it is evil in itself. Now, my brothers, the meaning of al-Hakim has become derived from where? From judgment and wisdom, or from iḥkām, and iḥkām means wisdom. Wisdom exists in the legislation and exists in the decree. In the decree, everything God decreed is for a wisdom, whether it is good or evil. Also in the legislation, everything God legislated is for a wisdom. God, the Mighty and Majestic, legislated for the married adulterer that he be stoned with what? With stones. If he were killed by the sword, would it be easier or not? Easier. But that he be stoned with stones and be publicly disgraced and this be announced is for a great wisdom, which is to deter others from committing this forbidden act; and furthermore, because this body that took pleasure entirely in the forbidden thing should receive the pain of punishment. Yes.
* Student: On the assumption: "I am an emigrant to my Lord": to the religion of my Lord. I say: is not the religion of his Lord present in every place? Does he go to people who call upon God?
* The Shaykh: No, it is not present in every place; if it were present in every place he would not have left his place, because these people of his denied him and rejected him and wanted to burn him.
* Student: That is, he emigrated with him, no, he emigrated to his religion.
* The Shaykh: To his religion, to a place where the religion of God is present. And for this reason, for example, Madinah became the abode of hijra when religion was established in it.
* Student: That is, he emigrated to a people who worship God.
* The Shaykh: Yes, to the religion of God which...
* Student: (...) there is no believer on earth except me..
* The Shaykh: Yes, where was he when he said this? In Egypt, not in al-Sham. He said it in Egypt, and it is correct. As for his saying "on earth," the correct view is that it does not mean the entire earth; the correct view is that it means the land of Egypt.
* Student: Ibrahim's wife (...)?
* The Shaykh: Yes, she was a believer.
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: Yes.
* * *
He said: (﴿And We gave him﴾ [al-'Ankabut 27] after Isma'il ﴿Isaac and Jacob﴾). Hiba (gift) means giving without reward or without return, and everything God bestows upon His servants is a favour from Him without return. (﴿Isaac and Jacob﴾ after Isaac). God made Ya'qub a gift to Ibrahim only because he was the son of his son; and it will come to us, God willing, in the benefits that this is evidence that the grandfather is a father, because God made the son of the son a gift to his grandfather.
﴿And We placed in his offspring prophethood and the Scripture﴾. Offspring of whom?
* Student: Ibrahim.
* The Shaykh: Ibrahim. Here the pronoun departed from the rule: it returned to the first mentioned noun. The general rule is that a pronoun refers to the nearest mentioned noun, but it may depart from this rule according to context, as in His saying: ﴿And He has not placed upon you in religion any hardship; the creed of your father Ibrahim. He named you "Muslims" before and in this﴾ [al-Hajj 78]; "He" refers to whom? To God, not to Ibrahim, although Ibrahim is the nearest mentioned noun.
And His saying: ﴿And We placed in his offspring prophethood﴾: He fronted the prepositional phrase and the adverbial, over the thing placed in it, namely prophethood and the Scripture; this is an indication of restriction (hasr). For this reason the scholars said: there is no prophet after Ibrahim except that he is from the offspring of Ibrahim. Ibrahim, peace and blessings be upon him, is given the kunya Abu al-Anbiya' (father of the prophets).
(﴿And We placed in his offspring prophethood﴾: so all the prophets after Ibrahim are from his offspring. ﴿And the Scripture﴾ meaning the scriptures) — it is singular but intended as a genus (i.e., the Torah, the Gospel, the Psalms and the Furqan). The Torah was revealed to Musa, the Gospel to 'Isa, the Psalms to Dawud, and the Furqan to Muhammad ﷺ.
(﴿And We gave him his reward in this world﴾ — which is good praise among all the people of religions — ﴿and indeed he is in the Hereafter among the righteous﴾). ﴿Atayna-hu﴾ means "We gave him," so it takes two objects: one is the pronoun hu in ﴿atayna-hu﴾, and the second is ﴿ajrahu﴾.
And his saying: ﴿his reward in this world﴾. Ajr means compensation; the compensation for a thing is called ajr, and from it ujra (wage) for the worker for his work.
And his saying: ﴿his reward in this world﴾. What is his reward in this world?
Shall we say that the author did not say "good praise among all religions," or is it more general than that? The correct view is that it is more general than that: from the coolness of his eye through his children, their spread and their multitude; and likewise good praise, as all religions claim to belong to him and want him to be from them. For this reason God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Ibrahim was neither a Jew,﴾ as the Jews claimed, ﴿nor a Christian,﴾ as the Christians claimed, ﴿but he was a hanif, a Muslim, and he was not of the polytheists﴾ [Al 'Imran 67]. Then God judged between the groups, saying: ﴿Indeed, the most worthy of Ibrahim are those who followed him, and this Prophet﴾ Muhammad ﷺ ﴿and those who believe; and God is the Ally of the believers﴾ [Al 'Imran 68].
And his saying: ﴿And We gave him his reward in this world, and indeed he is in the Hereafter among the righteous﴾. The lam in ﴿among the righteous﴾ is for emphasis, so the sentence is emphasized with inna and the lam.
And his saying: (﴿the righteous﴾, meaning those who have the high ranks), and what is meant here is the highest kinds of the righteous, who are the prophets or messengers, because Ibrahim, peace be upon him, is among the five possessors of resolve (ulu al-'azm), who are Muhammad ﷺ, Ibrahim, peace be upon him, Musa, 'Isa and Nuh.
And his saying: ﴿among the righteous﴾: when "the righteous" comes alone, it includes all four categories: the prophets, the truthful (siddiqun), the martyrs (shuhada') and the righteous (salihun), and God knows best.
* Student: Shaykh (...).
* The Shaykh: Why?
* The student: Because it is more eloquent (...).
* * *
* The Shaykh: First: that idols do not benefit their worshippers.
* And among its benefits also: that the most that obtains for them from these idols is mutual affection among them in this worldly life, upon falsehood.
* And among its benefits also: that people of falsehood may develop mutual affection to protect their falsehood and to prevail over the truth, but this does not last.
* From the benefits of the verse: that those who gathered upon falsehood, when the Day of Resurrection comes, some of them disown others and curse one another; because of His saying: ﴿Then on the Day of Resurrection some of you will disbelieve in others﴾.
* And among its benefits: affirmation of the Resurrection, because of His saying: ﴿Then on the Day of Resurrection some of you will disbelieve in others﴾. The Day of Resurrection was named, as we mentioned earlier, and I forgot to mention it in our last sessions: it was named the Day of Resurrection for three reasons:
* First: that people rise on it from their graves to the Lord of the worlds.
* Second: that the witnesses stand on it, as God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And on the day the witnesses stand﴾ [Ghafir 51].
* Third: that justice is established on it: ﴿And We shall set up the just balances for the Day of Resurrection﴾ [al-Anbiya' 47].
* Student: The witnesses, Shaykh (...).
* The Shaykh: The witnesses are those who testify for the messengers that they delivered, and against the nations that they were conveyed to; and likewise the limbs testify against a person for what he did.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 29, verse 21–27 (part 6 of 7):

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the affirmation of the Fire, based on His saying: ﴿And your refuge is the Fire﴾. Does it exist now or not?
* A student: It exists.
* The Shaykh: It exists, as evidenced by the saying of the Exalted: ﴿And fear the Fire which has been prepared for the disbelievers﴾ [Aal 'Imran 131]. So it exists now.
* Among the benefits of the verse: these polytheists will find no one to protect them from the punishment of Allah, based on His saying: ﴿And you will have no helpers﴾. No one will prevent them from the punishment of Allah the Exalted on the Day of Resurrection.
Can it be derived from the verse that the friendship of the righteous (al-muttaqun) on the Day of Resurrection remains, or not? Perhaps it can be derived by what is called qiyas al-'aks (reverse analogy), which the Prophet ﷺ established, for analogy (qiyas) is of two kinds: qiyas al-mumathalah wa al-muwafaqah (analogy of similarity and agreement) and qiyas al-'aks (reverse analogy). The Messenger ﷺ established reverse analogy in his saying when he said: «And in the intercourse of one of you there is a charity», meaning that when a person has intercourse with his wife, it is a charity. «They said: O Messenger of Allah, does one of us fulfil his desire and yet has a reward for it? He said: "Tell me, if he placed it in something unlawful, would he incur a burden?" The answer: yes, he would incur a burden. "Likewise, if he places it in what is lawful, he has a reward"»[[Recorded by Muslim (1006/53) from the hadith of Abu Dharr.]]. This is called qiyas al-'aks. We may say: if these polytheists disown one another on the Day of Resurrection and curse one another, then the righteous, the monotheists, the sincere are the opposite of that. I do not wish to establish the ruling itself, for the ruling is established in another verse, His saying: ﴿The intimate friends on that Day will be enemies to one another, except the righteous﴾ [az-Zukhruf 67].
Then He the Exalted said: ﴿So Lut believed in him﴾. Well, there is discussion here. We have not really discussed it; we took the benefits and forgot to discuss. His saying the Exalted: ﴿Then on the Day of Resurrection, some of you will disbelieve in others﴾: (yawm) is a time adverb. What is its governing element?
* A student: Its governing element is the verb (yakfuru, "disbelieve").
* The Shaykh: (yakfuru). And the second? Are there not two governing elements disputing over it?
* A student: yakfuru and yalʿanu (curse).
* The Shaykh: yakfuru and yalʿanu, yes.
And His saying: ﴿your refuge is the Fire﴾, its i'rab (grammatical analysis): is it "ma'wa"?
* A student: (...).
* The Shaykh: Its i'rab, what I want (...) ﴿and your refuge is the Fire﴾.
* The student: (...).
Student: It is not permissible for it to be the predicate (khabar).
* The Shaykh: Why?
* Student: Because it needs a justification (musawwigh) for it to be the predicate.
* The Shaykh: The custom is that it is the predicate...
* The student: Fronting the predicate here has no justification.
* The Shaykh: No, the justification is that it implies restriction (hasr).
* Student: Restriction would be if it were a prepositional phrase or an adverb.
* The Shaykh: No, absolutely not. Fronting what should be delayed implies restriction; this is a rule among them.
* Student: O Shaykh, is the fronting of the predicate among the reasons in this matter?
* The Shaykh: General, among the rhetoricians it is general: fronting what should be delayed.
* Student:
"And like: 'I have a dirham, and for me there is a need, / whose fronting of the predicate is obligatory.'"
* The Shaykh: Obligatory fronting is different from permissible fronting. Here we say: "The Fire is your refuge" is valid outside the Qur'an. We only said that it is permissible for "ma'wakum" to be a fronted predicate, because the original rule is that one informs about entities, not by entities. You say: "Zayd is standing." You inform about Zayd that he is standing. Here we inform about the Fire that it is a refuge; this is the original.
The original is that one informs about entities, not by entities, and the Fire is an entity, so both possibilities are permissible without doubt, and tomorrow this will be a middle solution.
We do not say that "ma'wakum" cannot be a subject (mubtada'), nor do we say that it cannot be a predicate.
* Student: It is not an adverb (...).
* The Shaykh: It is not necessary. The original fronting of the predicate, even if it is not an adverb, is permissible. You say: "Standing is Zayd" — there is no obstacle.
* Student: Is informing about entities with an adverbial phrase, for example, prohibited?
* The Shaykh: No, no, that is a second question. What is at issue is fronting and delaying; whether this or that, you say: "Standing is Zayd": "standing" is a fronted predicate and "Zayd" is a delayed subject. There is no obstacle.
His saying: ﴿So Lut believed in him﴾ [al-'Ankabut 26]. What do you say, why was it construed with (al-lam) here? Can it be construed with other than (al-lam)? Who knows?
* A student: Yes, it is construed with (al-fa'), and (al-lam), of course, is from affirmation and submission.
* The Shaykh: And following.
* The student: And (al-ba') is for affirmation.
* The Shaykh: And confidence in a thing. Can we say that the two particles alternate?
* Student: It is not possible.
* The Shaykh: Why?
* Student: You must say: "I believed in Allah (...)."
* The Shaykh: You do not say "I believed to Allah." Now, regarding other than Allah, is it permissible: "I believed in him and to him"?
* Student: It is permissible.
* The Shaykh: What is the evidence?
* Student: The evidence is the saying of the Exalted in the story of Pharaoh (...): ﴿Pharaoh said: Did you believe in him before I gave you permission?﴾ [al-A'raf 123]; this is in Surat al-A'raf, and in Surat ash-Shu'ara: ﴿He said: Did you believe in him before I gave you permission?﴾ [ash-Shu'ara 49].
* The Shaykh: "Did you believe in him" and "Did you believe to him." But since belief in Allah is not merely following, it must be contentment and tranquility; it is not correct to say "I believed to Allah." Now: ﴿He believes in Allah and believes to the believers﴾ [at-Tawbah 61]. He combined them: ﴿believes in Allah and believes to the believers﴾. What is Lut's relation to Ibrahim? The relation of Lut to Ibrahim?
* Student: The author says he is his nephew (ibn akhihi).
* The Shaykh: That he is his nephew; you attributed it to the author because you are not convinced by it?
* Student: Yes.
* The Shaykh: And what do you think?
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: Yes, the well-known view is that he is his nephew; this is the known position. And based on this well-known position, the saying of the Exalted presents a difficulty: ﴿And We placed in his offspring prophethood﴾ [al-'Ankabut 27], for Lut was a prophet. And the answer?
* Student: It is said that the prophethood being in his offspring after him...
* The Shaykh: After what?
* Student: After the death of Ibrahim.
* The Shaykh: Or after his migration.
* Student: Or after his migration.
* The Shaykh: After his migration; because Lut believed before Ibrahim migrated, so ﴿We placed in his offspring prophethood﴾ comes after he migrated.
This is closer than the view of some who say that this is an exception, so that ﴿We placed in his offspring prophethood﴾ means other than Lut, for he is not of his offspring.
* Student: The verse of al-An'am: Lut, from the apparent context, may be from Nuh or from Ibrahim; some exegetes said this. Does this not include it?
* The Shaykh: According to what the historians say: that he is his nephew?
* Student: Yes.
* The Shaykh: Indeed, here it resolves the difficulty, but we say based on this view. As for if it is established that he is from the offspring of Ibrahim, there is no difficulty; but he is not from his offspring, because it is well known that Ibrahim had only Isma'il and Ishaq, this is well known.
* Student: ﴿And We gave him Isaac and Jacob, each﴾ [al-An'am 84].
* The Shaykh: Jacob is his grandson.
* Student: Well known: ﴿each We guided, and Noah We guided before, and of his offspring, Dawud﴾ to the end of the verse [al-An'am 84].
* The Shaykh: ﴿Dawud, Sulayman, Ayyub, Yusuf, Musa and Harun; thus do We reward the doers of good (84). And Zakariyya, Yahya, 'Isa and Ilyas, each of the righteous (85). And Isma'il, al-Yasa', Yunus and Lut, and each We preferred over the worlds﴾ [al-An'am 84–86]. The apparent meaning of this verse, as Ibrahim said, is that he is of the offspring of Ibrahim. But the well-known fact, as long as he existed in his time, is that Ibrahim had only Isma'il and Ishaq; this is well known. Isma'il is the first and Ishaq is the second, so according to this, the saying "Lut is of the offspring of Nuh, and not of the offspring of Ibrahim" holds.
* Student: The historian did not say "after Ibrahim."
* The Shaykh: No, the offspring is known to be the descendants.
* Student: (...) but I say the difficulty is that it is not said that the offspring of Ibrahim (...).
* The Shaykh: In the verse we have is this, but we say that Lut is not of his offspring. If he is not of his offspring, then ﴿We placed in his offspring prophethood﴾ holds, but Lut was before he migrated, and before prophethood was in his offspring.
* From the benefits of the verse — we now begin ﴿So Lut believed in him﴾ — from the benefits of the verse: that Lut, peace be upon him, was among the followers of Ibrahim although he was a prophet; by His saying: ﴿So Lut believed in him﴾, although he was a prophet.
* And among its benefits: the virtue of Ibrahim, peace be upon him, through migration; for migration is among the best deeds, because a person leaves in it what is familiar of family and homeland, indeed even the homeland, to establish the religion of Allah.
* And among its benefits: the indication of sincerity, in His saying: ﴿emigrant to my Lord﴾.
* And among its benefits: the affirmation of two of Allah's names: al-'Aziz and al-Hakim, and the affirmation of what they include of attributes; for every name of Allah includes an attribute, but not every attribute includes a name. That is: every name includes an attribute, and not vice versa.
Meaning: names are not derived from attributes for Allah; rather all of Allah's names include attributes. For example, among the attributes of Allah the Exalted is plotting against those who deserve it, but we do not name Him "the Plotter."
Among His names: He is ﴿Mighty, Owner of Retribution﴾ [Aal 'Imran 4]. ﴿Owner of Retribution﴾ is an attribute, so we do not name Him "al-Muntaqim," as Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah chose, though the apparent speech of Ibn al-Qayyim in al-Badai' affirms the name al-Muntaqim, and he said it is among the paired names that are not mentioned singly; one does not say only "al-Muntaqim," but says "al-'Afuww al-Muntaqim."
So, the affirmation of what the name al-'Aziz includes of attributes is what?
Might (al-'izzah); and it, as the scholars said, has three categories.
And al-Hakim: what attribute does it include?
Wisdom (al-hikmah) and judgment (al-hukm), and its explanation has already passed.
* Student: (...) the name al-Jabbar.
* The Shaykh: Al-Jabbar in the Qur'an.
* Student: But (...) al-Muntaqim al-Jabbar.
