And ﴿he was distressed on their account and felt powerless to protect them﴾: meaning, regarding what happened to Lut, that he was distressed on their account and felt powerless to protect them. Was the cause his fear for them from his people, or was the cause that he himself feared that the punishment would encompass him?

* A student: The first.
* Another student: For the first, we say: it is *isti'nafiyya* (resumptive) or *ta'liliyya* (causal).
* The Shaykh: Yes, by Allah. In any case, it is suitable to be both resumptive and causal. What prevents it from being that he feared this and that? Is there an obstacle? He feared for them, and he also feared for himself that the punishment would encompass him, because when punishment descends it encompasses everyone, except those whom Allah saves. We recited yesterday His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Say: "My Lord, if You show me that which they are promised (93), my Lord, then do not place me among the wrongdoing people"﴾ [Al-Mu'minun 93–94]. Because every person is exposed to the possibility that the punishment will encompass him.
* Student: But (...) he did not know that they were messengers, what happened from his people.
* The Shaykh: In the beginning? Yes, perhaps he did not know that they were messengers.
* The student: ﴿The messengers of your Lord will never reach you﴾.
* The Shaykh: No, before it: ﴿We are messengers of your Lord﴾; they informed him.
* The student: ﴿And when Our messengers came to Lut, he was distressed on their account and felt powerless to protect them, and he said, "This is a trying day." (77) And his people came rushing to him, and before that they had been doing evil deeds. He said, "O my people, these are my daughters; they are purer for you. So fear Allah and do not disgrace me regarding my guests. Is there not among you a single rightly-guided man?" (78) They said, "You already know that we have no claim on your daughters, and you certainly know what we want." (79) He said, "If only I had power against you, or could take refuge in a strong support." (80) They said, "O Lut, we are messengers of your Lord; they will never reach you. So set out with your family in the darkness of the night, and let none of you look back, except your wife; indeed, what strikes them will strike her. Indeed, their appointed time is the morning. Is not the morning near?"﴾ [Hud 77–81].
* The Shaykh: Good. What is the aspect of correctness?
* The student: The correctness lies in the discussion, and the fear about..
* The Shaykh: That he was afraid for them.
* The student: His fear continued until he knew that they were the messengers of his Lord.
* Student: His saying: ﴿Do not fear and do not grieve﴾ [Al-'Ankabut 33] (...).
* The Shaykh: We will consider it later, God willing.

His saying: ﴿Indeed, We will save you﴾ [Al-'Ankabut 33] is read with a doubled and with a single letter; two readings: *munjūka* and *munajjīka*. *Munjūka* is from which verb? The verb is *anjā* (to save). *Munajjīka* is from *najjā*.

﴿Indeed, We will save you and your family, except your wife﴾. Here *ahlaka* (your family) is in the accusative, as a conjunction (*'aṭf*) on what?

* Student: On the pronoun.
* The Shaykh: On the pronoun in *munajjīka*. There is a difficulty here, because the pronoun in *munajjīka* is in the genitive position through being a possessive attachment. Here *ahl* has come in the accusative. What is the justification for the accusative if we say it is conjoined to the *kāf* in *munajjīka*?
* Student: Because the active participle (*ism al-fā'il*) sometimes functions like a verb and sometimes takes a genitive attachment.
* The Shaykh: Is that correct? Do you agree with this? He says: because the active participle sometimes functions like a verb and sometimes takes a genitive attachment.
* Student: (...) the attachment.
* The Shaykh: (...) the cause.
* Student: We say: *ahlaka* is conjoined to the position of the object.
* The Shaykh: The position of the attached noun. Good. Do we want evidence for this from the words of Ibn Malik?
* The student: "Put in the genitive or accusative the follower of *alladhī*..." Like this?
* The Shaykh:

وَاجْرُرْ أَوِ انْصِبْ تَابِعَ الَّذِي انْخَفَضْ ∗∗∗ كَمُبْتَغِــــــي جَـــــاهٍ وَمَــــــــالًامَــــــنْ نَهَــــــضْ

Yes, this is evidence from the words of Ibn Malik, and it is permissible: *kamubtaghī jāhin wa-mālan man nahaḍ*. Good. Is this like *mālan* or like *mālin*?

* Student: *Mālan*.
* The Shaykh: Like *mālan*. It is also permissible for the *wāw* to be the *wāw* of accompaniment (*ma'iyya*), and Ibn Malik said:

يُنْصَـــــــــبُ تَالِي الْــــوَاوِمَفْعُــــــــولًا مَعَــــــهْ ∗∗∗ فِي نَحْــــــــوِ سَـــــــيْرِي وَالطَّرِيــــــــقَمُسْرِعَـــــــــه

﴿Indeed, We will save you and your family, except your wife, who was among those who remained behind﴾. We say about it what was said before. (The accusative of *ahlaka* is conjoined to the position of the *kāf*.) (﴿Indeed, We are sending down﴾ with the single and doubled letter, *munzilūna* and *munazzilūna*, ﴿upon the people of this town a punishment﴾: a punishment, ﴿from the sky﴾.)

Regarding ﴿rijzan﴾: the author said, "a punishment." *Al-rijz* is not *al-rijs*. *Ar-rijz* is punishment; *ar-rijs* is impurity (*najs*).

Regarding ﴿from the sky﴾: does "sky" here mean the protected ceiling, or height?

* Student: The first.
* The Shaykh: How? What is the evidence?
* Student: Because it is the basic meaning.
* The Shaykh: Is the most common usage that "sky" means the protected ceiling?
* Student: Height.
* The Shaykh: Height is common, and "sky" is also common.
* Student: ﴿Indeed, We are sending down﴾ is height.
* The Shaykh: In any case, whether we say it is the protected ceiling, and that this punishment descended from the lowest heaven, or we say it means height, in every case it came to them from above. Its coming from above is stronger and more emphatic, because what comes from above is high and encompassing, and we seek refuge in Allah, unlike what comes from below, which is not like that.

He said: ﴿A punishment from the sky because of what﴾ with the deed by which ﴿they were defiant﴾, that is: because of their defiance.

The author's wording is strange and contains some contradiction. The *bā'* in His saying ﴿bimā﴾ is undoubtedly causal, and he parsed *mā* as a relative pronoun (*ism mawṣūl*), then estimated it as a verbal noun (*maṣdar*), which indicates that he made it a *maṣdariyya* (verbal-noun particle). This is one of the strange things.

Let us now see: if we parse it according to the first estimate, ﴿bimā﴾, he said, "with the deed by which," so *mā* is a relative noun functioning as an adjective to an omitted antecedent, the estimate being "with the deed." The relative noun, as you know, needs a clause as its complement and needs a returning pronoun linking the clause to it. The complement clause is His saying ﴿they were defiant﴾, and the returning pronoun he estimated with his words "by it": "by what they were defiant by." This is contrary to the familiar position of the grammarians, that if the returning pronoun is genitive, it must agree with the relative noun in the type of governing element and the type of preposition.

What is the evidence from the words of Ibn Malik for the requirement of this matter?

* Student: The evidence?
* The Shaykh: Do you know the basis of the issue?
* Student: Yes, that the returning pronoun must agree...
* The Shaykh: Yes, go on.
* Student:

كَذَا الَّذِي جُرَّ بِـ(مَا) الْمَوْصُولَ جَرْ ∗∗∗ كَمُــــــــــــــرَّ بالَّـــــــذِي مَــــــرَرتُفَــــهْـــــوَ بَـــــــــــرْ

* The Shaykh: Yes.

كَذَا الَّذِي جُرَّ بِـ(مَا) الْمَوْصُولَ جَرْ ∗∗∗ كَمُـــــــــــــــرَّ بالَّــــــــــــــــــذِيمَـــــــــــــــــــرَرتُ .....

Here the governing element differs. The correct view is that *mā* here is a *maṣdariyya*, that is, "by their being defiant" or "by their being wrongdoers" (*bi-kawnihim yafsuqūn*), so it is a verbal-noun particle and not a relative noun.

As for His saying ﴿yafsuqūn﴾: *fisq* originally means departing from obedience, and from it the saying "the fruit defiled (*fasaqat al-thamara*)" when it came out of its skin.

Defiance (*fisq*) is divided into two kinds: the major defiance that takes one out of the religion (*millah*), and the minor defiance that does not take one out of the religion.

The term agreed upon among the scholars is the second. When they use the word *fisq* without qualification, they mean what does not take one out of the religion. But in the Qur'an it is divided into these two kinds: defiance can be a major defiance that takes one out of the religion, and it can be a lesser defiance that does not take one out of the religion. However, both kinds take one out of justice ('adala), so the defiant person is not just.

What is the evidence from the Qur'an for defiance that takes one out of the religion?

* Student: ﴿As for those who were defiant, their refuge is the Fire﴾ [As-Sajda 20].
* The Shaykh: Their defiance here takes them out of the religion without doubt.
* Student: ﴿Thus the word of your Lord has come true against those who were defiant, that they will not believe﴾ [Yunus 33].
* The Shaykh: Yes. And likewise in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿As for those who were defiant, their refuge is the Fire﴾, in contrast to ﴿As for those who believed﴾.

As for defiance that does not take one out of the religion, what is an example, such as His saying, Exalted is He...?

* Student: ﴿And do not eat of that over which the name of Allah has not been mentioned, for indeed it is defiance﴾ [Al-An'am 121].
* The Shaykh: Yes. And others: ﴿O you who believe, if a defiant person brings you a report, then verify it﴾ [Al-Hujurat 6].

As for the cause of defiance, which is departing from obedience, it may be caused by leaving an obligation, and it may be caused by doing a prohibited act. It may be caused by leaving an obligation, as when a person abandons congregational prayer, he becomes defiant, because congregational prayer is obligatory. And it may be caused by doing a prohibition, as when a person shaves his beard, because shaving the beard is prohibited. However, the scholars say regarding a prohibition: if it is a major sin, one becomes defiant merely by committing it if one does not repent from it; and if it is a minor sin, one does not become defiant except by persisting in it.

Does one become defiant by shaving the beard if one does it only once?

* Student: No.
* The Shaykh: No. But if he persists, and every time it grows back he shaves it again, he becomes defiant.
* Student: The one who takes half of it?
* The Shaykh: He shaves the chin and leaves the sideburns?
* Student: Or reduces it.
* The Shaykh: No, there are people like that. I have seen a man who shaves the chin and leaves the sideburns; it exists.

In any case, this is forbidden, whether he shaves the sideburns and leaves the chin, or shaves the chin and leaves the sideburns. Many people think that the beard is the chin, but the chin is not the beard. The chin (*dhaqn*) is the meeting place of the two jaws, because the beard is the place where the teeth grow.

The *Qamus* also mentions that all hair on the face is part of the beard, meaning that trimming the hair of the cheeks is part of the beard. In any case, it is not like shaving, but it is disobedience, because the Messenger (ﷺ) said: "Let the beards grow" [agreed upon: al-Bukhari (5893) and Muslim (259/52), from Ibn 'Umar]. The basic ruling of a command is obligation, so if he persists in it, he becomes defiant.

* Student: The correct interpretation of His saying "We sent down upon them a punishment from the sky" is that it means the judgment is by it, because it descends from the sky.
* The Shaykh: Yes, this is not correct. The correct view is that the punishment itself descended from the sky, as in the other verse: ﴿We sent upon them a violent wind﴾ [Al-Qamar 34] (...).

﴿When Our messengers came to Lut﴾.

* Among its benefits: applying the term "messengers" to angels, from His saying ﴿Our messengers﴾. We mentioned previously the evidence that an angel is called a messenger.
* Among its benefits: the honoring of these messengers by attributing them to whom? To Allah, Glorified and Exalted; for a thing becomes honored by the honor of what it is attributed to.
* Among them: that prophets are like other human beings; they are affected by hardship, grief, joy and happiness. This is shown by His saying ﴿he was distressed on their account﴾. Human attributes do not contradict the perfection of messages. For this reason the Prophet (ﷺ), when he forgot, said: "I am only a human being like you; I forget as you forget" [agreed upon: al-Bukhari (401) and Muslim (572/89), from Ibn Mas'ud]. He also feels cold and heat, and he hungers and thirsts.
* Among them: the great caution of Lut (peace be upon him) regarding his people, because he was only distressed for them and felt powerless to protect them, out of fear for them from his people. They came in an enticing form, for it is mentioned that they came in the form of young men of beauty and handsomeness, a trial from Allah, Mighty and Majestic.
* Among the benefits of the verse also: deducing states from outward appearances. From where do we take this?
* Students: ﴿he was distressed on their account﴾.
* The Shaykh: No. It is that you deduce a man's state from his outward appearance. Their saying ﴿Do not fear and do not grieve﴾ is because they saw the signs in him, and for this reason they said, ﴿Do not fear and do not grieve﴾.

From it we can derive a benefit on which something else depends, namely: acting on indicators (*qara'in*). Acting on indicators is established, is it not?

In the story of Joseph: ﴿A witness from among her own family testified: "If his shirt is torn from the front, then she has spoken truly, and he is among the liars (26). But if his shirt is torn from the back, then she has lied, and he is among the truthful"﴾ [Yusuf 26–27]. Is this a clear proof or an indicator? An indicator. Likewise in the story of Solomon regarding the two women and their child, because the two women disputed: the younger and the older. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "I will bring the knife," or he called for a knife to split the child in two. The older woman agreed, because her son had been eaten by a wolf, and she said: "Let this one go with him." The younger woman said: "O Prophet of Allah, he belongs to her, because compassion overcame her." So by this indicator he knew it was the younger one's, and he judged it for her. This is one of the indicators.

Likewise in this law: the Prophet (ﷺ) in the story of the gold of Huyayy ibn Akhtab, when he asked about his wealth, where it was. They said: "O Muhammad, the wars and the years have consumed it." He said: "That is not possible; the wealth is large and the covenant is recent." Then he handed the man over to al-Zubayr ibn al-'Awwam and said: "Torment him." When he felt the torment he said: "Wait, I see Huyayy ibn Akhtab circling or wandering around this ruin" (a place of destruction), "so perhaps he buried it in this place." And they found it [narrated by Abu Dawud (3006) and Ibn Hibban (5199), the wording being his, from Ibn 'Umar].

This is acting on indicators, and there are many examples. The point is that our deducing a person's state from his outward appearance is acting on an indicator.

* Also among the benefits of the verse: it is appropriate to reassure the frightened so that fear leaves him, as in His saying ﴿Do not fear and do not grieve﴾. From this is what is used today in medicine: the doctor tells the patient, "This is a simple and easy matter," and reassures him so that his chest may be relieved.
* Among them: it is appropriate to remove what harms before what pleases is achieved.
* Student: ﴿Do not fear and do not grieve, indeed We will save you﴾.
* The Shaykh: ﴿Indeed We will save you.﴾ So they began by negating fear and grief, then followed it with good news. For this reason, a well-known saying among the scholars is: *al-takhliya qabl al-tahliya* (emptying before adorning): strip a thing of whatever defect it has, and then complete it with adornment.

From this comes the statement of sincerity. Which comes first, negation or affirmation? Negation: "There is no god but Allah."

* Among the benefits of the verse: association with a righteous person does not necessarily entail righteousness. From where is this taken?
* Students: ﴿except your wife﴾.
* The Shaykh: ﴿except your wife﴾, for his wife was connected to him, yet she did not become righteous. But is association with the righteous a cause of righteousness? Yes, it is a cause of righteousness; for this reason the Prophet (ﷺ) urged us to choose our companions.[[Among them is his saying: "The likeness of a good companion and a bad companion is like the bearer of musk and the blacksmith's bellows. The bearer of musk will either give you some, or you will buy some from him, or you will find its fragrance. The blacksmith's bellows will either burn your body or your clothes, or you will find a foul smell from it." Agreed upon: al-Bukhari (2101) and Muslim (2628/146), from Abu Musa.]]

﴿We sent upon them a violent wind, except﴾ [Al-Qamar 34]

I quote the translation of the passage as requested, rendering the spoken exchanges faithfully.

The gist of it: if it is authentically reported from the Prophet ﷺ that Jibril lifted these towns and overturned them, then there is no dispute; but if it is not authenticated, we do not say it, because it contradicts the apparent meaning of the verses.

* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: "Mu'tafikah" — he did not say "mu'tafakah" (the overturned ones). If it were the passive form, it would mean "the overturned."
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: No. The mu'tafikah are those who committed iftira' (falsehood and lying). His saying "ahwa" (Surah al-Najm 53:53) also points to this, since when they fell from the high dwellings, He caused them to fall.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Yes indeed, that is not a problem. The main point is that if this matter is authentically established, the discussion is over; if it is not, it is not the apparent meaning of the Qur'an.

Among the benefits of this noble verse: the affirmation of causes (asbab), based on His words "bima kanu yafsuqun" ("because they used to defy"), since the ba' here denotes causation.

Another benefit: disobedience is a cause of punishments and destruction. For this reason Allah made sins a form of corruption on the earth, as in His words "bima kanu yafsuqun."

In affirming causes there is a refutation of a group of innovators. Who are they?
* Student: The Ash'aris.
* Shaykh: And others?
* Student: The Jabriyyah.
* Shaykh: The Jabriyyah are the Jahmiyyah, because the Jahmiyyah have three jeems (three "j" letters, i.e., three sins of this kind). May Allah protect us from the jeems — of their jeems is what is of every jeem — and from the accursed Satan. What are the three jeems they have?
* Student: Jabr, irja', and the jeem of tajahhum...
* Shaykh: Ibn al-Qayyim says:
"Jabr, irja', and the jeem of tajahhum..."
Three jeems, yes. They say there is nothing in it, there are no effective causes. Even if you throw a stone at a glass and it shatters, they say: the stone did not break it; it broke at its presence, not by it.
This is not reasonable speech. When you place a paper in fire and it burns, they say: the fire did not burn it; there are no effective causes. Rather, this happened at the fire, not by it. If that were so, then if you put it near light before it falls into the fire, it would burn; and if the cause were not effective, we could say that it is fitting for us to bring the stone and place it by the glass, then it would break.
In any case, this view is sufficiently refuted by its own description. But they want to reach something beyond it: that the human being is compelled (majbar) in his actions. So if Allah punishes him while he is disobedient to Him, His punishment is not a proof against him, since Allah may punish without a cause, and causes, in their view, have no effect. We agree with them that causes are not effective by themselves, is that not so? As evidence, the burning fire became cool and safe for Ibrahim. But we say: they are effective by the decree of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic — the One who made them burn, so they burned.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 29, verses 28–34 (part 1 of 5):**

He said: (﴿And Lot, when he said to his people, "Do you indeed"﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 28]).

(*Lūṭan*, "Lot") The author said: "And mention Lot," so it is an object (*maf'ūl*) of a deleted verb.

The command to mention these virtuous prophets is not merely for praising them and raising their rank among people. It serves this purpose, and another purpose as well: to follow them, to imitate them, and to be patient as they were patient.

(﴿And Lot, when he said to his people, "Do you indeed"﴾ with the two hamzas made clear, the second hamza softened, and an alif inserted between them in both readings, in both places.)

﴿When he said to his people, "Do you indeed"﴾. His saying "with the two hamzas made clear" and so on: these are readings (*qirā'āt*). "Making the two hamzas clear" means you say: ﴿ءَأَئِنَّكُمْ﴾ ... no, it is ﴿أَئِنَّكُمْ﴾ with clear hamzas.

The second reading, he says: "softening the second": ﴿أَاِنَّكُمْ﴾, soft. Leave it between the *yā'* and the hamza.

"Inserting an alif between them in both readings": ﴿آأَئِنَّكُمْ﴾ on the clear reading, and on the softened reading: ﴿آاِنَّكُمْ﴾ softened.

His saying "in both places": which two places? In His saying ﴿Do you indeed come to the men﴾, and in ﴿When he said to his people, "Do you indeed"﴾.

This story, like other stories, appears in the Noble Qur'an in various forms. How do we reconcile them when it is one story?

In reconciling, we say: if it could have been repeated, then it was repeated in both forms.

If it could not have been repeated, then Allah, exalted is He, relates it according to its meaning, sometimes in this way and sometimes in that. Lot, peace be upon him, said in this verse, as Allah the Mighty and Majestic says he said: ﴿Do you indeed commit the immorality﴾.

* A student: ﴿إِنَّكُمْ﴾?
* The Shaykh: What I have is ﴿When he said to his people, "Do you indeed"﴾. The Mushaf has ﴿إِنَّكُمْ﴾, but the commentator (...) a hamza. He only mentioned what?
* A student: One hamza.
* The Shaykh: We have two hamzas. Read the tafsir: ﴿And Lot, when he said to his people, "Do you indeed"﴾ with the two hamzas made clear.
* A student: But (...) the Mushaf.
* The Shaykh: The Mushaf itself was printed according to the reading.
* A student: Our tafsir says: ﴿to his people, "Indeed you"﴾, then it says: with the two hamzas made clear.
* The Shaykh: It is an error, because the tafsir in the margin is copied from the original, and the original follows one reading.
* A student: But the commentator did not point to this reading (...).
* The Shaykh: You mean the commentator, indeed, did not point to it. He should have pointed to it.

I say: For example, you find here in the story of Lot, he said: ﴿Do you indeed commit the immorality that no one in the worlds has preceded you in﴾. In another verse: ﴿Do you commit the immorality while you see?﴾ [al-Naml: 54], or ﴿Do you commit the immorality that no one in the worlds has preceded you in?﴾ [al-A'raf: 80]. This is a difference, is it not? How do we reconcile them?

We reconcile them by the first way, which is simple: multiplicity of statement. Sometimes he says this to them, and sometimes he says that. There is no difficulty in this.

In the story of Pharaoh: ﴿He said to the chiefs around him, "Indeed this is a knowledgeable magician"﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 34], and in surah al-A'raf: ﴿The chiefs of Pharaoh's people said, "Indeed this is a knowledgeable magician"﴾ [al-A'raf: 109]. How do we reconcile?

We say: they all said this and that. If multiplicity is possible, whether from the speaker or in the speech, it is taken to mean that. If it is not possible, then it is a matter of relating it according to its meaning, and Allah, glorified and exalted is He, speaks of it in each place in a way that fits, and as eloquence requires. ﴿Do you indeed﴾.

* A student: ﴿Do you commit the immorality while you see?﴾ [al-Naml: 54]. Is the intended meaning not the town?
* The Shaykh: No, leave the interrogation aside. The discussion is about difference of wording. Here he said ﴿Do you indeed come﴾, and there he said ﴿Do you come﴾.

The interrogation in every place is for rebuke and affirmation.

He said: ﴿Do you indeed commit the immorality﴾.

The *lām* in His saying ﴿you indeed come﴾ is the *lām* of emphasis, and *ta'tūna* means "you come." His saying ﴿the immorality﴾: is the *alif-lām* here for the whole genus, or for the known referent?

* The students: For the known referent.
* The Shaykh: That is, the immorality known to you. The *alif-lām* was added to it because of its magnitude and its ugliness. This is why the word "the immorality" is used in this place. Regarding fornication, Allah the Mighty and Majestic said: ﴿And do not approach fornication; indeed it is an immorality﴾ [al-Isra': 32]. Regarding marrying forbidden kin: ﴿Indeed it was an immorality, hateful, and an evil way﴾ [al-Nisa': 22]. These are three expressions regarding sodomy: Allah described it as immorality in what He related from Lot. In the matter of fornication He said ﴿indeed it was an immorality﴾, and in marrying forbidden kin He said ﴿an immorality and hatefulness﴾. So is marrying forbidden kin greater than fornication or not?

Because it was described with two evil attributes, immorality and hatefulness. Sodomy is uglier than both in terms of description, for it is the immorality that is regarded as abominable by all people.

He said: (﴿the immorality﴾, that is, the anuses of men) — I seek refuge in Allah — the anuses of men. There is no doubt that this is immorality. Everyone finds it abominable, every person of sound intellect finds it abominable. As for one whose heart has been overturned, do not be surprised if he says it is not immorality, just as those who worship idols consider it a virtue and a good deed. These also, may Allah protect us, consider this matter good. It is astonishing that one of them has intercourse with a male in his youth, and this one who was penetrated, when he grows old, penetrates another, so he becomes both doer and done-to.

He said: (﴿What no one has preceded you in among the worlds﴾) The interrogation in His saying ﴿Do you indeed come﴾ is for denunciation and rebuke, and this denunciation is emphasized by the *lām*.

(﴿What no one has preceded you in among the worlds﴾) "Mā" is negating. ﴿min aḥad﴾ is the subject of *sabaqa*, but with the addition of the preposition for emphasis. That is: no one has preceded you in it. As for His saying "in it" (*bihā*): should we say that the *bā'* here means "upon" (*'alā*), "no one preceded you upon it"?

I do not say it means "upon." I say the *bā'* is in its own meaning: you were not preceded in it. This differs from "you did not precede them in it." If he had said "upon it," it would refer to those who lived in their time, and they were more ahead in it than these people.

But if he says "who preceded you in it," this requires precedence in time. His saying ﴿of any among the worlds﴾: the author said, "humans and jinn."

There is no doubt about humans. What about jinn?

* A student: Yes.
* Another student: Its apparent meaning is "the worlds," as in ﴿Praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-Fatiha: 2], which is general.
* The Shaykh: No, the problem is that if we take the generality, we would say: and the angels too. In any case it is permissible that ﴿the worlds﴾ is general with a particular intended meaning, namely the children of Adam. It is also permissible that it is general except for what reason excludes, as you mentioned regarding the angels.

Do we say it includes jinn, humans, and animals?

* A student: Animals are not accountable at all.
* The Shaykh: Are they not among the worlds?
* A student: They are among the worlds, but they are not accountable, and animals do not come except...
* The Shaykh: In any case...
* A student: They do not come; a male does not come to a male except donkeys, apart from that.
* The Shaykh: No, we do not know; in any case we do not know a similar thing about animals. But the answer is as you said: they are not accountable. The discussion concerns the accountable.

Now, this is in His saying ﴿What no one has preceded you in among the worlds﴾. He intends to increase the reproach against them, meaning: you are the ones who established this way. "Whoever establishes a bad practice will bear its burden and the burden of whoever acts upon it" [[Recorded by Muslim (1017/69) from the hadith of Jarir ibn 'Abd Allah.]]. It is as if he is saying to them: if you had been preceded in this immorality, you would have some kind of excuse. But you were not preceded in it, so you are the example in it, may Allah protect us.

﴿Do you indeed come to the men﴾. This sentence is a restatement of what preceded in the previous sentence, and an elaboration of it. He said: ﴿Do you indeed come to the men﴾. The apparent meaning of the noble verse is that even the grown man, may Allah protect us, they approach him.

When the male reaches adulthood, he is called a man: ﴿Do you indeed come to the men﴾. This is an allusion to intercourse, because the Qur'an uses euphemism. Indeed, even in the Arabic language, what is disliked to mention is referred to by what indicates it. Do you understand?

So, for example, Allah the Exalted said: ﴿So come to your tilth however you wish﴾ [al-Baqara: 223]. He expressed intercourse by "coming." Here too He expressed it by "coming."

Second: ﴿and you cut off the road﴾. *al-sabīl* is "the road." Their cutting off the road has two aspects. The first aspect: cutting off the known road, which is that they confront people to rob them, plunder them, and kill them. In our colloquial language this is called *al-ḥanshala*. That is one.

The second: cutting the road in that your conduct causes people to avoid the roads because of what you do to those who use them. This is why he said: (cutting off the path of passers-by by your committing immorality against whoever passes by you, so people abandon passing by you). This is also cutting off the road: if anyone passes by you on the road, you confront him with immorality, may Allah protect us. This is not taking money, killing, plundering, or robbery, but you commit immorality against him. Thus the roads are cut off. Is this not so?

* The students: Yes.
* The Shaykh: The roads are cut off. That is one, and these are two traits.

The third: (﴿and you commit the evil in your gatherings﴾). "Your gatherings" means your places of conversation. *Al-nādī*, *al-mantadā*, and *al-nadī* are all names for a place of talk and assembly among people. ﴿and you commit the evil in your gatherings﴾: some of you commit immorality with others.

As for His saying ﴿the evil﴾: the author explained it as "committing immorality," and on this view there is repetition. The more correct view is that *al-munkar* is more general than committing immorality. It is everything that is denounced by custom or by law. They mentioned among this that they would strike one another with their buttocks, that is, some of them would knock others with their hips. They mentioned among this that they would break wind, the well-known flatulence. They also mentioned among this that they would loosen their belts, that is, they would show off. But is this evil?

* Students: No, because it has been reported in the Sunnah.
* The Shaykh: This is not evil. Did some of them mention it? He said: among the things they did was that they loosened the buttons of their robes. The point is that we leave the verse as it is: *al-munkar* is everything denounced by custom or by law.

Likewise, shooting pebbles (*al-ḥadhf bi'l-ḥaṣā*) and similar things.

My view is that it is general in every matter, including speech that contains mockery, ridicule, and the like. This is evil. Has anything like this existed in this nation?

We say: yes, it has existed. In this nation there are those who did the deed of Lot's people, and in this nation there are communities such that if you inquire about them you will find them doing what Lot's people did. Among these are mockery, ridicule, noisy chatter, frivolity, and other things. The Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "You will certainly follow the ways of those who were before you" [[Recorded by al-Tirmidhi (2180) and Ahmad (21897), the wording being his, from the hadith of Abu Waqid al-Laythi.]].

* A student: Like cracking the fingers and fighting dogs against each other? Is this from their practices or not?
* The Shaykh: They mentioned the fighting of dogs against one another and of roosters.
* The student: And cracking the fingers?
* The Shaykh: And cracking the fingers. I do not know; perhaps cracking the fingers in an unfamiliar manner. Perhaps they gather, and one of them says: "Come on (...)".
* The student: (...).

* * *

* The Shaykh: His saying the Exalted: ﴿And Lot, when he said to his people﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 28], to its end.

* Benefiting from this: raising the mention of these callers to Allah, because His saying "mention" means: mention him in a place of praise. Raising the mention of the callers to Allah, the prophets and others. This is why Allah the Exalted said in the Qur'an regarding Mary: ﴿And mention in the Book Mary﴾ [Maryam: 16].

* Among the benefits of the verse: the virtue of Lot, peace be upon him.

* Among its benefits also: focusing on the matter in which people are immersed, even if something else is more important. Lot, now, did not focus on tawhid in this story. Is it not true that every messenger calls to tawhid? But he focused on this practice that was prevalent among people.

* From this a further point follows: some people, when they see a caller denouncing a specific thing in which people are immersed, say: "People are worse than this. Why do you speak about this? People are in a trap bigger than the sparrow." That is: when I spoke about entertainment, or gambling, or usury, he does not speak of this. There are people who do not pray; why do you not speak about this?

We say: there is no objection to callers focusing on what people are immersed in, even if something else not yet immersed in is more important, because the aim is to treat this disease that has spread among people.

* Among the benefits of the verse: the vileness of sodomy, may Allah protect us, which is a male having intercourse with a male. There is no doubt that it is among the greatest immoralities.

In this noble verse, the prescribed punishment (*ḥadd*) is not mentioned. Likewise, the Sunnah contains no clear authentic hadith on this matter concerning the punishment for the sodomite (*al-lūṭī*). For this reason the scholars differed on it in three opinions.

The first opinion: its punishment is execution in every case, that is, whether the doer and the one penetrated are married (*muḥṣan*) or not. Do you know who is the *muḥṣan*?

He is the one who has married and had intercourse in a valid marriage.

Some scholars said, and this is the second opinion: its punishment is like the punishment of the fornicator. That is, if he is married he is stoned, and if he is not married he is flogged and exiled.

Some scholars said: there is no prescribed punishment for it, and that the inner natural deterrent suffices. Whatever is loathsome in souls does not have a prescribed punishment, since the natural deterrent suffices. Like urine: urine is more filthy than wine, and wine has a prescribed punishment. Does urine have a prescribed punishment?

It has no prescribed punishment, because souls recoil from it and find it repulsive, so the natural deterrent is sufficient instead of the disciplinary deterrent. These are the three opinions.

As for the first opinion, they relied on the hadith that has come with this meaning, the saying of the Prophet, peace be upon him: "Whoever you find doing the deed of Lot's people, kill the doer and the one penetrated" [[Recorded by Abu Dawud (4462) and al-Tirmidhi (1456) from the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas.]]. It is a hadith whose lowest status is that it is good (*ḥasan*). Furthermore, the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, agreed on killing the sodomite, the doer and the one penetrated. They differed, however, on how he should be killed. Some said he should be burned with fire, some said he should be stoned, and others said he should be thrown from the highest place in the town. This is what Shaykh al-Islam, may Allah have mercy on him, chose: that the doer and the one penetrated are both killed, based on the hadith, the reports from the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, and on the meaning and sound analogy. This immorality, may Allah protect us, cannot be guarded against. If it has no strong deterrent, it spreads among people, may Allah protect us, and dominates. That is one point.

And because it destroys manhood and virility: a person becomes like a woman. Some of them, may Allah protect us, afflicted with this matter, beautify themselves and imitate women.

.. from shirk.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 29, verses 28–34 (part 2 of 5):

The evidence for the first point, that attributing a thing to its known cause, whether known through the senses or through the Law, is permissible, is that this verse and many other verses and many hadiths attribute things to their causes. The Messenger ﷺ said about his uncle Abu Talib: "Were it not for me, he would be in the lowest level of the Fire."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (3883) and Muslim (209 / 357), from the hadith of al-'Abbas ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib.]]

If a thing is attributed to its known cause, whether known through the senses or through the Law, but with Allah joined by a particle that implies equality, that is shirk (association of partners with Allah). It is either minor or major, and it may reach the level of major shirk if one believes that the cause has an influence like the influence of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.

If it is attributed to Allah and to other than Allah with a particle that implies sequence, then if the particle is (thumma, "then"), it is permissible, based on the saying of the Prophet ﷺ when a man said to him: "What Allah wills and you will." He said: "Have you made me an equal to Allah? Rather, what Allah alone wills."[[Narrated by Ahmad (1839) from the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas with the wording: "Have you made me an equal (ʿidl) to Allah?"]]

If it is joined by a particle that implies sequence and immediacy, such as (fa, "so"), for example: "Were it not for Allah, then so-and-so," what is your opinion? We have three particles: (wa, "and"), which is clearly forbidden as shirk; (thumma), which is permissible; and (fa). What about (fa)?

In reality, this (fa) is subject to two considerations. If we see that sequence exists in it, we say: what is the ruling? The ruling is permissibility.

If we see that the difference between it and (thumma), whose permissibility the texts have indicated, is that (thumma) indicates delay, an interval, and the distance of the second from the first, we say: it is appropriate that we not permit it. There is no doubt that caution and abstaining from it is better, although there is no doubt that it implies sequence, but there is a difference between it and (thumma).

* Student: O Shaykh, the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "Have you made me an equal to Allah? Say: What Allah wills, then you will."
* Shaykh: "What Allah alone wills," yes.
* Student: Alright, perhaps in another hadith he permitted only (thumma) and did not indicate prohibition of anything else?
* Shaykh: By Allah, this is what we told you. But the reason is that he forbade (wa) and permitted (thumma), and remained silent about (fa).
* Student: We place it at a level between the level of the thing and the level of...
* Shaykh: Permissibility. So is caution...?
* Student: It becomes forbidden.
* Shaykh: No. Caution is avoiding it. We do not definitively rule it forbidden, because the difference between it and (wa) is clear, and we do not definitively rule it permitted, because the difference between it and (thumma) is clear. So we say, as a precaution: we avoid this matter. And praise be to Allah, there is no forbidden thing except that the permissible is more than it, many times over. But people need a reminder, because this is also one of the matters which, although outside the lesson, the discussion is connected to one another. Some people, when advising or guiding people, say: "This is forbidden and not permissible," but they do not open for them a door that they may follow. This contradicts sound da'wah (calling to Islam).

We have mentioned that when a person mentions to people the forbidden path, it is part of the completeness of da'wah and reform that he mentions to them the permitted, open path.

We said that this is what the Book and the Sunnah indicate. Rather, in the Quran Allah, the Exalted, says: ﴿O you who have believed, do not say "Ra'ina" (a word the Jews used to mock the Prophet)﴾ [al-Baqarah 104]. This is forbidden. But ﴿say "Unzurna" (look at us)﴾ opened a door for them.

In the Sunnah, the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, said to Bilal, when he forbade him from buying a sa' (measure) for two sa's, or two sa's for three: "Sell the mixed dates for dirhams, then buy with the dirhams the choice dates."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (2202) and Muslim (1593 / 95), from the hadith of Abu Sa'id and Abu Hurayra.]] For a person to say to people: "O people, you see this thing is forbidden," and then not open for them a door that they may walk through, this is in reality a deficiency in da'wah.

* Student: It would be difficult.
* Shaykh: Difficult in pronunciation, you mean?
* Student: In pronunciation.
* Shaykh: Yes, praise be to Allah.
* Student: And the (wa) after is easier for you than...
* Shaykh: This similarity is verbal. May Allah bless you.
* Student: And in that expression (...).
* Shaykh: Correct. So in this state there is a stumbling block, as they say, a verbal stumbling block.
* Student: Praise be to Allah, it is not found in the speech of the common people here.
* Shaykh: No, it is not found. People, the common folk, now sometimes exaggerate. Our Shaykh 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sa'di told us that a man was asked: "How is your (...) like this?" They had a large house, what do they eat? He said: "We eat only (...)." I seek refuge in Allah. Sometimes the common people exaggerate.

I think we have finished some of the benefits of the verse...
* Student: That "family" (ahl) includes males and females.
* Shaykh: Yes, that "ahl" linguistically includes males and females.
* Student: O Shaykh, does it not establish that Lot, peace be upon him, invoked against them?
* Shaykh: Except, the saying (...).
* Student: Yes, I mean we said at first that it is not there.
* Shaykh: We first confirmed that he invoked against them from his saying: "My Lord, help me against them," by the supplication, because they had challenged him: ﴿They said: Bring us the punishment of Allah﴾ [al-'Ankabut 29].
* Student: O Shaykh, does what is derived from the verse (...) support the view of the one who said that the town was overturned upon them?
* Shaykh: This comes explicitly in the verse, more explicit than this: ﴿We are sending down upon the people of this town a punishment from the sky﴾ [al-'Ankabut 34] (...) said Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.
* Student: We mentioned that in da'wah we explain to people what is forbidden for them and explain what...
* Shaykh: That we open for them another door.
* Student: That we open for them a door (...).
* Shaykh: It is the general case that there is in it what (...), and I do not recall anything that does not have what (...).
* Student: I mean, the texts come absolute, without what opposes them. That is, the prohibition comes in verses...
* Shaykh: Yes, the prohibition comes in verses, but you find in other verses a permitted path mentioned: ﴿Allah has permitted trade and forbidden usury﴾ [al-Baqarah 275]. He forbade usury, but there is another permitted path. ﴿Prohibited to you is carrion﴾ [al-Ma'idah 3]; ﴿and He makes lawful for them the good things﴾ [al-A'raf 157]. That is, it is not necessary that they be joined together, and the texts are part of one another, with no contradiction.
* Student: O Shaykh, let us recall an example (...).
* Shaykh: Listening to the Quran, brother, and the Hadith.
* Student: Yes, but is this like this?
* Shaykh: I say, instead of spending your time on songs and music and other things, you have the Quran and good anashid (chants). You have a holiday. A person here claimed yesterday, saying: "We have a work schedule of twenty-four hours and we play cards, what should we do?" They want to rest... (...) Ramadan later? I see that playing football is better for you and more energizing, praise be to Allah, and you walk.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Yes, football benefits the body.
* Student: The work schedule means...
* Shaykh: No, no, but it is not a written schedule. A schedule is not everything that is known is said.
* Student: And they cannot recite the Quran?
* Shaykh: No, he says: we pray and rest, and talk, and recite the Quran among ourselves. But twenty-four hours, in reality it is hard that a person does only serious work. My point is that your colleague says: "We said it is forbidden (...) and what shall we bring him?" Praise be to Allah.
* Student: Every prophet has a supplication. Is this the supplication of Lot?
* Shaykh: Allah knows whether it is this one or another. But this one, there is no doubt that Allah answered his supplication.
* Student: The difference in invoking against the people. You said it is not appropriate that one invoke (...), for example he says: ﴿My Lord, do not leave upon the earth from among the disbelievers a single dweller﴾ [Nuh 26].
* Shaykh: Yes. Now, for us, this is correct, it contradicts wisdom. There must be... And for this reason he said: "A group of my nation will continue to be upon the truth, dominant over those who oppose them."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (7311) and Muslim (1921 / 171), from the hadith of al-Mughira ibn Shu'ba.]] If we supplicate that Allah wipe out the disbelievers, this means the meaning of this hadith is void.

We say: ﴿He said: "Indeed, in it is Lot"﴾ [al-'Ankabut 32]. ﴿Lot﴾ here is in the accusative because it is the postponed subject of (inna, "indeed").

﴿They said﴾, that is, the messengers, ﴿"We know best who is in it"﴾ [al-'Ankabut 32].

The saying ﴿We know best﴾ is an elative form (ism al-tafdil, the comparative/superlative form). Where is the one it is compared with?
* Student: Ibrahim.
* Shaykh: From you, that is? If you say Ibrahim, its meaning is "from you."
* Student: "We" in the sense of "we know."
* Shaykh: That is, the word ﴿best﴾ apparently is an elative form, and if it is an elative form, the comparison is definitely with the one mentioned, as you said: Ibrahim. But what is the reasoning? The reasoning is that this kind of expression is addressed to one whom the speaker wishes to inform of what the speaker has. As the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "We have more right to doubt than Ibrahim."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (4537) and Muslim (151 / 238), from the hadith of Abu Hurayra.]] Ibrahim, peace be upon him, said: ﴿My Lord, show me how You give life to the dead. He said: Have you not believed? He said: Yes, but for my heart to be assured﴾ [al-Baqarah 260]. The Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "We have more right to doubt than Ibrahim." The elative here is with regard to the one who is compared and the one compared with. Is there doubt in it? No. But the meaning is that if there were doubt in Ibrahim, we would have more right to it than him. So just as we do not doubt, Ibrahim does not doubt.

So the meaning of ﴿We know best﴾ is: just as you know, we also have knowledge of that.

His saying ﴿best of who is in it﴾ means: it includes Lot and others, because (man, "who") is a relative pronoun, one of the forms of generality.

﴿Surely We will deliver him﴾ is read with lightening and with doubling, two canonical readings. (nunajjiyanna) from the doubled form (najja), (nunjiyanna) from the form with the added hamza from (anja). Both are correct and the meaning is one.

His saying ﴿Surely We will deliver him﴾: deliverance (al-najat) means rescue from destruction.

﴿Surely We will deliver him and his family﴾ is coordinated with the pronoun. The sentence, as you see in His saying ﴿Surely We will deliver him﴾, is emphasized by three emphatics: the implied oath, the (lam), and what else?
* Student: The emphatic (nun).
* Shaykh: The emphatic (nun), yes. ﴿and his family, except his wife﴾: ﴿except his wife﴾ is an exception from ﴿his family﴾, and what is meant by "woman" here is the wife.

﴿She was among those who remained behind﴾: those left behind in punishment. As for His saying ﴿she was﴾, shall we say it is a past verb stripped of tense, as we have said in several verses such as ﴿And Allah is ever Forgiving and Merciful﴾ [al-Nisa' 96] and ﴿And Allah is ever Hearing and Seeing﴾ [al-Nisa' 134]?

It has already passed for us that (kanat, "was") in verses like these is stripped of tense, and what is meant is that its subject is characterized by its predicate. Here, ﴿she was among those who remained behind﴾: shall we say the purpose is only to show that she was among those who remained behind, so she is stripped of tense? Or shall we say that (kanat) indicates time, and what is meant is: she was, in Allah's knowledge, among those who remained behind?
* Student: The first.
* Shaykh: Yes, we say both are possible, and there is no contradiction between them. If you wish, say: she was in Allah's knowledge among those who remained behind.
And if you wish, say: ﴿she was﴾ means she was characterized by being among those who remained behind, that is, those remaining in punishment, meaning: she is not saved.
* Student: A woman was mentioned. What is the difference between saying "a wife of one of the Prophet's wives" and "his woman"?
* Shaykh: There is no difference. When it is said "the woman of so-and-so," she is...
* Student: The woman of Pharaoh.
* Shaykh: That is, his wife.
* Student: But I heard that when a woman's religion differs from her husband's, she is not called a wife.
* Shaykh: What?
* Student: He cites the saying of the Exalted: ﴿Gather those who did wrong and their wives﴾ [al-Saffat 22].
* Shaykh: No, their wives (azwajahum) means their companions. It is not that.
* Student: (...) and here likewise.
* Shaykh: The wife of Noah and the wife of Lot: if this rule is not broken, then it is a sound one.
* Student: ﴿And his wife was a carrier of firewood﴾ (...).
* Another student: The wife of Pharaoh.
* Shaykh: Yes, he is saying that a woman is not called a wife when she differs from her husband in religion.
* Student: Whether it is he or she.
* Shaykh: But what your colleague said: the word "woman" is applied to a wife where there is agreement in religion, like the saying of the Exalted about Abu Lahab: ﴿And his wife, the carrier of firewood﴾ [al-Masad 4], meaning: his wife.
So this rule has not remained sound. A person often seems to think that a matter is consistent, and forgets that it may be broken. In such cases one should be careful and say: "usually," so that if it is broken, there is no flaw in his expression.
* Student: The saying "best." There is an objection that it may occur to us that the angels know better than him, since he found...
* Shaykh: There is no objection if it is in the general sense. That is, Ibrahim may not know everyone in it. But Lot, and he addressed them about Lot, do you understand? So if we say, taking the whole group, Lot and his people, there is no barrier to the angels knowing more than Ibrahim, because we do not definitively say that Ibrahim knows everyone in it.
But if we say that what is meant is what was the object of the objection, which is his saying ﴿Indeed, in it is Lot﴾, then it is not on its literal basis. So the meaning is: we know as you know.
* Student: (...) is always connected to Lot, peace be upon him, and he was revealed to, or conveyed revelation to, so they all know his condition.
* Shaykh: Yes, they know, but more knowledgeable...
* Student: But they saved Lot and his family...
* Shaykh: Leave it, it will come, God willing.

He said: ﴿And when Our messengers came to Lot, he was distressed on their account﴾.

We say about ﴿lamma﴾ what we said before.

As for His saying ﴿an jā'at﴾, the ﴿an﴾ here, they say, is extra for emphasis, and every extra particle in the Quran is for emphasis according to the context.

﴿And when Our messengers came to Lot﴾: that is, their coming to him was confirmed. (﴿he was distressed on their account﴾: he grieved because of them.)

(sī'a) here is a past verb in the passive voice. He did not say su'a. Is it because the past verb takes a damma on its first letter when it is passive?
* Student: Because its middle radical is weak.
* Shaykh: Yes, weak, like qīla and bī'a.

And pronounce with the kasra or the ishmam (partial rounding) of the first letter of the triliteral, which is made weak in its middle, and the damma is for it like bū'a...

We know how to pronounce the pure kasra and the pure damma, so we say qūla. But I think the ishmam was difficult for us.
* Student: It is difficult to be certain. There are places in the Quran that are not difficult, but...
* Shaykh: No, this is this.

His saying ﴿he was distressed on their account﴾: the author, by his saying "because of them," indicated that the (bi) is causal, that is, evil befell him because of them. And Allah knows best.
* Student: The rule for the extra (an)?
* Shaykh: If the (an) is removed and the sentence remains correct, then it is extra. That is the rule.
* Student: It has no verbal rule.
* Shaykh: No, it has none. It is the general case that when it comes after (lamma), according to what is in the Quran, it comes as extra, so when...
His saying, the Exalted: ﴿He said: Indeed, in it is Lot. They said: We know best who is in it. We will surely deliver him and his family﴾.

* From the benefits of the verse: showing the tenderness and forbearance of Ibrahim, since he said ﴿Indeed, in it is Lot﴾. It seems that he, peace be upon him, wanted this town not to be destroyed because of the presence of this righteous man. That is one possibility. Another possibility is that he raised this statement in order to learn what the condition of Lot would be. Which of them is more likely?

The statement now may be understood as him saying this so that the punishment would be lifted from them because of this righteous man, and it may be understood that he raised it to see what Lot's condition would be.
* Students: The first.
* Another student: No, the second.
* Shaykh: Or the second?
* Student: The second is better.
* Shaykh: The answer was: ﴿We will surely deliver him and his family﴾. In my view, this favors the second: the meaning is, what will you do with this man?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Read the verse so that we can see clearly. Perhaps this is a separate proof that supports...
* Student: (...)

**The Shaykh:** Regarding His words, ﴿But when good news came to Abraham, he began to argue with Us concerning the people of Lot﴾ [Hud 74].

**Student:** ﴿O Abraham, give up this [argument]. Indeed, the command of your Lord has come﴾ [Hud 76].

**The Shaykh:** The discussion of His words ﴿argue with Us concerning the people of Lot﴾ supports the first possibility. So we say: he meant this and that, is that right? Nothing prevents Abraham, peace be upon him, from saying this for both purposes.

In any case, it shows his compassion, peace be upon him, which is well known of him, to the extent that he said: ﴿Whoever follows me is of me, and whoever disobeys me, indeed You are Forgiving and Merciful﴾ [Ibrahim 36].

* One of the benefits of the verse: it affirms that the angels speak and have knowledge, which indicates that they possess minds and the faculty of speech. This contrasts with those who say they have no minds, and this is one of the strangest claims: that these angels, who glorify [God] night and day without pause, and whom Allah described as honored servants, have no minds. Then who has a mind?

It also contrasts with those who say they are spirits, not bodies, because the apparent situation is that they are bodies that speak and talk, and they have minds and speech.

* Another benefit of the verse: it is permissible to attribute a thing to its cause. Evidence: His words ﴿We will surely save him and his family﴾. It is known that the saving comes from Allah, but since these were messengers of Allah, the act of Allah was attributed to them. That is, whatever Allah, Mighty and Majestic, decreed is their act. In this there is the attribution of a thing to its cause. We have already mentioned that attributing a thing to its cause has four forms:

The first form: that it is attributed to the cause without mentioning Allah.

And that it is attributed to the cause together with Allah using the conjunction "and" (wa).

And that it is attributed to the cause together with Allah using "then" (thumma).

And that it is attributed to the cause together with Allah using "then" (fa), is that not so?

The first category: is it permissible or not? The first category: attributing it to its cause without mentioning Allah.

* Student: It is not permissible.

* The Shaykh: It is not permissible. Do you agree with him?

* Student: No.

* The Shaykh: You do not agree with him.

* Student: Is this cause a known cause?

* The Shaykh: It is known that it is its cause, agreed upon as a legal or sensory cause. So you disagree? Fine. What is the evidence for its permissibility?

* Student: Among the evidence for its permissibility is the Prophet's ﷺ saying to Abu Talib: "Had I not been [there], he would have been in the lowest level of the Fire."

* The Shaykh: Yes, "Had I not been [there], he would have been in the lowest level of the Fire" [agreed upon; al-Bukhari (3883) and Muslim (209/357), from the hadith of al-Abbas ibn Abd al-Muttalib]. The truth is that what prevented him from being in the lowest level of the Fire is Allah, Mighty and Majestic, but His Messenger ﷺ was the cause.

* Student: And this verse also.

* The Shaykh: And this verse. Fine. If it is attributed to the cause together with Allah using "and," what do you say?

* Student: It is not permissible.

* The Shaykh: It is not permissible? What is the evidence?

* Student: Because (...) requires equality.

* The Shaykh: No, that is a reason. But we want the evidence.

* Student: The saying of a man to the Messenger ﷺ: "What Allah wills and you will." He said: "Have you made me a rival to Allah? Say: What Allah alone wills" [Ahmad (1839), from the hadith of Ibn Abbas with the wording: "Have you made me an equal to Allah?"].

* The Shaykh: Correct. Also, the reason implies that this cause is made equal to Allah, Mighty and Majestic. Fine, this ruling is that it is not permissible. But is it enough to say: it is not permissible?

* Student: It is shirk. It may be major, and it may be minor.

* The Shaykh: Major, major, with tanwin? No, no, we proceed with the first word without tanwin. And it may be minor, according to the state of heart of this one who associates [others with Allah]. It is shirk in every case.

If it is attributed to its cause together with Allah using "then" (thumma), what is its ruling?

* Student: It is permissible.

* The Shaykh: Permissible? What is the evidence?

* Student: Say: "What Allah wills, then you will."

* The Shaykh: Where?

* Student: "Then."

* The Shaykh: I want the evidence. If a narration contradicts it, who can recall it?

* Student: Meaning "then" indicates a necessary proof.

* The Shaykh: No, we want evidence. There is the hadith of Qutaylah, the dream that a man among the Muslims saw with a man.

* Student: The Prophet ﷺ said to them: "Say: What Allah wills, then Muhammad wills" [al-Nasa'i (3773), from the hadith of Qutaylah with the wording: "What Allah wills and you will"].

* The Shaykh: Yes.

* Student: The hadith of Ibn Abbas.

* The Shaykh: And the hadith of Ibn Abbas is an athar (a report from a companion).

So we say: this is indicated by the hadith of Qutaylah, and its discussion, God willing, will come in the book of Tawhid, and we will examine whether it is authentic or not. Likewise the athar of Ibn Abbas, which is well known, regarding His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So do not set up rivals to Allah while you know﴾ [al-Baqarah 22].

Then the reason is that "then" (thumma) indicates that the conjoined term is delayed relative to the term it is conjoined to, a delay that is immediate or a long one? 

* Student: A long one.

* The Shaykh: A long one, because "then" (thumma) indicates sequence with an interval.

If one connects it with its cause using "fa," what do you say?

* Student: We hesitated about it.

* The Shaykh: Yes, what is the reason for the hesitation?

* Student: Because "fa" indicates immediate sequence, so insofar as it indicates sequence, it is permissible.

* The Shaykh: It contradicts "and."

* Student: And insofar as it indicates immediate sequence...

* The Shaykh: It contradicts "then," and "then" has been reported as permissible, while "and" has been reported as forbidden. This one is in the middle. We said: it is better for a person to avoid it and turn to things that have no difficulty.

* One of the benefits of the verse: the wife is included among the family (ahl). From where is this taken?

* Student: From the angels' saying: ﴿We will surely save him and his family﴾, then they made an exception of his wife.

* The Shaykh: ﴿except his wife﴾. If someone said: this exception is disjunctive (munqati') and therefore does not indicate [inclusion], what is the answer?

* Student: What is the disjunctive exception?

* The Shaykh: Yes. The disjunctive exception is one where what is excepted is not of the same kind as what it is excepted from. So if someone said this, how would we counter him?

* Student: This is of the same kind as what is excepted.

* The Shaykh: Yes? He says it is not of its kind; he says she is not of the family.

* Student: The original principle in exception is connection (ittisal).

* The Shaykh: Correct.

* Student: Then the burden of proof is on the claimant.

* The Shaykh: This is the correct position. The original principle in exception is connection, because if she were not included in what is excepted, there would be no need to remove her. So this is the original principle.

* A benefit that follows from this one is that the wives of the Prophet ﷺ are from his family (ahl al-bayt)? Yes, from his family, without doubt, contrary to the Rafidah (a Shi'i sect) who exclude his wives from his family.

And the Qur'an contains clear proof of this: that the wives of the Messenger ﷺ are from his family. From where?

* Student: His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and his wives are their mothers﴾ [al-Ahzab 6].

* The Shaykh: No, no. The question is: what in the Qur'an clearly indicates that the wives of the Messenger ﷺ are from his family?

* Student: ﴿The mercy of Allah and His blessings be upon you, O people of the house﴾ [Hud 73].

* The Shaykh: No, that is about Abraham.

* Student: In the verse of hijab: ﴿O Prophet, say to your wives and your daughters and the women of the believers﴾ [al-Ahzab 59]. And at the end, clearly, at its conclusion: ﴿Allah only intends to remove from you the impurity, O people of the household, and to purify you with [complete] purification﴾ [al-Ahzab 33].

* The Shaykh: That is not in this verse.

* Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: No, he brought the verse of hijab.

* Student: No, no, he said: the verse of tabarruj (display).

* The Shaykh: The verse of tabarruj.

* Student: ﴿O Prophet, say to your wives: If you desire the worldly life and its adornment...﴾ [al-Ahzab 28], up to His saying: ﴿O wives of the Prophet, you are not like anyone among women﴾ [al-Ahzab 32]. Then Allah, Exalted, concluded the verse with His saying: ﴿Allah only intends to remove from you the impurity, O people of the household, and to purify you with [complete] purification﴾ [al-Ahzab 33].

* The Shaykh: Up to His saying: ﴿And establish prayer and give zakah and obey Allah and His Messenger. Allah only intends to remove from you the impurity, O people of the household, and to purify you with [complete] purification﴾ [al-Ahzab 33]. This is clear and explicit.

* One of the benefits of this noble verse: association with the righteous does not necessarily make the associate righteous. It is true that association with the righteous is among the causes of righteousness, but it is not necessary. From where is this taken?

* Student: ﴿except his wife﴾; she was his companion.

* The Shaykh: We want the verse, not a reason.

* Student: ﴿She was among those who remained behind﴾.

* The Shaykh: ﴿except his wife; she was among those who remained behind﴾, so she was among those destroyed, or among those who remained in destruction, even though she was the wife of a righteous man, a prophet of the prophets. So a wife should not rely on Allah due to her husband's righteousness. You will find this matter also in the story of prohibition (al-Tahrim), or not? Surah al-Tahrim, in order that the wives of the Messenger ﷺ not rely on Allah because they are wives of the Prophet.

* Student: Shaykh, the wife of Lot is among those who remained behind. As for the wife of Noah, we cannot mention the verses that those who remained behind [were drowned]; the wife of Noah was drowned...

* The Shaykh: Because Noah, and Allah knows best, no one remained except that they were destroyed, and we do not know whether she remained until the people were destroyed by the flood. We do not know.

* Student: (...) that there is a refutation in it of those who say that the wife of Noah went out with him and then (...).

* The Shaykh: Yes. And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and let none of you look back, except your wife﴾ [Hud 81] is not an exception from His saying ﴿and let none look back﴾, but an exception from the sentence before it.

* Student: Does this not contradict that? Because it is possible that if she looked back she would be among those who remained behind; that is, looking back was the decree or the cause of her being among those who remained behind. So is it not a contradiction?

* The Shaykh: So the refutation is not clear? In any case the refutation is very clear, and I think this has passed us before: ﴿and let none of you look back, except your wife﴾. We mentioned the scholars' disagreement over whether it is an exception from the last clause or from the first.

* Student: Shaykh, is here the attribution of knowledge to the self, ﴿We know best who is in it﴾; did they not say: "after Allah"?

* The Shaykh: This is a fine benefit, but everyone knows that a person knows.

* Student: A grammatical benefit, Shaykh.

* The Shaykh: What is it?

* Student: The permissibility of placing the predicate of inna before its subject when it is a prepositional phrase.

* The Shaykh: No, this is not a matter of difficulty. It is like: "The earth is beneath us, and the sky above us," there is no difficulty in it.

* Student: Shaykh, a hadith has been reported that the Prophet ﷺ gathered Fatimah, Ali, al-Hasan and al-Husayn, and said: "O Allah, these are the people of my household, so purify them with [complete] purification." Umm Salamah said: "And I, O Messenger of Allah, am I from the people of your household?" He said: "You are upon good" [al-Tirmidhi (3205), from the hadith of Umar ibn Abi Salamah].

* The Shaykh: Yes. Confirm this hadith and let us see its wording; otherwise the verse is explicit. The meaning would be, if this is established, that the people of his household are his kin.

* Among its benefits, then, in the verse: permissibility of swearing an oath without being asked to swear. From where is this taken? ﴿We will surely save him﴾, like this.

* Another of its benefits: consideration of an implied oath. That is, it is not required that we pronounce the oath. If someone said: "I will surely do such-and-such," would he be swearing? Yes, he would be swearing, because it is known that this sentence is an answer to an implied oath, so he would be swearing. And if he said: "If Allah gives me of His bounty, I will surely give charity," would that be a vow (nadhr)?

Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿And among them are those who made a covenant with Allah: If He gives us of His bounty, we will surely give charity and will surely be among the righteous. But when He gave them of His bounty, they were stingy with it﴾ [al-Tawbah 75-76]. So He made this a vow. This is because a vow has no specific formula; anything that indicates commitment is a vow in any wording. It may be a vow combined with an oath, which adds emphasis.

* Student: Shaykh, His saying: ﴿Indeed, in it is Lot﴾. Does mixing with the righteous and the presence of the righteous truly repel punishment?

* The Shaykh: Perhaps it does repel it. For this reason Allah, Exalted, said: ﴿And Allah would not punish them while you are among them﴾ [al-Anfal 33].

* * *

Allah, Exalted, said: ﴿And when Our messengers came to Lot, he was distressed for them﴾. This we have explained, and we clarified that (lamma) is conditional and (an) is superfluous.

His saying ﴿he was distressed for them﴾ is the response of (lamma).

﴿Was distressed (sii'a)﴾ is a past verb in the passive voice, and its deputy subject refers back to Lot; that is, distress came upon him.

His saying ﴿for them (bihim)﴾: the "ba'" indicates causation; that is, because of them.

* Student: Is the deputy subject implied?

* The Shaykh: No, it is a hidden pronoun.

* Student: Can the prepositional phrase here be the deputy subject?

* The Shaykh: A prepositional phrase does not stand in for the subject except when that is impossible.

* Student: It is not present, because this requires an intransitive verb?

* The Shaykh: It is now an intransitive verb, but if you make the prepositional phrase the deputy subject, you have made it transitive, because the deputy subject means that originally it was a direct object. So the meaning of ﴿was distressed for them﴾ is: Lot.

* Student: Is (sa'a) here intransitive or transitive in origin?

* The Shaykh: No. ﴿Sii'a bihim﴾ means: distress befell him, or evil afflicted him. But (sa'a) in origin is transitive, as you say: "This matter distressed me."

* Student: Transitive without a direct object, meaning with an adverbial, a prepositional phrase, or...

* The Shaykh: "So-and-so distressed me, this news distressed me," just as you say "it gladdened me." Is that clear?

His saying: ﴿and he was constrained in heart for them (wa daqa bihim dhar'an)﴾. What is the i'rab (grammatical analysis) of ﴿dhar'an﴾?

* Student: It is a specification (tamyiz).

* The Shaykh: This is a specification transferred from what? From the subject. And a specification, as we have seen, can be transferred from the subject or from the direct object.

An example of one transferred from the direct object is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And We caused the earth to burst forth with springs﴾ [al-Qamar 12]. This is a specification transferred from the direct object; its origin is "and We caused the springs of the earth to burst forth."

An example of one transferred from the subject: you say, for instance, "His chest expanded with them," that is, "his chest expanded."

Here, ﴿daqa bihim dhar'an﴾, its origin is: "his dhar' was constrained because of them." And what is the dhar'? The author explained it as the chest. He said: (﴿daqa bihim dhar'an﴾ means: a chest), that is, his chest was constrained because of them and did not expand; rather, he experienced grief and worry because of that.

It was also said, and this is the correct view, that dhar' means capacity; that is, he was constrained by them in capacity, so he became unable to bear them. This is its meaning in the Arabic language. Capacity was named dhar' from dhira' (forearm), because the forearm is the seat of bearing, and capacity is that by which a person is able to bear or unable to bear, that is, to carry a thing.

He said: ﴿and he was constrained in heart for them﴾. The reason is that they were men of handsome appearance in the form of guests, so he feared for them from his people, and they informed him that they were messengers of his Lord. This is the reason he was constrained by them, because his people, as Allah mentioned in another verse, when they heard of that ﴿came to him rushing toward him﴾ [Hud 78], that is, hastening, may Allah protect us, wanting these guests. This is one of Allah's trials for the servant: to place forbidden things before him in a form his soul desires, so that Allah may know who fears Him in the unseen.

So they, may Allah protect us, when these came, came to Lot seeking them. He would say to them: ﴿These are my daughters; they are purer for you. So fear Allah and do not disgrace me regarding my guests. Is there not among you a rightly guided man?﴾ [Hud 78]. So he was constrained by them out of fear for them from his people, because his people, as Allah, Exalted, said, were people of wickedness: ﴿And We saved him from the town that was committing wicked deeds﴾ [al-Anbiya' 74]. So he was feared for them.

But they said to him: ﴿Do not fear and do not grieve.﴾ Fear is about what is expected to happen in the future, and grief is about what has already occurred in the past.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 29, verses 28–34 (part 4 of 5):

They said: The word *al-huzn* (grief) may also be used for the future. They gave as an example the Prophet's (ﷺ) words to Abu Bakr: ﴿Do not grieve; indeed Allah is with us﴾ [At-Tawbah 40]. Here, *"lā taḥzan"* means "do not fear." It is also possible that it keeps its original meaning, namely "do not grieve over what has happened, our leaving and entering the cave and hiding in it," or that he feared that the punishment would overtake him, so he was afraid. And ﴿he was distressed on their account and felt powerless to protect them﴾: meaning, regarding what happened to Lut, that he was distressed on their account and felt powerless to protect them. Was the cause his fear for them from his people, or was the cause that he himself feared that the punishment would encompass him?

* A student: The first.
* Another student: For the first, we say: it is *isti'nafiyya* (resumptive) or *ta'liliyya* (causal).
* The Shaykh: Yes, by Allah. In any case, it is suitable to be both resumptive and causal. What prevents it from being that he feared this and that? Is there an obstacle? He feared for them, and he also feared for himself that the punishment would encompass him, because when punishment descends it encompasses everyone, except those whom Allah saves. We recited yesterday His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Say: "My Lord, if You show me that which they are promised (93), my Lord, then do not place me among the wrongdoing people"﴾ [Al-Mu'minun 93–94]. Because every person is exposed to the possibility that the punishment will encompass him.
* Student: But (...) he did not know that they were messengers, what happened from his people.
* The Shaykh: In the beginning? Yes, perhaps he did not know that they were messengers.
* The student: ﴿The messengers of your Lord will never reach you﴾.
* The Shaykh: No, before it: ﴿We are messengers of your Lord﴾; they informed him.
* The student: ﴿And when Our messengers came to Lut, he was distressed on their account and felt powerless to protect them, and he said, "This is a trying day." (77) And his people came rushing to him, and before that they had been doing evil deeds. He said, "O my people, these are my daughters; they are purer for you. So fear Allah and do not disgrace me regarding my guests. Is there not among you a single rightly-guided man?" (78) They said, "You already know that we have no claim on your daughters, and you certainly know what we want." (79) He said, "If only I had power against you, or could take refuge in a strong support." (80) They said, "O Lut, we are messengers of your Lord; they will never reach you. So set out with your family in the darkness of the night, and let none of you look back, except your wife; indeed, what strikes them will strike her. Indeed, their appointed time is the morning. Is not the morning near?"﴾ [Hud 77–81].
* The Shaykh: Good. What is the aspect of correctness?
* The student: The correctness lies in the discussion, and the fear about..
* The Shaykh: That he was afraid for them.
* The student: His fear continued until he knew that they were the messengers of his Lord.
* Student: His saying: ﴿Do not fear and do not grieve﴾ [Al-'Ankabut 33] (...).
* The Shaykh: We will consider it later, God willing.

His saying: ﴿Indeed, We will save you﴾ [Al-'Ankabut 33] is read with a doubled and with a single letter; two readings: *munjūka* and *munajjīka*. *Munjūka* is from which verb? The verb is *anjā* (to save). *Munajjīka* is from *najjā*.

﴿Indeed, We will save you and your family, except your wife﴾. Here *ahlaka* (your family) is in the accusative, as a conjunction (*'aṭf*) on what?

* Student: On the pronoun.
* The Shaykh: On the pronoun in *munajjīka*. There is a difficulty here, because the pronoun in *munajjīka* is in the genitive position through being a possessive attachment. Here *ahl* has come in the accusative. What is the justification for the accusative if we say it is conjoined to the *kāf* in *munajjīka*?
* Student: Because the active participle (*ism al-fā'il*) sometimes functions like a verb and sometimes takes a genitive attachment.
* The Shaykh: Is that correct? Do you agree with this? He says: because the active participle sometimes functions like a verb and sometimes takes a genitive attachment.
* Student: (...) the attachment.
* The Shaykh: (...) the cause.
* Student: We say: *ahlaka* is conjoined to the position of the object.
* The Shaykh: The position of the attached noun. Good. Do we want evidence for this from the words of Ibn Malik?
* The student: "Put in the genitive or accusative the follower of *alladhī*..." Like this?
* The Shaykh:

وَاجْرُرْ أَوِ انْصِبْ تَابِعَ الَّذِي انْخَفَضْ ∗∗∗ كَمُبْتَغِــــــي جَـــــاهٍ وَمَــــــــالًامَــــــنْ نَهَــــــضْ

Yes, this is evidence from the words of Ibn Malik, and it is permissible: *kamubtaghī jāhin wa-mālan man nahaḍ*. Good. Is this like *mālan* or like *mālin*?

* Student: *Mālan*.
* The Shaykh: Like *mālan*. It is also permissible for the *wāw* to be the *wāw* of accompaniment (*ma'iyya*), and Ibn Malik said:

يُنْصَـــــــــبُ تَالِي الْــــوَاوِمَفْعُــــــــولًا مَعَــــــهْ ∗∗∗ فِي نَحْــــــــوِ سَـــــــيْرِي وَالطَّرِيــــــــقَمُسْرِعَـــــــــه

﴿Indeed, We will save you and your family, except your wife, who was among those who remained behind﴾. We say about it what was said before. (The accusative of *ahlaka* is conjoined to the position of the *kāf*.) (﴿Indeed, We are sending down﴾ with the single and doubled letter, *munzilūna* and *munazzilūna*, ﴿upon the people of this town a punishment﴾: a punishment, ﴿from the sky﴾.)

Regarding ﴿rijzan﴾: the author said, "a punishment." *Al-rijz* is not *al-rijs*. *Ar-rijz* is punishment; *ar-rijs* is impurity (*najs*).

Regarding ﴿from the sky﴾: does "sky" here mean the protected ceiling, or height?

* Student: The first.
* The Shaykh: How? What is the evidence?
* Student: Because it is the basic meaning.
