"Their brother Shu'ayb, so he said: O my people, worship Allah and hope for the Last Day" — "O my people": "yā" is a vocative particle, and "qawmi" is a vocative noun — is it declined or indeclinable?

* Student: Declined.

* Shaykh: It is a vocative noun in the accusative, and the sign of its accusative is a visible kasrah at its end.

* Student: A presumed fathah.

* Shaykh: A presumed fathah on the omitted "ya'," ...

* Student: Because of the meeting of two quiescent letters.

* Shaykh: Because of the meeting of two quiescent letters. Therefore a presumed fathah on what precedes the omitted ya' of the speaker, because of the meeting of two quiescent letters; its manifestation was prevented by the occupation of the place by the harakah of harmony. Repeat the parsing: "qawmi" is a vocative noun...

* Student: A vocative noun.

* Shaykh: In the accusative.

* Student: In the accusative.

* Shaykh: A fathah.

* Student: A presumed fathah.

* Shaykh: On what precedes the ya'.

* Student: On what precedes the ya'.

* Shaykh: The omitted.

* Student: The omitted.

* Shaykh: For lightness.

* Student: For lightness, because of the meeting of two quiescent letters.

* Shaykh: Its manifestation was prevented by the occupation of the place by the harakah of harmony.

He said: "O my people, worship Allah and hope for the Last Day." "Worship Allah" means: humble yourselves to Him by obedience, because worship is derived from humbling oneself, and from it the saying: a "paved road" (mu'abbad), meaning: made smooth for travelers. So worship is the humbling of oneself to Allah, the Exalted, by obeying Him. And obedience is: carrying out the command and avoiding the prohibition, when used absolutely. But when it is coupled, as in: obedience and disobedience, obedience becomes concerning commands and disobedience concerning prohibitions.

He said: "Worship Allah," meaning: devote worship to Him alone; because of His words: "And We did not send before you any messenger except that We revealed to him that there is no deity except Me, so worship Me" [Al-Anbiya 25]. So what is meant here by worship is sincerely devoting worship to Allah, the Exalted.

"And hope for the Last Day": he said: (fear Him, and it is the Day of Resurrection).

Does "raja'" (hope) apply to desire for the beloved, or not? Correct, this is the basic meaning: desire for the beloved; therefore it is said: "tamanni and raja'."

And "raja'" is applied to the meaning of fear, so it is from the category of antonyms (al-adhdad), because in the Arabic language there are words that indicate a meaning and its opposite, called antonyms, and the philologists wrote books on this; you find one word suitable for this and for that, for a thing and its opposite.

So is "raja'" here in the sense of fear, or in the sense of desire for the beloved?

The author took it to mean fear, because the context is one of warning. It may be that what is meant is: the hope which is desire for the beloved, because the Last Day contains what is beloved and what is hateful, correct?

Allah the Exalted said: "So among them are the wretched and the happy. As for those who were wretched, they will be in the Fire" [Hud 105–106], "And as for those who were made happy, they will be in Paradise" [Hud 108].

If someone says to us: may we not interpret it as both meanings together: hope in Him out of fear of punishment and desire for reward; would that not be suitable?

It is suitable to include both matters. It has previously been mentioned to us that the preponderant view with me — and it is the view of some scholars — is the permissibility of using a homonym in both its meanings when no contradiction results, so that we say: a word that admits both in a way that does not contradict. What prevents its use in both its meanings? And Allah knows best.

* Student: His Exalted words (...).

* Shaykh: An explanation or clarification of what he was sent with.

And in His words "O my people" there is evident gentleness, because a man's people must support him and accept what he brought (...).

.. and avoiding the prohibition.

And His words: "and hope for the Last Day" [Al-'Ankabut 36]. He said: (fear Him). It may also mean: hope for what it contains of reward and recompense. It is suitable for this and that, and it is one of the antonymous words that indicate a thing and its opposite.

His words "the Last Day" are the Day of Resurrection, and it was called "the Last" because there is no day after it. People have four stages: a first stage in the womb, the second stage in this world, the third stage in the graves, and the final stage — when? The Day of Resurrection. Therefore it is called the Last Day, since it is the last thing, the last stage a human will have is this day; that is why it is called the Last Day.

"And do not commit corruption in the earth, being corrupters" [Al-'Ankabut 36]. "Do not commit corruption" means: do not corrupt. Accordingly, "corrupters" (mufsidin) — the author said about it: (an emphatic circumstantial qualifier of its agent). What is the meaning of "emphatic of it"? That is, of the same meaning. Is this emphasis verbal or semantic? Answer.

* Student: Semantic.

* Shaykh: Why?

* Student: It is not from the same root...

* Shaykh: It is not from the root of the verb. If he had said "wa la ta'thaw fi al-ardi 'athin," it would have been verbal. But here it is semantic, because he emphasized it by meaning, since "al-'utuww" — the author says: (from 'athi with a kasrah on the thaa: he corrupted). It is said: "'athiya ya'tha" like "fariha yafrahu." You do not know the doors, the doors of conjugation: how many are they?

* Student: Eight.

* Shaykh: Six; among them: the pattern "fa'ila yaf'alu, like fariha yafrahu and radiya yarda." And "'athiya" in the opinion of the author: ya'tha; and it may be from the pattern "fa'ala yaf'ulu: 'atha ya'thu." Both mean: he corrupted; therefore the author said: (he corrupted).

As for His words "and do not commit corruption in the earth, being corrupters": the prohibition here is clear, therefore the verb is jussive by the deletion of the nun: "la ta'thaw." By what does corruption occur? Is the meant corruption sensory — such as demolishing buildings, spoiling rivers, cutting trees, and the like — or the meant corruption is moral, or both?

* Students: Both.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 29, verse 35–40 (part 2 of 5):

* The Shaykh: Both. Corruption is not permissible even in material matters; for this reason "the Prophet (ﷺ) forbade the squandering of wealth."
I say: Corruption on earth includes corruption through sins and material, physical corruption. The evidence for this is that "the Prophet (ﷺ) forbade the squandering of wealth"[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (1477) and Muslim (593/12), from the hadith of al-Mughira ibn Shu'ba.]], and Abu Dawud[[We have not located it.]] narrated: "They were with the Prophet (ﷺ) on a journey, and they stopped at a land, and he forbade them from cutting its trees," because they are for shade, so cutting them is corruption of it.
What was the response of these people to this call, which calls to good and forbids evil; calling to good in His saying: ﴿Worship Allah and hope for the Last Day﴾, and forbidding evil in His saying: ﴿And do not commit abuse on the earth, spreading corruption﴾? The reply: ﴿So they denied him﴾ [al-'Ankabut 37].
Here He said: ﴿So they denied him﴾, although denial occurs only in news, whereas He said: ﴿Worship Allah﴾, ﴿and hope﴾, ﴿and do not commit abuse﴾, and all three of these clauses are imperative, not declarative. The apparent expectation would be that He say: "so they disobeyed him." Why then does He say: ﴿So they denied him﴾?
The answer: It is said that he gave them these commands, or these two commands and the prohibition, in his capacity as a messenger from Allah. ﴿So they denied him﴾ means: they denied his claim to prophethood. This is more emphatic than disobedience, because they rejected his messengership outright; they did not acknowledge the messengership and then say, "we will disobey you in this matter." Rather, they denied the messengership entirely, so this is more emphatic than saying "so they disobeyed him." Have you understood this or not?
* A student: Clear.
* The Shaykh: He said: ﴿So they denied him, and the quake seized them﴾. The fa' in His saying ﴿So they denied him﴾ is for sequence (ta'qib): the sequencing of this clause after what preceded it.
In His saying ﴿and the quake seized them﴾, the fa' may be for sequence, or it may be for causation (sababiyya). If we say it is for sequence, then it is evidence that they were punished immediately upon their denial. If we say it is for causation, then it does not necessarily follow that their punishment was close to their denial, because it is possible that Allah gave them respite after the denial and then seized them. Moreover, when we take it as causal, it does not rule out or prevent the punishment from being immediate. On this basis we say: it is preferable that it be causal, and the causal reading is preferable for three reasons:
The first reason: it indicates the wisdom of the punishment, which is the denial.
Second: it has a broader indication than the fa' being for ordering, because it includes what follows the denial immediately and what is delayed after it.
Third: we are spared the claim that Allah, glorified and exalted, did not give them respite, and we have no knowledge of that. Therefore choosing that the fa' here be causal is preferable.
His saying ﴿the quake seized them﴾ — "seized them" (akhadhathum) is more emphatic than "struck them" (asabathum), because seizing indicates that there is no leniency in it and that it is destructive. As for ar-rajfa, he says: "the severe earthquake." Is there another verse indicating that the Cry (as-sayha) seized them?
* A student: Yes, ﴿And the Cry seized them at morning﴾ [al-Hijr 83].
* The Shaykh: No.
* A student: Thamud — the Cry and the quake are both mentioned concerning them, but here, Shu'ayb is not mentioned.
* Another student: In Surah Hud, O Shaykh.
* The Shaykh: In Surah Hud, the Cry seized them: ﴿So they became in their homes prostrate (jathimin), as if they had never prospered there. Unquestionably, Madyan [was removed]﴾ [Hud 94, 95].
So ﴿the quake seized them﴾ and ﴿the Cry seized them﴾ are not contradictory, since both can occur together: the punishment was a cry; they were cried at and heard it, and the earth quaked beneath them, so they were punished by sound and punished by the act, by both together.
* A student: If we say the fa' is causal, then the denial comes after our seizing, O Shaykh, or the cause... i.e., the cause of the action is omitted; meaning: they denied because of what?
* The Shaykh: No, its meaning is not that the cause is what follows it. If it is said to be causal, the cause may be what follows it, and what follows it may be the effect; i.e., because of their denial they were seized. So the cause comes first. When we say it is causal, its meaning is not that it enters only upon the cause; it may enter upon the cause, and it may enter upon the effect.
He said: ﴿So the quake seized them, and they became﴾, and the fa' here we say is either conjunctive or causal; both are acceptable. ﴿Became (asbahu) in their abode, prostrate (jathimin)﴾: ﴿jathimin﴾ is in the accusative as the predicate of ﴿asbaha﴾. His saying ﴿in their abode, prostrate﴾, and in another verse: ﴿in their homes﴾ [Hud 67]. There is no contradiction, because "dar" is a singular noun in construct, and a singular noun in construct is generic. I say: "diyar" and "dar" are not contradictory, because "dar" is singular, and a singular in construct encompasses (ya'ummu). We ask the brother for an example from the Qur'an showing that a singular in construct is generic. Does anyone of you recall one?
* A student: His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And if you should count the favor of Allah, you could not enumerate it﴾ [al-Nahl 18].
* The Shaykh: His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And if you should count the favor of Allah, you could not enumerate it﴾. "Ni'ma" (favor) is singular, but certainly what is meant here is the plural, by evidence of His saying?
* A student: ﴿And if you should count﴾.
* The Shaykh: No, ﴿you could not enumerate it﴾, because one individual favor can be enumerated. So "dar" and "diyar" have no difference in meaning.
As for His saying ﴿jathimin﴾, the author said: "(kneeling on their knees, dead)." I seek refuge in Allah! This "jathim" means that, due to the severity of what befell them, they knelt on their knees, then became still and became jathimin.
He, Exalted, said: (﴿And﴾ We destroyed ﴿'Ad﴾ ﴿and Thamud﴾ [al-'Ankabut 38] with or without tanwin). What is ṣarf? It is tanwin. Ibn Malik said:
Ṣarf is a tanwin that comes to show a meaning, by which the noun becomes amkan (declinable).
So here it is permissible to have ṣarf in ﴿Thamudan﴾ and permissible to omit ṣarf, and both are readings: ﴿Thamuda﴾. Likewise all tribal names may, in principle, be read with or without ṣarf. Ṣarf is considered in view of the tribe as a living group, which is masculine, and non-ṣarf in view of the tribe as a community, which is feminine.
Accordingly, if we read ﴿Thamuda﴾ without ṣarf, we say it is conjoined to ﴿'Adan﴾, and the conjunct of an accusative is accusative, and it lacks tanwin because it is not declined, the preventing factor being the proper-noun status and feminine gender considered as a tribe. And for ﴿Thamudan﴾ with ṣarf, we say ﴿Thamudan﴾ is conjoined to ﴿'Adan﴾, the conjunct of an accusative is accusative, and it takes tanwin because it is masculine considered as a people.
His saying ﴿'Adan and Thamud﴾ are two objects of an omitted verb; the estimate, as the author said: "(We destroyed 'Ad and Thamud)." Where were 'Ad located? In al-Ahqaf, by His saying: ﴿And mention the brother of 'Ad, when he warned his people in al-Ahqaf﴾ [al-Ahqaf 21]. Thamud were the people of Salih in al-Hijr; the dwellings of Thamud are known until now.
He, Exalted, said: (﴿And it has become clear to you﴾ their destruction, ﴿from their dwellings﴾ in al-Hijr and Yemen). ﴿And it has become clear﴾ means appeared. ﴿To you﴾: the address is to whom?
* A student: To the Quraysh.
* The Shaykh: Yes, to the Quraysh, because this was clear to them and they know it.
His saying ﴿from their dwellings﴾: "min" according to the author's estimate is causal; i.e., "Our destruction of them became clear to you because of your seeing their dwellings," so it is causal.
Could we not make "min" partitive, so that the meaning is ﴿it has become clear to you from their dwellings﴾, i.e., some of their dwellings? It is possible, but I have not seen anyone parse it this way. That is, "min" could be partitive, meaning: it became clear to you a portion, and the portion has passed away, since what is observed now is some of these dwellings and traces. As for the author's estimate, he says the subject of ﴿tabayyana﴾ is omitted, the estimate being: "their destruction."
We forgot to say: is the subject omitted, or is it a concealed pronoun?
* A student: Omitted.
* The Shaykh: Is the subject omitted or concealed?
* A student: Omitted, not concealed, because it is a principal element.
* Another student: Concealed.
* Another student: A principal element is not concealed.
* The Shaykh: It is only said "omitted" in a place where it cannot be estimated, such as a verbal noun (maṣdar), as they said in His saying: ﴿Or feeding on a day of severe hunger, an orphan﴾ [al-Balad 14, 15]: they said the subject here is omitted, because it cannot be concealed in a verbal noun. But when it can be concealed, it is said to be concealed (mustatir). An omitted element may be a principal element or a secondary one. But in reality, the author's statement suggests that it is omitted; had the author said: "and it has become clear," i.e., "their destruction," and made it an explanation of the omitted element, it would have been better.
("from their dwellings" in al-Hijr and Yemen): is this "laff wa nashr" arranged or confused?
* Students: Confused.
* The Shaykh: Because "in al-Hijr" refers to Thamud, which is mentioned later in the Qur'an, and "and Yemen" refers to 'Ad. Such an arrangement is not appropriate; that is, the commentator or explainer of someone's words should not explain it in this order, because an ignorant person who does not know, if we did not know about their location, would ask: to whom does al-Hijr belong?
* Students: To 'Ad.
* The Shaykh: To 'Ad, and we say Yemen belongs to Thamud. Yes.
He said: ﴿And Satan made their deeds appear pleasing to them﴾. This is with the estimate of "qad": i.e., Satan has made their deeds appear pleasing to them, from disbelief and sins. "Zayyana" means: made fair and beautiful. So Satan made their deeds appear fair to them, from shirk and sins, and he said that shirk is good, because you worship these idols so that they bring you closer to the Creator: ﴿We worship them only that they may bring us nearer to Allah in position﴾ [al-Zumar 3].
Then you hope in them and call upon them, and what you seek is attained, because Allah, the Exalted, may test the worshippers, so that their aim is fulfilled at this point, not by it. We now say: "with him, not by him"; i.e., one may call upon an idol, or upon the Prophet (ﷺ), or upon an angel, and Allah decrees, as a trial and test, that this cause occurs at the time of his supplication. We believers know that it was not achieved by it, but it occurred in his case as a trial. Allah, glorified and exalted, may test a person through sin, and it is made easy for him and made fair to him.
It has already passed for us that Allah tested the Jews with what? With the fish: they came on Saturday and did not come on other days. Allah tested the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, with game that their hands and spears could reach while they were in ihram. Likewise the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "A man whom a woman of rank and beauty invited, and he said: Indeed I fear Allah"[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (1423) and Muslim (1031/91), from Abu Hurayra.]]. No one was present with them; for if someone had been present, he would have said "I fear people," but he said "I fear Allah." A person may thus be tested with sin.
Similarly, Satan says to them: these idols, if you worship them, will bring you near to Allah and be a means: ﴿We worship them only that they may bring us nearer to Allah﴾ [al-Zumar 3]. As for sins, Satan likewise makes them fair to a person and makes them easy for him, and says: "Go on and act, and the Lord is Forgiving and Merciful; act and repent; the world is before you. As long as you have not reached forty years, the prayers and fasting are not obligatory upon you; when you reach forty years and attain your maturity, then prayer and fasting become obligatory." This is found now among some ignorant Muslims.
His saying here: ﴿Satan made their deeds appear fair﴾ — what is the morphological form (wazn) of "al-shaytan"?
* A student: From the root "shaṭana."
* The Shaykh: In reality it has no weight, no significance; but its verbal form?
* A student: (fa'lan).
* Another student: According to the root or the difference of root: some say its root is "shaṭan," so in this sense it is on the pattern fa'lan, shaytan; and some say its root is "shā-ṭa" (...).
* The Shaykh: If we take it from "shaṭan," it is on the pattern of?
* A student: On the pattern of fay'āl. But if its pattern is "shāṭa," it is on the pattern fa'lān.
* The Shaykh: fa'lān, with nūn.
* A student: And the preferred view is "shāṭa," and Allah knows best.
* The Shaykh: "Shaṭana" means "he went far away."
* A student: No, "shāṭa" from...
* The Shaykh: "Shāṭa." If it were "shāṭa," would the nūn be...?
* A student: The nūn is augmentative.
* The Shaykh: If it is augmentative, is it declinable or not?
* A student: If it is augmentative, it is prohibited from ṣarf.
* The Shaykh: And in the Qur'an: ﴿We guarded it from every accursed shaytan﴾ [al-Hijr 17]: is it declined or not?
* A student: Declined.
* The Shaykh: It is declined. But you may say: this is indefinite and has no alif and nūn; if it is indefinite it is declined, because that which has the alif and nūn is prevented from ṣarf when it is a descriptive or a proper noun, and "shaytan" is not a descriptive. In any case, the closer view is that it is from "shaṭana," i.e., he went far from the mercy of Allah.
* A student: "Shaytan" is not a proper noun?
* The Shaykh: No, and it may be intended as a genus: a black dog is a shaytan; this is not a proper noun; i.e., a shaytan among the shayatin. That is why the jurists, in an expression, said: it is not permissible to delay the qada' (makeup) until another Ramadan, or: until another Ramadan?
* Students: Ramadan.
* The Shaykh: No, "until another Ramadan," because it is indefinite, not a proper noun.
* A student: Like the verse ﴿And We guarded it﴾ [al-Hijr 17].
* The Shaykh: Yes. In any case, what appears is that "shaytan" is from "shaṭana," i.e., when he is far away.
His saying: ﴿Satan made their deeds appear fair to them﴾ [al-Anfal 48]: here the beautification is attributed to Satan, and in another verse He attributed the beautification to Himself, saying: ﴿Indeed, those who do not believe in the Hereafter — We have made their deeds appear fair to them, so they wander blindly﴾ [al-Naml 4]. How do we reconcile the two verses, that Allah sometimes attributes the beautification to Himself and sometimes to Satan?
* A student: By considering the cause, and considering the true agent: the true agent of beautification is Allah, and the cause is Satan.
* The Shaykh: The one who beautifies is Allah?
* A student: The true agent of beautification is Allah.
* The Shaykh: Which of them directly performed the beautification?
* The student: Satan.
* The Shaykh: Then he is the real one.
* The student: He is only a cause, because everything is by the decree of Allah, Exalted.
* The Shaykh: The meaning is that beautification is attributed to Allah because it is by His decree and destiny, and beautification is attributed to Satan because he directly does it. Is that so? And it is so. It is attributed to Allah, Exalted, in creation and decree, and attributed to Satan directly.
He said: ﴿Satan made their deeds appear fair to them, so he averted them from the way﴾. ﴿He averted them from the way﴾ means: he turned them away. This is a transitive use of "ṣadda," since "ṣadda" can be intransitive and transitive. If you say: "The man turned away from the way of Allah and went astray," is it intransitive or transitive?
* A student: Intransitive.
* The Shaykh: "The man turned away from the way of Allah and went astray": this is intransitive. A verse like ﴿so He averted them from the way﴾ — "turned them away" — is transitive. He said: ﴿And when it is said to them, "Come to what Allah has revealed and to the Messenger," you see the hypocrites turning away from you with aversion﴾ [al-Nisa' 61]. The verbal noun now is on the pattern fu'ūl, as Ibn Malik said:
And fa'ala for the intransitive, like qa'ada, has fu'ūl for its verbal noun...

**Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 29, verses 35–40 (part 3 of 5):**

But (ṣadda), the transitive form: what is its verbal noun?

* Student: (ṣudūd).
* Shaykh: No. The verbal noun of the transitive ṣadda is (ṣaddan), following the words of Ibn Malik:
(faʿlun) is the standard verbal noun of the transitive form from three letters ∗∗∗ ...............................
Honestly, I wish I had not cited this, because you will say: it has become useful to us. In any case, (ṣadda) comes both intransitive and transitive.
What do you say about His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Those who disbelieved and barred (others) from the way of Allah, He has caused their deeds to go astray﴾ [Muhammad 1]? Is it intransitive or transitive?
* Student: It is both intransitive and transitive. The transitive is more general. If we estimate it, it is transitive, but...
* Shaykh: It is transitive, clearly, because ﴿those who disbelieved﴾ refers to their own barring, and the intransitive is indicated by ﴿those who disbelieved﴾. So ﴿barred from the way of Allah﴾ means others. This is the closest reading.
He says: ﴿So He barred them from the way, and they were discerning﴾. "From the way": the (al-) in His saying ﴿the way﴾ is for the mental definite reference that is known, and it is the way of truth. For this reason the author said: "the way of truth." It is the way of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and it is called the way of Allah because it leads to Him, and because He is the One who set it down for His servants, as in His saying: ﴿the path of Allah, to whom belongs whatever is in the heavens﴾ [al-Shura 53]. It may also be attributed to the believers, as in His saying: ﴿and follows a path other than the way of the believers﴾ [al-Nisa 115]. How do we reconcile the two?
Sometimes Allah attributes the way to Himself, as in His saying: ﴿and barred (others) from the way of Allah﴾ [al-Nisa 167], and sometimes He attributes it to the believers, as in His saying: ﴿and follows a path other than the way of the believers﴾ [al-Nisa 115]. How do you combine them?
* Student: It is all the way of Allah. The way of the believers is the way of Allah.
* Shaykh: It is the way of Allah, but why was it attributed to the believers once and to Allah once?
* Student: Because the believers are the ones who follow it.
* Shaykh: Well said, exactly. And it is attributed to Allah, as we said a little while ago, because it leads to Him, and He is the One who legislated it for His servants, made it clear, and established it for them.
He says: ﴿So He barred them from the way, and they were discerning﴾ ("people of insight"). That is, He, glorified and exalted, gave them of intellects and insight by which they could be guided. Allah mentioned this explicitly regarding the people of Ṣāliḥ, saying: ﴿As for Thamūd, We guided them, but they preferred blindness over guidance﴾ [Fussilat 17]. They had insight and they had knowledge, but they were arrogant, and we seek refuge in Allah. So He barred them from the way even though Allah had given them what would enable them to resist Satan. But they were overcome in their affair by what Satan made attractive to them.
* Student: Shaykh, what about the verses about the disbelievers that we mentioned: ﴿they do not understand﴾, ﴿deaf, dumb, blind, so they do not reason﴾ [al-Baqara 171]?
* Shaykh: Did we not say that intellect is of two kinds?
* Student: Here it is ﴿discerning﴾.
* Shaykh: Yes. ﴿Discerning﴾ means that they have insight, that is, they have minds with which they perceive, but they do not have minds by which they are guided. In the sense that they were not guided by them. They did not benefit from them. So they have insight and knowledge, but they did not benefit from it.
* Student: They have insight but did not benefit from it?
* Shaykh: Yes, they have insight, but there is no guidance through this insight.
* Student: Shaykh, is it insight in the sense of its means being weak?
* Shaykh: Yes. They were not guided by it. The meaning is that they had knowledge and sight by which they perceive things, but they did not benefit from it.
And He, Exalted, said: ﴿And [We destroyed] Qārūn, Pharaoh and Hāmān﴾ [al-ʿAnkabūt 39]. The author said "We destroyed," and this estimate is based on the context. That is, the context indicates that there is an implied element, which is "We destroyed."
Qārūn was a merchant from the Children of Israel, but as Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿he oppressed them﴾ [al-Qaṣaṣ 76]. Allah had given him great wealth, so much that its keys would weigh down a group of men, that is, a band of people. These keys were the keys of the treasuries. For this reason, when he did not believe in Moses, he was deluded by his wealth, and we seek refuge in Allah. So he did not believe in his Lord.
Pharaoh is well known. He was the king of Egypt who claimed to be lord and said: ﴿I am your lord, the Most High﴾ [al-Nāziʿāt 24]. Hāmān was his minister.
He placed Qārūn first because of the nobility of his lineage, since he was from the Children of Israel, and they are more noble than the Copts. He placed Pharaoh before Hāmān because of Pharaoh's higher rank over him.
As for His saying: ﴿Qārūn, Pharaoh and Hāmān﴾: if someone asks, "Is this order not an instance of beginning with the lowest?"
The answer is no. If it were an instance of beginning with the lowest, he would say: "Qārūn, Hāmān, and Pharaoh."
* Student: (...) believed in him. This refutes those who say he was a hypocrite. He used to read the Torah.
* Shaykh: Who?
* Student: Some people about Qārūn. They said that Qārūn had the most beautiful voice among people when reciting the Torah, but he was deluded by his wealth.
* Shaykh: We do not know about this. If there is no text for it, we do not know about it.
﴿And Pharaoh and Hāmān. And Moses certainly came to them﴾. All of these, Qārūn, Pharaoh and Hāmān, are not declined. What is the reason for non-declension?
* Student: Definiteness as a proper name, and being non-Arabic.
* Shaykh: Definiteness as a proper name and being non-Arabic.
(﴿And Moses certainly came to them﴾ before this, ﴿with clear proofs﴾, with manifest evidences, ﴿but they waxed arrogant in the land, and they were not those who could escape﴾.) ﴿And Moses certainly came to them﴾: this sentence, as we often encounter it, is emphasized with three emphases: the implied oath, the lām, and qad.
As for His saying: (﴿And Moses certainly came to them﴾ before this, ﴿Moses﴾), before what?
* Student: Before the destruction.
* Shaykh: Before the destruction, or before ʿĀd and Thamūd?
* Student: Before the destruction.
* Shaykh: Yes. ﴿Moses with the clear proofs﴾. The bāʾ here is for accompaniment, that is, he came to them accompanied by the clear signs. This is because Allah, Exalted, does not send a messenger except that He gives him the signs by which people can believe in someone like him. Wisdom and mercy require this. It is not known, nor is it wise, for a man among people to be sent to people and say, "I am the messenger of Allah," without a sign. Is that not so? So there must be a clear sign that indicates that he is a messenger. For this reason He said: ﴿with the clear proofs﴾, that is, with the clear signs.
The author said: "the manifest proofs." Among them, for example, is the staff, and among them the hand, and likewise the years of drought by which they were seized. But despite this, they did not benefit. We ask Allah for well-being.
He said: ﴿they waxed arrogant in the land﴾. "Waxed arrogant" means that they became proud, exalted themselves, and rose up against the truth, and did not accept it. You know what happened between Moses and Pharaoh in terms of debate and threats, until the matter reached the point where he said: ﴿I will surely make you one of those imprisoned﴾ [al-Shuʿarāʾ 29].
(﴿But they waxed arrogant in the land and were not those who could escape﴾, that is, escaping Our punishment.) That is, they were not those who could outrun Us. To "outrun" means to escape. For example, if you race a person and he outruns you, that is, escapes you and you fail to catch him, these people, despite their arrogance, greatness and haughtiness, never outran Allah, Mighty and Majestic.
As for Qārūn, Allah caused the earth to swallow him and his dwelling, and he remains in it until the Day of Resurrection. His house in which he sought protection did not benefit him, nor did his wealth which he hoarded.
As for Pharaoh and Hāmān, Allah, Mighty and Majestic, drowned them by means of what Pharaoh took pride in. He said to his people: ﴿O my people, is not the kingdom of Egypt mine, and these rivers flowing beneath me? Do you not see?﴾ [al-Zukhruf 51]. So Allah expelled him from Egypt and destroyed him by means of what he had boasted of. He boasted of the rivers, so he was destroyed by what? He was destroyed by water. Allah destroyed him, and Allah, Mighty and Majestic, did not escape Him. Although when Pharaoh was being destroyed, he thought he was victorious, because he had sent heralds to the cities, and they gathered the people and followed Moses and his people, considering them a small group in their grip. They said: "They have nothing but the sea. Either they will fall into the sea, or we will seize them with a seizure that shows no leniency." But the matter, praise be to Allah, turned out the opposite: Allah destroyed Pharaoh and his people, and saved Moses and his people.
He, Glorified and Exalted, said: (﴿So each﴾ of those mentioned ﴿We seized for his sin﴾ [al-ʿAnkabūt 40]).
* Student: Just as they were ahead of others, meaning that others had preceded them in this action.
* Shaykh: No. Do you mean in time?
* Student: Yes.
* Shaykh: No. They were also ahead in time, far ahead.
* Student: Is this wāw the wāw of ḥāl (circumstantial clause), ﴿and they were not those who could escape﴾?
* Shaykh: Yes, ﴿they waxed arrogant in the land﴾. No, the apparent reading is that it is the istiʾnāf (resumptive, new sentence), which is better.
* Student: ﴿and they were not those who could escape﴾?
* Shaykh: Yes, that is better.
﴿So each﴾. The author said: (of those mentioned). The common estimate is: "So each one," but the author prevented estimating "one" because (kullan) is with tanwīn, and he does not like to change the wording of the Qur'an. For this reason he said: (of those mentioned). The grammarians say that the tanwīn in (kull) here is tanwīn of ʿiwaḍ (compensation) in place of what?
* Student: In place of a nūn.
* Shaykh: Tanwīn of compensation in place of a word, that is, "each one." As you know, tanwīn can be compensation for a word, as here, or compensation for a letter, as in (jawārin) and (ghawāshin), or compensation for a sentence, as in (idhin) in ﴿and you at that time﴾ [al-Wāqiʿa 84], and (yawmaʾidhin), and similar.
He said: ﴿So each We seized for his sin﴾, that is, each of these, Allah, Mighty and Majestic, seized for his sin. The bāʾ in His saying ﴿for his sin﴾ is causal, and it is also of exchange and equivalence, that is, they were seized because of their sins, and in proportion to their sins they were seized. So the bāʾ here is causal and of compensation: they were seized because of sin, but Allah did not exceed in punishing them more than they deserved, but by the cause and the measure.
As for His saying ﴿for his sin﴾, in the Noble Qur'an there also occurs ﴿We destroyed them for their sins﴾ [al-Anʿām 6]. Reconciling the plural and the singular is easy: it can be said that the singular here is in the genitive construction, so it is general, that is, "for their sins." And sins are acts of disobedience, whether major or minor, and here they are without doubt among the greatest major sins.
﴿Among them﴾: this is the detail, because His saying ﴿for his sin﴾ is general, and it is specified by His saying: ﴿Among them is one upon whom We sent a violent wind﴾ ("We sent upon him"). He did not say "to him," because here it is sending punishment, so it is above them, and it is not sending address, so that we would say the object of this address is the one to whom it is sent. It is the sending of punishment.
(﴿We sent upon them a violent wind﴾, a sweeping wind with pebbles, like the people of Lot.)
* Student: ﴿Indeed We sent upon them a violent wind﴾ [al-Qamar 34].
* Shaykh: Yes, but this requires consideration, because what is understood about the people of Lot: was what was sent upon them from the sky, or not? A violent wind from the sky, and it was stones of baked clay, like what was sent upon the people of the Elephant, or not? And it was not pebbles stirred up by winds. We do not know that Allah sent winds upon the people of Lot. If it were winds carrying pebbles, Allah, Mighty and Majestic, would have made it clear, so that it would be said: "We sent upon him a violent wind, like the people of Lot." Is that right? Allah sent upon them a violent wind from the sky that pelted them with stones of baked clay.
﴿And among them is the one seized by the Cry﴾, like what?
* Students: Thamūd.
* Shaykh: The author says: (like Thamūd), the people of Ṣāliḥ. And the people of Madyan, the companions of Shuʿayb, were they not seized by the Cry?
* Students: Yes.
* Student: They were seized by the Earthquake, Shaykh.
* Shaykh: Which ones?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Here, but in another verse: ﴿The Cry seized them﴾ [al-Ḥijr 73].
(﴿And among them is the one whom We caused the earth to swallow﴾, like Qārūn, ﴿and among them is the one whom We drowned﴾, like the people of Noah, and Pharaoh and his people.) These were destroyed by drowning. As for Pharaoh and his people, they drowned in the Red Sea. And the second, who?
* Student: Noah, by the Flood.
* Shaykh: Noah, by the Flood, the great Flood, which Allah, Glorified and Exalted, commanded the sky so that it opened its gates with pouring water, and caused the earth to burst forth with springs. Look, glory be to Allah, at the expression. He did not say: "We caused the springs of the earth to gush forth." Had the expression been "We caused the springs of the earth to gush forth," much dry land would not have burst forth. Rather, the springs gushed out, but: ﴿We caused the earth to gush forth with springs﴾ [al-Qamar 12]. It is as if the whole earth became springs, to the point that the oven, which is the place where fire is kindled and the furthest place from water appearing in it, began to boil with springs. Glory be to Allah the Great! ﴿And the waters met for a matter already decreed﴾ [al-Qamar 12], until they rose over the peaks of the mountains, and the ship settled on al-Jūdī. Al-Jūdī is a very high mountain, to the point that the water carried it until it came to rest on this mountain, which indicates the abundance of these waters. Allah is Greatest!
If a person imagined that rain rose four meters, he would be astonished at that. But this, by the power of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, rose to hundreds of meters, and Allah is powerful over all things.
He said: ﴿And among them is the one whom We drowned, and Allah would not wrong them﴾, by punishing them without sin. Allah would not do this. ﴿Allah would not wrong them.﴾ The lām here, what do they call it?
* Student: Muzaḥlaqa.
* Shaykh: No, there are no slidings.
* Student: The lām of emphasis.
* Shaykh: Not the lām of emphasis either. My brothers, this is the lām of denial (lām al-juḥūd), because the lām of denial is the one preceded by a negated state, or we say to the students of al-Ājurrūmiyya: what precedes it, (mā kāna)?
* Student: Or (mā yakun).
* Shaykh: No, or (lam yakun). (mā kāna) or (lam yakun). Here, what precedes it is (mā kāna). ﴿Allah would not wrong them﴾, and injustice has two aspects (...). When He denied that Allah wronged them, He clarified where this injustice came from, saying: ﴿but they were wronging themselves﴾ [al-ʿAnkabūt 40]. ﴿Themselves﴾ is the predicate of (kāna), and the wāw is its subject.
* Student: No, ﴿themselves﴾ is a verbal sentence as the predicate of (kāna), and ﴿themselves﴾ is the object of ﴿they wrong﴾.
* Shaykh: ﴿Themselves they wrong.﴾
* Student: They were wronging themselves.
* Another student: It is the predicate of an omitted subject.
* Shaykh: No, the subject of (kāna) is the wāw in ﴿kānū﴾. If it were an emphasis, it would be in the accusative.
* Student: In the accusative, governed by ﴿yaẓlimūn﴾ by way of the construction of ishtighāl (the verb is occupied with the pronoun).
* Shaykh: By way of ishtighāl? What do you say now? Do you agree?
* Student: The noun is interpreted, and the predicate is a sentence.
* Shaykh: The discussion is about ﴿anfusahum﴾. What do we say about it?
* Student: It is the object of ﴿yaẓlimūn﴾.
* Shaykh: The object of ﴿yaẓlimūn﴾, by way of ishtighāl?
* Student: No, there is no pronoun here (...), it is not permissible to use ishtighāl here.
* Shaykh: So it is a fronted object of ﴿yaẓlimūn﴾, or not? And there is no ishtighāl, because ishtighāl, as Ibn Malik says:
If a pronoun of a preceding noun is occupied by a verb, diverting it from that noun by putting it in the accusative in form or in place.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 29, verse 35–40 (part 4 of 5):

Al-ishtighal (the grammatical construction of "occupation," in which a pronoun in the verb refers back to a preceding noun) must always have a pronoun in the occupied verb; that is why we call it ishtighal. Here, however, "أنفسهم" (anfusahum, "themselves") is a direct object placed before its verb "يظلمون" (yazlimun, "they wrong"), and placing it first has two benefits: a verbal benefit and a semantic benefit. The verbal benefit is observing the fawasil (the rhyming endings of the verses). That is, the ends of the verses. This is the verbal benefit: had he said, "ولكن كانوا يظلمون أنفسهم" (wa-lakin kanu yazlimuna anfusahum), it would not have harmonized with what came before and after it. The second, the semantic benefit, is restriction and exclusivity (al-hasr wal-ikhtisas); that is, "they wronged no one but themselves." In reality, it is they who did the wronging. As God the Exalted says in another verse: ﴿وَمَا ظَلَمْنَاهُمْ وَلَكِنْ كَانُوا هُمُ الظَّالِمِينَ﴾ [az-Zukhruf 76] "We did not wrong them, but they were the wrongdoers." As for us, we did not wrong them.

* Student: Shaykh, is there an implied reference to the people of Noah? That is, does the context make this one of them, and the story of Noah? Noah is only mentioned at the beginning of the surah. Is Noah not mentioned?
* Shaykh: Yes. So what of it?
* Student: "فمنهم" (faminhum, "among them") means among those mentioned: 'Ad and those before them, Qarun, Pharaoh and Haman, these who were mentioned. That is, "each of those mentioned, We seized for his sin." "Faminhum" is in order. The mention of the people of Noah here has a basis.
* Another student: The people of Noah are the cause mentioned at the beginning of the surah...
* Shaykh: It does not matter. In any case, from among the people. Do you want the pronoun to refer to the nearest mentioned party?
* Student: Yes, and its order: the sequence. Sometimes the Qur'anic order is sequential; it mentions the punishment in sequence according to the order.
* Shaykh: "Whoever was seized by the Blast," we say, like Thamud. But this is not in that order, because Shu'ayb came before these.
* Student: But we said Thamud were seized by the Blast, which fits Shu'ayb and the people of Madyan and Thamud.
* Shaykh: If we observe the order, is it not suitable here for Thamud or not? Or it is suitable, because it comes before Qarun: ﴿فَمِنْهُمْ مَنْ أَخَذَتْهُ الصَّيْحَةُ وَمِنْهُمْ مَنْ خَسَفْنَا بِهِ الْأَرْضَ﴾ "Among them is one seized by the Blast, and among them is one We caused the earth to swallow." Especially since the author says: ﴿فَكُلًّا﴾ "each" (of those mentioned). If he had said, "each of the wrongdoers," anyway the matter is simple, since there is an example of this and that.
God the Exalted says: ﴿وَلَقَد تَرَكْنَا مِنْهَا آيَةً بَيِّنَةً لِقَوْمٍ يَعْقِلُونَ﴾ [al-'Ankabut 35] "And We have left from it a clear sign for a people who reason."
* Among the benefits of this verse: the wisdom of God the Exalted in preserving the traces of the signs, ﴿وَلَقَد تَرَكْنَا مِنْهَا﴾, because the intention is their preservation.
* Among its benefits: that none benefit from the signs except people of intellect, by His saying: ﴿لِقَوْمٍ يَعْقِلُونَ﴾.
* Among them: the benefit of intellect. Whenever a person is given intellect, it is a blessing from God upon him; the more intelligent he is, the more it is a blessing from God. From where do we take the benefit of intellect? From the fact that its possessor benefits from it in the signs that God, the Mighty and Majestic, has left.
Then He said: ﴿وَإِلَى مَدْيَنَ أَخَاهُمْ شُعَيْبًا فَقَالَ يَا قَوْمِ اعْبُدُوا اللَّهَ وَارْجُوا الْيَوْمَ الآخِرَ﴾ and so on to the end [al-'Ankabut 36] "And to Madyan, their brother Shu'ayb. He said: O my people, worship God and hope for the Last Day..."
* Among the benefits of this verse: the affirmation of God's mercy and wisdom in sending messengers. The sending of messengers indicates mercy and wisdom. As for mercy, it is clear, because servants cannot benefit by their intellects in worshipping God, the Mighty and Majestic. For this reason the scholars say that acts of worship are tawqifi (determined by revelation). As for wisdom, it is so that people will have no proof against God after the messengers.
* Among the benefits of the verse: that the prophet is usually from his own people, because the prophets mentioned in the whole Qur'an are described with His saying: ﴿إِلَى قَوْمِهِ﴾ "to his people" and ﴿أَخَاهُمْ﴾ "their brother" and what is similar to that.
The wisdom behind this, meaning: from it arises * another benefit: that a messenger should ideally be known among his people, so that they assist him, help him, and do not deny him.
* Among the benefits of the verse: the obligation of worshipping God, by His saying: ﴿اعْبُدُوا اللَّهَ﴾.
* Among them: the obligation of preparing for the Last Day, by His saying: ﴿وَارْجُوا الْيَوْمَ الْآخِرَ﴾.
* Among them: the affirmation of the Last Day. Is it clear?
* Among them: the prohibition of corruption on earth, by His saying: ﴿وَلَا تَعْثَوْا فِي الْأَرْضِ مُفْسِدِينَ﴾ "and do not commit corruption on the earth, causing mischief." The basic principle in a prohibition is that it is forbidden.
* Among them: that the sharia combines both the positive and the negative. The positive is by what? By commands. The negative is by prohibitions. That is, the sharia consists of actions and abstentions; it is not merely actions, and nothing reforms the servants except this. A person may find commands suitable and prohibitions unsuitable, and he may find prohibitions suitable and commands difficult. So God the Exalted combined command and prohibition in His sharia.
* Among them: I said, the prohibition of corruption on earth?
* Student: Yes.
* Shaykh: And we mentioned in the tafsir that this corruption includes moral corruption through sins and physical corruption through destruction and ruin.
Then He said: ﴿فَكَذَّبُوهُ فَأَخَذَتْهُمُ الرَّجْفَةُ فَأَصْبَحُوا فِي دَارِهِمْ جَاثِمِينَ﴾ [al-'Ankabut 37] "But they denied him, and the quake seized them, and they became prostrate in their homes."
* Among the benefits of this verse: the explanation of what the messengers, peace be upon them, suffer from their peoples, by His saying: ﴿فَكَذَّبُوه﴾ "they denied him." There is no doubt that the denial of a person who is upon the truth affects him to the utmost degree. A person who has the truth and the signs, and came for the benefit of creation, and then they deny him: this is not an easy matter for the soul.
* Also among the benefits of the verse: the consolation of those who call to God, the Mighty and Majestic, when they are opposed in their call. How so? How is this consolation? That the messengers were denied, so they are even more deserving of it. For this reason God consoles the Prophet, peace be upon him, with such: ﴿فَإِنْ كَذَّبُوكَ فَقَدْ كُذِّبَ رُسُلٌ مِنْ قَبْلِكَ جَاءُوا بِالْبَيِّنَاتِ وَالزُّبُرِ وَالْكِتَابِ الْمُنِيرِ﴾ [Al 'Imran 184] "If they deny you, messengers before you were denied, who came with clear proofs, the scriptures, and the illuminating Book." And ﴿وَلَقَدْ كُذِّبَتْ رُسُلٌ مِنْ قَبْلِكَ فَصَبَرُوا عَلَى مَا كُذِّبُوا وَأُوذُوا﴾ [al-An'am 34] "And messengers before you were denied, and they were patient over what they were denied and harmed." So the one who calls to God should not disdain being denied, for this is the path of the messengers, peace be upon them, and their followers will be like them.
* Among the benefits of the verse: the hastening of punishment for the one who denies, but when? If we say that the fa' in His saying ﴿فَأَخَذَتْهُمُ﴾ is what? It is 'atifah (conjunctive, indicating sequence). But if we say it is sababiyyah (causal), it does not indicate this, because the effect may be delayed after the cause.
* Among them, among the benefits of the verse: the wisdom of God the Mighty and Majestic in punishing those who deny their messengers.
* Among them: that punishment is neither oppression nor injustice, because God the Exalted is exalted above wronging, and He wrongs no one. Had these people not been punished justly, God would not have punished them.
* Among them: the power of God the Exalted, by His saying: ﴿فَأَصْبَحُوا فِي دَارِهِمْ جَاثِمِينَ﴾. And how many were they? Their number? A people, a large tribe, whom God annihilated in a moment. This is evidence of His power, and that when He wills a thing, He says to it: "Be," and it is.
* Among them: that shelters do not benefit from God. It is taken from His saying: ﴿فِي دَارِهِمْ﴾ "in their homes." The home is a shelter for a person, where he seeks refuge from his enemy, but in relation to God, it neither prevents nor benefits. For this reason He said: ﴿أَصْبَحُوا فِي دَارِهِمْ﴾.
Then God the Exalted said: ﴿وَعَادًا وَثَمُودَ وَقَدْ تَبَيَّنَ لَكُمْ مِنْ مَسَاكِنِهِمْ وَزَيَّنَ لَهُمُ الشَّيْطَانُ أَعْمَالَهُمْ فَصَدَّهُمْ عَنِ السَّبِيلِ وَكَانُوا مُسْتَبْصِرِينَ﴾ [al-'Ankabut 38] "And 'Ad and Thamud, and it has become clear to you from their dwellings. Satan made their deeds attractive to them and barred them from the way, though they were discerning."
* Among the benefits of this verse: first, that one should take heed from the conditions of those who passed away. From where is this taken? ﴿وَقَدْ تَبَيَّنَ لَكُمْ مِنْ مَسَاكِنِهِمْ﴾ meaning: take heed and be admonished.
* Among them: the demonstration of God the Exalted's power, because 'Ad were among the strongest of God's servants, to the point that they said: ﴿مَنْ أَشَدُّ مِنَّا قُوَّةً﴾ [Fussilat 15] "Who is mightier than us in strength?" Yet God destroyed them with the gentlest of things. What is it?
* Student: The wind.
* Shaykh: With the wind. The wind, which is among the gentlest things, God destroyed them with it. This indicates the perfection of God the Exalted's power, and that however strong people become, their strength is nothing compared to the strength of God.
* Among the benefits of the verse: that Satan may be given power over the children of Adam, by His saying: ﴿وَزَيَّنَ لَهُمُ الشَّيْطَانُ أَعْمَالَهُمْ﴾.
* Among them: a warning against the beautification of deeds. I think we all understand that His saying ﴿زَيَّنَ﴾ "made attractive" and ﴿أَعْمَالَهُمْ﴾ "their deeds" indicates that these deeds are originally ugly, but they were made attractive, so one must beware of Satan's beautification.
If someone says: what is the criterion for Satan's beautification? A deed may appeal to me and seem attractive within myself, so I do it, but I do not know whether it is from Satan's beautification or from God's beautification. What is the criterion?
The criterion: if the deed is contrary to God's sharia, it is from Satan's beautification. If it conforms to God's sharia, it is from God's guidance and not from Satan's beautification.
* Among them: the affirmation of devils and their influence on the children of Adam, by His saying: ﴿وَزَيَّنَ لَهُمُ الشَّيْطَانُ أَعْمَالَهُمْ﴾.
* Among them: the refutation of the Jabriyyah (determinists) regarding the attribution of deeds to them. When they are attributed to them, it means that they are actually the doers.
* Also among the benefits of the verse: that evil deeds may be a cause of the servant's misguidance, by His saying: ﴿وَزَيَّنَ لَهُمُ الشَّيْطَانُ أَعْمَالَهُمْ فَصَدَّهُمْ﴾. There is no doubt that evil deeds are a cause of the servant's misguidance. ﴿فَبِمَا نَقْضِهِمْ مِيثَاقَهُمْ لَعَنَّاهُمْ وَجَعَلْنَا قُلُوبَهُمْ قَاسِيَةً يُحَرِّفُونَ الْكَلِمَ عَنْ مَوَاضِعِهِ وَنَسُوا حَظًّا مِمَّا ذُكِّرُوا بِهِ﴾ [al-Ma'idah 13] "So for their breaking of their covenant, We cursed them and made their hearts hard; they distort words from their places and have forgotten a portion of what they were reminded of." Evil deeds drag one another along until a person becomes blind, may God protect us, to the truth because of his disobedience.
* Among the benefits of the verse: the monstrousness of barring from the way while being discerning. From where is this taken? From His saying: ﴿وَكَانُوا مُسْتَبْصِرِينَ﴾, for the clause here is a circumstantial clause with the implied "qad": "so He barred them, though they had been discerning." The discerning person was on the verge of not barring, but, may God protect us, the strength of the cause and the weakness of the preventer is what necessitated that they bar others from the way of God.
* Among the benefits of the verse: the use or consideration of the indication of expressions by what the addressee understands. I mean that the "al" in His saying ﴿السَّبِيلِ﴾ "the way" is for prior reference (al-'ahd). Which kind of reference? The mental reference (al-'ahd al-dhihni).
* This is evidence that the addressee may be referred to what he understands in his mind from the indication of the address, and that is so.
So if someone says: this verse contains vagueness about "the way," we do not know which way?
We say: there is no vagueness in it, since there is something known to the addressee, and so there is no vagueness in it.
Then He said: ﴿وَقَارُونَ وَفِرْعَوْنَ وَهَامَانَ وَلَقَدْ جَاءَهُمْ مُوسَى بِالْبَيِّنَاتِ فَاسْتَكْبَرُوا فِي الْأَرْضِ وَمَا كَانُوا سَابِقِينَ﴾ [al-'Ankabut 39] "And Qarun, Pharaoh, and Haman. Moses had come to them with clear proofs, but they acted arrogantly in the land, yet they could not outrun (Us)."
* In it is the censure of these three individuals: Qarun, Pharaoh, and Haman.
* Also among its benefits: the cause of tyranny may be wealth, and it may be status and leadership. In Qarun's case, the cause of his tyranny was wealth; in Pharaoh's and Haman's case, status and leadership. These two causes are the cause of a person's arrogance against obedience to God, the Exalted.
* Among its benefits: the affirmation of the mission of Musa, peace be upon him, by His saying: ﴿وَلَقَدْ جَاءَهُمْ مُوسَى بِالْبَيِّنَاتِ﴾.
* Among its benefits: that Musa was a messenger to Pharaoh and to the Children of Israel. Was Pharaoh from the Children of Israel?
* Student: No.
* Shaykh: From where?
* Student: From the Copts.
* Shaykh: From the Copts. How do we reconcile this with the saying of the Messenger of God, ﷺ: "The prophet used to be sent only to his own people" [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (335), Muslim (521/3), from Jabir ibn 'Abdullah], while the people of Musa are the Children of Israel, and Musa was sent to Pharaoh and to the Children of Israel?
* Student: They were present in Egypt, in Pharaoh's kingdom, the Children of Israel. Then he [Pharaoh] enslaved them and prevented them from leaving. So it was required that he go to him first so that they would leave with him and worship God, the Mighty and Majestic, as He wished, and he [Pharaoh] prevented them. So it was necessary...
* Shaykh: That is: the presence of the Children of Israel in Pharaoh's kingdom, does wisdom require that he be sent to both of them?
* Student: That is not quite it. He [Pharaoh] prevented them and enslaved them in the land.
* Shaykh: Yes, and he also prevented Musa from taking the Children of Israel with him.
* Student: Yes. So it was necessary to direct him to him, to free them from this enslavement.
* Shaykh: Yes.
* Student: That the prophet is sent to his people, and whoever entered the religion from others (...).
* Shaykh: Very well, then Pharaoh would be a follower of the Children of Israel, although the original message was to whom? To Pharaoh. How can the one who is originally the primary target become the follower? So let us return to what he said.
* Student: Whether they were his people as followers or followers of others.
* Shaykh: So we return to this and say: it means that the Children of Israel cannot be reformed until the one who has control over them is reformed. Is this what you mean?
* Student: God's saying: ﴿وَنُرِيدُ أَنْ نَمُنَّ عَلَى الَّذِينَ اسْتُضْعِفُوا فِي الْأَرْضِ﴾ [al-Qasas 5] "And We wished to bestow favor upon those who were oppressed in the land."
* Shaykh: The important point now is that we all agree that the message was to whom? To Pharaoh and to the Children of Israel. Indeed, it was to Pharaoh primarily.
* Student: (...) says: send with us the Children of Israel, the Messenger of God to them.
* Shaykh: He called him to God. Indeed, the verses: "We sent Musa to Pharaoh," all indicate that the primary message was to Pharaoh.
* Student: It is permissible to say that God the Exalted's wisdom requires that He send to the peoples of the prophets, because they have zeal for him, inclination toward him, and support for him. Here with Pharaoh, he also has zeal and inclination toward him, considering that he raised him and that he grew up under his care, so he shared with the Children of Israel in this attribute.
* Shaykh: My view, and God knows best, is that the answer is one of two ways. The first way: that His saying, "The prophet used to be sent only to his own people," is not the first general statement to be specified. We can say: this is according to the majority and the general case, and we say that the evidence indicates Musa was sent to Pharaoh and to the Children of Israel. This answer is not forced; this answer contains no artificiality.
We can also say: the message was to Pharaoh because the Children of Israel could not become independent, nor fulfill the duty of the message and following Musa, unless Pharaoh was guided. For this reason they had no state or authority until God destroyed Pharaoh. So this means: Pharaoh was targeted first, because it was not possible to reach the Children of Israel and establish the call among them until this man either embraced Islam or was destroyed, as is what actually happened. Thus his message here is a means toward the goal. Musa, peace be upon him, was sent to the Children of Israel, but the message among the Children of Israel could not be realized until this man was guided or God decided his fate. What actually occurred is that God decided his fate after the signs and proofs that came, and so on.
* Student: And the other Copts, other than Pharaoh, were they not addressed by the call?
* Shaykh: It appears that the Copts in Egypt, indeed everyone under Pharaoh's authority, are included in this, because when Pharaoh believes, they will necessarily believe, since he has control over them.
* Student: Do we not say that "the people" is more general than (...) that the tribe of Musa is from the Children of Israel and his people are people (...)?
* Shaykh: If we say that what is meant by "people" is those among whom he was sent, then the meaning becomes: if the prophet were sent to all people, they would all become his people, and thus the implication of the end of the hadith is nullified. And it has passed us in the story of Shu'ayb that he was also sent to the companions of the Thicket (al-Aykah), and they were not from his people, as is evident from the fact that he did not say: "their brother."

The Answer: We say that this generality has been specified. The evidences indicate that some Messengers were sent to their own people and to others who followed them, and that no Messenger was sent to all of mankind except Muhammad (ﷺ).

His saying: ﴿And Moses had certainly come to them with clear proofs﴾.

* Among the benefits of the verse: Messengers are supported with clear signs, from His saying ﴿with clear proofs﴾. It is established from the Messenger (ﷺ) that he said: "There is no prophet except that he was given signs such that people believed because of their like"[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (7274) and Muslim (152/239) from Abu Hurayrah.]].
* Also among its benefits: the affirmation of mercy and wisdom in the signs of the prophets, isn't it so? Because the signs that accompany the Messengers are mercy toward creation and wisdom. Mercy, so that they may be a means of their guidance; and wisdom, so that the proof is established against them, lest someone say: "This Messenger did not bring us any sign, so he is a liar." So the affirmation of signs for the prophets includes mercy and wisdom. As for mercy, how do we say that giving the prophets signs includes mercy?
* A student: They could not worship except through the Messengers.
* The Shaykh: How?
* The student: If Allah sends the Messengers.
* The Shaykh: Yes indeed. We said: the signs given to the prophets include the affirmation of Allah's mercy and wisdom.
* A student: (...) lest they go astray (...).
* The Shaykh: Because the signs are a means to their guidance; when they see the signs, they are guided. Wisdom: how is that?
* A student: (...) he doesn't say: "His help did not come"?
* The Shaykh: No, that is not it. We are not asking about the wisdom of sending the Messengers, but the wisdom of giving the Messengers signs.
* A student: So that the proof is established against them.
* The Shaykh: Against whom?
* A student: Against the people.
* The Shaykh: It is said to them: "You denied those whose truthfulness was established by signs."
He said: ﴿with clear proofs﴾.
* Among the benefits of the verse: the vileness of the disbelief of these three: Qarun, Fir'awn and Haman, and that is by being arrogant toward the truth and turning away from it. For this reason He said: ﴿but they were arrogant in the land﴾.
* Among its benefits: the perfection of Allah's power, the Exalted, in that none of His creation can escape Him. From His saying: ﴿and they could not outrun [Us]﴾. Despite their greatness, their pride and their wealth, they could not outrun Allah. This is the realization of the saying of the Messenger (ﷺ) in the remembrances of prayer: "And no fortune benefits its possessor against You, for fortune"[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (844) and Muslim (593/137) from al-Mughirah ibn Shu'bah.]]. Whatever a person's greatness and abundance, his greatness and abundance will not benefit him.

And His saying: ﴿So each We seized for his sin: Among them were those upon whom We sent a storm of stones, and among them were those who were seized by the Blast, and among them were those whom We caused the earth to swallow, and among them were those We drowned﴾.

* Among the benefits of this verse: the completeness of Allah's power in sending these punishments, for they are all punishments that point to His power.
* Among them: the refutation of the statements of these atheists. When similar signs occur in the present time, they say: "These are natural disasters." Earthquakes come, which are the quaking, and they say: "This is a natural matter." Great floods come that destroy, and they say: "These are natural disasters." They take no lesson from them, and they regard them as a kind of punishment that befell earlier nations. Likewise the strong winds. This is from the death of hearts, may Allah protect us, that a person turns away from reflection and contemplation on these signs and attributes them to natural causes, as if, according to their claim, nature is what creates and acts without Allah.
* Among the benefits of the verse: the affirmation of Allah's wisdom, the Mighty and Majestic, from His saying: ﴿We seized for his sin﴾, whether we say the letter "bi" (ba') indicates causation or exchange.
* Among them: the affirmation of causes. Whenever a lam of purpose or a ba' of causation comes to you in the Qur'an, it indicates the affirmation of causes and wisdoms.
* Among them: the refutation of the Jabriyya (determinists), who deny causes, and those who agree with them among the Ash'ariyya (followers of al-Ash'ari). We, the Ahl al-Sunna wal-Jama'a (the People of the Sunnah and the Community), believe in causes, but we do not say that these causes have an effect by themselves. Rather, Allah, the Exalted, creates their effect.
* Among them: that the recompense is of the same kind as the deed. Which of the two possibilities for the ba' is this: the exchange or the correspondence? The recompense is of the same kind as the deed, from His saying: ﴿So each We seized for his sin﴾. Know that the recompense is of the same kind as the deed in legal penalties and in natural penalties. Legal penalties such as the hudud (the fixed penalties prescribed by the Shari'ah). The hudud are penalties fixed by the Shari'ah, and they are all in reality punishments. Cutting off the hand for theft is undoubtedly in accord with wisdom, because the hand is what takes. Cutting off the hands and feet on opposite sides for highway robbers is in accord with wisdom, because highway robbers attack people with their hands and feet. Stoning the adulterer rather than killing him with the sword is also in accord with wisdom. Likewise, all legal and natural punishments are in accord with wisdom, and this is shown by His saying: ﴿So each We seized for his sin﴾.
* Also among the benefits of the verse: His saying ﴿a storm of stones﴾, the Blast, the swallowing and the drowning. These four kinds of punishment are mentioned for a wisdom. His saying ﴿upon whom We sent a storm of stones﴾ is destruction that came from above; ﴿whom We caused the earth to swallow﴾ is from below; ﴿who were seized by the Blast﴾ is destruction by speech and sound.
His saying ﴿whom We drowned﴾ is destruction by water. This is so that it may be clear to people that punishments do not come in one kind; they come in many kinds, according to the condition of the one being punished.
* Among them: the clarification of the perfection of Allah's justice, from His saying: ﴿And Allah did not wrong them﴾. Is this attribute one of the negative attributes or the affirmative attributes?
* A student: Negative.
* The Shaykh: Negative. It has come before us several times that negative attributes are not praise unless they include an affirmation. Mere negation is not praise until it includes an affirmation. If Allah negates wrongdoing from Himself, that does not mean only that He does not wrong, but that, because of the perfection of His justice, He does not wrong. The meaning is not that He is unable to wrong; rather He is capable, the Exalted, of wronging, but because of the perfection of His justice He does not wrong. If He were unable to wrong, negating wrongdoing from Him would not be praise, isn't it so?
* A student: Yes.
* The Shaykh: For this reason they said, regarding the poet's saying:
A tribe that does not betray a covenant
and does not wrong people even by a mustard seed's weight.
Is the negation of wrongdoing from this group praise or blame?
* Students: Blame.
* The Shaykh: In this context it is blame, meaning: because of their weakness they do not wrong. Likewise the poet's saying:
But my people, though they are of noble lineage,
are not in any way evil, and they are not...
That is, they are not evil in any respect, and they do not do evil, and there is no evil in them at all. Even more eloquent than this is that they
repay the wrong of wrongdoers with forgiveness,
and the offense of the offenders with kindness.
If someone wrongs them, they meet him with forgiveness and pardon; likewise, if someone harms them, they respond with kindness. Its outward meaning is praise, and he says: "May Allah reward them with good." But in reality it is among the strongest blame, because it belittles them and says that they cannot avenge themselves or defend themselves. Rather, if they are harmed, they respond with kindness out of fear of greater harm, and if they are wronged, they forgive. For this reason the same poet said:
Would that I had people who, when they ride,
raid as horsemen and as riders on foot.
He wished that Allah would give him people in their place.
The point is that mere negation does not indicate perfection unless it includes praise and affirmation.
* Among the benefits of the verse: a person is the wrongdoer of his own soul by committing sins, from His saying: ﴿but they were wronging themselves﴾. So you are forbidden to commit sins, because it is a wrong to yourself. As for Allah, the Exalted, He does not wrong. We have the negation of attributes in general: it may include perfection, it may include deficiency, and it may be due to non-receptivity. So which of these applies to Allah?
* A student: Perfection.
* The Shaykh: Perfection. It may be for perfection, as in this verse and as in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿and no weariness touched Us﴾ [Qaf 38]. And it may be the negation of deficiency for what?
* A student: For non-receptivity.
* The Shaykh: For non-receptivity. Like saying: "This wall does not get tired," and "This wall does not wrong." Why? Because of non-receptivity. Is this praise for it? No, because it does not in the first place accept this attribute so as to be negated from it. And the negation may be due to inability, as we mentioned in the examples of the two verses:
But my people, though they are of noble lineage,
are not in any way evil, and they are not...
And for Allah, of these three categories, only the first applies, which is what includes perfection and praise. For this reason the scholars say that when Allah negates an attribute from Himself, two things are meant: the negation of that attribute, and the affirmation of the perfection of its opposite.
* A student: Shaykh, is the statement that the negation of wrongdoing from Allah is because He is the one who disposes of the dominion?
* The Shaykh: No, this is an error. This is the statement of the Jabriyya. It is not correct. They say that wrongdoing is impossible for Allah in His essence, not because Allah does not will it. They say: wrongdoing is for a person to dispose of another's property, and when Allah disposes of His own dominion, He is not a wrongdoer. So, according to their claim, it is permissible, and it is not wrongdoing, for Him to punish the obedient one who spent his night and day in obedience to Allah by punishing him with the punishment of the disbeliever. They consider this not to be wrongdoing, because it is said: Allah only disposes of His own dominion. On this basis, al-Safarini, may Allah have mercy on him, said:
And it is permissible for the Master to punish the creatures
without any sin or crime that has occurred.
So everything that comes from Him, the Exalted, is beautiful,
because He is not asked about what He does.
(...) in Allah, the Exalted, and that the attributes of Allah, the Exalted, are divided into two types: affirmative and negative. The affirmative are those that Allah affirmed for Himself, and they are only attributes of perfection. The negative are those that Allah negated from Himself, and they are only attributes of deficiency. The negative attributes revolve around two things: one is deficiency, and the second is resemblance to created beings. If we say that resemblance to created beings is a deficiency and we limit these two things to one thing, that would not be far off, for resembling what is deficient is considered a deficiency.
* It is derived from the verse, from its end, in His saying: ﴿but they were wronging themselves﴾, that the disobedient one is a wrongdoer to his own soul. The reason is that the soul is a trust with you. Just as you are forbidden to diminish it in a physical way, you are forbidden to diminish it in a spiritual way. That is, if a person wished to cut off his hand, his finger, or to harm his body, that would be forbidden. For this reason, whoever kills himself with something will be punished with it in Hell forever and ever[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (5778) and Muslim (109/175) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]]. So the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, made the one who kills himself like the one who kills another in being eternal in the Fire and in being punished with what he killed with.
On this basis we say: everyone who disobeys Allah is a wrongdoer to himself. From here we know the meaning of His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And who would turn away from the religion of Abraham except one who makes a fool of himself﴾ [al-Baqarah 130], and that turning away from the religion of Abraham is foolishness, because it is a wronging of oneself without the person being aware of it.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 29, verse 41–44 (part 1 of 3):

Then He, the Exalted, said: ﴿The example of those who take protectors other than Allah﴾ — idols, whom they hope will benefit them — ﴿is like the example of the spider﴾ [al-'Ankabut 41].

(Mathal and mithl) are like (shabah and shibh), in form and in meaning. So mathal means likeness (shabah), and it is an expression for comparing an intelligible thing with a perceptible thing, because representing intelligible matters through perceptible ones increases them in clarity, explanation and conception. Is this understood? And although they are not equal in every respect, they are equal in the respect in which the comparison is made.

His saying: ﴿The example of those who take protectors other than Allah﴾ means: those who made protectors. The intended meaning of "protectors" is the idols, and they were called protectors because their worshippers hope for their benefit, like a protector who benefits you by support, defence, bringing good, and similar things. Also, they are called protectors in that they themselves ..

.. This is why the people of Abraham said: ﴿Burn him and support your gods, if you are going to act﴾ [al-Anbiya' 68]. They support them and hope for support from them, and for this reason these idols were named (protectors).

His saying: ﴿other than Allah﴾ means: besides Him. The evidence that the intended meaning is "besides" in the sense of "other than" is that this occurs in several verses, such as His saying: ﴿You have no god other than Him﴾ [al-A'raf 59]. The expression "dun" (besides) is used because its rank is lowly in comparison to whom? To Allah, Mighty and Majestic. ﴿other than Allah, protectors﴾ [al-'Ankabut 41]. Their likeness, then, — who is meant by those who take protectors other than Allah? It refers to the polytheists, their likeness ﴿is like the example of the spider﴾ [al-'Ankabut 41]; that is, like the likeness of the spider. The spider is a well-known small creature that takes for itself a house made of web, and this house of web is what it weaves and emerges from. Allah, glory be to Him, is capable of all things. When this spider falls from a height, it immediately secretes this web and clings to it so that it does not fall to the ground; then, despite that, it secretes it and clings to it, and you find it hanging by this thread. When it wishes to climb up with it, it climbs, turning itself over and making its head the highest, and it climbs with this thread that it has just secreted. Then, when it is hunting — and it mostly hunts flies — what does it do with them? It binds them with these threads until it finishes them off. This is part of the saying of the Exalted: ﴿Our Lord is He who gave everything its creation, then guided it﴾ [Ta-Ha 50], guiding this creation to what is good for it. The point is that this spider took a house for itself, that is, made for itself a house. From what? From the web that it weaves.

The author said: (﴿took a house﴾ [al-'Ankabut 41] for itself, to which it retreats), and this is observed. ﴿And indeed the frailest﴾ [al-'Ankabut 41], the weakest ﴿of houses is the house of the spider﴾ [al-'Ankabut 41]. This is the word of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, who is the Knower of what we have not encompassed in knowledge. How many of Allah's creatures have houses, while we know of these houses only what we witness of them, and how much is hidden from us! Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, says: "The frailest of houses is the house of the spider." He emphasised this sentence ﴿And indeed the frailest of houses is the house of the spider﴾ with (inna) and the lam, in order to stress the weakness of these protectors, just as the houses in which spiders take refuge are weak; indeed they are the frailest and weakest of houses, for these protectors are likewise the weakest of protectors, since they do not benefit their worshippers. Rather, Allah says in the Qur'an: ﴿Indeed, you and what you worship besides Allah are fuel for Hell; you will arrive at it. (98) Had these been gods, they would not have arrived there, but all of them will abide therein﴾ [al-Anbiya' 98–99]. ﴿They would not have arrived there﴾: does this refer to the gods, or to those who claimed divinity for them?

It includes both. Understand: if they were truly gods, they would have protected themselves from entering the Fire, and they would have protected their worshippers from entering the Fire. But they are false gods that do not benefit. This is the aspect of resemblance in His saying: ﴿And indeed the frailest of houses is the house of the spider﴾. This comparison is what the rhetoricians call the representational comparison (al-tashbih al-tamthili); that is, it is composed of a whole sentence. If you say, "So-and-so is like the sea in generosity," this is a comparison, but it is a single comparison, in which you liken one individual to another individual. But if you bring something in which you liken a story to a story or a matter to a matter, then the comparison here is representational and compound, consisting of several aspects of the thing compared and the thing compared to, and the aspects of resemblance are also multiple. This comparison we call a representational comparison, because it is composed of a complete story. That is, it is not intended that the worshippers be likened to the spider alone and the worshipped ones to the houses alone; rather, the whole matter is intended to be likened to the whole matter, so that the picture becomes clear to the addressee.

His saying: ﴿And indeed the frailest of houses is the house of the spider﴾. The author, explaining this weakness, said: (it does not repel heat or cold). Yes indeed, it does not repel heat, nor cold, nor does it protect it from calamities, such as something falling upon it or the like. This house is the frailest of houses. Therefore, these idols do not benefit their worshippers. Accordingly, we say: those who worshipped these idols did not take refuge in a beneficial refuge, but in a refuge which is neither beneficial, nor preventive, nor protective. For this reason Allah likened that to the house of the spider. In another verse He likened these idols and their supplication to a man stretching his palms towards water so that it would reach his mouth. Will it reach him?

A person has water before him and he is thirsty, so he stretches his palms towards the water. Can it reach his mouth? It can never reach it. Likewise, these idols do not benefit their worshippers, just as this water does not reach the mouth of this thirsty person. Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿if they only knew﴾ [al-'Ankabut 41]; they would not have worshipped them.

﴿If﴾ here is conditional, the protasis is His saying ﴿they were﴾, and its apodosis is omitted; according to the author's explanation, what is its estimated form? "They would not have worshipped them." It should not be joined to what precedes it, because if you joined it to what precedes it, the frailty of the spider's house would be conditioned upon their knowledge, although it is the frailest of houses whether they know or do not know. Therefore it is necessary to pause at His saying: ﴿the house of the spider﴾. Then we say: ﴿if they only knew﴾. The author says: they would not have worshipped them. It is also possible that the apodosis is: ﴿if they only knew﴾, meaning: if they were of those possessing beneficial knowledge, this matter would not have been hidden from them; and since this matter is not hidden from them, they would not have engaged in worship.
