Of the extreme Qadariyyah (qadariyyah ghulat), who said that Allah does not know things related to creation until after they occur. We seek refuge in Allah. However, Shaykh al-Islam (Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah) said in his time that these extremists were few, that they had dwindled, because they saw that denying knowledge was a condemnation of themselves with disbelief, so they abandoned this and began denying the writing (of destiny) and the will (of Allah).

* Among the benefits of the verse: affirmation of these two noble names, al-'Aziz (the Almighty) and al-Hakim (the All-Wise), and affirmation of the attributes they contain, namely the attribute of might (al-'izzah) and the attribute of wisdom (al-hikmah). Likewise, what they contain of attributes by way of implication (dalalat al-iltizam). For the indication of a word upon its meaning is of three kinds: by correspondence (al-mutabaqah), by inclusion (al-tadammun), and by implication (al-iltizam). Whatever these two attributes necessarily entail of attributes is established. Are you understanding this?

The indication of a word upon what it signifies is by correspondence, inclusion and implication. Have these passed us before? Let us give an example: the word (dar, house). You know the inhabited house. The word (dar) indicates this mass of building, which includes rooms, chambers, roofs and courtyards. It indicates this by correspondence. As soon as I say the word (dar), you understand that (dar) contains chambers, rooms, roofs and courtyards. Its indication of this is an indication by correspondence. It indicates each chamber individually, or each room individually, or each roof individually, or each courtyard individually; it indicates them by inclusion, meaning that it includes such-and-such. Clear? It indicates that it has a builder by what? By implication, because a house does not stand except with a builder. This is the meaning of their saying that indication is by correspondence, inclusion and implication. So, for example, al-'Izzah and al-'Aziz: the word al-'Aziz indicates the attribute of might by correspondence. From the necessary consequence of might is that the Almighty is knowing, able and strong; its indication of these meanings is by implication. The indication of al-'Aziz upon the essence and the attribute together is by correspondence, and upon the essence alone or the attribute alone is by inclusion.

* A student: Did you not say, O Shaykh, that its indication upon the essence?

* The Shaykh: No, because al-'Aziz is a name. Its indication upon the essence alone or the attribute alone is by inclusion, and upon both together is by correspondence, and upon what the might necessarily entails of knowledge, power, strength and the like is by implication. For this reason, the name al-Hayy al-Qayyum includes all the attributes: these two names include all the attributes, because al-Hayy necessarily entails all the attributes of perfection, and al-Qayyum necessarily entails all the attributes of sovereignty, dominion, management and so forth. For this reason, it is related in a hadith that these two are the Greatest Name of Allah.[[Narrated by Abu Dawud (1496) from the hadith of Asma' bint Yazid.]]

Al-'Aziz al-Hakim: we have said that in them is affirmation of might, and al-Hakim contains affirmation of command and wisdom. In combining the two, a third attribute appears, which is that the might of Allah is joined with wisdom, unlike the might of other than Him, since the might of others may be devoid of wisdom.

* Among the benefits of the verse: it is fitting to reflect when verses are concluded with something that is contrary to the apparent situation; that is, you should not reject it if you find a verse ending in a way that differs from what the apparent situation or context requires. Reflect upon it, for the error is from you: ﴿If You punish them, indeed they are Your servants; and if You forgive them, indeed You, You are the Almighty, the All-Wise﴾ [al-Ma'idah 118]. The apparent requirement of the context would be to say: "Indeed You are the Forgiving, the Merciful," but He turned away from that. Do not say that this is a flaw at all; the flaw is from you, for this is the speech of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and it contains no flaw. His cosmic signs contain no flaw, and neither do His legislative signs. Therefore, one must reflect and pause. Here, in the verse before us, it may occur to a person that it should end with knowledge, but upon reflection, its ending with might and wisdom is more fitting. Then He, exalted, said: ﴿And these parables We present to the people, but none will understand them except the knowledgeable﴾ [al-'Ankabut 43].

* In this noble verse there is a benefit: the striking of parables, and that it is a kind of teaching and guidance, by His saying: ﴿And these parables We present﴾.

* Among its benefits: affirmation of the greatness of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. From where is this taken?

* A student: ﴿We present﴾.

* The Shaykh: ﴿We present﴾ from the "nun of greatness" (nun al-'azamah): ﴿We present them to the people﴾. Know, if you did not know before, that what Allah, exalted, attributes to Himself with the expression of greatness indicates the greatness of His own self, glorified and exalted; it may also be intended to refer to His angels and not Himself. This is common in the Qur'an, and likewise the first-person plural is common in the Qur'an. Among what Allah intends regarding His angels is like His saying: ﴿So when We have recited it, follow its recitation﴾ [al-Qiyamah 18]. Does this pronoun refer to whom? The pronoun of the subject? It refers to Jibril, but Allah attributed it to Himself because Jibril is His messenger. Likewise His saying: ﴿When fear had left Abraham and the good tidings had come to him, he began to argue with Us concerning the people of Lot﴾ [Hud 74]. ﴿He argued with Us﴾, while he did not argue with Allah but with the messengers. But taking what is attributed to Allah in the form of greatness as referring to His messengers and angels requires evidence; otherwise, the default is that it returns to Allah. As for what Allah attributes to Himself in the singular form, it is for Himself alone. We will give two examples for this. The first: His saying: ﴿And when My servants ask you concerning Me, indeed I am near; I respond to the invocation of the supplicant when he calls upon Me. So let them respond to Me and believe in Me that they may be guided﴾ [al-Baqarah 186]. All these pronouns are in the singular form. Thus His saying: ﴿Indeed I am near﴾ means the nearness of Himself to the one who calls upon Him; but this nearness does not necessitate that the Throne be empty of Him or that His elevation be negated, just as He descends to the lowest heaven and this does not necessitate that He be empty of the Throne or that this contradicts His elevation. But His saying: ﴿Then why, when it [the soul] has reached the throat, while you are at that time looking on — and We are closer to him than you, but you do not see﴾ [al-Waqi'ah 83–85]. Here ﴿closer﴾ contains a pronoun referring to ﴿We﴾, and ﴿We﴾ refers to whom? To Allah. Yet He is closer to him than we are, by His angels. What is the evidence?

The evidence is His saying: ﴿but you do not see﴾, for the angels attend the dying person to take his soul and sit near him as far as the eye can see, but we do not see them. So here, the nearness is for whom?

The nearness is for the angels, because Allah attributed it to Himself with the expression of greatness and evidence was found. This benefit is very important, and it will benefit you in the matter of the attributes and other matters: what Allah attributes to Himself in the singular form is for Himself, and what He attributes to Himself in the plural form is for Himself, but it may be for His angels by a contextual indicator. This is not impossible, as you have known.

Here He said: ﴿These parables We present﴾. Is it for Himself or for the angels? For Himself, because there is no indicator showing that it is for the angels.

And ﴿We present them to the people﴾: the first benefit, we said, is that there is in it the benefit of striking parables.

* Also among the benefits of the verse: the mercy of Allah, exalted, toward creation through the striking of parables for them, because striking parables, as we said, brings the intelligible closer to the minds, and a person's conception of the perceptible is stronger than his conception of the intelligible, is it not so?

Now, if I explained to you the rites of Hajj clearly, fully and manifestly, or took you to Hajj to the rites themselves, which is more effective?

The latter is more effective, because you perceive it with your eyes, whereas the former you conceive with your hearts and do not grasp it well. Thus striking parables contains mercy for creation, in that Allah, glorified and exalted, brings the intelligible near to us through the perceptible.

* Among the benefits of the verse: it is fitting to reflect upon parables, by His saying: ﴿but none will understand them except the knowledgeable﴾. The knowledgeable is the one who reflects and considers until he understands.

* Among the benefits of the verse: praise of the intellect, by His saying: ﴿and none will understand them﴾. By "intellect" here is meant the intellect of perception or the intellect of sound judgment?

* The students: The intellect of sound judgment.

* The Shaykh: The intellect of sound judgment. The intellect that benefits is the one that is praised.

* Also among them: the virtue of knowledge, by His saying: ﴿but none will understand them except the knowledgeable﴾. Whoever is not knowing of Allah, glorified and exalted, and of His signs, does not understand these meanings and says: "These are things that have no meaning." But the knowledgeable is the one who understands them, knows their purpose and meaning, and the aspects of their resemblance, until he reaches the degree of perfection.

Allah, exalted, said: ﴿Allah created the heavens and the earth with truth. Indeed in that is a sign for the believers.﴾

* In this verse there are benefits. First: that the creator of the heavens and the earth is Allah, or not? ﴿Allah created the heavens﴾, because we do not know otherwise.

If someone said: is there no restriction in the verse so that you can say that the Creator is Allah?

We say: Yes, there is no restriction by the well-known methods, but there is a restriction in that there exist only one heavens and one earth; if the Creator of them is Allah, the possibility that anyone else is their creator is negated.

* Among them: refutation of the naturalists (ahl al-tabi'ah), may God protect us, who say that the heavens and the earth have no creator, that they are things that interact, change and fluctuate, and that creation has no beginning and no end.

* Among them: affirmation that the heavens and the earth are created, and that they are not eternal. From where do we know this? The creation of the heavens: they are brought into existence after non-existence, and everything other than Allah exists after non-existence.

* Among them: that the heavens are plural. How many?

* Students: Seven heavens.

* The Shaykh: Yes, they are specified as seven in other verses.

* Also among them: that the earth is one?

* Students: No, this refers to the genus.

* The Shaykh: The intended meaning is the genus. Now, in the Qur'an, the earth is never mentioned in plural form, is it not? However, its plurality is indicated in His saying: ﴿Allah is the One who created seven heavens and of the earth the like thereof﴾ [al-Talaq 12]. Is the similarity here in attribute impossible or not? Because there is no comparison between the heavens and the earth, when similarity in attribute is impossible, we return to similarity in number, and the Sunnah has come explicitly to that effect, such as His ﷺ saying: "He will be collared with it from seven earths."[[Narrated by al-Bukhari (2452) from the hadith of Sa'id ibn Zayd ibn 'Amr, and Muslim (1612/142) from the hadith of 'Aishah.]]

* Among the benefits of the verse: that the creation of these heavens and earth is with truth, not in vain, nor in play, nor in falsehood, by His saying: ﴿with truth﴾.

* Also among them: that they contain truth. Their creation, as a原 origination, is with truth, and they also contain truth; nothing can occur in the heavens and the earth except with truth.

* Also among its benefits: the reassurance of a person regarding what Allah brings about in the heavens and the earth, or the arousing of reassurance. What is the basis of this? I have mentioned the benefit, so what is its basis? Good, what is the basis of its arousing reassurance?

* A student: With truth.

* The Shaykh: That it is with truth. Everything that happens, once you know it is with truth, you feel reassured. I do not say: why did it happen, and why did it not happen? If hunger, sickness, earthquakes and floods befall people, I know that this is with truth, so I am reassured, content and submit. In reality, there is no rest for a person except through this; a person cannot find rest except by believing in Allah's decree and destiny, and that it is the truth, and then he becomes fully reassured. Otherwise, he will be troubled, for there is no hour in which he does not find something that grieves him, whether in himself, his family, his companions, his land, or the Islamic lands generally. A person cannot be reassured and settled until he believes that all these things are true.

* A student: Disputing with destiny?

* The Shaykh: Disputing destiny by the Shari'ah is obligatory. Yes, there is also something else.

* The student: So you are reassured and yet you dispute?

* The Shaykh: Dispute by the Shari'ah; it is not by destiny.

* The student: No, I meant combining the two?

* The Shaykh: Combining them: for example, when destiny comes to us that grieves us, we dispute it by the Shari'ah, by patience. If we are patient, it does not grieve us. Likewise, disputing destiny by the Shari'ah. This is obligatory: you must confront destiny with what the Shari'ah requires. But disputing destiny with destiny is not permissible. You keep giving answers in Sufi terms, I do not know what...

* The student: No, not Sufi, O Shaykh, let us be cautious (...). It was what prompted me to mention this...

* The Shaykh: I did not wish you to mention this, because it requires... Note that some people may shy away from the word "dispute," and what is meant by dispute is confrontation.

* Among the benefits of the verse: that the creation of the heavens and the earth is a sign indicating what this creation necessitates of the attributes of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. We have mentioned that among them is what indicates the power of Allah, the wisdom of Allah, and His might, according to what the verse requires.

* Also among them: that the verses benefit no one except whom? Except the believers, by His saying: ﴿for the believers﴾.

* From this benefit a derived benefit follows: whenever the servant's faith is perfected, he benefits more from the signs. The path to obtaining this is what we have mentioned more than once, that when a ruling is attached to a description, it grows stronger with the strength of that description and weaker with its weakness. Every ruling attached to a description grows in strength with the strength of that description and in weakness with its weakness. So we say: therefore, whenever a person's faith is more perfect, there appears to him of the signs of Allah in these creatures what does not appear to those below him. Is the meaning of this clear, O people?

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 29, verse 41–44 (part 1 of 3):

Then He, the Exalted, said: ﴿The example of those who take protectors other than Allah﴾ — idols, whom they hope will benefit them — ﴿is like the example of the spider﴾ [al-'Ankabut 41].

(Mathal and mithl) are like (shabah and shibh), in form and in meaning. So mathal means likeness (shabah), and it is an expression for comparing an intelligible thing with a perceptible thing, because representing intelligible matters through perceptible ones increases them in clarity, explanation and conception. Is this understood? And although they are not equal in every respect, they are equal in the respect in which the comparison is made.

His saying: ﴿The example of those who take protectors other than Allah﴾ means: those who made protectors. The intended meaning of "protectors" is the idols, and they were called protectors because their worshippers hope for their benefit, like a protector who benefits you by support, defence, bringing good, and similar things. Also, they are called protectors in that they themselves ..

.. This is why the people of Abraham said: ﴿Burn him and support your gods, if you are going to act﴾ [al-Anbiya' 68]. They support them and hope for support from them, and for this reason these idols were named (protectors).

His saying: ﴿other than Allah﴾ means: besides Him. The evidence that the intended meaning is "besides" in the sense of "other than" is that this occurs in several verses, such as His saying: ﴿You have no god other than Him﴾ [al-A'raf 59]. The expression "dun" (besides) is used because its rank is lowly in comparison to whom? To Allah, Mighty and Majestic. ﴿other than Allah, protectors﴾ [al-'Ankabut 41]. Their likeness, then, — who is meant by those who take protectors other than Allah? It refers to the polytheists, their likeness ﴿is like the example of the spider﴾ [al-'Ankabut 41]; that is, like the likeness of the spider. The spider is a well-known small creature that takes for itself a house made of web, and this house of web is what it weaves and emerges from. Allah, glory be to Him, is capable of all things. When this spider falls from a height, it immediately secretes this web and clings to it so that it does not fall to the ground; then, despite that, it secretes it and clings to it, and you find it hanging by this thread. When it wishes to climb up with it, it climbs, turning itself over and making its head the highest, and it climbs with this thread that it has just secreted. Then, when it is hunting — and it mostly hunts flies — what does it do with them? It binds them with these threads until it finishes them off. This is part of the saying of the Exalted: ﴿Our Lord is He who gave everything its creation, then guided it﴾ [Ta-Ha 50], guiding this creation to what is good for it. The point is that this spider took a house for itself, that is, made for itself a house. From what? From the web that it weaves.

The author said: (﴿took a house﴾ [al-'Ankabut 41] for itself, to which it retreats), and this is observed. ﴿And indeed the frailest﴾ [al-'Ankabut 41], the weakest ﴿of houses is the house of the spider﴾ [al-'Ankabut 41]. This is the word of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, who is the Knower of what we have not encompassed in knowledge. How many of Allah's creatures have houses, while we know of these houses only what we witness of them, and how much is hidden from us! Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, says: "The frailest of houses is the house of the spider." He emphasised this sentence ﴿And indeed the frailest of houses is the house of the spider﴾ with (inna) and the lam, in order to stress the weakness of these protectors, just as the houses in which spiders take refuge are weak; indeed they are the frailest and weakest of houses, for these protectors are likewise the weakest of protectors, since they do not benefit their worshippers. Rather, Allah says in the Qur'an: ﴿Indeed, you and what you worship besides Allah are fuel for Hell; you will arrive at it. (98) Had these been gods, they would not have arrived there, but all of them will abide therein﴾ [al-Anbiya' 98–99]. ﴿They would not have arrived there﴾: does this refer to the gods, or to those who claimed divinity for them?

It includes both. Understand: if they were truly gods, they would have protected themselves from entering the Fire, and they would have protected their worshippers from entering the Fire. But they are false gods that do not benefit. This is the aspect of resemblance in His saying: ﴿And indeed the frailest of houses is the house of the spider﴾. This comparison is what the rhetoricians call the representational comparison (al-tashbih al-tamthili); that is, it is composed of a whole sentence. If you say, "So-and-so is like the sea in generosity," this is a comparison, but it is a single comparison, in which you liken one individual to another individual. But if you bring something in which you liken a story to a story or a matter to a matter, then the comparison here is representational and compound, consisting of several aspects of the thing compared and the thing compared to, and the aspects of resemblance are also multiple. This comparison we call a representational comparison, because it is composed of a complete story. That is, it is not intended that the worshippers be likened to the spider alone and the worshipped ones to the houses alone; rather, the whole matter is intended to be likened to the whole matter, so that the picture becomes clear to the addressee.

His saying: ﴿And indeed the frailest of houses is the house of the spider﴾. The author, explaining this weakness, said: (it does not repel heat or cold). Yes indeed, it does not repel heat, nor cold, nor does it protect it from calamities, such as something falling upon it or the like. This house is the frailest of houses. Therefore, these idols do not benefit their worshippers. Accordingly, we say: those who worshipped these idols did not take refuge in a beneficial refuge, but in a refuge which is neither beneficial, nor preventive, nor protective. For this reason Allah likened that to the house of the spider. In another verse He likened these idols and their supplication to a man stretching his palms towards water so that it would reach his mouth. Will it reach him?

A person has water before him and he is thirsty, so he stretches his palms towards the water. Can it reach his mouth? It can never reach it. Likewise, these idols do not benefit their worshippers, just as this water does not reach the mouth of this thirsty person. Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿if they only knew﴾ [al-'Ankabut 41]; they would not have worshipped them.

﴿If﴾ here is conditional, the protasis is His saying ﴿they were﴾, and its apodosis is omitted; according to the author's explanation, what is its estimated form? "They would not have worshipped them." It should not be joined to what precedes it, because if you joined it to what precedes it, the frailty of the spider's house would be conditioned upon their knowledge, although it is the frailest of houses whether they know or do not know. Therefore it is necessary to pause at His saying: ﴿the house of the spider﴾. Then we say: ﴿if they only knew﴾. The author says: they would not have worshipped them. It is also possible that the apodosis is: ﴿if they only knew﴾, meaning: if they were of those possessing beneficial knowledge, this matter would not have been hidden from them; and since this matter is not hidden from them, they would not have engaged in worship. In any case, this indicates the ignorance of these worshippers, however clever they may be and however skilled they are in managing worldly affairs; in this respect they are foolish, having neither knowledge nor reason. This verse reminds us of another verse in which many people also err, in Surat al-Takathur: ﴿No! If you knew with the certainty of knowledge﴾ [al-Takathur 5]. Some people join it and say: ﴿No! If you knew with the certainty of knowledge (5) you would surely see the Hellfire﴾ [al-Takathur 5–6]. This is a mistake, because the meaning is clearly corrupted by it; for if you joined it, then ﴿you would surely see﴾ would be the apodosis of ﴿if you knew﴾, and the matter is not so. Rather, ﴿you would surely see﴾ is an independent, self-standing sentence in which Allah informs that we will indeed see the Hellfire. Therefore one must pause at His saying: ﴿No! If you knew with the certainty of knowledge﴾.

* Student: Shaykh, if someone said that the spider does benefit from its house to some degree, as is the reality, while the idol-worshippers certainly do not benefit from theirs?

* The Shaykh: Yes, this is correct; it may be raised against us. But the intended point is that these idols are like this house, because it does not benefit. They now benefit from these idols in some kind of benefit, especially material benefit, for those who come to them for worship and seeking blessing gain a material benefit. But the true benefit they hope for, which is averting harm, they do not get.

* Student: O Shaykh, is it not said that (...) does not necessarily entail entering the obligatory? It may be that you are asked for something and it is not obligatory..?

* The Shaykh: No, the intended point of the comparison here is the lack of benefit: they neither benefit nor protect them. And in reality, even the spider's house neither benefits it nor protects it; the wind comes to it, the cold comes to it, the rain comes to it, dust clings to it, and it does not benefit from it with complete benefit.

* Student: It catches prey with it.

* The Shaykh: No, it does not catch prey with it. It catches prey with the web that comes out of it; these threads are what it catches with. As for the house itself, it does not catch with it. But what we see on it, it is what brings it, it brings it and places it there.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed Allah knows whatever they call upon besides Him, of anything. And He is the Mighty, the Wise﴾ [al-'Ankabut 42]. ﴿Indeed Allah knows what﴾ — ﴿what﴾: the author says: (in the sense of "that which"). So it is a relative pronoun. This grammatical analysis which the author adopted is what appears most evident from the verse, while some grammarians say ﴿what﴾ is interrogative, and the pause is on His saying ﴿Indeed Allah knows﴾: what is it that they call upon besides Him of anything, do they benefit? But this is far from the wording, so the author's analysis is correct: ﴿knows what they call upon besides Him﴾. Following the author's analysis, we must say: where is the returning pronoun of the relative clause?

* Student: The ha' (hu).

* The Shaykh: Where?

* Student: In "besides Him".

* The Shaykh: ﴿what they call upon besides Him﴾ — this ha' refers to Allah, not to ﴿what﴾?

* Student: It is omitted.

* The Shaykh: It is omitted, and this is regular: omitting an accusative returning pronoun is regular. So the estimated form is: Indeed Allah knows what they call upon of anything.

And His saying ﴿they call upon﴾ — he said: (they worship). So the supplication here is supplication of worship. Just as supplication may be supplication of worship, it is also supplication of request. As for supplication of request, it is in His saying: ﴿And when My servants ask you about Me, indeed I am near; I respond to the invocation of the supplicant when he calls upon Me﴾ [al-Baqarah 186]. You say: "O my Lord, forgive me; O my Lord, have mercy on me," and similar things. What is supplication of worship? It is that you worship Allah, glory be to Him, by what He has commanded you. And this is called supplication because what is the true condition of the worshipper? It is seeking the forgiveness and mercy of Allah; so he is, in reality, one who supplicates implicitly. Its evidence is the saying of the Exalted: ﴿And your Lord said: Call upon Me, I will respond to you. Indeed, those who are too proud to worship Me will enter Hell, humbled﴾ [Ghafir 60].

And His saying ﴿what they call upon﴾ means: what they worship. It is necessary to make supplication here inclusive of both worship and supplication of request. Do they call upon these idols with supplication of request or not?

* Student: They call upon them.

* The Shaykh: They call upon these idols with supplication of request as well; they ask them. A clear evidence of this is those who associate partners with the prophets and the saints, for they call upon them with supplication of request. They say: "O Messenger of Allah, forgive me," and "O Messenger of Allah, ease my affair," and similar things.

As for His saying (with the yā' and the tā'): how is it with the yā' and the tā'? That is, ﴿yad'ūna﴾ and ﴿tad'ūna﴾ are two canonical recitations. ﴿besides Him﴾: other than Him. ﴿of anything﴾: this is an explanation of ﴿what﴾; that is, whatever they call upon, for Allah is aware of it.

His knowledge of it — what is the meaning of His knowledge of it? That He knows the state of this invoked and worshipped one. And this is like a justification for His saying: ﴿The example of those who take protectors other than Allah is like the example of the spider﴾ [al-'Ankabut 41], confirming that this likeness corresponds to reality, because it proceeds from — what?

From knowledge: ﴿Indeed Allah knows﴾. For when He mentioned that they are like the spider, He clarified that this is from His knowledge: ﴿Indeed Allah knows what they call upon besides Him of anything﴾, and that this thing which is called upon does not benefit.

His saying ﴿And He is the Mighty﴾ — in His dominion — ﴿the Wise﴾ — in His creation.

If someone said: the appropriate thing would be to say "And He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing," because Allah says ﴿knows﴾, so the apparent requirement is that the verse end with knowledge?

We say: this is correct with respect to the apparent wording, but on reflection you find that ending it with might and wisdom is more eloquent, for they seek support from these idols, victory and dominance; and the greatest evidence for this is the saying of Abu Sufyan on the day of Uhud, when he said: "Exalt Hubal" [narrated by al-Bukhari (4043) from the hadith of al-Bara']. Their reliance on these idols is countered by the might of One who cannot be overcome, who is Allah; and for this reason He said: ﴿And He is the Mighty﴾, the Dominant over these idols and over their worshippers. Is this clear?

Thus the fitness of ﴿the Mighty﴾ is more forceful than the fitness of (the All-Knowing), because these people seek victory from their idols and wish them to prevail and dominate; so Allah made clear that He is the possessor of might. We have already mentioned that al-'Aziz is one of the names of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and that it includes might in three respects: might of worth (ʿizzat al-qadr), might of subjugation (ʿizzat al-qahr), and might of inaccessibility (ʿizzat al-imtina'). As for might of worth, it means that He, glory be to Him, has no equal in His greatness, majesty and worth. As for might of subjugation, it means that no one resembles Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, in His subjugation, sovereignty and dominion. As for might of inaccessibility, it means that He, glory be to Him, is free from every deficiency and every defect; He is too mighty to be reached by any flaw or imperfection. As for His saying ﴿the Wise﴾, Allah, glory be to Him, always pairs might with wisdom. Do you know why?

Because some mighty creatures are carried by their might to recklessness, to lack of deliberation, and to failing to place things in their proper places. Recall the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And when it is said to him, "Fear Allah," he is seized by pride in sin﴾ [al-Baqarah 206]. Is it wisdom that pride seizes him in sin, or not?

It is not wisdom; it is the opposite of wisdom. Therefore Allah, the Exalted, always pairs the Mighty with the Wise, indicating that His might, blessed and exalted is He, is joined with wisdom. Though He is Mighty, prevailing and dominant, possessing complete authority, He, glory be to Him, does not govern the affair except in a manner of far-reaching wisdom. Moreover, according to our explanation earlier, al-Hakim means the One who possesses judgment (dhu al-hukm) and wisdom (al-hikmah). It is quite evident that His might is joined with His judgment, and that He has absolute judgment over His servants, glory be to Him; therefore this name is always paired with this name. Know that the names of Allah, glory be to Him, have meanings when they stand alone, and when they are joined with others, a further meaning arises from this combination beyond the individual meaning of each name. This is a matter to reflect upon. For example, al-'Aziz has a meaning when alone, and al-Hakim has a meaning when alone; but when both are joined, a third meaning arises from them, in addition to the individual meaning, which is the complete meaning attained by the combination of these two names. We have already mentioned that al-Hakim is the One who possesses judgment and wisdom, and that judgment is divided into cosmic (kawni) and legislative (shar'i). We illustrated the cosmic with His saying: ﴿So I will not leave this land until my father permits me or Allah judges for me﴾ [Yusuf 80], and the legislative with His saying in Surat al-Mumtahanah: ﴿That is the judgment of Allah; He judges between you﴾ [al-Mumtahanah 10], and what encompasses both: ﴿Indeed Allah decrees what He intends﴾ [al-Ma'idah 1], and similar things.

Ibn 'Uthaymin's commentary on Surah al-'Ankabut, verses 41–44 (part 2 of 3):

As for wisdom (al-hikmah), it is affirmed for Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and it means placing things in their proper places. It applies to His cosmic decree (al-hukm al-kawni) and His legislative decree (al-hukm al-shar'i), considered from the standpoint of their place. It is also a purposive wisdom (hikmah ghaiyyah) and a formal wisdom (hikmah suriyyah). Formal wisdom means that the thing being in this specific form is in accordance with wisdom. Then its end is also wisdom, so wisdom exists in the end and in the state in which the matter is. This encompasses all of Allah's decrees, cosmic and legislative, subhanahu wa ta'ala. He said: ﴿And He is the Mighty, the Wise﴾.

﴿And these parables﴾ [al-'Ankabut 43] in the Qur'an ﴿We set forth for mankind﴾, we make them, ﴿but none understands them﴾, meaning: comprehends them, ﴿except those of knowledge﴾, the ones who reflect.

﴿These parables﴾: he used ﴿these﴾, which indicates distance. Does it indicate distance or nearness? Distance. For he did not say "and this parable," so that we might say he turned the speech away from its apparent meaning or from the requirement of its context. Is the parable just mentioned near or far?
Near. But he said ﴿these parables﴾, and the other parables, other than the parable of those who take idols, are distant relative to this place? Yes indeed, because they are scattered throughout the Qur'an, and so the verse came with ﴿these parables﴾ and did not say "this parable." It encompasses all the parables mentioned in the Qur'an. The parables in the Qur'an are many and varied, and some scholars have authored independent books on them. Al-Suyuti devoted a separate chapter to them in al-Itqan, and he explained the benefits for which parables are set forth. The most evident and immediate benefit of them is bringing intelligible matters closer to minds, since a parable is the presentation of an intelligible thing, which may be far from a person's conception, through a perceptible thing that is easy to conceive. He said: ﴿These parables We set forth for mankind﴾. When you say "daraba dhalika mathalan" (he set that forth as a parable), the meaning is "ja'ala" (made). ﴿He has set forth for you a parable from yourselves﴾ [al-Rum 28], meaning: made for you. So the verb "daraba" comes to mean "ja'ala" when it is joined to "mathal," whenever you find ﴿Allah sets forth a parable﴾ [Ibrahim 24] and similar, so know that the meaning of "daraba" here is "ja'ala." The root (d-r-b) is not limited to striking with the hand. It includes the sense of "making," and it includes the sense of converting currency from one mint to another, and other senses, according to the context that clarifies it.

As for His words ﴿We set them forth for mankind﴾, meaning: We make them parables for people in general. Allah set forth parables for all people in the Torah, the Gospel and the Qur'an. But who comprehends them and benefits from them? The people of knowledge: ﴿but none understands them except those of knowledge﴾. Those of knowledge means: those possessing knowledge and understanding, who benefit from their understanding and knowledge. For this reason the author said "those who reflect." This explanation is open to question, since knowledge comes after reflection, but because knowledge is not attained except through it, the author explained it that way. The truth is that "those of knowledge" means those possessing knowledge and understanding, who comprehend things and understand them, as opposed to the ignorant, who turn away and do not benefit from the understanding Allah has given them, for they do not comprehend these parables. And if they do not comprehend them, do they benefit from them? They do not benefit from them. Is it possible for us to confine the parables found in the Qur'an? In this place, it is not possible. So shall we take this up as a research topic, or is it not possible?
* Student: A book by Ibn al-Qayyim, a limited (...).
* The Shaykh: I do not want you to copy from a book first, a person. This is between you and Allah. You yourselves should reflect on the Qur'an. We all, praise be to Allah, read the Qur'an in Ramadan. Whenever a parable passes by a person, he should note it down. Then after noting these parables, he looks and returns to the authored books: has he missed anything or not? It is not known that... I do not want you to teach the brothers, but a person may go to any authored book on this and copy from it, but...
* Student: No, O Shaykh, we may read Ibn al-Qayyim's book, we just read it as a reading that helps me (...).
* The Shaykh: No. I think a person should first begin by himself. He begins with the Qur'an, notes the parables, and then afterwards returns to the book. There is no objection. He said: ﴿but none understands them except those of knowledge.﴾ So He generalized in setting forth the parable and particularized in understanding the parable. Where is the generalization in setting forth the parable? ﴿We set them forth for mankind﴾. And the particularization: ﴿but none understands them except those of knowledge﴾. This is a frequent style in the Qur'an, generalization followed by particularization: ﴿And Allah calls to the abode of peace and guides whom He wills to a straight path﴾ [Yunus 25]. He generalized in the call and particularized in guidance.

Allah said: ﴿Allah created the heavens and the earth with truth﴾ [al-'Ankabut 44], meaning: in truth. ﴿Indeed in that is a sign﴾ indicating His power, Exalted is He, ﴿for the believers﴾. ﴿Allah created the heavens and the earth.﴾ What is the meaning of "created"? It means: brought them into existence. Allah, Exalted is He, is the Creator of the heavens and the earth.
And ﴿Originator of the heavens and the earth﴾ [al-Baqarah 117]. The people of knowledge said: "Badi'" means "mubdi'" (originator), and innovation (ibda') is bringing a thing into existence without a prior pattern. From this comes the newly dug well (bi'r badi'), which has just been dug. So creation is more general than origination, but Allah, Mighty and Majestic, has shown in another verse that He is both Creator and Originator. He is the One who brought the heavens and the earth into existence, and He is the Originator of the heavens and the earth.
His words ﴿Allah created the heavens and the earth﴾ mean along with what is in them. What is in them, with respect to the children of Adam, is among them. Likewise plants, for man was created from clay of the earth, and plants also come from the earth, as is evident.
As for His words ﴿with truth﴾, the author said: "(meaning: in truth)." The prepositional phrase is in the accusative position as a circumstantial qualifier (hal) of the subject of "created," meaning: in truth. It may also be a purposive object (maf'ul min ajlih), meaning: He created them for the sake of truth, as He said: ﴿We did not create the heaven and the earth and what is between them in vain﴾ [Sad 27], and they are only truth. The author's explanation is supported by His words: ﴿And We did not create the heavens and the earth and what is between them in play﴾ [al-Dukhan 38]. Since He, Exalted is He, is not playing, He is in truth.
As for His words ﴿indeed in that is a sign﴾, the referent of ﴿that﴾ is the creation, which includes everything that proceeds from the creation of the heavens and the earth, for it is a sign. The very creation of the heavens and the earth is a sign pointing to Allah, because a thing's sign is what points to it rather than to something else. Here the heavens and the earth point to Allah, because no one can create the like of these heavens and earth. Is that not so?
Thus they are a sign of Him. The existence of these heavens and earth points to power, and the order in them, the absence of disorder and contradiction, points to wisdom. If you reflect on the many events of the heavens and the earth, you will find that each one points to power, and of course to knowledge: ﴿Does He not know who created? And He is the Subtle, the All-Aware﴾ [al-Mulk 14], and to wisdom. And each has a particular indication of what it points to by itself. This is something that, if you contemplate it, many signs will become apparent to you. ﴿A sign for the believers.﴾ Does he mean that it points only to Allah's power?
No, it points to Allah's power, to His knowledge, to His wisdom, to His mercy, to His strength, and every event of the heavens and the earth, each thing in them, points to the attribute specific to it.
As for His words ﴿for the believers﴾, the author said: "(They are singled out for mention because they are the ones who benefit from them in faith, unlike the disbelievers)." This is correct. The cosmic signs benefit only the believer; the disbeliever does not benefit. The disbeliever says: "This is nature that operates by itself, and it takes revenge on people by itself, and brings good to people by itself," and gains nothing. The believer benefits from that. Likewise, the legislative signs: the believer benefits from them, and the non-believer does not benefit: ﴿And when a surah is revealed, some of them say, "Which of you has this increased in faith?" As for those who believed, it has increased them in faith, and they rejoice. But as for those in whose hearts is disease, it has added to their filth to their filth, and they die while they are disbelievers﴾ [al-Tawbah 124–125]. So both cosmic and legislative signs benefit none but the believer.
If someone says: "The believer is already a believer, so how does he benefit?"
We say: Yes. Benefit from what? From an increase in faith: ﴿As for those who believed, it has increased them in faith.﴾ And an increase in faith is without doubt a great benefit, because faith either increases, or decreases, or remains as it is. The last is rare, that faith neither increases nor decreases. It is either increasing or decreasing, and this is the usual case. However, I doubt the existence of the third division, that it neither increases nor decreases, because failure to increase faith leads to its decrease, since faith increases through obedience, as is understood by all: when obedience is lost, decrease occurs. The rational division is only that it is either increasing, decreasing, or remaining in its state, and whether the third case can be conceived or actually occurs, Allah knows best. He said: ﴿Indeed in that is a sign for the believers (44). Recite what has been revealed to you of the Book and establish prayer﴾ [al-'Ankabut 44–45].
* Student: Those who said (...) and those who said faith does not increase or decrease?
* The Shaykh: They have no evidence; that is, the ones who say faith does not increase or decrease have a weak reasoning. They are the Murji'ah, who say faith is the affirmation of the heart, and affirmation does not vary; or the Mu'tazilah and the Khawarij, who say faith is not divisible: either it exists entirely in full or is entirely absent. He said: ﴿Recite what was revealed﴾..
* Student: But doesn't the verse refer to creation with truth, all of it?
* The Shaykh: It refers to both of them together, and the creation of the heavens with truth, with this restriction, refers to both of them together.
* Student: O Shaykh, some scholars say, regarding the decrease and increase of faith, that whoever abandons what benefits him will inevitably be tested with what harms him, and this is one of the divine customs. Where did those commentators take this statement from (...), which he mentions, so I do not know from where? He says: always, if a person abandons anything that benefits him, Allah, Exalted is He, will necessarily test him with what harms him (...) the reasoning (...).
* The Shaykh: What is its reasoning? Whoever abandons what benefits him is tested with what harms him. What is the reasoning for that, brothers?
* Student: As a punishment, I mean, because Allah, Exalted is He, says: ﴿O mankind, indeed you are laboring toward your Lord with labor, and you will meet Him﴾ [al-Inshiqaq 6]. Man must do something.
* The Shaykh: Yes, this is its reasoning. Man must be a worker and an aspirer; every person must have aspiration and work. If this work is not in what benefits, it must be in what harms.
If someone says: this statement entails nullifying the category of the permissible (mubah) in the domain of obligation, as is mentioned of one of the Mu'tazilah, I think al-Ka'bi, who is called al-Ka'bi, and I think he was a Mu'tazili, who says there is no category of the permissible in the Shari'ah, because it follows that this permissible thing you occupy yourself with would necessarily keep you from the forbidden, so it would be obligatory. Things would be either obligatory or forbidden. But the scholars refuted him with evidence from reason and transmission and said: this is not correct. The harm of doing the permissible, if it involves neglecting an obligation, is not because it is permissible, but because of neglecting the obligation. If one does the permissible without that resulting in neglecting an obligation or committing a prohibited act, no sin is incurred. The point is that the meaning of the statement is that a person must be active: either in what benefits him or in what harms him. I seek Allah's forgiveness!
* Student: Are there no discussions related to the topic of the Names and Attributes and their explanation, only the Names and their explanation (...) verified in books?
* The Shaykh: I have seen only Ibn al-Qayyim's commentary on the Nuniyyah, and Shaykh 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sa'di explained it in Tawdih Tawhid al-Anbiya', and there is also a book, Sharh Asma' Allah, by one of the linguists.
* Student: al-Zajjaj?
* The Shaykh: And al-Zajjaj.
* Student: Tafsir of the Names.
* The Shaykh: Yes, he explained it, but I no longer know about my confidence in this man. (...).
In this verse, is the setting forth of parables for people, or do we place it in the verse that follows? ﴿And these parables We set forth﴾; the following verse is clearer.

* From this noble verse: a proof of the foolishness of those polytheists, who relied on what has no reliance for worshipping idols; this is derived from His words ﴿like the spider's house, which it has taken for itself﴾.
* Among its benefits too: the condemnation of these polytheists and the lowering of their rank, since they were compared to what? To spiders. Undoubtedly, comparing a human to an animal is a humiliation and a lowering of his rank, because Allah says: ﴿And We have honored the children of Adam and carried them on land and sea and provided for them of the good things and preferred them over much of what We have created, with definite preference﴾ [al-Isra' 70].
* Among the benefits of the verse: that these idols never benefit their worshippers; they do not benefit them, nor do they ward off harm from them. They do not bring good nor repel harm. From where is this derived? From their being compared to a spider's house.
* And among them: the permissibility of setting forth a parable with something lowly according to what the situation requires. From where do we take this?
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: No. ﴿Like the spider's house﴾, for it is one of the lowest of creatures. Allah, Exalted is He, said in Surat al-Baqarah: ﴿Indeed, Allah is not shy to present an example: a mosquito or what is above it﴾ [al-Baqarah 26]. Allah has set forth parables by the fly, by the donkey, by the dog, by the mosquito, and by the spider, all according to what the situation requires.
* Among the benefits of the verse: that the weakest of houses and the frailest is the spider's house. From here we derive that one should not say: "This is weaker than a spider's house," or not?
* Student: Yes.
* The Shaykh: Consider it: "weaker than a spider's house."
* Student: Because nothing is weaker than a spider's house.
* Another student: (...).
* The Shaykh: No, Allah is the One sought for help (...) weaker than a spider's house. Why do we say it is not appropriate? Why? Because He said: ﴿the weakest of houses﴾. So you cannot say of any house that it is weaker than a spider's house. If you say of a house: "weaker than a spider's house," that is not appropriate, because Allah says: "the weakest of houses is the spider's house." But if it is something other than a house, you might say, for example: "This man's argument is weaker than a spider's house." What do you think?
* Student: There is no harm.
* The Shaykh: This is no harm; there is no contradiction of the Qur'an. What is prohibited as contradicting the Qur'an is to say of a house that it is weaker than a spider's house. (...) the path of guidance. But note: what is meant by the knowledge that is the path of guidance? Is it knowledge of the natures of things and what Allah created in the universe, or knowledge of Allah, Mighty and Majestic?
It is knowledge of Allah and His signs, cosmic and legislative, and not merely that a person is acquainted with what is in this universe, for he may be acquainted with it and not benefit. From here we derive the error of many people who interpret His words: ﴿Only those of His servants who have knowledge fear Allah﴾ [Fatir 28] as meaning those with knowledge of the universe. If that were so, astronomers, geologists and their like would be those who fear Allah, and those with knowledge of the Shari'ah of Allah would be behind them in fear, and this is impossible. Then Allah, Exalted and Glorified, said: ﴿Allah created the heavens and the earth with truth; indeed in that is a sign for the believers﴾ [al-'Ankabut 44].
* From this noble verse it is derived that the Creator of the heavens and the earth is Allah.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 29, verse 41–44 (part 3 of 3):

He said: ﴿Indeed, Allah knows whatever they invoke besides Him of things; and He is the Almighty, the All-Wise.﴾ This verse indicates that Allah did not liken these polytheists to the spider except with knowledge. The verse is in the nature of a justification for what precedes it, meaning that He, glorified and exalted, did not say "like the spider" except with knowledge: He knows these idols, that they do not benefit, and that there is no benefit in them.

* Among its benefits: affirmation of Allah's knowledge regarding created things. This is a refutation of whom? Of the extreme Qadariyyah (qadariyyah ghulat), who said that Allah does not know things related to creation until after they occur. We seek refuge in Allah. However, Shaykh al-Islam (Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah) said in his time that these extremists were few, that they had dwindled, because they saw that denying knowledge was a condemnation of themselves with disbelief, so they abandoned this and began denying the writing (of destiny) and the will (of Allah).

* Among the benefits of the verse: affirmation of these two noble names, al-'Aziz (the Almighty) and al-Hakim (the All-Wise), and affirmation of the attributes they contain, namely the attribute of might (al-'izzah) and the attribute of wisdom (al-hikmah). Likewise, what they contain of attributes by way of implication (dalalat al-iltizam). For the indication of a word upon its meaning is of three kinds: by correspondence (al-mutabaqah), by inclusion (al-tadammun), and by implication (al-iltizam). Whatever these two attributes necessarily entail of attributes is established. Are you understanding this?

The indication of a word upon what it signifies is by correspondence, inclusion and implication. Have these passed us before? Let us give an example: the word (dar, house). You know the inhabited house. The word (dar) indicates this mass of building, which includes rooms, chambers, roofs and courtyards. It indicates this by correspondence. As soon as I say the word (dar), you understand that (dar) contains chambers, rooms, roofs and courtyards. Its indication of this is an indication by correspondence. It indicates each chamber individually, or each room individually, or each roof individually, or each courtyard individually; it indicates them by inclusion, meaning that it includes such-and-such. Clear? It indicates that it has a builder by what? By implication, because a house does not stand except with a builder. This is the meaning of their saying that indication is by correspondence, inclusion and implication. So, for example, al-'Izzah and al-'Aziz: the word al-'Aziz indicates the attribute of might by correspondence. From the necessary consequence of might is that the Almighty is knowing, able and strong; its indication of these meanings is by implication. The indication of al-'Aziz upon the essence and the attribute together is by correspondence, and upon the essence alone or the attribute alone is by inclusion.

* A student: Did you not say, O Shaykh, that its indication upon the essence?

* The Shaykh: No, because al-'Aziz is a name. Its indication upon the essence alone or the attribute alone is by inclusion, and upon both together is by correspondence, and upon what the might necessarily entails of knowledge, power, strength and the like is by implication. For this reason, the name al-Hayy al-Qayyum includes all the attributes: these two names include all the attributes, because al-Hayy necessarily entails all the attributes of perfection, and al-Qayyum necessarily entails all the attributes of sovereignty, dominion, management and so forth. For this reason, it is related in a hadith that these two are the Greatest Name of Allah.[[Narrated by Abu Dawud (1496) from the hadith of Asma' bint Yazid.]]

Al-'Aziz al-Hakim: we have said that in them is affirmation of might, and al-Hakim contains affirmation of command and wisdom. In combining the two, a third attribute appears, which is that the might of Allah is joined with wisdom, unlike the might of other than Him, since the might of others may be devoid of wisdom.

* Among the benefits of the verse: it is fitting to reflect when verses are concluded with something that is contrary to the apparent situation; that is, you should not reject it if you find a verse ending in a way that differs from what the apparent situation or context requires. Reflect upon it, for the error is from you: ﴿If You punish them, indeed they are Your servants; and if You forgive them, indeed You, You are the Almighty, the All-Wise﴾ [al-Ma'idah 118]. The apparent requirement of the context would be to say: "Indeed You are the Forgiving, the Merciful," but He turned away from that. Do not say that this is a flaw at all; the flaw is from you, for this is the speech of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and it contains no flaw. His cosmic signs contain no flaw, and neither do His legislative signs. Therefore, one must reflect and pause. Here, in the verse before us, it may occur to a person that it should end with knowledge, but upon reflection, its ending with might and wisdom is more fitting. Then He, exalted, said: ﴿And these parables We present to the people, but none will understand them except the knowledgeable﴾ [al-'Ankabut 43].

* In this noble verse there is a benefit: the striking of parables, and that it is a kind of teaching and guidance, by His saying: ﴿And these parables We present﴾.

* Among its benefits: affirmation of the greatness of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. From where is this taken?

* A student: ﴿We present﴾.

* The Shaykh: ﴿We present﴾ from the "nun of greatness" (nun al-'azamah): ﴿We present them to the people﴾. Know, if you did not know before, that what Allah, exalted, attributes to Himself with the expression of greatness indicates the greatness of His own self, glorified and exalted; it may also be intended to refer to His angels and not Himself. This is common in the Qur'an, and likewise the first-person plural is common in the Qur'an. Among what Allah intends regarding His angels is like His saying: ﴿So when We have recited it, follow its recitation﴾ [al-Qiyamah 18]. Does this pronoun refer to whom? The pronoun of the subject? It refers to Jibril, but Allah attributed it to Himself because Jibril is His messenger. Likewise His saying: ﴿When fear had left Abraham and the good tidings had come to him, he began to argue with Us concerning the people of Lot﴾ [Hud 74]. ﴿He argued with Us﴾, while he did not argue with Allah but with the messengers. But taking what is attributed to Allah in the form of greatness as referring to His messengers and angels requires evidence; otherwise, the default is that it returns to Allah. As for what Allah attributes to Himself in the singular form, it is for Himself alone. We will give two examples for this. The first: His saying: ﴿And when My servants ask you concerning Me, indeed I am near; I respond to the invocation of the supplicant when he calls upon Me. So let them respond to Me and believe in Me that they may be guided﴾ [al-Baqarah 186]. All these pronouns are in the singular form. Thus His saying: ﴿Indeed I am near﴾ means the nearness of Himself to the one who calls upon Him; but this nearness does not necessitate that the Throne be empty of Him or that His elevation be negated, just as He descends to the lowest heaven and this does not necessitate that He be empty of the Throne or that this contradicts His elevation. But His saying: ﴿Then why, when it [the soul] has reached the throat, while you are at that time looking on — and We are closer to him than you, but you do not see﴾ [al-Waqi'ah 83–85]. Here ﴿closer﴾ contains a pronoun referring to ﴿We﴾, and ﴿We﴾ refers to whom? To Allah. Yet He is closer to him than we are, by His angels. What is the evidence?

The evidence is His saying: ﴿but you do not see﴾, for the angels attend the dying person to take his soul and sit near him as far as the eye can see, but we do not see them. So here, the nearness is for whom?

The nearness is for the angels, because Allah attributed it to Himself with the expression of greatness and evidence was found. This benefit is very important, and it will benefit you in the matter of the attributes and other matters: what Allah attributes to Himself in the singular form is for Himself, and what He attributes to Himself in the plural form is for Himself, but it may be for His angels by a contextual indicator. This is not impossible, as you have known.

Here He said: ﴿These parables We present﴾. Is it for Himself or for the angels? For Himself, because there is no indicator showing that it is for the angels.

And ﴿We present them to the people﴾: the first benefit, we said, is that there is in it the benefit of striking parables.

* Also among the benefits of the verse: the mercy of Allah, exalted, toward creation through the striking of parables for them, because striking parables, as we said, brings the intelligible closer to the minds, and a person's conception of the perceptible is stronger than his conception of the intelligible, is it not so?

Now, if I explained to you the rites of Hajj clearly, fully and manifestly, or took you to Hajj to the rites themselves, which is more effective?

The latter is more effective, because you perceive it with your eyes, whereas the former you conceive with your hearts and do not grasp it well. Thus striking parables contains mercy for creation, in that Allah, glorified and exalted, brings the intelligible near to us through the perceptible.

* Among the benefits of the verse: it is fitting to reflect upon parables, by His saying: ﴿but none will understand them except the knowledgeable﴾. The knowledgeable is the one who reflects and considers until he understands.

* Among the benefits of the verse: praise of the intellect, by His saying: ﴿and none will understand them﴾. By "intellect" here is meant the intellect of perception or the intellect of sound judgment?

* The students: The intellect of sound judgment.

* The Shaykh: The intellect of sound judgment. The intellect that benefits is the one that is praised.

* Also among them: the virtue of knowledge, by His saying: ﴿but none will understand them except the knowledgeable﴾. Whoever is not knowing of Allah, glorified and exalted, and of His signs, does not understand these meanings and says: "These are things that have no meaning." But the knowledgeable is the one who understands them, knows their purpose and meaning, and the aspects of their resemblance, until he reaches the degree of perfection.

Allah, exalted, said: ﴿Allah created the heavens and the earth with truth. Indeed in that is a sign for the believers.﴾

* In this verse there are benefits. First: that the creator of the heavens and the earth is Allah, or not? ﴿Allah created the heavens﴾, because we do not know otherwise.

If someone said: is there no restriction in the verse so that you can say that the Creator is Allah?

We say: Yes, there is no restriction by the well-known methods, but there is a restriction in that there exist only one heavens and one earth; if the Creator of them is Allah, the possibility that anyone else is their creator is negated.

* Among them: refutation of the naturalists (ahl al-tabi'ah), may God protect us, who say that the heavens and the earth have no creator, that they are things that interact, change and fluctuate, and that creation has no beginning and no end.

* Among them: affirmation that the heavens and the earth are created, and that they are not eternal. From where do we know this? The creation of the heavens: they are brought into existence after non-existence, and everything other than Allah exists after non-existence.

* Among them: that the heavens are plural. How many?

* Students: Seven heavens.

* The Shaykh: Yes, they are specified as seven in other verses.

* Also among them: that the earth is one?

* Students: No, this refers to the genus.

* The Shaykh: The intended meaning is the genus. Now, in the Qur'an, the earth is never mentioned in plural form, is it not? However, its plurality is indicated in His saying: ﴿Allah is the One who created seven heavens and of the earth the like thereof﴾ [al-Talaq 12]. Is the similarity here in attribute impossible or not? Because there is no comparison between the heavens and the earth, when similarity in attribute is impossible, we return to similarity in number, and the Sunnah has come explicitly to that effect, such as His ﷺ saying: "He will be collared with it from seven earths."[[Narrated by al-Bukhari (2452) from the hadith of Sa'id ibn Zayd ibn 'Amr, and Muslim (1612/142) from the hadith of 'Aishah.]]

* Among the benefits of the verse: that the creation of these heavens and earth is with truth, not in vain, nor in play, nor in falsehood, by His saying: ﴿with truth﴾.

* Also among them: that they contain truth. Their creation, as a原 origination, is with truth, and they also contain truth; nothing can occur in the heavens and the earth except with truth.

* Also among its benefits: the reassurance of a person regarding what Allah brings about in the heavens and the earth, or the arousing of reassurance. What is the basis of this? I have mentioned the benefit, so what is its basis? Good, what is the basis of its arousing reassurance?

* A student: With truth.

* The Shaykh: That it is with truth. Everything that happens, once you know it is with truth, you feel reassured. I do not say: why did it happen, and why did it not happen? If hunger, sickness, earthquakes and floods befall people, I know that this is with truth, so I am reassured, content and submit. In reality, there is no rest for a person except through this; a person cannot find rest except by believing in Allah's decree and destiny, and that it is the truth, and then he becomes fully reassured. Otherwise, he will be troubled, for there is no hour in which he does not find something that grieves him, whether in himself, his family, his companions, his land, or the Islamic lands generally. A person cannot be reassured and settled until he believes that all these things are true.

* A student: Disputing with destiny?

* The Shaykh: Disputing destiny by the Shari'ah is obligatory. Yes, there is also something else.

* The student: So you are reassured and yet you dispute?

* The Shaykh: Dispute by the Shari'ah; it is not by destiny.

* The student: No, I meant combining the two?

* The Shaykh: Combining them: for example, when destiny comes to us that grieves us, we dispute it by the Shari'ah, by patience. If we are patient, it does not grieve us. Likewise, disputing destiny by the Shari'ah. This is obligatory: you must confront destiny with what the Shari'ah requires. But disputing destiny with destiny is not permissible. You keep giving answers in Sufi terms, I do not know what...

* The student: No, not Sufi, O Shaykh, let us be cautious (...). It was what prompted me to mention this...

* The Shaykh: I did not wish you to mention this, because it requires... Note that some people may shy away from the word "dispute," and what is meant by dispute is confrontation.

* Among the benefits of the verse: that the creation of the heavens and the earth is a sign indicating what this creation necessitates of the attributes of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. We have mentioned that among them is what indicates the power of Allah, the wisdom of Allah, and His might, according to what the verse requires.

* Also among them: that the verses benefit no one except whom? Except the believers, by His saying: ﴿for the believers﴾.

* From this benefit a derived benefit follows: whenever the servant's faith is perfected, he benefits more from the signs. The path to obtaining this is what we have mentioned more than once, that when a ruling is attached to a description, it grows stronger with the strength of that description and weaker with its weakness. Every ruling attached to a description grows in strength with the strength of that description and in weakness with its weakness. So we say: therefore, whenever a person's faith is more perfect, there appears to him of the signs of Allah in these creatures what does not appear to those below him. Is the meaning of this clear, O people?

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 29, verse 41–44 (part 1 of 3):

Then He, the Exalted, said: ﴿The example of those who take protectors other than Allah﴾ — idols, whom they hope will benefit them — ﴿is like the example of the spider﴾ [al-'Ankabut 41].

(Mathal and mithl) are like (shabah and shibh), in form and in meaning. So mathal means likeness (shabah), and it is an expression for comparing an intelligible thing with a perceptible thing, because representing intelligible matters through perceptible ones increases them in clarity, explanation and conception. Is this understood? And although they are not equal in every respect, they are equal in the respect in which the comparison is made.

His saying: ﴿The example of those who take protectors other than Allah﴾ means: those who made protectors. The intended meaning of "protectors" is the idols, and they were called protectors because their worshippers hope for their benefit, like a protector who benefits you by support, defence, bringing good, and similar things. Also, they are called protectors in that they themselves ..

.. This is why the people of Abraham said: ﴿Burn him and support your gods, if you are going to act﴾ [al-Anbiya' 68]. They support them and hope for support from them, and for this reason these idols were named (protectors).

His saying: ﴿other than Allah﴾ means: besides Him. The evidence that the intended meaning is "besides" in the sense of "other than" is that this occurs in several verses, such as His saying: ﴿You have no god other than Him﴾ [al-A'raf 59]. The expression "dun" (besides) is used because its rank is lowly in comparison to whom? To Allah, Mighty and Majestic. ﴿other than Allah, protectors﴾ [al-'Ankabut 41]. Their likeness, then, — who is meant by those who take protectors other than Allah? It refers to the polytheists, their likeness ﴿is like the example of the spider﴾ [al-'Ankabut 41]; that is, like the likeness of the spider. The spider is a well-known small creature that takes for itself a house made of web, and this house of web is what it weaves and emerges from. Allah, glory be to Him, is capable of all things. When this spider falls from a height, it immediately secretes this web and clings to it so that it does not fall to the ground; then, despite that, it secretes it and clings to it, and you find it hanging by this thread. When it wishes to climb up with it, it climbs, turning itself over and making its head the highest, and it climbs with this thread that it has just secreted. Then, when it is hunting — and it mostly hunts flies — what does it do with them? It binds them with these threads until it finishes them off. This is part of the saying of the Exalted: ﴿Our Lord is He who gave everything its creation, then guided it﴾ [Ta-Ha 50], guiding this creation to what is good for it. The point is that this spider took a house for itself, that is, made for itself a house. From what? From the web that it weaves.

The author said: (﴿took a house﴾ [al-'Ankabut 41] for itself, to which it retreats), and this is observed. ﴿And indeed the frailest﴾ [al-'Ankabut 41], the weakest ﴿of houses is the house of the spider﴾ [al-'Ankabut 41]. This is the word of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, who is the Knower of what we have not encompassed in knowledge. How many of Allah's creatures have houses, while we know of these houses only what we witness of them, and how much is hidden from us! Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, says: "The frailest of houses is the house of the spider." He emphasised this sentence ﴿And indeed the frailest of houses is the house of the spider﴾ with (inna) and the lam, in order to stress the weakness of these protectors, just as the houses in which spiders take refuge are weak; indeed they are the frailest and weakest of houses, for these protectors are likewise the weakest of protectors, since they do not benefit their worshippers. Rather, Allah says in the Qur'an: ﴿Indeed, you and what you worship besides Allah are fuel for Hell; you will arrive at it. (98) Had these been gods, they would not have arrived there, but all of them will abide therein﴾ [al-Anbiya' 98–99]. ﴿They would not have arrived there﴾: does this refer to the gods, or to those who claimed divinity for them?

It includes both. Understand: if they were truly gods, they would have protected themselves from entering the Fire, and they would have protected their worshippers from entering the Fire. But they are false gods that do not benefit. This is the aspect of resemblance in His saying: ﴿And indeed the frailest of houses is the house of the spider﴾. This comparison is what the rhetoricians call the representational comparison (al-tashbih al-tamthili); that is, it is composed of a whole sentence. If you say, "So-and-so is like the sea in generosity," this is a comparison, but it is a single comparison, in which you liken one individual to another individual. But if you bring something in which you liken a story to a story or a matter to a matter, then the comparison here is representational and compound, consisting of several aspects of the thing compared and the thing compared to, and the aspects of resemblance are also multiple. This comparison we call a representational comparison, because it is composed of a complete story. That is, it is not intended that the worshippers be likened to the spider alone and the worshipped ones to the houses alone; rather, the whole matter is intended to be likened to the whole matter, so that the picture becomes clear to the addressee.

His saying: ﴿And indeed the frailest of houses is the house of the spider﴾. The author, explaining this weakness, said: (it does not repel heat or cold). Yes indeed, it does not repel heat, nor cold, nor does it protect it from calamities, such as something falling upon it or the like. This house is the frailest of houses. Therefore, these idols do not benefit their worshippers. Accordingly, we say: those who worshipped these idols did not take refuge in a beneficial refuge, but in a refuge which is neither beneficial, nor preventive, nor protective. For this reason Allah likened that to the house of the spider. In another verse He likened these idols and their supplication to a man stretching his palms towards water so that it would reach his mouth. Will it reach him?

A person has water before him and he is thirsty, so he stretches his palms towards the water. Can it reach his mouth? It can never reach it. Likewise, these idols do not benefit their worshippers, just as this water does not reach the mouth of this thirsty person. Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿if they only knew﴾ [al-'Ankabut 41]; they would not have worshipped them.

﴿If﴾ here is conditional, the protasis is His saying ﴿they were﴾, and its apodosis is omitted; according to the author's explanation, what is its estimated form? "They would not have worshipped them." It should not be joined to what precedes it, because if you joined it to what precedes it, the frailty of the spider's house would be conditioned upon their knowledge, although it is the frailest of houses whether they know or do not know. Therefore it is necessary to pause at His saying: ﴿the house of the spider﴾. Then we say: ﴿if they only knew﴾. The author says: they would not have worshipped them. It is also possible that the apodosis is: ﴿if they only knew﴾, meaning: if they were of those possessing beneficial knowledge, this matter would not have been hidden from them; and since this matter is not hidden from them, they would not have engaged in worship. In any case, this indicates the ignorance of these worshippers, however clever they may be and however skilled they are in managing worldly affairs; in this respect they are foolish, having neither knowledge nor reason. This verse reminds us of another verse in which many people also err, in Surat al-Takathur: ﴿No! If you knew with the certainty of knowledge﴾ [al-Takathur 5]. Some people join it and say: ﴿No! If you knew with the certainty of knowledge (5) you would surely see the Hellfire﴾ [al-Takathur 5–6]. This is a mistake, because the meaning is clearly corrupted by it; for if you joined it, then ﴿you would surely see﴾ would be the apodosis of ﴿if you knew﴾, and the matter is not so. Rather, ﴿you would surely see﴾ is an independent, self-standing sentence in which Allah informs that we will indeed see the Hellfire. Therefore one must pause at His saying: ﴿No! If you knew with the certainty of knowledge﴾.

* Student: Shaykh, if someone said that the spider does benefit from its house to some degree, as is the reality, while the idol-worshippers certainly do not benefit from theirs?

* The Shaykh: Yes, this is correct; it may be raised against us. But the intended point is that these idols are like this house, because it does not benefit. They now benefit from these idols in some kind of benefit, especially material benefit, for those who come to them for worship and seeking blessing gain a material benefit. But the true benefit they hope for, which is averting harm, they do not get.

* Student: O Shaykh, is it not said that (...) does not necessarily entail entering the obligatory? It may be that you are asked for something and it is not obligatory..?

* The Shaykh: No, the intended point of the comparison here is the lack of benefit: they neither benefit nor protect them. And in reality, even the spider's house neither benefits it nor protects it; the wind comes to it, the cold comes to it, the rain comes to it, dust clings to it, and it does not benefit from it with complete benefit.

* Student: It catches prey with it.

* The Shaykh: No, it does not catch prey with it. It catches prey with the web that comes out of it; these threads are what it catches with. As for the house itself, it does not catch with it. But what we see on it, it is what brings it, it brings it and places it there.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed Allah knows whatever they call upon besides Him, of anything. And He is the Mighty, the Wise﴾ [al-'Ankabut 42]. ﴿Indeed Allah knows what﴾ — ﴿what﴾: the author says: (in the sense of "that which"). So it is a relative pronoun. This grammatical analysis which the author adopted is what appears most evident from the verse, while some grammarians say ﴿what﴾ is interrogative, and the pause is on His saying ﴿Indeed Allah knows﴾: what is it that they call upon besides Him of anything, do they benefit? But this is far from the wording, so the author's analysis is correct: ﴿knows what they call upon besides Him﴾. Following the author's analysis, we must say: where is the returning pronoun of the relative clause?

* Student: The ha' (hu).

* The Shaykh: Where?

* Student: In "besides Him".

* The Shaykh: ﴿what they call upon besides Him﴾ — this ha' refers to Allah, not to ﴿what﴾?

* Student: It is omitted.

* The Shaykh: It is omitted, and this is regular: omitting an accusative returning pronoun is regular. So the estimated form is: Indeed Allah knows what they call upon of anything.

And His saying ﴿they call upon﴾ — he said: (they worship). So the supplication here is supplication of worship. Just as supplication may be supplication of worship, it is also supplication of request. As for supplication of request, it is in His saying: ﴿And when My servants ask you about Me, indeed I am near; I respond to the invocation of the supplicant when he calls upon Me﴾ [al-Baqarah 186]. You say: "O my Lord, forgive me; O my Lord, have mercy on me," and similar things. What is supplication of worship? It is that you worship Allah, glory be to Him, by what He has commanded you. And this is called supplication because what is the true condition of the worshipper? It is seeking the forgiveness and mercy of Allah; so he is, in reality, one who supplicates implicitly. Its evidence is the saying of the Exalted: ﴿And your Lord said: Call upon Me, I will respond to you. Indeed, those who are too proud to worship Me will enter Hell, humbled﴾ [Ghafir 60].

And His saying ﴿what they call upon﴾ means: what they worship. It is necessary to make supplication here inclusive of both worship and supplication of request. Do they call upon these idols with supplication of request or not?

* Student: They call upon them.

* The Shaykh: They call upon these idols with supplication of request as well; they ask them. A clear evidence of this is those who associate partners with the prophets and the saints, for they call upon them with supplication of request. They say: "O Messenger of Allah, forgive me," and "O Messenger of Allah, ease my affair," and similar things.
