And for this reason there was reported from some of the early generations (salaf): "Whoever his prayer does not restrain from immorality and wrongdoing, he increases from God only in distance."[[Recorded by Sa'id ibn Mansur in his Tafsir (1705), and from his route al-Tabarani in al-Mu'jam al-Kabir (8543), from Ibn Mas'ud as his own statement. He also related it in al-Mu'jam al-Kabir (11025) as a hadith from Ibn 'Abbas traced back to the Prophet ﷺ.]] And we seek refuge in God.

What is the wisdom in its restraining from immorality and wrongdoing?

**Student:** Because it is a connection with God, and when a person connects with God, He magnifies his prohibition and magnifies his command.

**Shaykh:** Well done. The matter of God becomes great in a person's soul when he is connected with God, the Mighty and Majestic. Then also, when he wants to commit immorality and wrongdoing, he remembers the time when he was connected with God, the Mighty and Majestic, and so it restrains him. I told you when explaining: some people may pray a prayer, one of those prayers that is complete according to their state, and they find the taste of this prayer in their hearts for as long as God wills, for a long period, remembering the sweetness of this intimate conversation and its beauty, and it restrains them from immorality and wrongdoing.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And the remembrance of Allah is greater﴾.

First: the grammatical analysis (i'rab) of this sentence? You are not experts in i'rab?

**Student:** (...)?

**Shaykh:** Its i'rab.

**Student:** Ha.

**Shaykh:** The lām and all of it.

**Student:** ﴿And the remembrance of Allah﴾ is in the nominative.

**Shaykh:** The lām before it.

**Student:** The lām of (dhikr)?

**Shaykh:** Yes.

**Student:** (dhikr): a nominative subject, its sign of nominative case is the ḍamma, and (dhikr) is in construct, and the word (Allah) is a genitive noun in apposition, (akbar) is the predicate of the subject.

**Shaykh:** The predicate of the subject. Well done.

Is the construction here the genitive of the verbal noun to its subject or to its object?

**Student:** To its object.

**Shaykh:** To its object.

**Student:** No, to its subject.

**Shaykh:** To its subject?! Be definite.

**Student:** To its subject.

**Shaykh:** What is the difference between the two interpretations?

**Student:** The difference: this is the name of God upon the Qur'an, and the remembrance of God...

**Shaykh:** Which of the two interpretations is this?

**Student:** On the basis that the construct is to its subject.

**Shaykh:** Yes.

**Student:** As for if it is to its object, it is the remembrance of God by people, meaning what they mention God with, according to the second interpretation.

**Shaykh:** Good. Meaning: you are saying it is suitable for this and for that?

**Student:** No, it is according to an interpretation...

**Shaykh:** Its construction is to the subject.

**Student:** To its subject.

**Shaykh:** What do you say? What do you say about both constructions, to the subject and to the object, and about the interpretation he gave?

**Student:** He here said: it is a construction to the object.

**Shaykh:** A construction to the object?

**Student:** Because he mentioned the prayer...

**Shaykh:** What is the meaning on the interpretation that it is construct to the object?

**Student:** The preventing.

**Shaykh:** What is the meaning on this interpretation?

**Student:** The meaning: that the one who remembers God, may He be exalted, this is among the greatest things, or it prevents him from many things...

**Shaykh:** Meaning: your remembrance of God is greater and more significant than the prohibition of immorality and wrongdoing.

**Student:** Yes.

**Shaykh:** Is that so?

**Student:** The prohibition of immorality and wrongdoing?!

**Shaykh:** Yes, because He said: ﴿Indeed, prayer prohibits immorality and wrongdoing, and the remembrance of Allah is greater﴾.

**Student:** (...) the Qur'an, (...) meaning.

**Shaykh:** It is construct to the object, and the meaning then is: and your remembrance of God is greater than the prohibition of immorality and wrongdoing; that is, the remembrance of God that is in prayer is greater than immorality and wrongdoing, or in the general sense as the author chose.

On the interpretation that it is construct to the subject, what is the meaning?

**Student:** (...) only construct to the object.

**Shaykh:** Only to the object?

**Student:** Yes.

**Shaykh:** Yes.

**Student:** The remembrance of God, may He be exalted and majestic, of the person in the highest assembly.

**Shaykh:** Yes, greater...

**Student:** Greater than his doing, until when (...).

**Shaykh:** Yes, greater than his doing.

Because the matter is that God remembers you, not that you remember God, as in His saying: ﴿Say: If you should love Allah, then follow me; Allah will love you﴾ [Al 'Imran 31]. He did not say: follow me, you will love God. He said: ﴿will love you﴾, since the matter concerns God's love for the person. So on this basis the meaning is: and the remembrance of God of you while you pray is greater than what you gain from prayer in terms of restraint from immorality and wrongdoing. Is it not possible for us to say that it is suitable for this and that? Let it be for this and for that?

There is no contradiction between them. We stated the rule in tafsir: if a verse is open to two meanings that do not contradict each other, it is taken to both meanings. But if one of them contradicts the other, what do we do?

We adopt the stronger one, because a verse cannot bear two contradictory meanings, but the stronger one is adopted.

**Student:** As a matter of reward.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 29, verse 45–58 (part 3 of 3):

* The Shaykh: Yes, it is by way of recompense, as is established in the sacred hadith: "Whoever remembers Me within himself, I remember him within Myself; and whoever remembers Me in an assembly, I remember him in an assembly better than it."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (7405) and Muslim (2675/21) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]]
* A student: Is every waw (و) here resumptive (mustaʼnafah)?
* The Shaykh: Yes, indeed. It may be resumptive on both possibilities.
Regarding His words: ﴿And the remembrance of Allah is greater﴾, "greater" (akbar): where is the thing it is compared to?
* A student: The prohibition of indecency (al-fahshaa').
* The Shaykh: Yes, the prohibition of indecency and wrongdoing. And if we wish, we can say: the object of comparison has been omitted for generality.
* A student: Shaykh, someone may say: the speaker intends only one meaning.
* The Shaykh: Yes, the speaker intends only one meaning. But as long as his words can bear both meanings without contradiction, what tells us that He intended only one? This is the speech of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and the speech of Allah, glorified and exalted, is broad in meaning. So as long as the wording is suitable for both meanings without any contradiction between them, we cannot say that He intended only this one.
His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And Allah knows what you do﴾. This verse is a declarative sentence. A declarative sentence conveys Allah's knowledge of what we do. So what is the purpose of it? Is its purpose encouragement (targhib) or warning (tarhib)?
* A student: Warning.
* The Shaykh: Encouragement?
* A student: Warning.
* The Shaykh: Warning? That is, He knows what we do and will recompense us for it? What made you know that it is only for warning?
* A student: (...).
* The Shaykh: You say: warning. What made you know?
* A student: (...) the verse.
* The Shaykh: What verse?
* A student: (...).
* Another student: For encouragement and warning.
* The Shaykh: For encouragement and warning. These are two opinions. Which is more correct?
* A student: The correct view is that it is for warning.
* The Shaykh: For warning?
* A student: Yes.
* The Shaykh: What is the evidence?
* A student: Because it indicates watchfulness; when a person knows that Allah is watching him...
* The Shaykh: He fears Him.
* A student: He has some fear.
* The Shaykh: And when he knows that Allah knows what he does, and nothing of it is lost, does he not become eager to obey?
* A student: This is weak in this verse.
* Another student: It is for encouragement and warning: ﴿He knows what you do﴾, so He rewards the good-doer for his goodness and the wrongdoer for his wrongdoing.
* The Shaykh: It is for encouragement and for warning. Here, it is closer to encouragement, because what precedes it is a command, not a prohibition. If it were a prohibition, it would be closer to warning: "Do not commit adultery, for Allah knows what you do" is warning; "Do righteous deeds, for Allah knows what you do" is encouragement, which is clear. Nevertheless, we say that it applies to both together, because it includes the encouragement of obeying the command and the warning against disobeying and defying it.
In truth, we have extended this discussion as if it were a full lesson, but there is no harm in that, because we want a person to have opened to him, as much as possible, some of the knowledge of the Qur'an and its secrets.
* A student: The evidence that the address includes both the Messenger and others.
* The Shaykh: Which one?
* A student: I am asking you for the evidence that the address includes the Messenger and the whole Ummah?
* The Shaykh: Yes.
* A student: What is the evidence?
* The Shaykh: The address directed to the Messenger applies to him and to the Ummah. The evidence: who knows it?
* A student: ﴿Say: If you should love Allah, then follow me; Allah will love you﴾ [Al 'Imran 31].
* The Shaykh: Yes.
* A student: ﴿There has certainly been for you in the Messenger of Allah an excellent example﴾ [al-Ahzab 21].
* The Shaykh: No, this in fact is evidence for the obligation of following his example. But the evidence that an address directed to him applies to him and to the Ummah, when no proof indicates otherwise, is the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And a believing woman, if she gives herself to the Prophet and the Prophet wishes to marry her, [this is] exclusively for you, not for the [other] believers﴾ [al-Ahzab 50]. It shows us that, were it not for His saying ﴿exclusively﴾, the ruling would apply to him and to others. This indicates that, when unrestricted, an address directed to the Messenger ﷺ applies to him and to the Ummah.
Another verse also indicates this, which is His saying, when He mentioned that Allah permitted him the wife of Zayd ibn Harithah. What did He say?
He said: ﴿So that there will be no discomfort for the believers concerning the wives of their adopted sons﴾ [al-Ahzab 37].
Recite the verse: ﴿And [remember] when you said to the one on whom Allah bestowed favor and you bestowed favor, "Keep your wife and fear Allah," while you concealed within yourself that which Allah is to disclose, and you feared the people, while Allah has more right that you fear Him. So when Zayd had no longer any need for her, We married her to you﴾ [al-Ahzab 37]. Now, the ruling applies to whom?
* The students: To the Messenger ﷺ.
* The Shaykh: To the Messenger ﷺ. Nevertheless, He gave a general reason, saying: ﴿So that there will be no discomfort for the believers﴾; He did not say "for you," but ﴿for the believers concerning the wives of their adopted sons when they have no longer any need for them﴾. This is evidence that an address directed to him applies to him and to the Ummah. Is it clear?
* A student: Shaykh, do we also learn from the first verse an indication of the intended meaning?
* The Shaykh: Which one?
* A student: Because it begins with His saying: ﴿Indeed, We have made lawful to you your wives﴾ [al-Ahzab 50]?
* The Shaykh: I would say there is evidence in it, and this also supports it.
* A student: We could say, for example: He made the address singular to the Messenger, then stated the ruling about the woman: ﴿exclusively for you﴾ [al-Ahzab 50]...
* The Shaykh: This is evidence that the address directed to him applies to him and to the Ummah.
What concerns me in a student of knowledge is not that he memorizes issues; memorizing issues is simple. I think the recorder has a stronger memory for issues than we do, right?
(...) It is nothing. If you give the recorder a thousand issues and come to it twenty years later, will it give them back to you or not?
It will give them back to you. But what matters for the student of knowledge is that he understands. Among understanding is grasping implication (dalalah), the implication from the Qur'an and also from the Sunnah. Through this, Allah opens to a person a great deal of knowledge that perhaps no one else perceives. For this reason, when 'Ali ibn Abi Talib was asked: "Did the Prophet ﷺ entrust you with anything?" he said: "No, except what is in this sheet, or an understanding that Allah grants a person regarding the Qur'an." See, "or an understanding"; and there is no doubt that 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, had a great deal of understanding of the Qur'an.[[Narrated by al-Bukhari (111) from the hadith of 'Ali ibn Abi Talib.]]
So the point is that I love for the student of knowledge to be eager for understanding. The Prophet ﷺ said: "Many a one who conveys the message understands it better than one who hears it."[[Narrated by al-Bukhari (1741) from the hadith of Abu Bakrah.]] Memorization is like pharmacy: the pharmacist has all the medicines, but understanding, deduction and derivation are like the physician, who directs the medicines and benefits from them. The pharmacist keeps them for you, but the physician is the one who benefits and benefits others. So the most important thing to me in a student of knowledge, in the interpretation of the Qur'an and likewise in the Sunnah, is understanding, deduction and derivation. I think it has passed us that the indication of a word upon its meaning is of three types: correspondence (mutabaqah), inclusion (tadammun) and entailment (iltizam).
Correspondence and inclusion are simple; the least of students of knowledge can know them.
But entailment (iltizam) is the important one, and from it branch issues that none can count but Allah.
When a person is granted success in the implication of entailment, he attains much good in this matter.
[[The author's speech has been abridged due to its great length.]]

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 29, verse 45–58 (part 1 of 3):

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Recite what has been revealed to you of the Book﴾ [Al-Ankabut 45].
﴿Recite what has been revealed to you of the Book﴾. ﴿Recite﴾ (utlu) includes verbal recitation (al-tilawah al-lafziyyah) and recitation in terms of its rulings (al-tilawah al-hukmiyyah). Verbal recitation is that you read the Qur'an. Recitation in terms of its rulings is that you act upon its rulings, and this is the recitation of following (tilawat al-ittiba'), from their saying: "Fulan talaa fulan" (so-and-so followed so-and-so). What is the meaning of talaahu?
* Students: That he followed him.
* The Shaykh: Yes, he followed him. So the command to recite here includes both this and that: ﴿Those to whom We have given the Book recite it as it should be recited; those believe in it﴾ [Al-Baqarah 121].
As for his saying, glorified and exalted is He: ﴿Recite﴾, the address is to the Messenger, peace and blessings of Allah be upon him, and it is not directed to everyone who may be addressed. This is because He said: ﴿what has been revealed to you﴾, and this restricts it to the Messenger ﷺ, since no one else has had revelation sent to him. Nevertheless, the address to the Messenger, peace and blessings of Allah be upon him, is also an address to him and to the ummah, by the evidence of His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, in the Messenger of Allah you have a good example for whoever hopes for Allah and the Last Day﴾ [Al-Ahzab 21]. Except what evidence establishes as specific to him, in which case the evidence is followed, such as His saying: ﴿And a believing woman, if she gives herself to the Prophet and the Prophet wishes to marry her﴾ [Al-Ahzab 50]. Had the verse stopped at this, it would have been permissible for the ummah to do the same, but He said: ﴿exclusively for you, excluding the believers﴾ [Al-Ahzab 50]. This indicates that the address directed to the Messenger ﷺ is for him and for his ummah, unless there is evidence that it is specific to him.
He said: ﴿Recite what has been revealed to you of the Book﴾. ﴿Ma﴾ is a relative pronoun indicating generality. As for his saying: ﴿has been revealed to you﴾, wahy (revelation) linguistically is informing swiftly and secretly. Informing swiftly and secretly is called wahy. For example, suppose you are among a people and you want to inform someone of something; you say, for instance, "such-and-such" with your hand, so that those around you do not understand, but your companion understands, without you saying: "O so-and-so, get up so we may go to so-and-so." Is this called wahy?
No, this is not wahy, because it is clear and has no concealment. But linguistically, informing swiftly and secretly is called wahy. In the Shari'ah, however, it is Allah's informing one of His prophets or messengers with the Shari'ah; this is wahy in the legal sense. And here, what is intended? Wahy in the legal sense. It has levels, which Allah mentioned in Surah Ha Mim 'Asaqa (Ash-Shura). He said: ﴿what has been revealed to you of the Book﴾. ﴿Min﴾ here is explanatory (bayaniyyah), explaining ﴿ma﴾ in his saying: ﴿what has been revealed to you﴾. As for his saying: ﴿the Book﴾, it refers to the Qur'an. It is called a Book because it is written in the mushafs, because it is written in the Preserved Tablet (al-lawh al-mahfuz), and because it is written in the hands of the angels: ﴿No! Indeed, it is a reminder. So whoever wills may remember it. In sheets held in honor, exalted and purified, by the hands of scribes, noble and dutiful﴾ [Abasa 11–16].
The form kitab (fi'al) in the sense of maf'ul (object) is common in the Arabic language, and I think the examples that passed us are not absent from your minds now, such as firash (a bed) meaning mafrush (spread out), ghirас (planting) meaning maghrus (planted), and bina' (a building) meaning mabni (built).
He said: ﴿Recite what has been revealed to you of the Book and establish the prayer﴾ [Al-Ankabut 45]. ﴿Establish the prayer﴾ means: perform it in its complete form, because establishing a thing is making it upright, with no crookedness or deficiency.
As for his saying: ﴿establish the prayer﴾, the address is to the Messenger ﷺ, and it is known that he establishes the prayer, and that he is the most upright of those who pray in prayer. So how was the address directed to him with ﴿establish the prayer﴾?
We say: the address is directed to one who is characterized by it, and what is meant is continuity upon it, not renewal of it, because he already has it. But continuity upon it is like His saying: ﴿O you who believe, believe in Allah﴾ [An-Nisa' 136]. ﴿O you who believe, believe﴾: the address is not idle, so that we would say it is achieving what is already achieved. The believer is a believer; we say: what is meant? Continuity upon that. So when the address or command is directed to one who is characterized by it, what is meant is continuity upon it.
As for his saying, glorified and exalted is He: ﴿establish the prayer﴾. Earlier we said that recitation includes following and acting upon its rulings. Is establishing the prayer not from following it and acting upon its rulings?
Yes. So its being conjoined to his saying ﴿recite﴾ is from the conjunction of the particular to the general ('atf al-khass 'ala al-'amm), and the conjunction of the particular to the general is an indication of the elevation of its status. There is no doubt that the prayer is the best of bodily acts, so it was singled out for mention. Then, does conjoining the particular to the general mean mentioning it twice, or does it mean it was singled out for mention from among the general?
On this there are two opinions among the scholars. Some say that mentioning the particular after the general means that the indication of generality was removed from it and then it was singled out for mention. Others say it is included in the first generality and then singled out for mention, so it is mentioned twice. Both indicate its nobility; that is, both views indicate the nobility of what is mentioned. But which is stronger? The latter: that it is mentioned twice, once by way of the general and once by way of the specific. The benefit appears if you say: "Honor the students and Muhammad," and Muhammad is among the students according to the view that he is included in the general, then singled out for mention. We then know that this man is a student and his name is Muhammad. But if we say he was removed from the general and singled out for mention, then we must search for this Muhammad: is he a student or not?
It requires a qarinah (indicator) showing that he is among the students. The correct view, as you have said, is that it is stronger: that mentioning the particular after the general means mentioning it twice.
Then He, glorified and exalted, said, giving the reason for the command to establish the prayer: ﴿Indeed, the prayer forbids immorality and wrongdoing﴾ [Al-Ankabut 45]. Is this reason related to the addressee or to the thing addressed? Pay attention, brothers, since the matter has a difficulty: is the reason here related to the addressee or to the thing he is addressed with? Who is the addressee?
* Student: The Messenger, peace and blessings of Allah be upon him.
* The Shaykh: Good. And the thing addressed?
* Student: The prayer.
* The Shaykh: The prayer. He addressed him with establishing the prayer. So is this reason for establishing the prayer as such, or is it a reason connected to the addressee, that is, connected to the one addressed?
If we say it is connected to the addressee, the meaning becomes that the prayer forbids you from immorality and wrongdoing, and this would imply that immorality and wrongdoing could occur from the Messenger ﷺ. If we say it is the reason connected to the thing addressed, which is the prayer, then we say that the prayer as such forbids immorality and wrongdoing, and this is a description that is true of whom? Of other than the Messenger ﷺ. So this reason is for the thing addressed, the prayer, and not for the one addressed, who is the Messenger ﷺ, since we know he is protected from immorality and wrongdoing. Is it clear, brothers? And this is the required reading.
As for his saying: ﴿Indeed, the prayer forbids immorality and wrongdoing﴾. The word ﴿tanha﴾ (forbids) here and in the previous verse: is the intended prayer the obligatory prayer, or the obligatory and voluntary together?
* Student: All of them.
* The Shaykh: It is general. As for his saying: ﴿Indeed, the prayer forbids immorality﴾, ﴿tanha﴾ means it prevents, but the expression of nahy (forbidding) is more eloquent than the expression of man' (preventing), since one who prevents may not be warning, whereas in nahy there is a warning. It is as if the prayer has a secret that requires a person to keep away from immorality and wrongdoing; it rebukes his conscience and says to him: Why do you do this? Why do you act so?
As for his saying: ﴿forbids immorality and wrongdoing﴾: ﴿al-fahsha'﴾ is everything that is considered abominable among sins, such as adultery, theft, drinking wine, killing a soul, and the like. ﴿Al-munkar﴾ is what is less than that. The conjunction of ﴿al-munkar﴾ to ﴿al-fahsha'﴾ is the conjunction of the general to the particular, since every fahsha' is munkar, but not every munkar is fahsha'.
The author said: (﴿from immorality and wrongdoing﴾ according to the Shari'ah; that is, it is of its nature to do so as long as the person is in it). As for his saying: (that is, it is of its nature to do so), this is correct. But "as long as the person is in it" is not correct. Rather, it forbids immorality and wrongdoing whether or not the person is in it, and whether or not he remains in it. That is, its benefit is not specific to when a person is engaged in praying, which is well known; he is not one who commits immorality and wrongdoing. Rather, the great benefit is that it affects your heart in a way that requires keeping you away from immorality and wrongdoing, and this is the fruit and the result. The fruit and result are not merely that when you pray you no longer commit immorality and wrongdoing. Therefore the author's restriction with his words "as long as he is in it" is open to question and is not correct. Rather, it is unrestricted: it forbids immorality and wrongdoing, meaning that what occurs through it necessitates for the heart distance from immorality and wrongdoing. The reason for this is that the praying person converses with his Lord, as the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said, so there is a bond between him and his Lord, and this bond gains the heart faith and light. For this reason the Prophet, peace and blessings of Allah be upon him, said: "Prayer is light" [Narrated by Muslim (223/1) from the hadith of Abu Malik al-Ash'ari].
It is known that when the heart acquires light, it does not incline toward immorality and wrongdoing. Whenever it intends to do something, it recalls that a few hours earlier it was standing before Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, so it feels shame and withdraws. This is a matter that is observed: a person sometimes recalls standing in a prayer twenty years or more ago, a prayer he prayed on some day, as if he saw his Lord, "worship Allah as if you see Him," in the utmost excellence, and he finds the taste of that prayer after a long time. This remembrance does not leave his heart; this recollection must affect his restraint from immorality and wrongdoing. This is the meaning of His saying: ﴿Indeed, the prayer forbids immorality and wrongdoing﴾. But what is meant by ﴿Indeed, the prayer﴾ is the prayer that is actually established, not every prayer forbids immorality and wrongdoing. By Allah, if our prayer forbade us from immorality and wrongdoing, we would all be sound, we would all be sound. But now we ask Allah to deal with us in His pardon: a person enters the prayer with a heart and leaves with the same heart or worse. Note that acts of worship, if they do not affect your heart for good, are a harm; what does not benefit you through the verses harms you, as the Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "The Qur'an is a proof for you or against you" [Narrated by Muslim (223/1) from the hadith of Abu Malik al-Ash'ari].
This matter is one that many Muslims suffer from: he says, "I am not affected by the prayer, my heart is not present, I am not humbled; so what is the remedy?" Some people may also doubt this report, while the report of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, is true. He says: "I pray, but I do not see that it forbids me from immorality and wrongdoing. I pray with the congregation in the mosque, then I go out to my shop and deal in usury, deal in fraud, deal in lying; I pray with the imam in the mosque, then I find in myself rancor and hatred toward the Muslims and aversion to some of the Shari'ah of Allah, and the like. Where is the one that forbids immorality and wrongdoing?"
We say: the affliction is not in the prayer; the affliction is in the one who prays. Otherwise, every believer, I mean every believer, knows with certainty that the prayer forbids immorality and wrongdoing, because this is the report of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and it is true. It is impossible otherwise, since He, exalted be He, knows everything, so He said that from knowledge, and His speech is the most truthful speech.
And His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And the remembrance of Allah is greater﴾ [Al-Ankabut 45]. The author said: (﴿And the remembrance of Allah is greater﴾ than other acts of obedience). First: what is the type of the lam in His saying ﴿wa-ladhikru Allah﴾? It is the lam of the beginning (lam al-ibtida'), yes, because the sentence is not a oath. As for his saying: (﴿dhikru Allah﴾), dhikr is a verbal noun (masdar) annexed to the name of Allah. Is it annexed to its subject or to its object?
* Student: To its object.
* The Shaykh: ﴿And the remembrance of Allah is greater﴾: that is, "and your remembrance of your Lord is greater." Or "and Allah's remembrance of you through the prayer is greater than its forbidding immorality and wrongdoing"?
* Student: No, "and your remembrance of your Lord."
* The Shaykh: The first. And the second?
* Student: It is possible.
* The Shaykh: No, the second is also valid, and the matter concerns Allah's remembrance of you, not your remembrance of Allah, just as the matter concerns Allah's love for you, not your love for Allah. Consider His saying: ﴿Say: If you love Allah, then follow me﴾ [Al-'Imran 31]. Is it "follow me, you love Allah" or "follow me, Allah will love you"?
Allah will love you; that is the matter. So the matter is that you be remembered, not that you remember. And just as this is true of the Creator with the creature, it is also true of creatures with one another: when you love so-and-so or remember so-and-so, what do you gain if so-and-so turns away from you?
You gain nothing but hardship and affliction. For this reason is the case of Barirah with her husband Mughith [Narrated by al-Bukhari (5283) from the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas]: he remembered her, but she did not remember him nor desire him, while he loved her intensely. So the matter is that you be remembered by Allah. But be assured that when you remember Allah from the heart, Allah's remembrance of you is greater than your remembrance of Him: "Whoever remembers Me in himself, I remember him in Myself," and the self of Allah, the Exalted, is greater than your self without doubt; "and whoever remembers Me in an assembly, I remember him in an assembly better than theirs" — better than them or like them? "better than them" [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (7405) and Muslim (2675/2) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah]. So when you truly remember your Lord, Allah remembers you with a remembrance greater and more majestic than your remembrance of Him. Therefore ﴿And the remembrance of Allah is greater﴾: we say it is suitable for both meanings.
As for his saying: (﴿And the remembrance of Allah is greater﴾ than other acts of obedience), is the intended meaning here the remembrance separate from the prayer, or the remembrance that is within the prayer? Let us see what the author holds.
* Student: The separate one.
* The Shaykh: The apparent meaning of the author's words is that it is the separate remembrance; that is, the prayer forbids immorality and wrongdoing, and the remembrance of Allah is greater in forbidding immorality and wrongdoing and greater. It may also be intended to be the remembrance of Allah that is within the prayer and that which occurs through it. Is "within it and through it" the same, or is there a difference between them?
No, there is a difference. The remembrance of Allah within it is like glorification, magnification, and recitation; and the remembrance of Allah through it means what arises from the remembrance of Allah because of it.

And His saying: ﴿And Allah knows what you do﴾, so that He may recompense you for it. This sentence is informative in form, but it has a great meaning. The purpose of this sentence is not that we should know, or be informed, that Allah knows what we do; rather, its purpose is a warning against doing what contradicts our Shari'ah, whether by committing what is forbidden or by abandoning what is commanded.

And His saying, the Exalted: ﴿He knows what you do﴾. ﴿Ma﴾ is a relative pronoun indicating generality; it includes?
* Student: Everything we do.
* The Shaykh: Everything we do, whether saying or action, in what relates to His right and in what relates to the rights of His servants.
﴿He knows what you do﴾. He said: (so that He may recompense you for it). This result is clear. When will the recompense for it take place?
* Student: In this world.
* The Shaykh: In the world and on the Day of Resurrection. As for the recompense for it, that is, for what we do, it may be legal, through the action of the servant, and it may be cosmic (kawniyyah), through the action of Allah. The recompense is legal through the action of the servant, such as the hudud. Are the hudud a legal punishment or a cosmic one?
* Student: Legal.

**Shaykh:** It is legislative (shar'iyyah) when it results from the servant's action, the servant being the one commanded to perform it. It is cosmic and predestined (kawniyyah qadariyyah) when it results from God's action, as when a person falls ill, loses wealth, and the like.

**Student:** Can what befalls a person of illnesses (...) be a punishment from God?

**Shaykh:** It may be a punishment, and it may be a trial and a test, as God the Exalted said: ﴿And We will surely test you with something of fear and hunger and a loss of wealth and lives and fruits. But give good tidings to the patient﴾ [al-Baqarah 155]. Then it is a test. And it may be a punishment, based on His saying: ﴿And whatever affliction strikes you is for what your hands have earned﴾ [al-Shura 30]. So a person may be afflicted as a punishment for a sin, or as a test.

The afflictions that come to the Messenger ﷺ, are these from which category? They are from the category of testing, so that the person may reach the level of perfection, because patience, as you know, is a high and great station in the religion, and ﴿Indeed, the patient will be given their reward without account﴾ [al-Zumar 10]. But patience is not possible without something to be patient over. There must be things that come upon a person from God's decree, which he endures.

**Student:** He, may He be exalted, says: ﴿And We test you with evil and with good as a trial﴾ [al-Anbiya' 35]. This falls under that.

**Shaykh:** It falls under that.

**Student:** What is meant by the trial (fitnah)?

**Shaykh:** The trial in relation to good is the trial of gratitude, and in relation to evil it is the trial of patience.

**Student:** In His saying: ﴿Indeed, prayer prohibits immorality and wrongdoing﴾ [al-'Ankabut 45], you first mentioned that it could possibly occur from the Messenger ﷺ, immorality or wrongdoing?

**Shaykh:** No, it is not possible.

**Student:** It is not possible?

**Shaykh:** No, it is not possible (...).

He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿Recite what has been revealed to you of the Book and establish prayer﴾, to the end of the verse [al-'Ankabut: 45].

The command in His saying ﴿Recite﴾ is addressed to whom?

**Student:** To the Messenger ﷺ.

**Shaykh:** And is it not suitable for it to be addressed to everyone who can be addressed?

**Student:** It was revealed to him, but it is for the Ummah after him.

**Shaykh:** No, I mean: is it not valid for us to make it addressed to everyone who can be addressed?

**Student:** No, because this is not possible (...) ﴿to you﴾.

**Shaykh:** Even ﴿to you﴾ always comes.

**Student:** For everyone who can be addressed, meaning among the Muslims, or among humanity in general? Among the Muslims?

**Shaykh:** Among the Muslims. Is this valid or not valid?

**Student:** Yes, if it were for the Muslims it would not be valid, because he, meaning...

**Shaykh:** Did we go over this? We have learned it.

**Student:** It is not valid for it to be general.

**Shaykh:** Why?

**Student:** Because He said: ﴿what has been revealed to you﴾, and others were not revealed to.

**Shaykh:** And others were not revealed to. Correct.

**Student:** ﴿And establish prayer﴾.

**Shaykh:** It does not contradict it. It is also for him. A command addressed specifically to the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, could it be for him and for others?

**Student:** Sometimes it is for him, and sometimes it is for him and for others.

**Shaykh:** Well done. In a verse like this one.

**Student:** This one is shared.

**Shaykh:** For him and for others, yes. What is the evidence that the address directed to him is for him and for others?

**Student:** His saying: ﴿Recite what has been revealed to you﴾.

**Shaykh:** No, (...) for him.

**Student:** His saying: ﴿And establish prayer﴾.

**Shaykh:** No.

**Student:** ﴿Indeed, prayer prohibits﴾.

**Shaykh:** No, the evidence is separate; it is not from the verse.

**Student:** Not from the verse?

**Shaykh:** No.

**Student:** Could it be His saying: ﴿O Prophet, why do you prohibit what Allah has made lawful for you?﴾ [al-Tahrim 1], then He said: ﴿Allah has already ordained for you﴾ [al-Tahrim 2]. Likewise: ﴿O Prophet, when you divorce women﴾ [al-Talaq 1].

**Shaykh:** No. What I mean is: if the address is specifically to the Messenger ﷺ, and it is clear that it is specific to him, then it is divided into two categories. One category is where the ruling does not extend beyond him to others. The other category is where the ruling extends beyond him to others, by evidence such as His saying: ﴿Say: If you should love Allah, then follow me; Allah will love you﴾ [Al 'Imran 31], and His saying: ﴿Certainly in the Messenger of Allah you have an excellent example﴾ [al-Ahzab 21].

As for what you mentioned, and like ﴿O Prophet, when you divorce women﴾, the address is to him, and what is meant is him and the Ummah, by evidence that He said: ﴿when you divorce﴾ and ﴿Allah has ordained for you﴾. A verse like the one you mentioned has an address that is shared by the force of the wording's indication, not by the force of following his example.

So now the address directed to the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, has three categories:

The first category: evidence indicates, by the force of the specific wording, that it is for him and for others. Such as?

**Student:** ﴿O Prophet, when you divorce﴾.

**Shaykh:** ﴿When you divorce women﴾. He said ﴿O Prophet﴾, then He said ﴿when you divorce﴾. And such as ﴿O Prophet, why do you prohibit﴾, then He said ﴿Allah has ordained for you﴾.

The second category: it is specific to him and does not extend beyond him to others in practice, not by the force of the wording. Such as: ﴿Did We not expand for you your breast? And We removed from you your burden, which had weighed upon your back, and We raised high for you your remembrance﴾ [al-Sharh 1–4]. All of this is specific to the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, and does not extend beyond him to others.

The third: that which is specific to him by the force of the address, but it encompasses others by the force of following his example, by separate evidence. Such as this verse. The Messenger was commanded with it, but in reality we too must recite what God revealed to His Prophet and establish prayer.

His saying: ﴿Recite﴾, this is an imperative verb built on the vowel damma, and we are not aware that an imperative verb is built on damma. How would you answer this?

**Student:** It is built on the elision of the waw.

**Shaykh:** On the elision of the waw, correct. Its origin is (talā yatlū) with a waw. The imperative verb, they say, is derived from the present tense. They say the imperative is a present-tense verb in the jussive mood, but remove from it the letter of the present tense. This is a useful rule for you: the imperative is a present-tense verb in the jussive mood from which the letter of the present tense has been removed.

For example, if someone says to you: form the imperative from (khāfa), what do you say?

**Student:** (khif).

**Shaykh:** (khif) is wrong.

**Student:** (khaf).

**Shaykh:** (khaf). What is the evidence?

Give me a present-tense verb in the jussive mood and remove from it the yā' of the present tense. You say: (lam yakhif) or (lam yakhaf)?

**Student:** (lam yakhaf).

**Shaykh:** (lam yakhaf). Remove the yā'?

**Student:** (khaf).

**Shaykh:** (khaf). Form an imperative from (nāma).

**Student:** (nam).

**Shaykh:** (nam) or (nim)?

**Student:** (nam).

**Shaykh:** (nam). The evidence: in the jussive present you say (lam yanam), you do not say (lam yanim). Remove the yā' of the present tense and it becomes (nam). Do you understand? This is a rule that benefits a person in such matters that are obscure, because many students, when you say to them: form the imperative from (khāfa), say?

**Student:** (khif).

**Shaykh:** (khif). And one says (khuf).

**Student:** He stresses the fā'?

**Shaykh:** No, he does not stress it, but he puts a damma on the khā', khuf.

**Student:** (nim), with a kasra on the nūn.

**Shaykh:** (nim)?!

**Student:** Why, Shaykh?

**Shaykh:** No, (nimm), with the mīm stressed, from namīmah (tale-bearing), with a doubled mīm: (namma yanimmu nimm).

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Recite what has been revealed to you﴾. Is this recitation verbal, or verbal and meaningful?

**Student:** All of it.

**Shaykh:** All of it. Verbal recitation, such as what?

**Student:** Such as reciting the Qur'an.

**Shaykh:** Reciting the Qur'an. And the meaningful?

**Student:** Application.

**Shaykh:** Yes indeed, application, meaning: following.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿what has been revealed to you of the Book and establish prayer﴾. This conjunction, of what is it a conjunction?

**Student:** The specific over the general.

**Shaykh:** The specific over the general, because among what was revealed to him is establishing prayer.

His saying: ﴿Indeed, prayer prohibits immorality and wrongdoing﴾. What is meant by the prohibition here? Its literal meaning?

**Student:** ﴿Indeed, prayer prohibits immorality and wrongdoing﴾, yes indeed.

**Shaykh:** ﴿prohibits immorality﴾: is it meant literally, or is the prohibition meant?

**Student:** No, it is not literal.

**Shaykh:** Or is it restraint? It restrains from immorality.

**Student:** It only restrains from immorality.

**Shaykh:** Is restraint meant?

**Student:** Because, meaning, it has...

**Shaykh:** No, we did not ask about the definition. First let us see the ruling. Is the meaning of "prohibition" here restraint, or the literal meaning of prohibiting?

**Student:** The literal meaning of prohibiting.

**Shaykh:** So if a person prays, he hears the prayer telling him: do not commit adultery, do not steal.

**Student:** Rather, restraint.

**Shaykh:** Is restraint meant?

**Student:** Yes indeed, that prayer restrains from immorality and wrongdoing.

**Shaykh:** While he is engaged in it, or even after he finishes it?

**Student:** Even after finishing it.

**Shaykh:** Even after finishing.

What is the wisdom in expressing it as prohibition rather than restraint?

**Student:** So that it includes even when a person is outside the prayer, after the prayer; it includes that.

**Shaykh:** We mentioned a meaning other than this. Does anyone among you recall it?

**Student:** Prohibition is stronger.

**Shaykh:** Prohibition is stronger than restraint.

**Student:** Yes indeed, prohibition is stronger than restraint.

**Shaykh:** Because it produces in the heart an aversion to this thing and a repulsion from it, while mere restraint does not entail that. Do you understand or not? That is: I may restrain a person from a disobedience, but his heart remains attached to it, not averse to it. But prohibition necessitates repulsion. So prayer necessitates restraint from sins or immorality and wrongdoing, and it also necessitates aversion to them and repulsion from them, as if a caller in your heart were forbidding you from this thing.

Question: Is this verse consistent with reality or not?

**Student:** Consistent.

**Shaykh:** Consistent with reality?

**Student:** Generally, because...

**Shaykh:** Generally.

**Student:** Because prayer requires (...) prayer (...).

**Shaykh:** Yes, but now the word "generally" implies fifty-one percent. Then an objection arises for us: the verse is general, it is not a majority statement. So the question now: is it consistent with reality or not?

**Student:** You mean in relation to (...).

**Shaykh:** I mean consistency with reality: the reality of people now. Does their prayer restrain them from immorality and wrongdoing?

**Student:** A part of the prayer, that they be humble (...).

**Shaykh:** Yes?

**Student:** The person who prays the prayer, meaning with its pillars...

**Shaykh:** This is known. We believe in this: that if a person prays a complete prayer in the required manner, it restrains him. We must believe this because it is the report of God.

The question now: is it consistent with reality or not?

**Student:** No, it is not consistent.

**Shaykh:** It is not consistent with most people. So is there a flaw in our prayer or not?

**Student:** Yes indeed.

**Shaykh:** Our prayer has a flaw. If your heart does not change when you leave the prayer, know that the prayer is deficient, because this is the report of the One who knows the secret and what is more hidden, God the Mighty and Majestic, and He spoke truly, and the truest speech is His. Is it clear?

And for this reason there was reported from some of the early generations (salaf): "Whoever his prayer does not restrain from immorality and wrongdoing, he increases from God only in distance."[[Recorded by Sa'id ibn Mansur in his Tafsir (1705), and from his route al-Tabarani in al-Mu'jam al-Kabir (8543), from Ibn Mas'ud as his own statement. He also related it in al-Mu'jam al-Kabir (11025) as a hadith from Ibn 'Abbas traced back to the Prophet ﷺ.]] And we seek refuge in God.

What is the wisdom in its restraining from immorality and wrongdoing?

**Student:** Because it is a connection with God, and when a person connects with God, He magnifies his prohibition and magnifies his command.

**Shaykh:** Well done. The matter of God becomes great in a person's soul when he is connected with God, the Mighty and Majestic. Then also, when he wants to commit immorality and wrongdoing, he remembers the time when he was connected with God, the Mighty and Majestic, and so it restrains him. I told you when explaining: some people may pray a prayer, one of those prayers that is complete according to their state, and they find the taste of this prayer in their hearts for as long as God wills, for a long period, remembering the sweetness of this intimate conversation and its beauty, and it restrains them from immorality and wrongdoing.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And the remembrance of Allah is greater﴾.

First: the grammatical analysis (i'rab) of this sentence? You are not experts in i'rab?

**Student:** (...)?

**Shaykh:** Its i'rab.

**Student:** Ha.

**Shaykh:** The lām and all of it.

**Student:** ﴿And the remembrance of Allah﴾ is in the nominative.

**Shaykh:** The lām before it.

**Student:** The lām of (dhikr)?

**Shaykh:** Yes.

**Student:** (dhikr): a nominative subject, its sign of nominative case is the ḍamma, and (dhikr) is in construct, and the word (Allah) is a genitive noun in apposition, (akbar) is the predicate of the subject.

**Shaykh:** The predicate of the subject. Well done.

Is the construction here the genitive of the verbal noun to its subject or to its object?

**Student:** To its object.

**Shaykh:** To its object.

**Student:** No, to its subject.

**Shaykh:** To its subject?! Be definite.

**Student:** To its subject.

**Shaykh:** What is the difference between the two interpretations?

**Student:** The difference: this is the name of God upon the Qur'an, and the remembrance of God...

**Shaykh:** Which of the two interpretations is this?

**Student:** On the basis that the construct is to its subject.

**Shaykh:** Yes.

**Student:** As for if it is to its object, it is the remembrance of God by people, meaning what they mention God with, according to the second interpretation.

**Shaykh:** Good. Meaning: you are saying it is suitable for this and for that?

**Student:** No, it is according to an interpretation...

**Shaykh:** Its construction is to the subject.

**Student:** To its subject.

**Shaykh:** What do you say? What do you say about both constructions, to the subject and to the object, and about the interpretation he gave?

**Student:** He here said: it is a construction to the object.

**Shaykh:** A construction to the object?

**Student:** Because he mentioned the prayer...

**Shaykh:** What is the meaning on the interpretation that it is construct to the object?

**Student:** The preventing.

**Shaykh:** What is the meaning on this interpretation?

**Student:** The meaning: that the one who remembers God, may He be exalted, this is among the greatest things, or it prevents him from many things...

**Shaykh:** Meaning: your remembrance of God is greater and more significant than the prohibition of immorality and wrongdoing.

**Student:** Yes.

**Shaykh:** Is that so?

**Student:** The prohibition of immorality and wrongdoing?!

**Shaykh:** Yes, because He said: ﴿Indeed, prayer prohibits immorality and wrongdoing, and the remembrance of Allah is greater﴾.

**Student:** (...) the Qur'an, (...) meaning.

**Shaykh:** It is construct to the object, and the meaning then is: and your remembrance of God is greater than the prohibition of immorality and wrongdoing; that is, the remembrance of God that is in prayer is greater than immorality and wrongdoing, or in the general sense as the author chose.

On the interpretation that it is construct to the subject, what is the meaning?

**Student:** (...) only construct to the object.

**Shaykh:** Only to the object?

**Student:** Yes.

**Shaykh:** Yes.

**Student:** The remembrance of God, may He be exalted and majestic, of the person in the highest assembly.

**Shaykh:** Yes, greater...

**Student:** Greater than his doing, until when (...).

**Shaykh:** Yes, greater than his doing.

Because the matter is that God remembers you, not that you remember God, as in His saying: ﴿Say: If you should love Allah, then follow me; Allah will love you﴾ [Al 'Imran 31]. He did not say: follow me, you will love God. He said: ﴿will love you﴾, since the matter concerns God's love for the person. So on this basis the meaning is: and the remembrance of God of you while you pray is greater than what you gain from prayer in terms of restraint from immorality and wrongdoing. Is it not possible for us to say that it is suitable for this and that? Let it be for this and for that?

There is no contradiction between them. We stated the rule in tafsir: if a verse is open to two meanings that do not contradict each other, it is taken to both meanings. But if one of them contradicts the other, what do we do?

We adopt the stronger one, because a verse cannot bear two contradictory meanings, but the stronger one is adopted.

**Student:** As a matter of reward.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 29, verse 45–58 (part 3 of 3):

* The Shaykh: Yes, it is by way of recompense, as is established in the sacred hadith: "Whoever remembers Me within himself, I remember him within Myself; and whoever remembers Me in an assembly, I remember him in an assembly better than it."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (7405) and Muslim (2675/21) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]]
* A student: Is every waw (و) here resumptive (mustaʼnafah)?
* The Shaykh: Yes, indeed. It may be resumptive on both possibilities.
Regarding His words: ﴿And the remembrance of Allah is greater﴾, "greater" (akbar): where is the thing it is compared to?
* A student: The prohibition of indecency (al-fahshaa').
* The Shaykh: Yes, the prohibition of indecency and wrongdoing. And if we wish, we can say: the object of comparison has been omitted for generality.
* A student: Shaykh, someone may say: the speaker intends only one meaning.
* The Shaykh: Yes, the speaker intends only one meaning. But as long as his words can bear both meanings without contradiction, what tells us that He intended only one? This is the speech of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and the speech of Allah, glorified and exalted, is broad in meaning. So as long as the wording is suitable for both meanings without any contradiction between them, we cannot say that He intended only this one.
His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And Allah knows what you do﴾. This verse is a declarative sentence. A declarative sentence conveys Allah's knowledge of what we do. So what is the purpose of it? Is its purpose encouragement (targhib) or warning (tarhib)?
* A student: Warning.
* The Shaykh: Encouragement?
* A student: Warning.
* The Shaykh: Warning? That is, He knows what we do and will recompense us for it? What made you know that it is only for warning?
* A student: (...).
* The Shaykh: You say: warning. What made you know?
* A student: (...) the verse.
* The Shaykh: What verse?
* A student: (...).
* Another student: For encouragement and warning.
* The Shaykh: For encouragement and warning. These are two opinions. Which is more correct?
* A student: The correct view is that it is for warning.
* The Shaykh: For warning?
* A student: Yes.
* The Shaykh: What is the evidence?
* A student: Because it indicates watchfulness; when a person knows that Allah is watching him...
* The Shaykh: He fears Him.
* A student: He has some fear.
* The Shaykh: And when he knows that Allah knows what he does, and nothing of it is lost, does he not become eager to obey?
* A student: This is weak in this verse.
* Another student: It is for encouragement and warning: ﴿He knows what you do﴾, so He rewards the good-doer for his goodness and the wrongdoer for his wrongdoing.
* The Shaykh: It is for encouragement and for warning. Here, it is closer to encouragement, because what precedes it is a command, not a prohibition. If it were a prohibition, it would be closer to warning: "Do not commit adultery, for Allah knows what you do" is warning; "Do righteous deeds, for Allah knows what you do" is encouragement, which is clear. Nevertheless, we say that it applies to both together, because it includes the encouragement of obeying the command and the warning against disobeying and defying it.
In truth, we have extended this discussion as if it were a full lesson, but there is no harm in that, because we want a person to have opened to him, as much as possible, some of the knowledge of the Qur'an and its secrets.
* A student: The evidence that the address includes both the Messenger and others.
* The Shaykh: Which one?
* A student: I am asking you for the evidence that the address includes the Messenger and the whole Ummah?
* The Shaykh: Yes.
* A student: What is the evidence?
* The Shaykh: The address directed to the Messenger applies to him and to the Ummah. The evidence: who knows it?
* A student: ﴿Say: If you should love Allah, then follow me; Allah will love you﴾ [Al 'Imran 31].
* The Shaykh: Yes.
* A student: ﴿There has certainly been for you in the Messenger of Allah an excellent example﴾ [al-Ahzab 21].
* The Shaykh: No, this in fact is evidence for the obligation of following his example. But the evidence that an address directed to him applies to him and to the Ummah, when no proof indicates otherwise, is the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And a believing woman, if she gives herself to the Prophet and the Prophet wishes to marry her, [this is] exclusively for you, not for the [other] believers﴾ [al-Ahzab 50]. It shows us that, were it not for His saying ﴿exclusively﴾, the ruling would apply to him and to others. This indicates that, when unrestricted, an address directed to the Messenger ﷺ applies to him and to the Ummah.
Another verse also indicates this, which is His saying, when He mentioned that Allah permitted him the wife of Zayd ibn Harithah. What did He say?
He said: ﴿So that there will be no discomfort for the believers concerning the wives of their adopted sons﴾ [al-Ahzab 37].
Recite the verse: ﴿And [remember] when you said to the one on whom Allah bestowed favor and you bestowed favor, "Keep your wife and fear Allah," while you concealed within yourself that which Allah is to disclose, and you feared the people, while Allah has more right that you fear Him. So when Zayd had no longer any need for her, We married her to you﴾ [al-Ahzab 37]. Now, the ruling applies to whom?
* The students: To the Messenger ﷺ.
* The Shaykh: To the Messenger ﷺ. Nevertheless, He gave a general reason, saying: ﴿So that there will be no discomfort for the believers﴾; He did not say "for you," but ﴿for the believers concerning the wives of their adopted sons when they have no longer any need for them﴾. This is evidence that an address directed to him applies to him and to the Ummah. Is it clear?
* A student: Shaykh, do we also learn from the first verse an indication of the intended meaning?
* The Shaykh: Which one?
* A student: Because it begins with His saying: ﴿Indeed, We have made lawful to you your wives﴾ [al-Ahzab 50]?
* The Shaykh: I would say there is evidence in it, and this also supports it.
* A student: We could say, for example: He made the address singular to the Messenger, then stated the ruling about the woman: ﴿exclusively for you﴾ [al-Ahzab 50]...
* The Shaykh: This is evidence that the address directed to him applies to him and to the Ummah.
What concerns me in a student of knowledge is not that he memorizes issues; memorizing issues is simple. I think the recorder has a stronger memory for issues than we do, right?
(...) It is nothing. If you give the recorder a thousand issues and come to it twenty years later, will it give them back to you or not?
It will give them back to you. But what matters for the student of knowledge is that he understands. Among understanding is grasping implication (dalalah), the implication from the Qur'an and also from the Sunnah. Through this, Allah opens to a person a great deal of knowledge that perhaps no one else perceives. For this reason, when 'Ali ibn Abi Talib was asked: "Did the Prophet ﷺ entrust you with anything?" he said: "No, except what is in this sheet, or an understanding that Allah grants a person regarding the Qur'an." See, "or an understanding"; and there is no doubt that 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, had a great deal of understanding of the Qur'an.[[Narrated by al-Bukhari (111) from the hadith of 'Ali ibn Abi Talib.]]
So the point is that I love for the student of knowledge to be eager for understanding. The Prophet ﷺ said: "Many a one who conveys the message understands it better than one who hears it."[[Narrated by al-Bukhari (1741) from the hadith of Abu Bakrah.]] Memorization is like pharmacy: the pharmacist has all the medicines, but understanding, deduction and derivation are like the physician, who directs the medicines and benefits from them. The pharmacist keeps them for you, but the physician is the one who benefits and benefits others. So the most important thing to me in a student of knowledge, in the interpretation of the Qur'an and likewise in the Sunnah, is understanding, deduction and derivation. I think it has passed us that the indication of a word upon its meaning is of three types: correspondence (mutabaqah), inclusion (tadammun) and entailment (iltizam).
Correspondence and inclusion are simple; the least of students of knowledge can know them.
But entailment (iltizam) is the important one, and from it branch issues that none can count but Allah.
When a person is granted success in the implication of entailment, he attains much good in this matter.
[[The author's speech has been abridged due to its great length.]]

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 29, verse 45–58 (part 1 of 3):

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Recite what has been revealed to you of the Book﴾ [Al-Ankabut 45].
﴿Recite what has been revealed to you of the Book﴾. ﴿Recite﴾ (utlu) includes verbal recitation (al-tilawah al-lafziyyah) and recitation in terms of its rulings (al-tilawah al-hukmiyyah). Verbal recitation is that you read the Qur'an. Recitation in terms of its rulings is that you act upon its rulings, and this is the recitation of following (tilawat al-ittiba'), from their saying: "Fulan talaa fulan" (so-and-so followed so-and-so). What is the meaning of talaahu?
* Students: That he followed him.
* The Shaykh: Yes, he followed him. So the command to recite here includes both this and that: ﴿Those to whom We have given the Book recite it as it should be recited; those believe in it﴾ [Al-Baqarah 121].
As for his saying, glorified and exalted is He: ﴿Recite﴾, the address is to the Messenger, peace and blessings of Allah be upon him, and it is not directed to everyone who may be addressed. This is because He said: ﴿what has been revealed to you﴾, and this restricts it to the Messenger ﷺ, since no one else has had revelation sent to him. Nevertheless, the address to the Messenger, peace and blessings of Allah be upon him, is also an address to him and to the ummah, by the evidence of His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, in the Messenger of Allah you have a good example for whoever hopes for Allah and the Last Day﴾ [Al-Ahzab 21]. Except what evidence establishes as specific to him, in which case the evidence is followed, such as His saying: ﴿And a believing woman, if she gives herself to the Prophet and the Prophet wishes to marry her﴾ [Al-Ahzab 50]. Had the verse stopped at this, it would have been permissible for the ummah to do the same, but He said: ﴿exclusively for you, excluding the believers﴾ [Al-Ahzab 50]. This indicates that the address directed to the Messenger ﷺ is for him and for his ummah, unless there is evidence that it is specific to him.
He said: ﴿Recite what has been revealed to you of the Book﴾. ﴿Ma﴾ is a relative pronoun indicating generality. As for his saying: ﴿has been revealed to you﴾, wahy (revelation) linguistically is informing swiftly and secretly. Informing swiftly and secretly is called wahy. For example, suppose you are among a people and you want to inform someone of something; you say, for instance, "such-and-such" with your hand, so that those around you do not understand, but your companion understands, without you saying: "O so-and-so, get up so we may go to so-and-so." Is this called wahy?
No, this is not wahy, because it is clear and has no concealment. But linguistically, informing swiftly and secretly is called wahy. In the Shari'ah, however, it is Allah's informing one of His prophets or messengers with the Shari'ah; this is wahy in the legal sense. And here, what is intended? Wahy in the legal sense. It has levels, which Allah mentioned in Surah Ha Mim 'Asaqa (Ash-Shura). He said: ﴿what has been revealed to you of the Book﴾. ﴿Min﴾ here is explanatory (bayaniyyah), explaining ﴿ma﴾ in his saying: ﴿what has been revealed to you﴾. As for his saying: ﴿the Book﴾, it refers to the Qur'an. It is called a Book because it is written in the mushafs, because it is written in the Preserved Tablet (al-lawh al-mahfuz), and because it is written in the hands of the angels: ﴿No! Indeed, it is a reminder. So whoever wills may remember it. In sheets held in honor, exalted and purified, by the hands of scribes, noble and dutiful﴾ [Abasa 11–16].
The form kitab (fi'al) in the sense of maf'ul (object) is common in the Arabic language, and I think the examples that passed us are not absent from your minds now, such as firash (a bed) meaning mafrush (spread out), ghirас (planting) meaning maghrus (planted), and bina' (a building) meaning mabni (built).
He said: ﴿Recite what has been revealed to you of the Book and establish the prayer﴾ [Al-Ankabut 45]. ﴿Establish the prayer﴾ means: perform it in its complete form, because establishing a thing is making it upright, with no crookedness or deficiency.
As for his saying: ﴿establish the prayer﴾, the address is to the Messenger ﷺ, and it is known that he establishes the prayer, and that he is the most upright of those who pray in prayer. So how was the address directed to him with ﴿establish the prayer﴾?
We say: the address is directed to one who is characterized by it, and what is meant is continuity upon it, not renewal of it, because he already has it. But continuity upon it is like His saying: ﴿O you who believe, believe in Allah﴾ [An-Nisa' 136]. ﴿O you who believe, believe﴾: the address is not idle, so that we would say it is achieving what is already achieved. The believer is a believer; we say: what is meant? Continuity upon that. So when the address or command is directed to one who is characterized by it, what is meant is continuity upon it.
As for his saying, glorified and exalted is He: ﴿establish the prayer﴾. Earlier we said that recitation includes following and acting upon its rulings. Is establishing the prayer not from following it and acting upon its rulings?
Yes. So its being conjoined to his saying ﴿recite﴾ is from the conjunction of the particular to the general ('atf al-khass 'ala al-'amm), and the conjunction of the particular to the general is an indication of the elevation of its status. There is no doubt that the prayer is the best of bodily acts, so it was singled out for mention. Then, does conjoining the particular to the general mean mentioning it twice, or does it mean it was singled out for mention from among the general?
On this there are two opinions among the scholars. Some say that mentioning the particular after the general means that the indication of generality was removed from it and then it was singled out for mention. Others say it is included in the first generality and then singled out for mention, so it is mentioned twice. Both indicate its nobility; that is, both views indicate the nobility of what is mentioned. But which is stronger? The latter: that it is mentioned twice, once by way of the general and once by way of the specific. The benefit appears if you say: "Honor the students and Muhammad," and Muhammad is among the students according to the view that he is included in the general, then singled out for mention. We then know that this man is a student and his name is Muhammad. But if we say he was removed from the general and singled out for mention, then we must search for this Muhammad: is he a student or not?
It requires a qarinah (indicator) showing that he is among the students. The correct view, as you have said, is that it is stronger: that mentioning the particular after the general means mentioning it twice.
Then He, glorified and exalted, said, giving the reason for the command to establish the prayer: ﴿Indeed, the prayer forbids immorality and wrongdoing﴾ [Al-Ankabut 45]. Is this reason related to the addressee or to the thing addressed? Pay attention, brothers, since the matter has a difficulty: is the reason here related to the addressee or to the thing he is addressed with? Who is the addressee?
* Student: The Messenger, peace and blessings of Allah be upon him.
* The Shaykh: Good. And the thing addressed?
* Student: The prayer.
* The Shaykh: The prayer. He addressed him with establishing the prayer. So is this reason for establishing the prayer as such, or is it a reason connected to the addressee, that is, connected to the one addressed?
If we say it is connected to the addressee, the meaning becomes that the prayer forbids you from immorality and wrongdoing, and this would imply that immorality and wrongdoing could occur from the Messenger ﷺ. If we say it is the reason connected to the thing addressed, which is the prayer, then we say that the prayer as such forbids immorality and wrongdoing, and this is a description that is true of whom? Of other than the Messenger ﷺ. So this reason is for the thing addressed, the prayer, and not for the one addressed, who is the Messenger ﷺ, since we know he is protected from immorality and wrongdoing. Is it clear, brothers? And this is the required reading.
As for his saying: ﴿Indeed, the prayer forbids immorality and wrongdoing﴾. The word ﴿tanha﴾ (forbids) here and in the previous verse: is the intended prayer the obligatory prayer, or the obligatory and voluntary together?
* Student: All of them.
* The Shaykh: It is general. As for his saying: ﴿Indeed, the prayer forbids immorality﴾, ﴿tanha﴾ means it prevents, but the expression of nahy (forbidding) is more eloquent than the expression of man' (preventing), since one who prevents may not be warning, whereas in nahy there is a warning. It is as if the prayer has a secret that requires a person to keep away from immorality and wrongdoing; it rebukes his conscience and says to him: Why do you do this? Why do you act so?
As for his saying: ﴿forbids immorality and wrongdoing﴾: ﴿al-fahsha'﴾ is everything that is considered abominable among sins, such as adultery, theft, drinking wine, killing a soul, and the like. ﴿Al-munkar﴾ is what is less than that. The conjunction of ﴿al-munkar﴾ to ﴿al-fahsha'﴾ is the conjunction of the general to the particular, since every fahsha' is munkar, but not every munkar is fahsha'.
The author said: (﴿from immorality and wrongdoing﴾ according to the Shari'ah; that is, it is of its nature to do so as long as the person is in it). As for his saying: (that is, it is of its nature to do so), this is correct. But "as long as the person is in it" is not correct. Rather, it forbids immorality and wrongdoing whether or not the person is in it, and whether or not he remains in it. That is, its benefit is not specific to when a person is engaged in praying, which is well known; he is not one who commits immorality and wrongdoing. Rather, the great benefit is that it affects your heart in a way that requires keeping you away from immorality and wrongdoing, and this is the fruit and the result. The fruit and result are not merely that when you pray you no longer commit immorality and wrongdoing. Therefore the author's restriction with his words "as long as he is in it" is open to question and is not correct. Rather, it is unrestricted: it forbids immorality and wrongdoing, meaning that what occurs through it necessitates for the heart distance from immorality and wrongdoing. The reason for this is that the praying person converses with his Lord, as the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said, so there is a bond between him and his Lord, and this bond gains the heart faith and light. For this reason the Prophet, peace and blessings of Allah be upon him, said: "Prayer is light" [Narrated by Muslim (223/1) from the hadith of Abu Malik al-Ash'ari].
It is known that when the heart acquires light, it does not incline toward immorality and wrongdoing. Whenever it intends to do something, it recalls that a few hours earlier it was standing before Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, so it feels shame and withdraws. This is a matter that is observed: a person sometimes recalls standing in a prayer twenty years or more ago, a prayer he prayed on some day, as if he saw his Lord, "worship Allah as if you see Him," in the utmost excellence, and he finds the taste of that prayer after a long time. This remembrance does not leave his heart; this recollection must affect his restraint from immorality and wrongdoing. This is the meaning of His saying: ﴿Indeed, the prayer forbids immorality and wrongdoing﴾. But what is meant by ﴿Indeed, the prayer﴾ is the prayer that is actually established, not every prayer forbids immorality and wrongdoing. By Allah, if our prayer forbade us from immorality and wrongdoing, we would all be sound, we would all be sound. But now we ask Allah to deal with us in His pardon: a person enters the prayer with a heart and leaves with the same heart or worse. Note that acts of worship, if they do not affect your heart for good, are a harm; what does not benefit you through the verses harms you, as the Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "The Qur'an is a proof for you or against you" [Narrated by Muslim (223/1) from the hadith of Abu Malik al-Ash'ari].
This matter is one that many Muslims suffer from: he says, "I am not affected by the prayer, my heart is not present, I am not humbled; so what is the remedy?" Some people may also doubt this report, while the report of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, is true. He says: "I pray, but I do not see that it forbids me from immorality and wrongdoing. I pray with the congregation in the mosque, then I go out to my shop and deal in usury, deal in fraud, deal in lying; I pray with the imam in the mosque, then I find in myself rancor and hatred toward the Muslims and aversion to some of the Shari'ah of Allah, and the like. Where is the one that forbids immorality and wrongdoing?"
We say: the affliction is not in the prayer; the affliction is in the one who prays. Otherwise, every believer, I mean every believer, knows with certainty that the prayer forbids immorality and wrongdoing, because this is the report of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and it is true. It is impossible otherwise, since He, exalted be He, knows everything, so He said that from knowledge, and His speech is the most truthful speech.
And His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And the remembrance of Allah is greater﴾ [Al-Ankabut 45]. The author said: (﴿And the remembrance of Allah is greater﴾ than other acts of obedience). First: what is the type of the lam in His saying ﴿wa-ladhikru Allah﴾? It is the lam of the beginning (lam al-ibtida'), yes, because the sentence is not a oath. As for his saying: (﴿dhikru Allah﴾), dhikr is a verbal noun (masdar) annexed to the name of Allah. Is it annexed to its subject or to its object?
* Student: To its object.
* The Shaykh: ﴿And the remembrance of Allah is greater﴾: that is, "and your remembrance of your Lord is greater." Or "and Allah's remembrance of you through the prayer is greater than its forbidding immorality and wrongdoing"?
* Student: No, "and your remembrance of your Lord."
* The Shaykh: The first. And the second?
* Student: It is possible.
* The Shaykh: No, the second is also valid, and the matter concerns Allah's remembrance of you, not your remembrance of Allah, just as the matter concerns Allah's love for you, not your love for Allah. Consider His saying: ﴿Say: If you love Allah, then follow me﴾ [Al-'Imran 31]. Is it "follow me, you love Allah" or "follow me, Allah will love you"?
Allah will love you; that is the matter. So the matter is that you be remembered, not that you remember. And just as this is true of the Creator with the creature, it is also true of creatures with one another: when you love so-and-so or remember so-and-so, what do you gain if so-and-so turns away from you?
You gain nothing but hardship and affliction. For this reason is the case of Barirah with her husband Mughith [Narrated by al-Bukhari (5283) from the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas]: he remembered her, but she did not remember him nor desire him, while he loved her intensely. So the matter is that you be remembered by Allah. But be assured that when you remember Allah from the heart, Allah's remembrance of you is greater than your remembrance of Him: "Whoever remembers Me in himself, I remember him in Myself," and the self of Allah, the Exalted, is greater than your self without doubt; "and whoever remembers Me in an assembly, I remember him in an assembly better than theirs" — better than them or like them? "better than them" [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (7405) and Muslim (2675/2) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah]. So when you truly remember your Lord, Allah remembers you with a remembrance greater and more majestic than your remembrance of Him. Therefore ﴿And the remembrance of Allah is greater﴾: we say it is suitable for both meanings.
As for his saying: (﴿And the remembrance of Allah is greater﴾ than other acts of obedience), is the intended meaning here the remembrance separate from the prayer, or the remembrance that is within the prayer? Let us see what the author holds.
* Student: The separate one.
* The Shaykh: The apparent meaning of the author's words is that it is the separate remembrance; that is, the prayer forbids immorality and wrongdoing, and the remembrance of Allah is greater in forbidding immorality and wrongdoing and greater. It may also be intended to be the remembrance of Allah that is within the prayer and that which occurs through it. Is "within it and through it" the same, or is there a difference between them?
No, there is a difference. The remembrance of Allah within it is like glorification, magnification, and recitation; and the remembrance of Allah through it means what arises from the remembrance of Allah because of it.

And His saying: ﴿And Allah knows what you do﴾, so that He may recompense you for it. This sentence is informative in form, but it has a great meaning. The purpose of this sentence is not that we should know, or be informed, that Allah knows what we do; rather, its purpose is a warning against doing what contradicts our Shari'ah, whether by committing what is forbidden or by abandoning what is commanded.

And His saying, the Exalted: ﴿He knows what you do﴾. ﴿Ma﴾ is a relative pronoun indicating generality; it includes?
* Student: Everything we do.
* The Shaykh: Everything we do, whether saying or action, in what relates to His right and in what relates to the rights of His servants.
﴿He knows what you do﴾. He said: (so that He may recompense you for it). This result is clear. When will the recompense for it take place?
* Student: In this world.
* The Shaykh: In the world and on the Day of Resurrection. As for the recompense for it, that is, for what we do, it may be legal, through the action of the servant, and it may be cosmic (kawniyyah), through the action of Allah. The recompense is legal through the action of the servant, such as the hudud. Are the hudud a legal punishment or a cosmic one?
* Student: Legal.

**Shaykh:** It is legislative (shar'iyyah) when it results from the servant's action, the servant being the one commanded to perform it. It is cosmic and predestined (kawniyyah qadariyyah) when it results from God's action, as when a person falls ill, loses wealth, and the like.

**Student:** Can what befalls a person of illnesses (...) be a punishment from God?

**Shaykh:** It may be a punishment, and it may be a trial and a test, as God the Exalted said: ﴿And We will surely test you with something of fear and hunger and a loss of wealth and lives and fruits. But give good tidings to the patient﴾ [al-Baqarah 155]. Then it is a test. And it may be a punishment, based on His saying: ﴿And whatever affliction strikes you is for what your hands have earned﴾ [al-Shura 30]. So a person may be afflicted as a punishment for a sin, or as a test.

The afflictions that come to the Messenger ﷺ, are these from which category? They are from the category of testing, so that the person may reach the level of perfection, because patience, as you know, is a high and great station in the religion, and ﴿Indeed, the patient will be given their reward without account﴾ [al-Zumar 10]. But patience is not possible without something to be patient over. There must be things that come upon a person from God's decree, which he endures.

**Student:** He, may He be exalted, says: ﴿And We test you with evil and with good as a trial﴾ [al-Anbiya' 35]. This falls under that.

**Shaykh:** It falls under that.

**Student:** What is meant by the trial (fitnah)?

**Shaykh:** The trial in relation to good is the trial of gratitude, and in relation to evil it is the trial of patience.

**Student:** In His saying: ﴿Indeed, prayer prohibits immorality and wrongdoing﴾ [al-'Ankabut 45], you first mentioned that it could possibly occur from the Messenger ﷺ, immorality or wrongdoing?

**Shaykh:** No, it is not possible.

**Student:** It is not possible?

**Shaykh:** No, it is not possible (...).

He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿Recite what has been revealed to you of the Book and establish prayer﴾, to the end of the verse [al-'Ankabut: 45].

The command in His saying ﴿Recite﴾ is addressed to whom?

**Student:** To the Messenger ﷺ.

**Shaykh:** And is it not suitable for it to be addressed to everyone who can be addressed?

**Student:** It was revealed to him, but it is for the Ummah after him.
