We have already discussed the grammatical analysis (*i'rab*) of such a construction: ﴿Have they not seen﴾, and we said that regarding it there is (a difference of opinion) among the scholars...
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: (﴿and people are being snatched away from around them﴾, through killing and captivity, beyond them). He, exalted be He, said: (﴿Then in falsehood﴾, meaning the idol, ﴿do they believe, and in the blessing of Allah do they disbelieve﴾ by their associating others with Him?)
The interrogative here is for rebuke: ﴿Then in falsehood﴾, and it is said of it as is said of ﴿Have they not seen﴾: namely, is the hamzah (interrogative particle) after the *fa'* (conjunction), with the *fa'* delayed? Or is it in its place, with the coordination being with the preceding sentences?
Regarding ﴿in falsehood﴾, the author said: (the idol). This is open to review, unless the author intended it as an example, and that among the things that are false are idols. Otherwise, it includes everything that has no good in it, whether an idol, worldly life, leadership, or anything else. Everything other than the Truth is falsehood. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The truest word spoken by a poet is the word of Labid: 'Surely everything other than Allah is vain.'" [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (3841) and Muslim (2256/3) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.] Based on this, we say: falsehood is more general than what the author mentioned.
His saying: ﴿they believe﴾ means they affirm and feel secure in it. You find them, in false matters, content, affirming, and following. But ﴿in the blessing of Allah they disbelieve﴾: ﴿Then in falsehood do they believe, and in the blessing of Allah do they disbelieve﴾.
His saying: ﴿in the blessing of Allah﴾ means: by what He has bestowed upon them of wealth, standing, leadership, and other things. ﴿They disbelieve﴾, because these blessings require what? Gratitude, by returning to obedience to Allah. If a person remains in disobedience to Allah while blessings continue to flow upon him, he thereby becomes a disbeliever.
And it is possible to say, regarding the Muslims: ﴿in the blessing of Allah they disbelieve﴾ refers to the material, physical blessing and the immaterial, heart-based blessing. Is Islam not the greatest of blessings upon us? If a person disbelieves in it and does not fulfill its obligations, he is rebuked for this. It is said: "Are you not a Muslim?" He will say: "Yes." "Then why did you not pray? Why did you not give zakah? Why did you not fast? Why did you not do such-and-such of the obligations?"
So gratitude for the blessing of Islam is obligatory, just as gratitude to Allah for His blessings upon us, such as wealth, children, security, and comfort, and similar things, is obligatory. Indeed, gratitude for Islam is more binding, and disbelief in Islam is more dangerous, because Allah says: ﴿And if you turn away, He will replace you with another people, then they will not be like you﴾ [Muhammad 47:38], and He says: ﴿And if these disbelieve in it, We have entrusted it to a people who are not disbelievers in it﴾ [al-An'am 6:89]. Allah may remove Islam from a people who do not fulfill its obligations, just as He removes security and prosperity from a people who do not give thanks for that security and prosperity. The blessings are one, and their path is one.
And His saying: ﴿and in the blessing of Allah﴾: is it singular or plural?
* Students: Plural.
* The Shaykh: Good. Why then did He say "the blessing of Allah"?
* Student: It is a singular noun in construct form (*mufrad mudaf*).
* The Shaykh: A singular noun in construct form, and so it is general. The proof is His saying: ﴿And if you count the blessing of Allah﴾. Look: ﴿if you count the blessing of Allah, you could not enumerate it﴾ [al-Nahl 16:18]. If it were singular, there would be no need to count it or to enumerate it, as it is well known.
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: No, it is not made dual except in terms of type; it is not made dual. He said: ﴿and in the blessing of Allah they disbelieve﴾. What does the phrase ﴿in the blessing of Allah﴾ relate to?
* Student: To ﴿they disbelieve﴾.
* The Shaykh: To ﴿they disbelieve﴾. It has been placed first to convey exclusivity (*hasr*), as if they disbelieve in nothing except the blessing of Allah. This is a semantic benefit. And there is also in it a verbal benefit: namely, observing the rhyme endings of the verses (*fawasil*).

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 29, verse 63–67 (part 1 of 4):

His saying, "And if you asked them, 'Who sends down water from the sky and thereby revives the earth after its death?'" The "lam" here is the lam of oath, and the answer to the oath is: "they will surely say, 'Allah'" [al-Ankabut 63]. "And if you asked them, 'Who sends down from the sky...'" — "man" (مَن) here is a relative pronoun in the nominative as subject (mubtada'), its relative clause (silah) is the verb "nazzala", and the answer to the oath is "they will surely say, 'Allah'". Is this i'rab correct or not?
* Students: No, it is wrong.
* The Shaykh: It is wrong. "Man" (مَن) is an interrogative pronoun, because it occurs after the question: "And if you asked them, 'Who sent down...'" On this basis, "man" is the subject (mubtada'), and "nazzala" with its clause is the predicate of the subject. His saying "man nazzala" is with the doubled "zay" (nazzala, intensive form). In some verses it is "anzala min as-sama'" [al-An'am 99]. The difference between "nazzala" and "anzala" is that "nazzala" indicates that a thing descends gradually, bit by bit, as Allah the Exalted said about the Qur'an: "And [it is] a Qur'an which We have separated [in revelation] that you might recite it to the people over a long period, and We have sent it down in stages" [al-Isra' 106].
And His saying, "nazzala min as-sama'" — because descent occurs from above. The meaning of "as-sama'" (the sky) here is "the height," not the protected ceiling, as evidenced by His saying: "Indeed, in the creation of the heavens and the earth, and the alternation of the night and the day, and the ship which runs through the sea with that which benefits people, and what Allah sends down from the sky of water, and gives life thereby to the earth after its death... and the clouds subjected between the sky and the earth" [al-Baqarah 164], and rain descends from the clouds: "Do you not see that Allah drives the clouds, then joins them, then makes them into a heap, and you see the rain emerge from within them" [al-Nur 43]. Thus we know that the meaning of "as-sama'" here is what? "The height." Everything that is above you is "sama'," because it derives from (sama, yasmu), meaning it rose and was elevated.
And His saying, "min as-sama' ma'an" — the wisdom in its descent from the sky is that when it descends from above, it covers what is below and what is high; if it flowed from the earth, it would not reach the high places before it destroyed what is below. But by the wisdom of Allah, it descends from above.
He said, "ma'an fa-ahya bihi al-ard" — the "fa" here indicates sequence and immediacy, but when it connects to a clause, it also indicates causation together with sequence and immediacy. This differs from when it precedes a noun, in which case it does not indicate causation. You say: "Zayd stood up, then 'Amr," which does not mean that Zayd's standing was the cause of 'Amr's standing, but that 'Amr's standing came after Zayd's standing. When it connects to a verb, however, it generally indicates sequence with causation. Accordingly, His saying "fa-ahya bihi al-ard" means that the water is the cause of the earth's revival. Now, His saying "fa-ahya bihi," does the earth come to life immediately or later?
* Students: Later.
* The Shaykh: Later. But since the cause is effective, the effect follows it immediately, like His saying: "Do you not see that Allah sends down water from the sky, and the earth becomes green?" [al-Hajj 63]. The earth does not become green merely by the water descending at night, but this is a necessitating cause. Since it is a necessitating cause, it is as if the effect exists at once. They said: Among this is their saying: "So-and-so married, and a child was born to him," although this is weaker than what we have here. But when he says "a child was born to him," we know with certainty that he was not begotten the night of his marriage or not? There is no difficulty in this; marriage is the cause of birth, and the sequence follows it. It is not necessary that it be immediate, but when the cause is necessitating and inevitable, the effect is as if it follows the cause directly.
And His saying: "fa-ahya bihi al-ard min ba'di mawtiha" — "ahya" (revive) and "mawt" (death) are applied to inanimate matter. So does it live and die or not? Inanimate matter lives and dies, and everything's life and death is according to its nature. Do not think that life and death are attributed only to what can move. Concerning these idols, Allah says: "And those whom they invoke besides Allah create nothing, while they are created. [They are] dead, not alive" [al-Nahl 20–21]. "Dead, not alive." So everything that has no movement and no growth can be called dead, even if it is something life does not inhabit.
And His saying: "ahya bihi al-ard min ba'di mawtiha" — is the meaning of "the earth" here the vegetation, or is it the earth itself? It has been said: the meaning is the earth itself, and by the mixing of water into it, it becomes living, and by its drying it becomes dead. It has also been said: the meaning is what is upon it of grass, crops and the like, i.e., the vegetation, and that the earth is not truly "earth" in the sense of being beneficial to people except through the vegetation above it, so its life and death are the life and death of its vegetation.
And His saying, the Exalted: "they will surely say, 'Allah'" — we say about it what has preceded: the lam occurs in the answer to the oath, and "yaqulunna" originally was "yaqulunanna." Have you seen? The grammarians said: the first nun was deleted because of the succession of similar sounds. Why do we not say: one of the two nuns of the emphatic nun was deleted? They said: because the emphatic nun was introduced for a purpose, which is emphasis, while the nun of the raf' (nominative ending) is always deleted in the case of the nasb (accusative), the jazm (jussive), the takhfif (lightening), and the like, so it was more appropriate for deletion. Thus we deleted the nun of raf' because of the succession of similar sounds. What is the reason for the deletion of the waw? Because of the meeting of two sukun (unvocalized letters), since the doubled emphatic nun consists of two letters, the first of which is unvocalized. When it is unvocalized, the weak letter before it, the soft vowel letter, is deleted, as Ibn Malik said:
"... and if it is a soft letter, its deletion is required."
And His saying, "Allah": we say it is the predicate of a deleted subject, or a subject whose predicate is deleted.
* A student: The reason for (...).
* The Shaykh: Allah knows best. We do not know how they say that mixing water with it is life. They say that this is a life appropriate to it. In truth, as I said a little while ago, life and death in vegetation are more evident, because it is the place of benefit. Perhaps one may cite as evidence His saying: "Or like one who passed by a town, while it was fallen upon its roofs. He said, 'How will Allah revive this after its death?'" [al-Baqarah 259]. The thing that is fallen upon its roofs is the vegetation or the earth? The vegetation. So "How will Allah revive this after its death" attributes death to the vegetation. This means that this supports the view that the revival of the earth and its vegetation means the revival of its vegetation and its death.
* A student: His saying, the Exalted: "You see the earth barren, but when We send down water upon it, it stirs and swells" [Fussilat 39].
* The Shaykh: Yes. Some scholars said: the earth itself stirs, and it swells, that is, with the water it rises. This is the matter in it, but the apparent view, and Allah knows best, is that the closer opinion is that the meaning is the vegetation.
His saying: "They will surely say, 'Allah.' Say: 'Praise be to Allah.'" "Say: 'Praise be to Allah'" — He did not say here "How are they turned away?" There He said: "How are they deluded?" (fa-anna yu'fakun), because the indication of creation and governance for lordship, which necessitates acknowledgment of divinity, is evident. Here He said: "Say: Praise be to Allah," because their acknowledgment of the first and the second, and that the whole matter is in Allah's hand, necessitates not merely that Allah exists, but that Allah deserves to be praised. For this reason He said: "Say: Praise be to Allah." The proof has been established against you, the clear evidence has stood against you, and the perfection of Allah the Mighty and Majestic has become manifest. Do you understand? The first contains negation (takhliyah), the second contains affirmation (tahliyah), the affirmation of Allah's perfection. That is, "Praise be to Allah" for the establishment of the clear evidence against you and the manifestness and clarity of the proof.
As for the author's saying, "How then do they associate partners with Him?", he brought it in the manner of His saying in the first verse, "How are they deluded?" But in my view, the second verse contains the establishment of proof on another matter which they deny, namely the Resurrection, for they deny it. The reality of the matter is that one who denies the Resurrection will associate partners with Allah and will do whatever he wishes, because the denier of the Resurrection believes there is no reward and no reckoning, and whoever believes so, will he act? He does not act. For this reason, as you see, Allah the Exalted always combines in the Qur'an belief in Him with belief in the Last Day; He always combines them, because belief in the Last Day is what drives a person to action, for whoever does not believe there is a recompense, how will he act? What appears to me is that the second verse was brought to oblige them to acknowledge the Resurrection.
* A student: Some verses: "So He revives thereby the earth after its death" [al-Baqarah 164].
* The Shaykh: Yes indeed, "after its death." Yes. The benefit: this revival may be close to the death of the earth, meaning that rain descends close to the drought, and sometimes it is delayed, so "min" (from/after) indicates the delay.
He said: "Say: Praise be to Allah," for the establishment of the proof against you. Now, "al-hamdu lillah" (praise belongs to Allah): what is praise (hamd)? Is it commendation? Most people say: it is commendation for good qualities. This is not correct, for commendation (thana') is other than praise (hamd). This is shown by the saying of the Prophet ﷺ, indeed by the saying of Allah, that commendation is other than praise in the sacred hadith, the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, that Allah, glorified and exalted, said: "I have divided the prayer between Me and My servant into two halves. When he says: 'Praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds' [al-Fatihah 2], He says: My servant has praised Me. When he says: 'The Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful' [al-Fatihah 3], He says: My servant has commended Me. When he says: 'Master of the Day of Judgment' [al-Fatihah 4], He says: My servant has glorified Me." [Related by Muslim (395/38) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.] This is clear evidence that commendation is other than praise, otherwise it would be repetition. Also, the meaning requires it, for "thana'" derives from "thaniyah," meaning return, for when you bend a staff, its end returns to its end. From it also comes the word "ithnan" (two), meaning one and one, in which there is return. The point is that "hamd" cannot be correctly explained as "thana'." So what is it? We say: it is describing the praised one with perfection, but we add also: together with love and magnification, so that flattery (madh) is excluded, for flattery is describing the one praised with perfection, but it may be out of love and magnification, or it may be out of fear and not love. This man who stood before an oppressive, tyrannical king and said: "You are the noble king, the benevolent, just one who wrongs no one" — is this flattery or not? It is flattery, but out of love and magnification? Not at all; it is a lie. So we say: praise (hamd) is describing the praised one with perfection together with love and magnification. Further, it is also distinguished from flattery in that flattery may conform to reality or may not, while praise must necessarily conform to reality.
He said: And His saying, "al-hamdu lillah": the scholars say that the "al" in "al-hamd" is for comprehensiveness (istighraq), so all praises belong to Allah. The lam in His saying "lillah," is it the lam of ownership or of its like? Ibn Malik says:
"And the lam is for ownership and its like..."
* A student: Its like.
* The Shaykh: Its like. So praise is due to Allah and specific to Allah, and what is meant is complete praise. As for mere praise, it is not specific to Allah; a person may be praised for one quality according to the measure of that quality, but complete and comprehensive praise belongs to Allah alone and is specific to Allah alone.
"Say: Praise be to Allah, but most of them do not know" — they do not realize their contradiction in this. Is "bal" here for transitional (intiqali) or for nullifying (ibtali) retraction?
* A student: Transitional.
* The Shaykh: Transitional. That is: after the matter has been established and the proof has stood, and the Creator has become worthy of commendation or praise, at that point it is correct to record ignorance against them, which is His saying: "But most of them do not reason." Most of these do not reason, meaning that they have such foolishness as is evident, for if they had intellects, their acknowledgment of what they acknowledged would have obliged them to acknowledge what they denied, or not? Yes, if they had genuine, rightly-guided intellects, their acknowledgment of what they acknowledged would have obliged them to acknowledge what they denied. They acknowledged that the One who created the heavens and the earth and subjected the sun and the moon is Allah, and that the One who sent down water from the sky and thereby revived the earth after its death is Allah. So where is intellect, while you deny the Resurrection and associate partners with the Creator?! Here there is no intellect.
From here we derive that those who claim they are the people of intellect, yet deny some of the attributes of Allah the Mighty and Majestic, arguing that intellect does not affirm them, we derive from this that they do not have intellect, for intellect obliges them to acknowledge what they denied, just as they acknowledged what they acknowledged.
For example — we will strike only two examples: the Ash'aris, and the discussion is with them and with whoever else, a fortiori, say: "We affirm for Allah will (irada), and we deny mercy (rahmah); Allah has no mercy." Why, O people? They say: "Yes, because will is indicated by reason, and mercy, reason has shown its invalidity." Look at what they say: "Reason has not indicated it; reason has shown its invalidity."
Now, explain: they say, "Will is indicated by reason through specification (takhsis): the specification of the sky being sky, the earth being earth, man being human, the donkey being an animal, and the like, i.e., a non-speaking animal. This indicates what? It indicates will: He willed the donkey to be a donkey, so it was a donkey; and He willed man to be a human, so he was a human; and He willed the sky to be sky, so it was sky," and so on.
Is this an indispensable proof for will? A clear proof, or not clear? Clear. Now mercy? They say: reason has shown its denial, why? They say: because mercy is softness and tenderness, and Allah, the Majestic and Exalted, is not described by softness and tenderness.
We said to them: You have argued from reality to will; we argue against you from reality to mercy, and the indication of reality for mercy is greater than the indication of reality for will. If you were to say to a common person, "What is your rational proof for will?" — by Allah, I do not know. Does the common person perceive that specification is evidence for will?
* A student: No.
* The Shaykh: Good. But if you say to the common person: Allah's sending down rain after drought so that the earth becomes fertile, and Allah's provision of wealth to the poor, so that he becomes rich after poverty, does this not indicate that Allah is merciful or not? What does he say? He says: yes. So the indication of the reality of the countless blessings of Allah for the mercy of Allah is more eloquent than the indication of specification for will. Is it clear? This is very clear.
Therefore, in reality, if they had intellect, as they claim that they are the people of intellect, their argument for mercy from reality would be more eloquent than their argument for will from reality. Is it clear? But the flaw and trial they have brought: they said that mercy means softness and tenderness, and Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, is exalted above that?

Our answer to this comes from three aspects. The first aspect: we say that this implication applies only to the mercy of the created being, and the mercy of the Creator is not the mercy of the created being; we do not liken them. This is the first.

Second thing: we say that whoever claims gentleness and tenderness are negated from God is merely (...), and gentleness toward others in order to deliver kindness to them is not a attribute of deficiency.

The third aspect: we say that mercy is not the same as gentleness and tenderness. It may be that this king shows mercy, for example, to one of his subjects and is compassionate toward him, while he remains in his might and sovereignty, and does not feel within himself that in this state he has fallen from the rank of strength and resolve. Isn't that so? Say: no, or yes?!

* The students: Yes.

* The Shaykh: For example, this powerful king in his authority shows mercy to a poor person among the members of his nation, while he feels that he remains in his might and nothing has harmed it in that. Then we say, by reason...

(Ma) is a negating particle and not a Hijazi one here, because the negation was nullified by (illa). And Ibn Malik says:
Acting like laysa was given to ma, provided it is not followed by in, with the negation still remaining...
And here the negation has not remained.

And His saying: ﴿And what is this worldly life﴾ [al-'Ankabut 64]. The demonstrative here is for belittling and for the lowness of its rank. Using a demonstrative to belittle is found in the Arabic language, as in His saying about the disbelievers: ﴿Is this the one who mentions your gods?﴾ [al-Anbiya' 36]; meaning: what is this contemptible, humiliated one who reviles the gods, when they are great and exalted, and the like.

And His saying: ﴿the worldly life﴾ is the abode in which we are, and it was described as "worldly" for two reasons: because it is near in time, and because it is near in rank.

And His saying ﴿the life﴾ came here to contrast it with the second life.

And His saying: ﴿except amusement and play﴾. This restriction is real: the world, which is the world, is confined to these two matters: amusement and play. As for the difference between them, it has been said: play is with the limbs, and amusement is with the tongue, based on the Most High's saying: ﴿And among the people is one who purchases idle talk to mislead from the way of Allah﴾ [Luqman 6]. And the Most High said: ﴿Those who are in vain discourse, playing﴾ [at-Tur 12].

It has also been said: amusement is in the heart, which is its heedlessness and its indulgence in diversions and in what distracts it from obedience to Allah, while play is in the limbs, of the tongue and other than the tongue. And this is closer to the truth: that amusement is in the hearts and play is in the limbs. This is the closer view.

Accordingly, the outcome of the world is that it is amusement with which a person diverts himself: heedlessness and wandering right and left. Likewise it is play, even the serious matters of the world are play, because they pass away and do not remain, or their owner departs from them. So it is like the play of children, who entertain themselves with it while they are children, then abandon it when they grow up, become wise, and recognize what they are upon.

The author said: (As for acts of devotion, they belong to the matters of the Hereafter, because their fruit appears there).

His saying: (As for acts of devotion) is an answer to an implied question, as if someone said: how can the world be amusement and play, when a person does righteous deeds in it: he prays, pays zakat, fasts, performs Hajj, honors his parents, maintains his kinship ties, and the like? Is this play?

* A student: No.

* The Shaykh: The author says: it is not play. Is this not in the world? He says: Yes, it is in the world, but its fruit appears in the Hereafter; therefore he said: (As for acts of devotion) -and they are from the world- (they belong to the matters of the Hereafter because their fruit appears there). The author spoke truly, for righteous deeds are not from the deeds of the world; therefore, if a person intends by them the world, they become void and he has no reward for them.

Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah said: whoever performs Hajj in order to take (worldly gain), then he has no share (khalaq) in the Hereafter; meaning, no portion. What the Shaykh said is confirmed by the Most High's saying: ﴿Whoever desires the worldly life and its adornment, We will pay them in full for their deeds therein, and they will not be deprived therein. Those are the ones for whom there is nothing in the Hereafter but the Fire, and what they did therein will be voided, and what they used to do is worthless﴾ [Hud 15-16].

It is also supported by his ﷺ saying: «Ruined is the servant of the dinar, ruined is the servant of the dirham» [Reported by al-Bukhari (2886) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah], and so on. The conclusion is that the deeds of the Hereafter are not from the deeds of the world; rather, if the deeds of the world are intended by them, they become void.

He said: ﴿And indeed the Hereafter abode, that is the true life﴾. This sentence is emphasized with three emphases. I say: explain to us the emphases in this.

* A student: The waw.

* The Shaykh: The waw is not for emphasis; the waw is not one of the emphasis particles.

* The student: (...).

* The Shaykh: ﴿And indeed the Hereafter abode, that is the true life﴾.

* A student: (inna), and the lam, and the pronoun.

* The Shaykh: And the separating pronoun: ﴿that is the true life﴾. Note that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, emphasized that al-hayawan, meaning life, but it came in this pattern for intensification: (hayawan) is fa'alan for intensification; otherwise al-hayawan means life, and the pattern of (hayawan) is fa'alan, so the alif and nun were added for intensification.

His saying: ﴿And indeed the Hereafter abode﴾: it is what will be on the Day of Resurrection.

﴿that is the true life﴾: he said (meaning life), but the alif and nun were added to it for intensification; meaning it is the real life. Therefore the disbeliever on the Day of Resurrection says: ﴿Oh, I wish I had sent forth for my life﴾ [al-Fajr 24]. His life in the world, he sends forth for it; indeed it is his garden. But the real life is the life of the Hereafter, because the life of this world is in reality not life. First: because it is troubled, every purity in it has a turbidity. Second: because it does not remain, is it not so? Third: because a person is threatened in it, he does not know when his term will come to him, in the morning or in the evening; how many a person has left his family and did not return except as a corpse, and how many a person was on his chair and did not finish writing what he was writing with his right hand. Is this life? The answer:

* The students: No.

* The Shaykh: No, it is not life in reality. Therefore the poet says:
There is no pleasure in living while its delights are troubled by remembering death and old age.
However pleasant life becomes for you, if you reflect, you will grow old and leave this life, and it will not be pleasant for you, and you will die, so no life will remain for you at all.

In sum: the Hereafter abode, our Lord spoke truly, Most High, is the true life. It is what the intelligent person should strive for. Remarkably, whoever strives for the Hereafter gains both the world and the Hereafter, and whoever strives only for the world loses both the world and the Hereafter. The evidence: ﴿Whoever desires the tilth of the Hereafter, We will increase him in his tilth﴾ [ash-Shura 20]. What is the meaning of ﴿We will increase him﴾? It means: We give him the tilth of the Hereafter together with the world, based on His saying: ﴿Whoever does righteousness, male or female, while being a believer, We will surely cause him to live a good life﴾ [an-Nahl 97]. This is the prompt reward, and ﴿We will surely reward them their due for the best of what they used to do﴾ is the deferred reward, and ﴿Whoever desires the tilth of the Hereafter, We will increase him in his tilth﴾.

* A student: (...).

* The Shaykh: No, We give him some of it, and We do not give him what he wants: ﴿We give him of it﴾ [Ali 'Imran 145]. And this promise is also conditioned by will, as in the verse of al-Isra': ﴿Whoever desires the immediate, We hasten for him therein what We will, for whom We want﴾ [al-Isra' 18]. He is not the one who desires it entirely, nor part of what he desires: ﴿what We will, for whom We desire; then We have made for him Hell, he will burn in it, reproached and banished﴾. So, the true life is in reality the Hereafter.

Is the waw in al-hayawan here original or converted? It has been said: it is converted from a yaa', and that it was changed to a waw so that it would not be confused with the dual; so, if one said "wa inna al-akhirata lahiya al-hayayan," it would be confused with the dual, so it was changed to a waw. This is an opinion of Sibawayh, based on the view that hayah is from the root ḥ-y-y, from ḥayiya yahyā.

It has also been said: the waw is original, and the waw in "hayah" is the root, but it was changed to yaa' in ḥayiya. Why? Because of its movement and the preceding kasra, so it became yaa'. This, in any case, is morphology, a purely morphological discussion.

As for the Most High's saying: ﴿if they only knew﴾: this is a new (independent) clause; ﴿law﴾ here is not connected to what precedes it, but is independent, so it is conditional, and the answer of the condition is omitted, which the author estimated with his saying:
(﴿if they only knew﴾ that, they would not have preferred the world over it).
In reality, his saying "they would not have preferred the world over it" is correct as an answer, but the answer is more eloquent than what the commentator estimated; that is why Allah omitted it, so that the mind would reach its estimation to every extent; so that the mind can estimate everything: ﴿if they only knew﴾ they would have worked for it night and day, not merely that they would not have preferred the world; it means that whoever puts the world before the Hereafter has no knowledge; if he knew the truth, and were among people of knowledge and understanding, he would not have put it first.

﴿So when they board the ship, they call upon Allah, sincere to Him in religion﴾ [al-'Ankabut 65]. The pronoun in ﴿when they board﴾ refers to the polytheists. That is, ask these people about their gods: do they turn to them in times of hardship, or do they acknowledge that none relieves the hardship except Allah? The answer: the second; they acknowledge that their idols do not benefit them, and they previously acknowledged that the One who created the heavens and the earth is who? Allah; that the One who sends down water from the sky is Allah; that the One who subjected the sun and the moon is Allah; and that the One who removes distress, based on what is mentioned in this verse, is who? Allah.

﴿When they board the ship﴾: is al-fulk the ships or the ship? It is suitable, because it is applicable to both the plural and the singular. Allah, Blessed and Most High, said: ﴿until when you are in the ship and they sail with them by a good wind﴾ [Yunus 22]; this is plural. And the singular?

* A student: "idha rakibu" (...).

* The Shaykh: No.

* A student: (...).

* The Shaykh: No, on al-fulk?

* The student: On al-fulk.

* The Shaykh: And it is singular?

* The student: Yes.

* The Shaykh: Good. He said: ﴿When they board the ship, they call upon Allah, sincere to Him in religion﴾. ﴿they call upon Allah﴾: ﴿they call﴾ is the response of ﴿idha﴾, and it is composed of a verb and a subject. Here there is a difficulty: it was previously established that when the past tense verb is attached to the plural waw, it is built on damma and the plural waw is made sukun. Here it is not built on damma, and the plural waw is not made sukun. You say: qamu (they stood); the letter before the waw is damma, and the plural waw is sukun. Here ﴿da'awu﴾: neither is the letter before the waw damma, nor is the waw made sukun. So how is this difficulty resolved?

* A student: (...).

* The Shaykh: No (...) before the waw. Now, when the plural waw is attached to the past verb, the letter before it takes damma and the waw takes sukun.

* The student: (...).

* The Shaykh: Now what we have is the opposite.

* The student: da'awu.

* The Shaykh: ﴿da'awu Allah﴾.

* The student: (...).

* The Shaykh: No.

* The student: (...).

* The Shaykh: One.

* The student: (...).

* The Shaykh: No. What we have now is one.

* The student: (...).

* The Shaykh: So the waw that is present, what is it?

* The student: (...).

* The Shaykh: Or the waw of the verb.

* The student: The waw of (...).

* The Shaykh: That is, the waw of the verb. Good, this is an answer... yes.

* A student: (...) the waw (...) the waw of the doer (...) because the waw is the waw of the doer (...).

* The Shaykh: The waw was deleted.

* The student: The waw (...).

* The Shaykh: Good, and what brought the fatha?

* A student: It remained on the original: the damma is the original of the waw (...).

* The Shaykh: And is this the answer? Yes.

* A student: (...) the waw of the plural: that the letter before the waw of the plural is deleted and fatha is put (...) da'aw, the original of the verb: (da'a) (...) the letter of weakness (...) so it was deleted (...) before it.

* The Shaykh: And the fatha remained?

* The student: As a sign of it.

* The Shaykh: As an indication of it, on that basis. Good, the damma of the waw in ﴿da'awu﴾?

* A student: (...).

* The Shaykh: (qamu) is not (...) sukun.

* A student: (...).

* The Shaykh: Good:
............................... And if it is a soft letter, its deletion is deserved.

* A student: (...).

* The Shaykh: (...).

* A student: (...).

* The Shaykh: Is his answer correct, the first one or not?

* A student: (...).

* The Shaykh: Yes, that the alif was deleted, the alif deleted from the verb?

* A student: (...) the alif, the alif of the verb (...).

* Another student: (...).

* The Shaykh: No, let no one speak, everybody, except the one in charge.

* A student: (...).

* The Shaykh: That is not correct.

* The student: (...).

* The Shaykh: Is it the pronoun?

* The student: Yes, and it was deleted because of the meeting of two sukuns.

* The Shaykh: It seems there will be disagreement among you; perhaps we will cut the path.

* A student: (...).

* The Shaykh: No, the correct one: its origin is that it is deleted with the alif; the alif of the verb was deleted and the fatha remained as an indication of it, and the existing waw is the waw of the pronoun, but it was moved with damma because of the meeting of two sukuns. Where are the two sukuns? If the waw remained sukun and the hamza of (al) remained sukun, it would not work. So if someone says: the rule is that you delete the waw because:
............................... And if it is a soft letter, its deletion is deserved.
We say: deleting the waw here is not possible; if we deleted the waw, it would necessitate returning the alif of the verb; then when we return it, we would have no evidence of the pronoun, so the existence of the pronoun is necessary, and it was moved with damma because it is the cognate of the waw, since the appearance of kasra on the waw is very heavy, and damma is closer to its cognate waw. This is present in the Qur'an; there are several examples of this.

And His saying: ﴿da'awu Allah mukhlisina lahu al-din﴾ [al-'Ankabut 65]. ﴿da'awu﴾: is it supplication of worship or a request?

* A student: A request.

* The Shaykh: A request. And His saying: ﴿mukhlisina lahu al-din﴾ is a state (hal) of the subject of ﴿da'awu﴾. Ikhlas is cleansing a thing of what mixes with it; so the meaning of ﴿mukhlisina lahu﴾ is: they do not associate with this supplication a supplication to any idol.

And His saying: ﴿lahu al-din﴾: the author said: (that is, the supplication), because supplication is worship, so it is from the religion; therefore he said:
(﴿mukhlisina lahu al-din﴾ meaning: they do not call upon anyone with Him, because they are in a hardship that none removes except Him).

They in that case acknowledge and are compelled; it is not possible for any of them to call upon an idol in this state, because he knows that the idol does not benefit him; so they call upon none but Allah. This is a third proof against them, rather a fourth.

The first proof: the creation of the heavens and the earth. The second: the subjugation of the sun and the moon. The third: sending down water from the sky and giving life to the earth; four (...). And the fifth: their sincere supplication to Allah in the state of hardship.

* A student: These are the greatest proofs against them.

* The Shaykh: Yes indeed, these are among the greatest proofs against them.

He said: ﴿So when He delivered them to the land, behold, they associate others with Him﴾. ﴿Lamma﴾ (لَمَّا) here is a conditional particle. Its verb of condition is ﴿delivered them﴾ (نَجَّاهُمْ), and its response is ﴿behold, they associate﴾ (إِذَا هُمْ يُشْرِكُونَ). The grammarians call ﴿idha﴾ (إِذَا) the particle of suddenness (fuja'iyyah), and suddenness is something that arrives unexpectedly. The meaning is that when they were delivered to land, they suddenly and hastily associated others with Allah. And what are they associating? Shirk (associating partners with Allah). We seek refuge in Allah. The reward for the blessing should be disbelief.

﴿So when He delivered them to the land﴾. Who delivered them? Allah. That is, He rescued them from the hardship they were in, ﴿to the land﴾, which is the shore of safety.

(﴿behold, they associate﴾ with Him.)

﴿behold, they associate﴾ is a nominal sentence (jumlah ismiyyah), which indicates that this becomes a fixed attribute of theirs. They persist, may Allah protect us, in shirk, hastening to it. This is the utmost of baseness, because a human being by his nature and innate disposition does not disbelieve in the one who has bestowed favour upon him, but rather thanks him.

As for these people, merely by the blessing they associate others with Allah, we seek refuge in Allah. This resembles the speech of someone who sings on some Arab radio stations about the war they call the Six-Day War. You know it? It was a war with the Jews, in which Syria, Jordan and Egypt fought. It was a war that, may Allah protect us, destroyed their morale and took their lands. But during the days of the battle, one of the announcers would say: "Tomorrow we will enter Tel Aviv, and Umm Kulthum will sing to us." But Umm Kulthum sang over their remains.

Is this in reality a promise of disbelief in the blessing, or not? The Messenger ﷺ entered Makkah at the conquest with his head bowed low, humbling himself before Allah, Mighty and Majestic.[[Narrated by Abu Ya'la (3393), and al-Hakim in al-Mustadrak (4413), from the hadith of Anas ibn Malik.]] Yes, there is a difference between this and that. This state, for example, if we conquer the lands of the disbelievers and singing girls sing to us and play instruments for us, this resembles ﴿So when He delivered them to the land, behold, they associate others with Him﴾.

Allah the Exalted said: (﴿So that they may disbelieve in what We have given them﴾ [al-'Ankabut 66] of the blessing, ﴿and so that they may enjoy themselves﴾ by gathering together in the worship of idols. In another reading, with the lam sukun: an imperative of threat.)

His words: ﴿So that they may disbelieve in what We have given them﴾. Is the lam here the lam of command (lam al-amr) or the lam of causation (lam al-ta'lil)?
* Student: Causation.
* The Shaykh: Yes, there are two readings. If we make the second lam sakin in His words ﴿and let them enjoy themselves﴾, which is the second reading, the lam becomes the lam of command, an imperative of threat, because Allah does not command disbelief, neither as a command of guidance nor as a command of obligation. And if we kasr the second lam: ﴿and so that they may enjoy themselves﴾, the lam becomes the lam of "so that" (kay).

Then, if the lam in His words ﴿so that they may disbelieve in what We have given them﴾ is not a lam of command, is it the lam of causation or the lam of consequence (lam al-'aqibah)? The answer: it is the lam of consequence, because Allah did not deliver them to land so that they would associate others with Him in order that they would disbelieve. Rather, their outcome became disbelief. Is the lam of consequence known in the Arabic language? Yes, it is known. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Then the family of Pharaoh picked him up, so that he would become an enemy to them and a source of grief﴾ [al-Qasas 8].

If someone asked us: Did the family of Pharaoh pick up Moses for this purpose? We would say: No, but this became the outcome. Had they known that he would be an enemy to them and a source of grief...
* Student: They did not pick him up.
* The Shaykh: Yes, or they picked him up and then destroyed him. They did not pick him up for this purpose, but the outcome was this. So here the outcome is that they disbelieved in what We had given them.

As for His words ﴿with what We have given them﴾: is the ba' here for causation, or is the verb (kafara, disbelieved) transitive through it, as in "kafara bihi" (disbelieved in him)? Yes, this is closer. That is, ﴿so that they may disbelieve in what We have given them﴾ means the verb (kafara) is transitive to its object through the ba', and the meaning is like "disbelieved in Allah, disbelieved in the Messenger, and disbelieved in such-and-such." His words ﴿what We have given them﴾ mean what We bestowed upon them of blessing. And what is the blessing? Their deliverance from drowning.

﴿and so that they may enjoy themselves﴾. He said: (by gathering together in the worship of idols).
It may also be said that ﴿and so that they may enjoy themselves﴾ refers to the blessings as well, the blessings they were given. They disbelieved in them, so they did not thank for them, and they enjoyed them until their end and their destination.

The author says: (In another reading with the lam sukun, an imperative of threat): ﴿and let them enjoy themselves﴾. Now the common people recite it ﴿and let them enjoy themselves﴾. Do we correct them or not? Do we correct them?
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: We correct them.
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: Yes, because the reading is wrong. We correct them because they recite it incorrectly. If you say (...) ﴿and let them enjoy themselves﴾, where will you return to? We return to the mushaf. When we return to the mushaf, we find it kasr. Their recitation of it with sukun is not out of knowledge but out of error and lack of knowledge. But if a student of knowledge came and recited it ﴿and let them enjoy themselves﴾, we would not correct him, because the student of knowledge may have recited it with this reading.
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: If in fact it is correct but he did not intend the lam of command, then it is not correct. His recitation is wrong, and he did not intend the lam of command.
* Student: (...) the lam of command (...) the Arabic language (...).
* The Shaykh: Yes, but they intended what the Arabic language indicates. For example: "I bear witness that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah." What did they intend by "Messenger"?
* Student: As a predicate (khabar).
* The Shaykh: As a predicate. So they intended what the Arabic language requires, the other one.
* Student: And this?
* The Shaykh: No, this one did not intend the imperative.
* Student: He does not know.
* The Shaykh: He does not know. But he intended what is in the mushaf. If we correct him, we say: because you now intend the reading in the mushaf and you erred. But if he says: Yes, I made it sakin because I am on the second reading, we say: we do not correct him.
* Student: If a man recites in the reading of Warsh and he comes to a verse like this and recites it in the second reading, do we not correct him? He intends it, I mean.
* The Shaykh: No, if he intends it, we do not correct him, except as I told you earlier: in front of the common people, one should not recite contrary to the reading that is in their hands, because this causes confusion for them and makes the Qur'an, which was respected in their souls, lose its sanctity. The layman does not appreciate these matters. He sees that this indicates a defect in the Noble Qur'an and says: What kind of thing is this, it changes?
We have mentioned that the student of knowledge should recite the readings himself, between himself and himself. He should recite all the readings, because they are all Sunnah. But with regard to the common people, one should not recite among them something other than what was known among them.
* Student: Naming supplication as religion.
* The Shaykh: The reason supplication is named religion is that it is an act of worship. The person who calls upon his Lord is devoting himself to Him through this supplication. Therefore, especially the one who knows feels that he will be rewarded for it, so it is religion.

As for His words ﴿then they will come to know﴾: (﴿then they will come to know﴾ the outcome of that).
(Sawfa, "soon") the grammarians say it indicates emphasis but with a delay. For this reason they call it al-taswif (postponement), unlike sa (سَ), which indicates certainty with nearness.

His words ﴿then they will come to know﴾ are a declarative sentence, and what is meant is a threat, like His words: ﴿No! You will come to know. Then, no! You will come to know﴾ [al-Takathur 3, 4], in Surat Alhakum. And the Exalted said in Surat an-Naba': ﴿No! They will come to know. Then, no! They will come to know﴾ [an-Naba' 4, 5]. So the punishment, we seek refuge in Allah, is surely descending upon them.

﴿Did they not see that We made a sanctuary secure?﴾ [al-'Ankabut 67]. ﴿Did they not see﴾: the discussion of this structure has already passed, that the hamzah is the interrogative particle and the waw is a conjunction. Is the hamzah moved from its place or not? We mentioned that there is disagreement about this, and we mentioned that the easier view is that the hamzah is interrogative and the waw conjoins what precedes it.

His words ﴿Did they not see﴾: the author says (did they not know). That is because seeing (ru'yah) is of two kinds: knowledge-seeing (ilmiyyah) and sight-seeing (basariyyah). If it is transitive to two objects, it is knowledge-seeing, as when you say: "I saw knowledge beneficial." And if it is transitive to one object, it is sight-seeing, as when you say: "I saw so-and-so."

Knowledge-seeing is very common in the Qur'an, including His words: ﴿Indeed they see it as far away, but We see it as near﴾ [al-Ma'arij 6-7], meaning We know it as near. The first ﴿they see it﴾ is seeing of supposition (ru'yat zann): ﴿indeed they see it as far away﴾.

And His words the Exalted: (﴿Did they not see﴾, i.e., know, ﴿that We made﴾ in their land, Makkah, ﴿a sanctuary secure﴾).
Why did He specify it to the people of Makkah? Because of His words: ﴿while people are snatched away from around them﴾.

﴿We made a sanctuary secure﴾: the haram (sanctuary) is that which has sanctity (hurmah), that is, veneration. Veneration is called hurmah because by this veneration what would otherwise be permissible is prohibited. What is among the sanctities of Makkah?
* Student: Prohibition of killing game.
* The Shaykh: The prohibition of killing game, fighting within it, cutting trees, cutting grass, and other things. Even harmless animals must be safe.

As for His words ﴿a sanctuary secure﴾: the people of metaphor (ahl al-majaz) say that "secure" refers to whoever is in it. The correct view is that the sanctuary itself is secure. For this reason Allah, glory be to Him, protected it from everyone, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Have you not considered how your Lord dealt with the companions of the elephant?﴾ [al-Fil 1]. And the Prophet ﷺ prohibited fighting in it.[[Agreed upon: al-Bukhari (1834) and Muslim (1353 / 445), from the hadith of 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abbas. On the same subject: from Abu Hurayrah, 'Amr ibn Sa'id, and others.]] So it is itself secure, and when it is secure, whoever is in it is secure.

His words ﴿while people are snatched away from around them﴾: the author says (by killing and taking captive, around them). In the time of ignorance, those outside the sanctuary were not safe. They were raided, killed, taken captive, and their wealth and women were seized. But the people of Makkah were secure, to the extent that a person would find the killer of his father within the sanctuary and would not kill him, even with the intensity of their zeal. But go out of the sanctuary and you find killing, captivity, plunder and everything.

This is a great blessing from Allah upon Quraysh, and it was incumbent upon them to meet this blessing with thankfulness and with belief in the Messenger ﷺ. Moreover, the Messenger ﷺ was one of them, whom they knew and called "the Trustworthy" before he brought the message, and they sometimes made him their judge. But when he was sent with the message, may Allah protect us, and he opposed their desires, they disbelieved in him.
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: It is said regarding it: the sanctuary itself did not change, and the removal of stones from it did not remain, and people were not prevented from Hajj, even while (...).

Among the benefits:
* Student: (...) ﴿And if you asked them﴾ (...).
* The Shaykh: That is, ﴿And if you asked them﴾: who sent down, or who created?
* Student: Who sent down.
* The Shaykh: Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And if you asked them who sends down water from the sky and gives life thereby to the earth after its death, they will surely say, "Allah"﴾ [al-'Ankabut 63].
* Among the benefits of this verse: first, the wisdom of Allah, glory be to Him, in sending down rain from the sky.
* And among its benefits: no one can send down rain from the sky except Allah. Whatever these people, to whom Allah gave what He gave of crafts, may attempt, they will never be able to send down rain from the sky, because this belongs exclusively to Allah, Mighty and Majestic.
* And among the benefits of the verse: the power of Allah, glory be to Him, to give life to the dead: ﴿and gives life thereby to the earth after its death﴾.
* And among its benefits: that inanimate matter may be described as having life and death: ﴿gives life thereby﴾, ﴿after its death﴾. We mentioned another example of this matter regarding idols: ﴿And those they invoke besides Allah create nothing, and they are created. They are dead, not alive﴾ [an-Nahl 20, 21].
* And among its benefits: analogy from the unseen to the seen (qiyas al-gha'ib 'ala al-shahid). Qiyas (analogical reasoning) is the drawing of a ruling on an unknown matter from a known one by a shared cause.
* Student: The unseen is the resurrection or the raising again, and the seen is the giving of life to the earth?
* The Shaykh: Yes. The unseen is the giving of life to people after death, and the seen is the giving of life to the earth.
* And among its benefits: the establishment of valid analogy (qiyas), or the recognition of valid analogy, contrary to those who deny it or go to extremes in it. People have divided into two groups: some went to extremes, and some fell short. That is, some denied analogy absolutely, like Ibn Hazm, who denies it yet sometimes uses analogy. And some went to extremes in it and exceeded the limit, to the point that they analogized the attributes of the Creator to the attributes of the created, like the Mushabbihah (anthropomorphists), for example.
* And among the benefits of the verse: the goodness of the Qur'an's argumentation and debate, and that its arguments and debates are binding. The reason is that their acknowledgment of this matter binds them to acknowledge the Oneness of Lordship and the perfection of Allah's attributes.
* And among them: the obligation to proclaim praise and thanks to Allah, Mighty and Majestic, before the polytheists, because of His words: ﴿Say: "All praise is due to Allah"﴾.
* And among them: that the acknowledgment of the polytheists of what belongs exclusively to Allah the Exalted, of power, is in reality a perfection of Allah, Mighty and Majestic. For this reason Allah commanded His Prophet to praise Him, or to describe Him with praise, when He said: ﴿they will surely say, "Allah"﴾. From this it is derived that the polytheists' acknowledgment of the attributes that belong exclusively to Allah is considered among the perfect attributes of Allah for which He deserves praise.
* And among them: that most of these polytheists are ignorant, because of His words: ﴿But most of them do not know﴾ [an-Nahl 75], meaning they do not know what Allah deserves of attributes of perfection.
* Student: ﴿They do not reason﴾.
* The Shaykh: ﴿They do not reason﴾, yes, correct. Most of them are foolish, most of them are fools who do not reason. If they were reasonable, they would know the necessary consequences and what they entail, and they would acknowledge them.
* And among the benefits of this verse: that the Ash'ariyyah and their like have, in what they adopted of affirming some attributes and denying others, neither rational argument nor transmitted evidence. As for transmitted evidence, it is obvious; they have no proof. Likewise, they also have no sound rational reflection, for they deny what they themselves affirm, or something similar to it, or less than it, do they not? Examples of this have passed before us.
So we say: whoever acknowledges some of Allah's attributes and actions and denies others is evidence of the weakness of his intellect. The intended meaning of "intellect" here is not the intellect of madness, nor the opposite of madness, but the intellect of right guidance and rectitude.
* Student: How can some of them be described as having intellect?
* The Shaykh: Yes, because some of them acknowledged and believed.
* Student: He is now relating about them, speaking about them...
* The Shaykh: They are in general terms, and whoever has intellect, then reflects and considers, believes and returns.

﴿And this worldly life is nothing but amusement and play. And indeed, the Hereafter—that is the [true] life, if they only knew﴾ [al-'Ankabut 64].
* Among the benefits of this verse: the demonstration of the lowliness of this world, and that it is nothing at all, or is it relative to the Hereafter?
* Student: Relative to the Hereafter.
* The Shaykh: The apparent meaning of the verse is absolute: "it is nothing but amusement and play," everything in it is amusement and play. So we may say it is in absolute terms, and we may say it is in comparison with the Hereafter, because of His words: ﴿and indeed, the Hereafter—that is the [true] life﴾.
* Student: (...) meaning it is restricted, because there are things in it, like prayer for example...
* The Shaykh: The author answered this, saying: (Indeed, acts of nearness to Allah belong to the Hereafter because their effect appears in it). The same author answered this point. So whatever is among the deeds of the Hereafter is not included among the deeds of this world.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 29, verses 63–67 (part 4 of 4):

* Among the benefits of the verse: it is not permissible to intend by the deeds of the Hereafter anything of this world. What is the reason for this? This is a benefit, not a question. We said that it is deduced from this verse that it is not permissible to intend worldly gain by them. What is the basis of this inference?
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: No.
* Student: Because the world (...) and the Hereafter (...).
* The Shaykh: Because these matters are done for the sake of the Hereafter, so you may not take a worldly exchange for them. This issue has also been subject to disagreement among the scholars in the chapter on *ijarah* (contract of hire).
* Among the benefits of this verse: the perfection of the life of the Hereafter, based on His saying: ﴿Indeed, the Final Abode is the true life﴾. That is so, because the Final Abode is everlasting, either in goodness or in evil.
* Among the benefits of the verse: the exhortation to knowledge, based on His saying: ﴿if only they knew﴾.
* Among its benefits: that among knowledge, indeed among the best of the sciences, is the distinguishing between beneficial matters and harmful matters. This discernment is of the greatest kind. When a person is truly granted it, he is granted much good. When he is granted the ability to distinguish between beneficial and harmful things, and to distinguish between matters that resemble one another in knowledge, he attains much good.
Some scholars have done something of this kind, so they began writing books titled *al-Furuq* (The Distinctions) and *al-Taqasim* (The Divisions). For example, they mention: the difference between *fard* (obligatory) and *nafl* (supererogatory), the difference between the *adhan* (call to prayer) and the *iqamah* (second call), the difference between *ju'alah* (reward-based contract) and *ijarah*, the difference between a gift (*'atiyyah*) and a bequest (*wasiyyah*), the difference between such-and-such and such-and-such. They mention the distinctions. These are beneficial for the student of knowledge. And here He said: ﴿if only they knew﴾: had they known the difference between this world and the Hereafter, they would not have preferred the life of this world over the Hereafter.
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: In books.
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: No, we do not know of it, I do not know it. But he always, in fairness, says: so-and-so mentioned it in *al-Furuq wal-Taqasim* and similar works. Shaykh 'Abd al-Rahman has a small treatise on this subject, but it does not cover it fully; it is only beneficial in this chapter.
* Student: The book of al-Qarafi?
* The Shaykh: Al-Qarafi? Yes, but I have not seen it.
* Student: The Shaykh's treatise?
* The Shaykh: The Shaykh's treatise is called *al-Qawa'id* (The Principles). It is small, not large: *al-Qawa'id wal-Taqasim*. This...
* Student: (...) *al-Huruf wal-Qawa'id* (The Letters and the Principles).
* The Shaykh: Yes indeed.

He said: ﴿So when they board ships, they call upon Allah, sincere to Him in religion; but when He delivers them to the land, at once they associate others with Him﴾, and so on to the end [al-'Ankabut 29:65].

* Student: O Shaykh, regarding intending the world and intending the Hereafter: you see those who call themselves "the gnostics" (*al-'arifun*) saying, for example: "I do not act for the sake of Paradise, nor out of fear of the Fire." They call this "the worship of slaves," or (...).
* The Shaykh: (...) ﴿So when they board ships, they call upon Allah, sincere to Him in religion﴾, to the end.
* Among the benefits of this verse: the clarification that the polytheists, in the past, were sincere in times of hardship.
* Among its benefits: the implicit acknowledgment by the polytheists that their gods do not benefit them. Had they believed in their benefit, they would have called upon them in this state. But they know that these gods do not benefit them.
* Among its benefits: is the shirk of earlier peoples lighter than the shirk of those who committed shirk from this nation, or not? Because the polytheists of this nation do not call upon Allah. They call upon their awliya' (saints/protectors) and those whom they have taken as rivals to Allah, may Allah protect us. For example, the Rafidah (Shi'ah extremists) call upon 'Ali: "O 'Ali! O 'Ali!"
* Student: Near the Ka'bah (...).
* The Shaykh: Yes indeed. I heard a man among them calling out near the Maqam, raising his voice: "O 'Ali, O 'Ali!" He raised his voice (...). A man from the *hisbah* (enforcers of public morality) came to him, rebuked him, and said: "You commit shirk beneath the Ka'bah! Get out!" He said: "I am only saying: O 'Ali. And Allah says in the Qur'an: ﴿And He is the Most High, the Mighty﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:255]." That is, he means he is calling upon Allah. This is from *taqiyyah* (dissimulation) which they adopt, and it is the path of the hypocrites.

So there is no doubt, as it appears to me, and Allah knows best, that he does not intend Allah. He intends 'Ali. Because had he intended Allah, he would have said "O Lord," or "O Allah," or something similar. But when he fell into the snare of justice and monotheism (...) the discussion, he claimed this invocation. The conclusion is that the shirk of whoever commits shirk in this nation is greater than the shirk of the polytheists in the past.
* Among the benefits of the verse: that seeking refuge in Allah the Mighty and Majestic is a matter of innate *fitrah* (natural disposition). The proof is that these people were overcome by their *fitrah* until they ﴿called upon Allah, sincere to Him in religion﴾.
* Among the benefits of the verse: that supplication is part of religion, based on His saying:
(﴿they called upon Allah, sincere to Him in religion﴾, meaning: supplication)
There is no doubt that supplication is part of religion and worship, because in it is the utmost humility and the acknowledgment of Allah's perfection, the Mighty and Majestic. Is that not so? In it is the utmost humility and the acknowledgment of Allah's perfection, the Mighty and Majestic, and this is worship.
When you say "O Lord," its meaning is that you are in need of Allah the Mighty and Majestic, and its meaning is that Allah is perfect, is He not? Yes indeed. For this reason the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, pledged allegiance to the Prophet (ﷺ) that they would not ask people for anything. A man's whip would fall from his camel, so he would dismount, pick it up, and not say: "Hand it to me, so-and-so!" [Narrated by Muslim (1043/108) from the hadith of 'Awf ibn Malik al-Ashja'i.]
Whereas today, unfortunately, you find a person humbling himself to the utmost degree in asking for money while not in need of it. These people will come on the Day of Resurrection with not a morsel of flesh on their faces, may Allah protect us. The point is that supplication is humility, and for this reason it is worship.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that these polytheists, when they are saved from hardship, disbelieve in the blessing: ﴿when He delivers them to the land, at once they associate others with Him﴾.
* Among its benefits: the foolishness of one who makes blessings a cause of arrogance and insolence. This involves a clear resemblance to the polytheists. Those who make blessings a cause of arrogance and insolence are the ones resembling the disbelievers, because it is obligatory upon the one on whom Allah has bestowed a blessing to increase in worship of Allah, glorified and exalted be He, since worship is a form of gratitude. So when Allah bestows a blessing upon you, increase your gratitude to Him.
For this reason: "When the Messenger (ﷺ) entered Makkah as a conqueror, he lowered his head so much that it nearly touched the saddle-peak of his mount" [Narrated by Abu Ya'la (3393) and al-Hakim in *al-Mustadrak* (4413) from the hadith of Anas ibn Malik]. Peace and blessings be upon him. All of this was out of humbling himself before the Bestower, glorified and exalted be He. So do not make Allah's blessings upon you a cause of arrogance and insolence. Rather, make them a cause of gratitude and humility before Allah, glorified and exalted be He, so that these blessings may increase and become true blessings.
And His saying: ﴿so that they may disbelieve in what We have given them, and so that they may enjoy themselves; but they will come to know﴾ [al-'Ankabut 29:66]. We interpret this verse as being imperative (a command).
* From it is derived: a warning to the people of disbelief and to forbidden enjoyment, because the command here is for threat. Allah does not command anyone to disbelieve, nor to enjoy in a forbidden way.
* And it is derived from it, according to the reading in which the *lam* is causal (*lam al-ta'lil*): that the outcome of those who associated others with Allah has become what? Disbelief and fleeting enjoyment. For this reason He said after it: ﴿but they will come to know﴾.
* From it is derived: a warning to those disbelievers whose only concern is enjoyment of this world.
* Among its benefits: strong caution against what some Muslims today have fallen into, where their only concern has become what? Enjoying this world alone. You find that most of what they speak about is luxury, indulgence, and similar things. But diseases of the heart, ailments of the heart, and deviations of the heart, few speak about them, although they are the root.
Pampering the bodies while the hearts are diseased: what benefit is there in it? There is no benefit except that when Allah's retribution descends, a person's regret increases, may Allah protect us. But pampering the heart through obedience to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, this is what brings benefit to the body and to everything: ﴿Whoever does righteousness, whether male or female, while he is a believer – We will surely cause him to live a good life, and We will surely reward them according to the best of what they used to do﴾ [al-Nahl 16:97].
Then Allah, exalted be He, reminded these disbelievers of a great blessing that no one other than them obtains, so He said:
(﴿Have they not seen﴾ [al-'Ankabut 29:67]: meaning, have they not known)
We have already discussed the grammatical analysis (*i'rab*) of such a construction: ﴿Have they not seen﴾, and we said that regarding it there is (a difference of opinion) among the scholars...
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: (﴿and people are being snatched away from around them﴾, through killing and captivity, beyond them). He, exalted be He, said: (﴿Then in falsehood﴾, meaning the idol, ﴿do they believe, and in the blessing of Allah do they disbelieve﴾ by their associating others with Him?)
The interrogative here is for rebuke: ﴿Then in falsehood﴾, and it is said of it as is said of ﴿Have they not seen﴾: namely, is the hamzah (interrogative particle) after the *fa'* (conjunction), with the *fa'* delayed? Or is it in its place, with the coordination being with the preceding sentences?
Regarding ﴿in falsehood﴾, the author said: (the idol). This is open to review, unless the author intended it as an example, and that among the things that are false are idols. Otherwise, it includes everything that has no good in it, whether an idol, worldly life, leadership, or anything else. Everything other than the Truth is falsehood. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The truest word spoken by a poet is the word of Labid: 'Surely everything other than Allah is vain.'" [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (3841) and Muslim (2256/3) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.] Based on this, we say: falsehood is more general than what the author mentioned.
His saying: ﴿they believe﴾ means they affirm and feel secure in it. You find them, in false matters, content, affirming, and following. But ﴿in the blessing of Allah they disbelieve﴾: ﴿Then in falsehood do they believe, and in the blessing of Allah do they disbelieve﴾.
His saying: ﴿in the blessing of Allah﴾ means: by what He has bestowed upon them of wealth, standing, leadership, and other things. ﴿They disbelieve﴾, because these blessings require what? Gratitude, by returning to obedience to Allah. If a person remains in disobedience to Allah while blessings continue to flow upon him, he thereby becomes a disbeliever.
And it is possible to say, regarding the Muslims: ﴿in the blessing of Allah they disbelieve﴾ refers to the material, physical blessing and the immaterial, heart-based blessing. Is Islam not the greatest of blessings upon us? If a person disbelieves in it and does not fulfill its obligations, he is rebuked for this. It is said: "Are you not a Muslim?" He will say: "Yes." "Then why did you not pray? Why did you not give zakah? Why did you not fast? Why did you not do such-and-such of the obligations?"
So gratitude for the blessing of Islam is obligatory, just as gratitude to Allah for His blessings upon us, such as wealth, children, security, and comfort, and similar things, is obligatory. Indeed, gratitude for Islam is more binding, and disbelief in Islam is more dangerous, because Allah says: ﴿And if you turn away, He will replace you with another people, then they will not be like you﴾ [Muhammad 47:38], and He says: ﴿And if these disbelieve in it, We have entrusted it to a people who are not disbelievers in it﴾ [al-An'am 6:89]. Allah may remove Islam from a people who do not fulfill its obligations, just as He removes security and prosperity from a people who do not give thanks for that security and prosperity. The blessings are one, and their path is one.
And His saying: ﴿and in the blessing of Allah﴾: is it singular or plural?
* Students: Plural.
* The Shaykh: Good. Why then did He say "the blessing of Allah"?
* Student: It is a singular noun in construct form (*mufrad mudaf*).
* The Shaykh: A singular noun in construct form, and so it is general. The proof is His saying: ﴿And if you count the blessing of Allah﴾. Look: ﴿if you count the blessing of Allah, you could not enumerate it﴾ [al-Nahl 16:18]. If it were singular, there would be no need to count it or to enumerate it, as it is well known.
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: No, it is not made dual except in terms of type; it is not made dual. He said: ﴿and in the blessing of Allah they disbelieve﴾. What does the phrase ﴿in the blessing of Allah﴾ relate to?
* Student: To ﴿they disbelieve﴾.
* The Shaykh: To ﴿they disbelieve﴾. It has been placed first to convey exclusivity (*hasr*), as if they disbelieve in nothing except the blessing of Allah. This is a semantic benefit. And there is also in it a verbal benefit: namely, observing the rhyme endings of the verses (*fawasil*).

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 29, verse 68–69 (part 1 of 2):

Then He, glorified and exalted, said: ﴿And who is more unjust than one who fabricates a lie against Allah﴾ [al-'Ankabut 68]. That is, who associates partners with Him.

As for His saying ﴿man﴾ (who), the exegete says: "That is, no one." Accordingly, the interrogative here carries the sense of negation. The benefit of using an interrogative in place of a negation is that it carries the meaning of a challenge, as if it were said: "If you are truthful, then inform me that anyone is more unjust." So this is the benefit of the interrogative in the place of negation: that it carries the meaning of a challenge.

He said: ﴿And who is more unjust than one who fabricates a lie against Allah﴾, that is, no one is more unjust ﴿than one who fabricates a lie against Allah﴾. As for His saying "no one is more unjust than one who fabricates" (iftara), meaning invents, "a lie against Allah," the author said: "by associating partners with Him." This is also a deficient explanation, unless he means what? Unless he means an illustration: whoever associates partners with Allah has fabricated a lie against Allah. How so? Because he claims that there is another god with Allah, and that is a lie. Whoever says that Allah has forbidden such-and-such, when He has not forbidden it, has fabricated a lie against Allah. Have you understood?

Whoever says that Allah intended by His speech such-and-such and not such-and-such has fabricated a lie against Allah. Whoever says that Allah does not literally have a hand, or does not literally have a face, or does not literally have good pleasure, and similar things, has fabricated a lie against Allah. Fabricating a lie against Allah has many kinds and countless instances. So whoever speaks about Allah, or about His actions, or about His rulings, saying something that Allah and His Messenger did not say, is one who fabricates a lie against Allah.

As for His saying ﴿man aẓlamu﴾ (who is more unjust), a difficulty arises for us: in some cases this same form occurs in another matter, where it is said: ﴿man aẓlamu﴾ [al-Baqarah 114]. Allah, glorified and exalted, has combined both in one verse: ﴿And who is more unjust than one who fabricates a lie against Allah, or says, "It has been revealed to me," when nothing has been revealed to him, or one who says, "I will send down the like of what Allah has sent down"﴾ [al-An'am 93].

Several matters: "And who is more unjust than one who goes about to create as I create" [agreed upon; al-Bukhari (5953) and Muslim (2111/101) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah], and ﴿And who is more unjust than one who prevents the mosques of Allah from having His name mentioned therein﴾ [al-Baqarah 114]. What do we say, when we have explained ﴿man aẓlamu﴾ as meaning "no one is more unjust"? How then do we reconcile these texts?

* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Good, is it clear?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Yes. That is, either we say: no one is more unjust in this specific sense; for example, fabricating a lie may be against Allah and may be against others. Which of them is more unjust?
* Student: One who fabricates against Allah.
* Shaykh: One who fabricates against Allah. One who prevents the mosques of Allah: prevention may be preventing mosques, may be preventing markets, may be preventing someone from entering his own house, for example. Which of them is a greater prevention?
* Student: The mosques of Allah.
* Shaykh: The mosques of Allah. And thus we make each matter specific to what the context requires.

Or we say: all of them share in being the most unjust; that is, there is no one more unjust than this, nor more unjust than this, nor more unjust than this, nor more unjust than this, and so on to the end. The meaning becomes that they all share in what? In being the most unjust (...).

So whoever says that there is a partner with Allah has fabricated a lie against Allah, and whoever says that one of Allah's names is such-and-such, when it is not among His names, has fabricated a lie against Allah.

The Christians call God "the Father," and the philosophers say that He is the "effective cause," and this is a lie against Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. Likewise, lying against Allah concerning His attributes, whose examples have already been mentioned. Lying against Allah concerning His rulings is like one who says: "This is lawful," when it is not lawful, or "This is forbidden," when it is not forbidden, and similar things. So Allah, exalted is He, has made clear that there is no one more unjust than this. It has already been mentioned that this verse and similar ones with ﴿man aẓlamu﴾ can be reconciled in one of two ways.

Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Or denies the truth when it has come to him﴾. ﴿Denies the truth (al-haqq)﴾: al-haqq is that which is established. If it is a report, it is truthfulness (al-sidq); if it is rulings, it is justice ('adl).

As for His saying ﴿lammā jā'ahu﴾ (when it came to him): ﴿lammā﴾ here means "when" (ḥīna): when it came to him, he denied it. The phrase ﴿when it came to him﴾ is used because before it reaches him he is not held accountable for it, for Allah says: ﴿And We would never punish until We have sent a messenger﴾ [al-Isra' 15]. So Allah, exalted is He, in His mercy and justice, does not punish anyone until the proof of the Law has been established against him by its reaching him.

As for His saying: (﴿Is there not in Hell an abode (mathwa) for the disbelievers?﴾ ma'wā (refuge) ﴿for the disbelievers﴾, that is, therein is that, and he is one of them).

The author's words "that is, therein is that" indicate that the purpose of the interrogative here is confirmation (taqrir). The usual case is that when the interrogative hamza enters upon a negative particle, it is generally for confirmation. Examples of this are numerous, such as: ﴿Did We not expand for you your breast?﴾ [al-Sharh 1]; ﴿Is not Allah sufficient for His servant?﴾ [al-Zumar 36]; ﴿Is not Allah the most just of judges?﴾ [al-Tin 8]; ﴿Is not He who is able to bring the dead to life capable of that?﴾ [al-Qiyamah 40], and similar examples. All of this shows that the hamza here is for confirmation.

His saying here: ﴿Is there not in Hell an abode?﴾ means: in Hell there is an abode. This is why the author said: "that is, therein is that, and he is one of them." "He" refers to ﴿one who fabricates a lie against Allah, or denies the truth when it has come to him﴾; he is one of them, that is, one of the disbelievers.

His saying ﴿mathwa﴾: al-mathwa is al-ma'wa (refuge), but a refuge that is a place of residence to which one returns as one's place of dwelling. So one says "thawā fī kadhā," meaning he dwelt in such-and-such, that is, he stayed there in a lasting residence.

His saying ﴿lilkāfirīn﴾ (for the disbelievers) is in reality a manifest noun in place of a pronoun, for the context would require saying "Is there not in Hell an abode for him?" but instead the explicit noun was used in place of the pronoun. We have mentioned that using the explicit noun in place of the pronoun yields three benefits:

* Student: Emphasis.
* Shaykh: (...) the pronoun of separation (ḍamīr al-faṣl).
* Student: Generalization of the ruling (...).
* Shaykh: Correct. First: generalization of the ruling, such that it is general to him and to others. Good, that is one.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Yes, correct: that the ruling applies to him with this description; that is, for example, in our example he is a disbeliever, so this benefits the recording of this on the referent, namely that he is characterized by this attribute. The third benefit:
* Student: Causation (ta'līl).
* Shaykh: Causation, yes, indicating the cause when the term is derived: ﴿Is there not in Hell an abode for the disbelievers?﴾ The implied meaning: because of their disbelief.

If he had said: "Is there not in Hell an abode for him?" we would not have derived these three benefits. So the benefits are therefore:

First: indicating generalization.
Second: passing judgment on the referent of the pronoun by what this description requires.
Third: indicating the cause, or pointing to the cause, and this applies when the term is derived.

Then He, exalted is He, said: (﴿And those who strive for Us﴾ [al-'Ankabut 69], in Our cause ﴿We will surely guide them to Our ways﴾, that is, the paths of travel toward Us).

﴿Those who strive﴾ is the subject, and the clause ﴿We will surely guide them to Our ways﴾ is its predicate. As you see, the predicate is emphasized with three emphatics: the oath, what else? And the lam, and the nun of emphasis.
