﴿Those who strive (jāhadū)﴾: that is, they exerted effort (jahd) in reaching the goal. This is jihad: exerting effort to reach the goal is called jihad.

As for His saying ﴿for Us (fīnā)﴾, the author said: "in Our cause" (fī ḥaqqinā), that is, in the religion of Allah and in what is due to Him, glorified and exalted, and in explaining the Law of Allah, glorified and exalted. This includes enjoining good and forbidding evil, and includes restraining the soul from what is forbidden and obligating it to what is required. All of this is jihad for the sake of Allah. It also includes fighting the disbelievers to raise the word of Allah. So the verse is general: whoever exerts effort for the sake of Allah, his reward is given quickly, before the deferred reward.

﴿We will surely guide them to Our ways﴾: guidance of indication (dalālah) and guidance of success (tawfīq). Here it includes both matters. This is why He said ﴿We will surely guide them to Our ways﴾ and did not say "guide them to..." but said ﴿Our ways﴾, so the guidance was transitive to the second object directly. When guidance is transitive to the second object directly, it includes both indication and success.

Among its parallels is His saying in Surat al-Fatihah: ﴿Guide us to the straight path﴾ [al-Fatihah 6]. He did not say "guide us to the path," but said ﴿guide us the path﴾, so as to include guidance to it and guidance within it. Guidance to it is indication to it, that it points you to this; and guidance within it is that He grants you success to act within the framework of this path.

So ﴿We will surely guide them to Our ways﴾ includes what? The guidance of both matters: the guidance of indication and knowledge, and the guidance of success and direction. This is a promise from Allah, Mighty and Majestic, confirmed with these three emphatics, for those who believe in this promise, because it comes from the Lord, great and exalted, who does not break His promise, due to the completeness of His knowledge, power, and truthfulness as well: knowledge, truthfulness, and power. Breaking a promise happens only through the absence of one of these three. What are they? Knowledge, truthfulness, and power.

No one breaks a promise to you except an ignorant person who promised you something while thinking it would happen and it did not happen as he thought; or a person who is a liar, who promised you and deceived you; or a person who is incapable though truthful and knowing the causes but unable. As for Allah, Mighty and Majestic, all three of these are negated concerning Him: ignorance, lying, and incapacity. So, due to the completeness of His power, knowledge, and truthfulness, He does not break His promise.

I say: whoever believes in this, and we praise Allah, we do believe in it, must strive in the right of Allah; he struggles. This is the fulfillment of what has come in the many reports that when a person acts upon his knowledge, Allah, exalted is He, increases him in knowledge: He confirms the knowledge he acted upon and increases him in knowledge. This is why it has been said: "Bind knowledge by action." And it has been said: "Knowledge calls out to action; if it answers, it stays; otherwise it departs." It calls, saying: "Come." If the person answers and acts upon his knowledge, it remains and also increases. Allah says: ﴿We will surely guide them to Our ways﴾; this is an increase. And if it does not answer, knowledge departs. This is a truth supported by reality and by what is known from the Law. As for reality: when a person begins to act upon his knowledge, his action upon knowledge is in fact a study of it. Is that not so? Yes or no?

* Students: Yes.
* Shaykh: Yes. So acting upon knowledge is a study of it. You know how the Messenger of Allah ﷺ used to pray, and you apply that in all your prayers. Do you forget it or not?
* Student: We do not forget it.
* Shaykh: You do not forget it, because application is study.

Second, from the legal perspective, Allah, exalted is He, says: ﴿And Allah increases in guidance those who are guided﴾ [Maryam 76]. So whoever is guided, Allah, exalted is He, increases him in guidance and knowledge, in reality. We know this and recite it constantly, but heedlessness, forgetfulness, and neglect often overcome us, and we do not realize that this is true, and that whoever knows and acts, Allah, exalted is He, increases him in firmness in his knowledge and in favor beyond what he knows.

* Shaykh: No, I am asking you now, answer me.

As for His saying ﴿sublanā (our ways)﴾, the pronoun here, "nā," is a plural pronoun. What do you say about this plural pronoun?

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 29, verses 68–69 (part 2 of 2):

The author's statement, "(﴿with the doers of good﴾ [means] the believers)," is an incomplete explanation, because *al-muhsinin* (the doers of good, *ihsan*) is more specific than "the believers." For this reason the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Iman (faith) is that you believe in Allah, His angels..." and so on to the end of the hadith, and then said: "Ihsan (excellence) is that you worship Allah as if you see Him."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (50) and Muslim (9 / 5), from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]] So every person who is a *muhsin* in the legal sense of *ihsan*, not merely in the customary sense, is a believer, but not vice versa.

I say: "in the legal sense" is to distinguish it from customary *ihsan*, for customary *ihsan* occurs even among disbelievers. Is that not so? But the legal *ihsan*, which the Messenger (ﷺ) explained with his words "that you worship Allah as if you see Him," is more specific than faith.

As for his statement, "(with help and support)": yes, it is correct that He is with them in that way, but He is not with them in their place, because it is impossible for Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, to be with people in their places, whether they are *muhsinin* or not. This is because such a statement necessitates the negation of His highness (*'uluww*). Those among the early Jahmiyya (a sect that denied Allah's attributes) who held it were consistent in this, as were the later ones, as we have explained more than once. What do they say about the location of Allah?

* Student: (...)

* Shaykh: No, no. They say that He is neither inside the world nor outside it, neither above the world nor beneath it, neither connected to it nor separate from it. This is what the doctrine of the Jahmiyya settled upon, and the Ash'ariyya (the Ash'ari school) followed them in it. They hold this pure negation, and we seek refuge with Allah. As for the early Jahmiyya, they said that He, may He be exalted, is in the earth and not in the heavens; He is not high above in the heavens. It is among the wonders that they denied highness despite the agreement of the evidences upon it, and affirmed indwelling despite the agreement of the evidences in rejecting it.

Highness has already been established for us: the Book, the Sunnah, reason, the innate nature (*fitrah*), and the consensus of the early generations of this Ummah all indicate it. Is that not so? The Book is full of what indicates this, to the extent that some scholars said: "In the Book there are a thousand proofs for the highness of Allah." The Sunnah is likewise full of evidence for the highness of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, in various forms: by statement, by action, and by tacit approval.

The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Will you not trust me, when I am the trustworthy one of the One who is in the heaven?"[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (4351) and Muslim (1064 / 144), from the hadith of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri.]] He also said: "The Throne is above that, and Allah is above the Throne."[[Narrated by al-Tabarani in al-Mu'jam al-Kabir (8987), and Ibn Khuzaymah in al-Tawhid (594), from the hadith of 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud.]]

He (ﷺ) pointed with his finger to the heaven, calling Allah to witness that he had conveyed the message to his Ummah, at the greatest gathering of the Muslims. When was that? On the Day of 'Arafah, when he said: "O Allah, bear witness."[[Narrated by Muslim (1218 / 147), from the hadith of Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah.]] And in the Friday sermon he supplicated his Lord, raising his hands toward Him, saying: "O Allah, give us rain."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (1014) and Muslim (897 / 8), from the hadith of Anas ibn Malik.]] Is this a practice of action or of speech? It is a practice of action.

As for tacit approval, he (ﷺ) asked the slave girl: "Where is Allah?" She said: "In the heaven." He said: "Free her, for she is a believer."[[Narrated by Muslim (537 / 33), from the hadith of Mu'awiyah ibn al-Hakam al-Sulami.]]

* Student: (...)

* Shaykh: Yes. As for the indication of reason on this, it is also clear, for we say: is highness an attribute of perfection or an attribute of deficiency? It is an attribute of perfection, and no one denies this. Lowness is an attribute of deficiency, and Allah, glory be to Him, deserves perfection, or perfection is due to Him, and He is exalted above all deficiency. As for the innate nature, ask the child, the elderly person, and the common, ignorant person who does not...

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 29, verse 68–69 (part 1 of 2):

Then He, glorified and exalted, said: ﴿And who is more unjust than one who fabricates a lie against Allah﴾ [al-'Ankabut 68]. That is, who associates partners with Him.

As for His saying ﴿man﴾ (who), the exegete says: "That is, no one." Accordingly, the interrogative here carries the sense of negation. The benefit of using an interrogative in place of a negation is that it carries the meaning of a challenge, as if it were said: "If you are truthful, then inform me that anyone is more unjust." So this is the benefit of the interrogative in the place of negation: that it carries the meaning of a challenge.

He said: ﴿And who is more unjust than one who fabricates a lie against Allah﴾, that is, no one is more unjust ﴿than one who fabricates a lie against Allah﴾. As for His saying "no one is more unjust than one who fabricates" (iftara), meaning invents, "a lie against Allah," the author said: "by associating partners with Him." This is also a deficient explanation, unless he means what? Unless he means an illustration: whoever associates partners with Allah has fabricated a lie against Allah. How so? Because he claims that there is another god with Allah, and that is a lie. Whoever says that Allah has forbidden such-and-such, when He has not forbidden it, has fabricated a lie against Allah. Have you understood?

Whoever says that Allah intended by His speech such-and-such and not such-and-such has fabricated a lie against Allah. Whoever says that Allah does not literally have a hand, or does not literally have a face, or does not literally have good pleasure, and similar things, has fabricated a lie against Allah. Fabricating a lie against Allah has many kinds and countless instances. So whoever speaks about Allah, or about His actions, or about His rulings, saying something that Allah and His Messenger did not say, is one who fabricates a lie against Allah.

As for His saying ﴿man aẓlamu﴾ (who is more unjust), a difficulty arises for us: in some cases this same form occurs in another matter, where it is said: ﴿man aẓlamu﴾ [al-Baqarah 114]. Allah, glorified and exalted, has combined both in one verse: ﴿And who is more unjust than one who fabricates a lie against Allah, or says, "It has been revealed to me," when nothing has been revealed to him, or one who says, "I will send down the like of what Allah has sent down"﴾ [al-An'am 93].

Several matters: "And who is more unjust than one who goes about to create as I create" [agreed upon; al-Bukhari (5953) and Muslim (2111/101) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah], and ﴿And who is more unjust than one who prevents the mosques of Allah from having His name mentioned therein﴾ [al-Baqarah 114]. What do we say, when we have explained ﴿man aẓlamu﴾ as meaning "no one is more unjust"? How then do we reconcile these texts?

* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Good, is it clear?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Yes. That is, either we say: no one is more unjust in this specific sense; for example, fabricating a lie may be against Allah and may be against others. Which of them is more unjust?
* Student: One who fabricates against Allah.
* Shaykh: One who fabricates against Allah. One who prevents the mosques of Allah: prevention may be preventing mosques, may be preventing markets, may be preventing someone from entering his own house, for example. Which of them is a greater prevention?
* Student: The mosques of Allah.
* Shaykh: The mosques of Allah. And thus we make each matter specific to what the context requires.

Or we say: all of them share in being the most unjust; that is, there is no one more unjust than this, nor more unjust than this, nor more unjust than this, nor more unjust than this, and so on to the end. The meaning becomes that they all share in what? In being the most unjust (...).

So whoever says that there is a partner with Allah has fabricated a lie against Allah, and whoever says that one of Allah's names is such-and-such, when it is not among His names, has fabricated a lie against Allah.

The Christians call God "the Father," and the philosophers say that He is the "effective cause," and this is a lie against Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. Likewise, lying against Allah concerning His attributes, whose examples have already been mentioned. Lying against Allah concerning His rulings is like one who says: "This is lawful," when it is not lawful, or "This is forbidden," when it is not forbidden, and similar things. So Allah, exalted is He, has made clear that there is no one more unjust than this. It has already been mentioned that this verse and similar ones with ﴿man aẓlamu﴾ can be reconciled in one of two ways.

Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Or denies the truth when it has come to him﴾. ﴿Denies the truth (al-haqq)﴾: al-haqq is that which is established. If it is a report, it is truthfulness (al-sidq); if it is rulings, it is justice ('adl).

As for His saying ﴿lammā jā'ahu﴾ (when it came to him): ﴿lammā﴾ here means "when" (ḥīna): when it came to him, he denied it. The phrase ﴿when it came to him﴾ is used because before it reaches him he is not held accountable for it, for Allah says: ﴿And We would never punish until We have sent a messenger﴾ [al-Isra' 15]. So Allah, exalted is He, in His mercy and justice, does not punish anyone until the proof of the Law has been established against him by its reaching him.

As for His saying: (﴿Is there not in Hell an abode (mathwa) for the disbelievers?﴾ ma'wā (refuge) ﴿for the disbelievers﴾, that is, therein is that, and he is one of them).

The author's words "that is, therein is that" indicate that the purpose of the interrogative here is confirmation (taqrir). The usual case is that when the interrogative hamza enters upon a negative particle, it is generally for confirmation. Examples of this are numerous, such as: ﴿Did We not expand for you your breast?﴾ [al-Sharh 1]; ﴿Is not Allah sufficient for His servant?﴾ [al-Zumar 36]; ﴿Is not Allah the most just of judges?﴾ [al-Tin 8]; ﴿Is not He who is able to bring the dead to life capable of that?﴾ [al-Qiyamah 40], and similar examples. All of this shows that the hamza here is for confirmation.

His saying here: ﴿Is there not in Hell an abode?﴾ means: in Hell there is an abode. This is why the author said: "that is, therein is that, and he is one of them." "He" refers to ﴿one who fabricates a lie against Allah, or denies the truth when it has come to him﴾; he is one of them, that is, one of the disbelievers.

His saying ﴿mathwa﴾: al-mathwa is al-ma'wa (refuge), but a refuge that is a place of residence to which one returns as one's place of dwelling. So one says "thawā fī kadhā," meaning he dwelt in such-and-such, that is, he stayed there in a lasting residence.

His saying ﴿lilkāfirīn﴾ (for the disbelievers) is in reality a manifest noun in place of a pronoun, for the context would require saying "Is there not in Hell an abode for him?" but instead the explicit noun was used in place of the pronoun. We have mentioned that using the explicit noun in place of the pronoun yields three benefits:

* Student: Emphasis.
* Shaykh: (...) the pronoun of separation (ḍamīr al-faṣl).
* Student: Generalization of the ruling (...).
* Shaykh: Correct. First: generalization of the ruling, such that it is general to him and to others. Good, that is one.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Yes, correct: that the ruling applies to him with this description; that is, for example, in our example he is a disbeliever, so this benefits the recording of this on the referent, namely that he is characterized by this attribute. The third benefit:
* Student: Causation (ta'līl).
* Shaykh: Causation, yes, indicating the cause when the term is derived: ﴿Is there not in Hell an abode for the disbelievers?﴾ The implied meaning: because of their disbelief.

If he had said: "Is there not in Hell an abode for him?" we would not have derived these three benefits. So the benefits are therefore:

First: indicating generalization.
Second: passing judgment on the referent of the pronoun by what this description requires.
Third: indicating the cause, or pointing to the cause, and this applies when the term is derived.

Then He, exalted is He, said: (﴿And those who strive for Us﴾ [al-'Ankabut 69], in Our cause ﴿We will surely guide them to Our ways﴾, that is, the paths of travel toward Us).

﴿Those who strive (jāhadū)﴾: that is, they exerted effort (jahd) in reaching the goal. This is jihad: exerting effort to reach the goal is called jihad.

As for His saying ﴿for Us (fīnā)﴾, the author said: "in Our cause" (fī ḥaqqinā), that is, in the religion of Allah and in what is due to Him, glorified and exalted, and in explaining the Law of Allah, glorified and exalted. This includes enjoining good and forbidding evil, and includes restraining the soul from what is forbidden and obligating it to what is required. All of this is jihad for the sake of Allah. It also includes fighting the disbelievers to raise the word of Allah. So the verse is general: whoever exerts effort for the sake of Allah, his reward is given quickly, before the deferred reward.

In reality there is a disagreement among the grammarians: some hold that it is a noun, and this is undoubtedly the correct view, while others hold that it is a particle. It has two dialectal forms: the vowel "a," which is the more common, and the sukun (unvowelled). Ibn Malik said:

"And ma'a, with ma' in it, is rare; and it is said with fath and kasr for sukun that is joined."

The conclusion is that the correct view regarding ﴿la-ma'a﴾ is that it is a noun functioning as an adverb of place/circumstance, accusative in the adverbial sense, since it indicates companionship; ﴿ma'a﴾ is the governing term, and ﴿al-muhsinin﴾ is its genitive complement.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 29, verses 68–69 (part 2 of 2):

The author's statement, "(﴿with the doers of good﴾ [means] the believers)," is an incomplete explanation, because *al-muhsinin* (the doers of good, *ihsan*) is more specific than "the believers." For this reason the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Iman (faith) is that you believe in Allah, His angels..." and so on to the end of the hadith, and then said: "Ihsan (excellence) is that you worship Allah as if you see Him."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (50) and Muslim (9 / 5), from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]] So every person who is a *muhsin* in the legal sense of *ihsan*, not merely in the customary sense, is a believer, but not vice versa.

I say: "in the legal sense" is to distinguish it from customary *ihsan*, for customary *ihsan* occurs even among disbelievers. Is that not so? But the legal *ihsan*, which the Messenger (ﷺ) explained with his words "that you worship Allah as if you see Him," is more specific than faith.

As for his statement, "(with help and support)": yes, it is correct that He is with them in that way, but He is not with them in their place, because it is impossible for Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, to be with people in their places, whether they are *muhsinin* or not. This is because such a statement necessitates the negation of His highness (*'uluww*). Those among the early Jahmiyya (a sect that denied Allah's attributes) who held it were consistent in this, as were the later ones, as we have explained more than once. What do they say about the location of Allah?

* Student: (...)

* Shaykh: No, no. They say that He is neither inside the world nor outside it, neither above the world nor beneath it, neither connected to it nor separate from it. This is what the doctrine of the Jahmiyya settled upon, and the Ash'ariyya (the Ash'ari school) followed them in it. They hold this pure negation, and we seek refuge with Allah. As for the early Jahmiyya, they said that He, may He be exalted, is in the earth and not in the heavens; He is not high above in the heavens. It is among the wonders that they denied highness despite the agreement of the evidences upon it, and affirmed indwelling despite the agreement of the evidences in rejecting it.

Highness has already been established for us: the Book, the Sunnah, reason, the innate nature (*fitrah*), and the consensus of the early generations of this Ummah all indicate it. Is that not so? The Book is full of what indicates this, to the extent that some scholars said: "In the Book there are a thousand proofs for the highness of Allah." The Sunnah is likewise full of evidence for the highness of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, in various forms: by statement, by action, and by tacit approval.

The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Will you not trust me, when I am the trustworthy one of the One who is in the heaven?"[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (4351) and Muslim (1064 / 144), from the hadith of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri.]] He also said: "The Throne is above that, and Allah is above the Throne."[[Narrated by al-Tabarani in al-Mu'jam al-Kabir (8987), and Ibn Khuzaymah in al-Tawhid (594), from the hadith of 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud.]]

He (ﷺ) pointed with his finger to the heaven, calling Allah to witness that he had conveyed the message to his Ummah, at the greatest gathering of the Muslims. When was that? On the Day of 'Arafah, when he said: "O Allah, bear witness."[[Narrated by Muslim (1218 / 147), from the hadith of Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah.]] And in the Friday sermon he supplicated his Lord, raising his hands toward Him, saying: "O Allah, give us rain."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (1014) and Muslim (897 / 8), from the hadith of Anas ibn Malik.]] Is this a practice of action or of speech? It is a practice of action.

As for tacit approval, he (ﷺ) asked the slave girl: "Where is Allah?" She said: "In the heaven." He said: "Free her, for she is a believer."[[Narrated by Muslim (537 / 33), from the hadith of Mu'awiyah ibn al-Hakam al-Sulami.]]

* Student: (...)

* Shaykh: Yes. As for the indication of reason on this, it is also clear, for we say: is highness an attribute of perfection or an attribute of deficiency? It is an attribute of perfection, and no one denies this. Lowness is an attribute of deficiency, and Allah, glory be to Him, deserves perfection, or perfection is due to Him, and He is exalted above all deficiency. As for the innate nature, ask the child, the elderly person, and the common, ignorant person who does not...
